events.title: Nvidia reverses, metals crash ahead of Anthropic IPO
events.summary: Is this what it takes to clear room for $1.5 trillion of new supply? Slumping crypto prices, a big Nvidia reversal despite good earnings, and now a sharp drop-off in metals prices from gold to copper — cross-asset selling has traders wondering if Anthropic's incoming IPO is spurring a rotation trade with the aim of freeing up cash to buy stock in the AI giant when it goes public on Thursday. Meanwhile, metals prices fell across the board, led by a 5% sell-off in copper futures to the lowest since April. Gold futures lost more than 3% to $3,744, the lowest since September 2025, despite Treasury yields slipping on the session. Almost 300,000 options traded on the SPDR GLD Shares ETF (GLD) , with a slight bias towards calls. The catch for gold bugs is that more calls looked like they were initiated by sellers, according to Cboe LiveVol data, which show 52,000 calls sold on the bid versus 45,000 calls bought on the ask.

events.title: Sam Altman says his life is so weird that he’s unphased by Andrew Garfield portraying him in upcoming movie
events.summary: Hollywood has found plenty of material and cinematic inspiration from a string of Silicon Valley scandals and power struggles in recent years. “ You Can See Everything ,” the documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, smashed box office expectations, and Netflix’s limited series “The Altruists” comes out Thursday to tell the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the downfall of FTX. As the founder and CEO of OpenAI, one of the most influential companies of the century, Sam Altman isn’t going to escape the Hollywood treatment, either. In “Artificial,” a biographical comedy-drama opening in theaters on Christmas, the lauded actor Andrew Garfield will portray Altman in a film that chronicles OpenAI’s rise and the internal turmoil that erupted when he was briefly ousted in 2023. “If you had told me 20 years ago that someone was going to make a movie about me, I think that would have struck me as… that would have been a very weird thing,” Altman said on stage at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “Now it doesn’t feel like it’s in like the top 10 weirdest things about my life.” Garfield is best known for his role as Spider-man, but his big break came in 2010, when he played as Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin in “The Social Network” alongside Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg. (That film also had a sequel of sorts this year called “ The Social Reckoning ,” but it bombed at the box office.) So, if Altman isn’t fazed by the looming release of “Artificial,” what’s actually the weirdest thing in his life? “The fact that we are ushering in this technology that we have all of these very real concerns about, and that we have, we find ourselves in a role of such significance and such responsibility to make that go well,” Altman said. “That’s a that is a crazy situation to find yourself in.” Sure, that is pretty weird, Sam. It’s also weird that you use ChatGPT for parenting advice and don’t respect olive oil . But I’d wager to say it’s even weirder that there’s an upcoming film about the time your colleagues briefly ousted you because they were concerned that you can’t be trusted . Say what you want about Mark Zuckerberg (I certainly have), but at least he’s honest about what he thinks about “The Social Network.” “It was weird, man,” Zuckerberg reflected on a podcast last year. “They got all these very specific details of what I was wearing, or these specific things correct, but then the whole narrative arc around my motivations and all this stuff were like, completely wrong… The whole arc is like, I’m somehow motivated by trying to find a girlfriend, [but] I was dating Priscilla [Chan] before I started Facebook.” Zuckerberg said he knew his employees would be tempted to see the movie, so he organized a company outing when it was released, even though the film hardly paints a flattering portrait of him. Zuckerberg even had enough of a sense of humor to buy a prop from the film at auction. He owns an Ardsley High School T-shirt that Eisenberg wore in the movie and even wore it himself in a video with YouTubers Colin and Samir. Eisenberg hasn’t been particularly complimentary of Zuckerberg, saying that he doesn’t want to think of himself as “associated with somebody like that.” And while “Artificial” hasn’t hit theaters yet, Garfield doesn’t seem to have a much more favorable opinion of the tech founder he portrays. “I don’t know Sam Altman. I’ve never met him,” Garfield told Esquire . “But I think anyone who takes on that level of responsibility for a company or technology that you know is going to do a hell of a lot of damage to the soul of humanity [must have] a certain ability to dissociate.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Data centres could ignite a 'climate bomb' in Australia, report finds
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Pollution from data centre rollout could rival coal power stations, report says The rollout of data centres has the potential to accelerate or slow down Australia's clean energy transition. ( ABC: Graphic by Sharon Gordon ) A new report from the Climate Council examines nine major data centres proposed for Australia, warning that increased energy demand could mean more pollution. The peak body for data centre developers says they are already offsetting 70 per cent of their demand with renewable energy. The federal government is expected to deliver a national mandatory framework around large data centres and AI infrastructure in the coming months. Australia's rapid data centre rollout could add 39 million tonnes of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere in a decade if allowed to be powered primarily by fossil fuels, the Climate Council has warned. This is based on nine proposed data centres the report identifies as the biggest potential polluters because of their electricity demand. That is roughly the same as the annual emissions of a country like Sweden. Climate Council chief executive Amanda McKenzie said the demand by the artificial intelligence expansion could set back Australia's climate targets. "If they extend the life of coal, if they bring on new gas … it's a very big increase in our climate pollution," Ms McKenzie said. Australia currently has around 165 operational data centres, making it one of the top five locations around the globe even before a series of hyper-scale data centres have been developed. The Climate Council's map showing the rollout of data centres, proposed and operational, in Australia. ( Supplied: Climate Council ) The energy market operator forecasts that within a decade, data centres could use as much electricity as nearly all the homes in New South Wales and Victoria today. Ms McKenzie said the plan for most data centres was simply to plug them into the existing grid, which is still mostly powered by fossil fuels. Ms McKenzie said Australia needed mandatory national standards that would require large projects to bring on new renewable energy and storage within three years of approvals. The federal government is expected to introduce legislation for large data centres and AI infrastructure early next year, with developers expected to bring on their own new clean energy to match their demand. A large-scale data centre proposed for Queensland's Western Downs was included in the data. ( Supplied: Urbis ) But fossil fuels are still on the table for Queensland and the Northern Territory, which campaigned to keep gas generation in the energy mix. In response to the report, Data Centres Australia, the peak body for data centre developers, said the industry was committed to renewable energy. Chief executive Belinda Dennett said the report was based on "speculative" demand. She said operational data centres were already offsetting 70 per cent of their energy use with renewable energy agreements. She said multi-billion-dollar AI companies are focused on the speed of energy connection, rather than the cost. "Rather than slow down this data centre build out that is happening right now, how do we make sure we can build renewable energy projects more quickly?" Ms Dennett said. University of Technology renewable energy researcher Chris Briggs said the data centre industry could tip the scales towards a climate positive or a climate negative future. Chris Briggs says the advent of data centres could bring more renewable energy into the grid. ( Supplied: ) He said the Climate Council's report was based on a "worst case scenario" but acknowledged it was "certainly a possibility". "We could effectively turn back the energy transition or push it in a different direction," Dr Briggs said. He said if the renewables rollout did not accelerate, it would incentivise data centres to invest in coal and gas generation. It can take years to bringing on new solar and wind energy projects farms takes years , while the developer behind Anthropic's first data centre leased in Australia has said "the industry doesn't work in years, months but thinks in weeks and days." Around Australia, communities with proposed data centres are worried their concerns will be steamrolled by global AI companies. Protesters gathered outside an economic forum in Dalby about a proposed data centre, leased by Anthropic.

events.title: Trust, but prepare: How to make sense of AI's age of upheaval
events.summary: Most Americans are baffled and alarmed by the daily, if not hourly, explosion of technical glitches hitting air travel, banks and work products like Microsoft Outlook. The outages seem genuinely scary and related. So what the hell is going on? The most likely answer : This is the first true wave of unintended consequences of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence hitting us at once. The big picture: In short, AI is exceptionally good at building software, and therefore exceptionally good at spotting and exploiting bugs in large technical, software-based systems. The glitches come from a mix of sources — some innocuous, some scary, including: routine updates to aging infrastructure; humans scrambling to patch vulnerabilities discovered by AI; hackers exploiting existing weaknesses; and bad actors using swarms of AI agents to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. That's the new reality that government officials and AI experts believe we're entering. They expect this period of disruption and heightened vulnerability to persist for months, as powerful new AI tools expose weaknesses buried in decades-old systems. The catchphrase gaining currency : " Software Beirut " — a period of cascading failures, many of our own making, that could grow worse before things get better. What this means for YOU : Understand the different causes, detailed below, and resist the temptation to panic every time something goes haywire. It's easy to hop on social media and let the algorithm drag you into doomsday thinking. You should also prepare : Reset and protect your passwords . Keep more cash on hand if possible, in case your bank is down for a day or two. Buy some basic emergency supplies in case power or water do go out. Sadly, we believe this season of glitches and possible cyberattacks will persist. Better to be prepared. Here's a more detailed look at the different causes of these glitches or breakdowns: 1. Updates to old systems: The government says last Friday's nationwide airspace outage was simply a case of replacing old copper wires with new fiber that went very, very badly. Aging infrastructure can struggle to accommodate new components. In this case, a network problem overwhelmed legacy equipment, triggering a cascade that grounded flights across the country. 2. AI spotting bugs and humans rushing to fix them: This is one of cyber expert Nicole Perlroth's core scenarios, which went viral this week. AI can find vulnerabilities faster than humans can investigate and patch them. In the frantic sprint to fix those weaknesses before hackers exploit them, systems can break. According to the Washington Sun , banking executives and NSA officials have told lawmakers that rushed efforts to patch AI-discovered vulnerabilities contributed to some of this week's outages. 3. Bad actors attacking vulnerable systems : Across Europe, supermarket refrigerators are being hacked , spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food. No one had "protect the fridges" on their security to-do list this year. But the attacks show how hackers can exploit even the most mundane internet-connected systems — with devastating real-world consequences. 4. AI enabling new forms of cyberattacks : Google said this week it had identified, for the first time, bad actors using AI to find weaknesses and launch cyberattacks entirely on their own — with no human in the loop. If it wasn't already clear, Google warned that "the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point." The bottom line: Most companies and much of government are woefully unprepared for the new era of AI-powered cyberattacks. Their systems are old, clunky and riddled with vulnerabilities. Fortifying them will take enormous amounts of money, time and persistence. The good news: We can see the danger coming, and still have (a little) time to protect ourselves for what may come next. Axios' Ben Berkowitz and Zachary Basu contributed.

events.title: One app, many ways to pay: How DBS is shaping the next wave of digital payments with PayLah!
events.summary: Building on over a decade of innovation, DBS is charting PayLah’s next chapter with more ways to pay and more personalised experiences for customers across generations DBS is extending PayLah! to more cross-border QR payments, including China, offering customers a convenient way to pay overseas. For millions of Singaporeans, paying with DBS PayLah! has become part of their daily routines – from buying meals at hawker centres to paying at heartland shops and malls. What began as a peer-to-peer mobile wallet more than a decade ago has grown into one of Singapore’s most widely used payment platforms, with over three million users. DBS is now building on this foundation, extending the convenience of PayLah! beyond Singapore’s shores and into more payment situations. From shops across the Causeway to storefronts in China, PayLah! users can scan to pay just as they do at Singapore’s hawker centres – where PayLah! accounts for more than 60 per cent of QR transactions. “The way people pay has evolved significantly over the past decade, and so have their expectations. Today, customers value not just the ability to pay digitally, but how simple and seamless the experience is,” said Chan Sow Han, head of Payments and Unsecured Lending at DBS Singapore. “Our focus is to build on what customers already know and use, extending that ease of payment across more situations and locations so they can use PayLah! to pay wherever they are, while continuing to enhance the experience to better serve their needs.” QR payments are widely used across Asia, but payment systems and practices differ across markets. In China, for instance, customers may scan a merchant’s QR code or present their own for the cashier to scan. DBS is addressing this through its latest expansion of PayLah!, which enables users to make QR payments at over 100 million participating Alipay+ and Weixin Pay merchants across China. On top of existing UnionPay QR connectivity, DBS is the first and only bank in Singapore to support both payment methods across China’s three major QR payment ecosystems. The development marks another milestone in DBS’ efforts to extend the payment habits Singaporeans are accustomed to at home across international borders. According to DBS, in 2022, it became the first bank in Singapore to enable consumers to make QR payments globally using a local app, through its partnership with UnionPay International. Since then, PayLah!’s overseas reach has grown through partnerships with payment networks. These include DuitNow in Malaysia, PromptPay in Thailand and QRIS in Indonesia, allowing customers to scan to pay when travelling to these destinations. This year, DBS said it also became the first Singapore bank to connect to Taiwan’s TWQR network, allowing PayLah! users to scan to pay at over 250,000 participating merchants in Taiwan. “While QR payments are increasingly common across Asia, different markets have their own payment systems and ways of transacting. Our approach has been to work with established payment networks and partners to bridge these differences, so customers can enjoy a more consistent payment experience when travelling,” said Chan. The TravelLah! Debit Card offers zero foreign exchange fees and zero DBS fees on overseas ATM withdrawals, with no cap on the amount or frequency. These efforts have translated into growing customer usage. Last year, PayLah!’s cross-border QR transaction volumes have grown 2.5 times year-on-year, while the number of unique users has doubled. Average spending per customer on PayLah!’s overseas QR transactions has also increased by approximately 30 per cent in the same period. Recognising that customers have different payment preferences when travelling, DBS also introduced the TravelLah! Debit Card in September 2026, complementing PayLah!’s overseas QR payment capabilities with a debit card option. Available to customers aged 16 and above, TravelLah! offers zero foreign exchange fees, using Visa exchange rates without additional mark-ups from DBS. Customers can pay in more than 150 currencies worldwide and view indicative exchange rates directly on the PayLah! app, giving them greater visibility over prevailing rates before they spend. TravelLah! also offers zero DBS fees on overseas ATM withdrawals, with no cap on the amount or frequency of overseas withdrawals. The accompanying TravelLah! Debit Card Wallet within DBS PayLah! held in Singapore dollars can be topped up as needed, allowing customers to set aside funds for their travels without having to pre-convert or manage multiple currencies. Cardholders can also redeem complimentary basic travel insurance, subject to terms and conditions. The card has attracted interest among younger customers, with around half of those who signed up in its first month aged between 16 and 29. Beyond expanding where and how customers can pay, DBS is also enhancing PayLah! to better serve the needs of different customer groups.

events.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
events.summary: Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera. The company is introducing Easy Lens CLI, which builds on its existing Easy Lens tool , which lets creators generate Lenses from a single prompt on the web and mobile. Easy Lens CLI brings that same idea into developers’ existing workflows, allowing AI assistants to handle the technical work while creators focus on the vision for the Lens itself. The launch indicates that Snapchat is looking to lower the barrier to creating AR content, while making its platform more accessible to developers who are increasingly using AI coding assistants. Instead of requiring creators to learn how to use Snapchat’s own development tools, the company is bringing Lens creation into the AI coding workflows they already use, which could in turn expand the pool of people who build for Snapchat. Developers enrolled in Snapchat’s Lens+ Payouts program can earn from the Lenses they create with Easy Lens CLI. Snapchat says it paid out $1.8 million to Lens+ community creators last month. Lens creators can describe the Lens they want in plain language, and their AI assistant handles the process from start to finish, Snapchat says. That includes building with more than 100 AR building blocks and 50 AI asset generators, generating previews, and publishing them to Snapchat and tracking their performance. With Easy Lens CLI, Snapchat says developers can create everything from Web Lens games with leaderboards to camera effects and beauty filters. AI assistants can generate assets, build and test Lenses, address errors, and send updated versions directly to the creator’s phone. The new capability can take a game from an initial idea to a published Lens in a single day, without developers having to write code themselves, Snapchat says. The tool is aimed at different types of creators. The company notes that game developers can bring existing browser games to Snapchat as Web Lenses, while AI creators can use assets from their preferred tools to build Lenses in their own style. Additionally, agencies and brands can turn existing campaign videos, images, and other brand assets into AR experiences with less production time. Easy Lens CLI runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux. events.title: Heated debate escalates into on-air fight on Armenian TV

events.title: I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways
events.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump arrived in Shenzhen late Wednesday afternoon. He joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for an APEC banquet that evening. I was in the room as the leaders gathered and witnessed the interactions between the three leaders. SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time. Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held Nov. 17 to 19. Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping . "At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation. Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin. But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media. But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days. Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation. Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi. It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C. And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons. This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening. Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so. China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult. But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit. Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit. After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted. It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked. Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage. "The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries. During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak. They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon. The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.

events.title: Former OpenAI researcher says he’ll donate his equity to AI safety: 'Everything else is a distraction'
events.summary: AI engineerJacob Coxon said he's donating his equity in OpenAI to AI safety research. Adam Gray/Getty Images Jacob Coxon is giving up what could be a massive windfall in the name of AI safety. The ex-OpenAI researcher said he's donating his equity to AI safety causes. Coxon's warnings about AI safety went viral in September, sparking a national conversation. Jacob Coxon is forking over what could be a massive personal windfall in the name of AI safety. The ex-OpenAI researcher, who also worked at Anthropic before he recently quit, said on Wednesday that he's committed to selling his equity in OpenAI and donating the proceeds to AI safety causes. "We need to pause or drastically slow down the race to superintelligence," he said on X. "Everything else is a distraction." In doing so, Coxon is forgoing what could be millions of dollars in profit that would become liquid when OpenAI goes public , an event that CEO Sam Altman has said is on the horizon. Coxon made serious waves in September when he left Anthropic and issued a series of dire warnings that it and OpenAI were "gambling with our lives." "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," he said in an X post on September 8 that has since racked up 175 million views. "This is not a marketing stunt." Coxon worked at OpenAI from 2023 until 2026, before leaving for Anthropic. Since then, the 27-year-old from England has done the rounds with media to advocate for AI safeguards and, principally, a pause on recursive self-improvement, the process by which AI models train themselves. In a November 9 talk at Stanford, Coxon called his stake in OpenAI "blood money" but balked at giving it up at the time. "I like money, bro," he said. "My parents were like worried I was having a psychotic break. I think if I'd also given away all the money they'd be even more convinced of that." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Fed officials expect more rate hikes, worry about AI impact on inflation, minutes show
events.summary: At the Fed's October meeting, almost all participants said that further rate hikes "would likely be appropriate," according to newly released minutes. AI was a major topic of discussion, and was viewed as a driver of both inflation and potential financial instability. Officials said they expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond. Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday. Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk." More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December. The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective." In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December. Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability. Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint." "Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms." Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off. Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Consumer prices rose more than expected in October, complicating Fed's inflation fight 3 unexpected reasons the October jobs report was so strong Bessent blames Lutnick’s Commerce as he slams Nvidia chip ‘leakage’ to China Analysis: The Fed's chairman sees an AI revolution coming. Now he has to figure out what it means Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal." Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target. The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach. However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act. At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting that includes low odds of a half-point move, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures traders also are pricing a solid likelihood of two more increases in 2027.

events.title: It's Thursday somewhere: Some hardcore 'GTA 6' fans flew to New Zealand to play ASAP
events.summary: Gamers have giant expectations for "GTA 6." Early reviews say they won't be disappointed. Rockstar Games "GTA 6" comes out on Thursday. Streamers flew to New Zealand, where it's already Thursday, to play. "GTA 6" is the industry's most hotly anticipated game — and it's been years in the making. Reviewers and gamers have described a massive map, detailed storylines, and even a good love story. "Grand Theft Auto 6" comes out on Thursday. So gamers hopped on a plane to a magic land where it's already game time. On Wednesday (in America), YouTube and Twitch live feeds were filled with popular streamers playing "Grand Theft Auto 6." They didn't get early access — instead, they were logging on from New Zealand, where it's already Thursday, and the game is officially live . "I landed at the airport, and it was crazy," Wynn Curtis, the Buffalo, New York-based streamer who goes by Wynnsanity on YouTube, said from across the world. "All I saw were streamers everywhere, dude." The game, available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S and X for $79.99 or $99.99, is the first mainline "Grand Theft Auto" release in 13 years. Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of "GTA" studio Rockstar Games, reportedly spent between $1 billion and $1.5 billion during the game's eight-year development cycle . That long wait has spun up a crazy amount of excitement. Business Insider previously reported that multiple workforce management software companies saw a spike in PTO requests for November 19, its official release date. Several techie companies gave their employees an extra paid day off to let them play. And, apparently, the anticipation inspired some streamers to fly across the world. "Let's get a 'W New Zealand' in chat," Toronto-based Andre Rebelo-Soares, popularly known as TypicalGamer on YouTube and Twitch, said on Wednesday during his "GTA 6" livestream from the future. Officials in New Zealand didn't let the opportunity go to waste: On Instagram, the country's official tourism account boasted about its time advantage. "One perk of seeing the sun first? Getting GTA 6 first too," the caption read. "We heard a few of you are trying the New Zealand trick to join us. We get it, and we'd love to have you." View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Zealand (@purenewzealand) A 'masterpiece' to follow up an icon? Flying to New Zealand to play a video game may seem extravagant, but early reviews indicate the 18-hour flight might be worth it. On Wednesday morning, video gaming pundits — who said they've had secret early access for the past three weeks — released their thoughts after a trip through Rockstar Games' fictional Miami. "GTA 6," they said, has asked them to shoot their way out of drug deals gone wrong, cross paths with Florida man-style NPCs, and even assemble an IKEA-style coffee table. The consensus: It's freaking cool. "It is an explorer's delight, a master class in design, and an all-time classic," Jason Schreier, the video game industry reporter for Bloomberg News, wrote on X. Playing through GTA VI over the last three weeks reminded me of playing Breath of the Wild or Elden Ring for the first time. It is an explorer's delight, a master class in design, and an all-time classic. — Jason Schreier (@jasonschreier) November 18, 2026 Its predecessor, "GTA 5," was iconic in its own right. That game followed three crime-doers — Michael, Franklin, and Trevor. The lovably curmudgeonly characters committed offenses across a warped rendition of Los Angeles, where game subplots poked fun at social media narcissism, car radios mocked right-wing paranoia, and trips down the Westwood Boulevard-like street (aptly renamed "Morningwood Boulevard") ridiculed vanity. It was a massive hit. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games' corporate owner, said earlier this month that it has sold nearly 235 million units of "GTA 5". Reviewers say "GTA 6" pulls off the same trick on a larger scale: a giant criminal sandbox full of crass humor and sharper social commentary, but with a more emotionally grounded and romantic story centered on a new set of likable lawbreakers, Jason and Lucia. "It's all impressively done and rendered with technological aplomb," reviewer Yussef Cole wrote for The New York Times . "Instead, the game's artistry is felt most in its Bonnie and Clyde duo." events.title: Hairdressing friendship ends in bankruptcy after failed private loan
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Former friends regret vendor finance deal after buyer goes bankrupt Brieanna Forrest-Gribble, who is now bankrupt, says she will never partake in vendor finance again. ( ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager ) A hairdressing business owner lost thousands after selling her salon to a trusted friend through vendor finance. An insolvency expert says rising interest rates and living costs are driving more businesses towards these private loans. A small business advocacy group is calling for greater regulation and education around vendor finance. When Evelina Kemp sold her Port Macquarie hair salon to her friend and employee Brieanna Forrest-Gribble, the pair skipped the bank and agreed to a private loan. Eighteen months later, the salon has closed, Ms Forrest-Gribble has declared bankruptcy, and Ms Kemp is still owed tens of thousands of dollars. The pair used vendor finance, where the seller, rather than a bank, lends the buyer the money to purchase the business. But small business advisers warn the arrangement can leave sellers out of pocket if the buyer cannot pay. Brieanna Forrest-Gribble says the business was running at a loss as soon as she took over. ( Supplied ) Both Ms Kemp and Ms Forrest-Gribble told the ABC they agreed to the $50,000 private sale because they trusted each other. "I thought I've got [Evelina] by my side that can help me to make sure I'm doing everything right," Ms Forrest-Gribble said. "It just sounded like it was something that could set me and my kids up for life. According to documents obtained by the ABC, Ms Forrest-Gribble paid Ms Kemp a $15,000 deposit and signed a loan contract to repay Ms Kemp $35,000 in weekly instalments, interest-free for a year. Brieanna Forrest-Gribble operated Noya Studios in Port Macquarie until July 2026. ( ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager ) But within weeks, Ms Forrest-Gribble was struggling to pay back the loan. "I was drowning from the start. It just got worse until I couldn't anymore," she said. Ms Kemp initially offered to pay Ms Forrest-Gribble the rent money for leasing a chair in the salon directly towards the loan. But by January 2026, Ms Kemp was fired after several disagreements between the two. The salon business eventually closed in July 2026, and the pair ended up in court over the debt. Ms Forrest-Gribble was ordered to pay $45,680.93 to Ms Kemp, which included legal fees and income lost, but she declared bankruptcy, leaving Ms Kemp unpaid. Evelina Kemp regrets choosing to go down the route of vendor finance. ( ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager ) Not-for-profit The Affiliation for Business Resilience & Turnaround (ABRT) said vendor finance enquiries had jumped 70 per cent in the last year. ABRT chair Eddie Griffith said the number of enquiries rose from 590 in August 2025 to 1011 in October 2026, driven by sellers trying to recover the balance of a loan or by buyers who could not pay back their loan. "We're seeing an increase in vendor finance because the small business community is being squeezed," he said. Eddie Griffith says vendor finance should always be the last option. ( Supplied: Eddie Griffith ) "We have tighter lending with banks, rising interest rates, uncertainty with the property market and that makes access to credit more difficult. "It's this whole perfect storm with small business owners where it's becoming very hard to profitably run a small business." Mr Griffith said tough market conditions were pushing more sellers towards vendor finance, often with buyers they knew and trusted. "It can get the best sale price, it could be the highest amount you receive; it's someone who knows the business and a lot of the time someone they probably trust," he said. Brieanna Forrest-Gribble closed down her business in July when she became bankrupt. ( ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager ) Mr Griffith said vendor finance is very high risk, with the seller acting as the bank. He said out of the hundreds of small businesses he's seen using vendor finance in the past year, around 40 per cent declared bankruptcy. "Although they might make the first few payments, the truth is if things go wrong, the sheer concept of vendor finance means they very rarely have security for the balance that's due," he said. Mr Griffith said vendor finance needs to be tracked by government bodies like the Australian Small Business and Family Enterprise Ombudsman (ASBFEO) and the Australian Financial Security Authority (AFSA). Brieanna Forrest-Gribble announced the closure of Noya Studios on social media on July 26.

events.title: Hourly workers are living with 7.86% inflation. No wonder they voted against the AI boom
events.summary: On Nov. 3, in 40 of 41 local votes across 10 states, Americans chose to limit data centers. Many observers read that as voters choosing a recession over the biggest industrial buildout of their lifetimes . I read it differently. Hourly workers are short on paycheck, and the warehouses near those data centers are short on hourly workers. The backlash and the buildout are one problem seen from two ends. I see both ends because my company staffs those warehouses, which also means a tight labor market is good for our business. The figures below come from our shift and survey data unless I note otherwise. Look at the paycheck Headline inflation was 3.7% in September . The Bureau of Labor Statistics itself says the CPI “ does not necessarily measure your own experience with price change .” For hourly workers, the gap is wide. In our survey of 3,083 hourly workers this summer , 69.4% said they earn under $30,000 a year across all their jobs, and only about half have a savings account. So I rebuilt the number around how these workers spend. I call it FeelFlation. We took each category’s share of take-home pay and weighted it by how much that category’s cost rose in the 12 months through September (figures rounded): Rent or mortgage: 28% of take-home pay, costs up 3% Interest on debt: 16%, up 21% Transportation: 15%, up 11% Discretionary spending: 13%, up 2.6% Food: 10.9%, up 3% Insurance premiums: 10%, up 12% Healthcare: 7%, up 2.6% The weighted total is 7.86%, more than double the headline. The interest increase is our estimate from Consumer Financial Protection Bureau data, combining higher interest rates with balances that stay unpaid longer. If anything, 7.86% understates the squeeze, since newer data put insurance premiums up 16%. Three categories do most of the damage: interest, insurance premiums and transportation. Together they take 41% of the paycheck and drive nearly 80% of the increase. Interest alone adds more than three points, and it’s a cost the official gauge leaves out. The CPI tracks the prices of what people buy and excludes the interest on the credit cards and auto loans they use to pay for it. Gas prices make people angry because they see them every day. A debt bill that eats one dollar in six does more damage, quietly. Hourly pay on our platform rose 3.1% over the same 12 months. The things these workers pay for rose 4.76 percentage points faster than their pay, and they’re responding the only way they can. In that same survey , 67.6% said they pick up an extra shift rather than borrow when an unexpected bill hits. Look at the warehouse Now the other end. In Columbus, Ohio, the share of posted warehouse shifts filled on our platform fell from 87.9% in 2024 to 82.8% this year. More than 1 in 6 warehouse shifts there now goes unfilled. Fill rates fell in every data-center metro we track. Northern Virginia went from 96.2% to 92.6%, Dallas-Fort Worth from 93.5% to 91.4%, and Phoenix from 91.5% to 90.1%. Across the four metros combined, the rate dropped 1.8 points, to 90.3%. Columbus fell nearly three times as far. Peak season is days away, and these warehouses are heading into it short. Two caveats. First, our warehouse volume in these metros has more than doubled since 2024, to 17,342 shifts from 7,258, so part of the drop reflects demand outrunning supply. That’s what a shortage is. Second, we can’t trace an individual worker from a warehouse to a data center job site. My read is that the buildout draws the most skilled hourly workers first, and warehouses compete for the rest of a shrinking pool. Net immigration fell from about 3.5 million in 2023 to roughly 410,000 in 2025 , according to the Congressional Budget Office. One problem, two ends The backlash and the buildout feed each other. A worker whose paycheck is going backward hears the industry promise trillions in value and the end of their job in the same breath. Then they get asked to host a power-hungry data center down the road. They vote no. And the data centers that do get built can’t staff the warehouses that supply them. Silicon Valley spent the past 18 months telling Main Street that AI would make a few people unfathomably rich and put everyone else out of work. Voters took the industry at its word. Now it has to show working people what the boom is worth to them. What would help Growth without more workers isn’t an option. Washington should match legal immigration for skilled trades to what the buildout needs. Two other changes would reach paychecks faster. Put overtime money in the weekly check. Through 2028, workers can deduct the premium portion of their overtime pay , the “half” in time-and-a-half, from federal taxable income, up to $12,500 a year. But the break arrives with the annual tax return, and Social Security and Medicare taxes still apply . A two-to-three-year overtime tax holiday would deliver that money every payday instead of in a refund months later. It would reward the extra shift workers already choose over debt and help cover the shifts warehouses can’t fill. Share the upside. AI labs and data center owners are raising money on the promise of future productivity. Part of that upside, including equity, should reach the hourly workers who build, supply and staff these facilities. A town would look at a data center differently if it came with a raise. Voters ran the numbers on Nov. 3. Now the industry has until the next ballot to run its own. events.title: ‘Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah’: LeBron James sues the sports betting app whose AI version of him said it
events.summary: In an ad, LeBron James sits in an NBA locker room in a No. 23 jersey with “Bron” printed across the back, scrolling through bets on his phone. He stops on a photo of Phoenix Suns forward Dillon Brooks, one of his best-known on-court rivals. “Dillon Brooks? On Kalshi? Hell nah,” he says, in James’ voice. Except it isn’t James. It’s an AI-generated version of him, made by a two-person startup to sell a sports betting app called Bron. And James, who has an exclusive endorsement deal with Kalshi-rival Polymarket, is now suing. King James has been at the center of many notable brand deals—spanning massive contracts with Nike , Sprite , and of course, Polymarket . But the NBA’s oldest active player, and his company LBJ Trademarks LLC, is accusing the app’s creator PlayVision Inc. of exploiting his likeness in an AI-generated ad—and using an alleged affiliation with the star to promote itself. The suit, filed on Nov. 17 in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York against the app’s parent company and its cofounders Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby,  alleges trademark infringement, false endorsement and false advertising. According to the complaint, the founders are PlayVision’s only employees, and it includes  an argument that the company deliberately chose the name Bron and used an AI version of James in its marketing to capitalize on his global recognition. “The word ‘Bron’ has no dictionary definition and no special meaning in the context of sports analytics, wagering, or artificial intelligence,” the filing read. “Rather, in the context of anything sports-related, it refers to only one man—LeBron James.” The lawsuit describes the campaign as an effort to create the false impression that James was affiliated with the app, which offers sports betting research tools—including bet tracking and odds comparisons. The complaint is seeking an injunction preventing the defendants from using James’ name and likeness, repayment of profits generated through the alleged infringement, and compensatory and punitive damages.  The complaint accuses the appmakers of violating James’ right of publicity under a 1903 New York law, stemming from a woman whose portrait appeared without her consent on 25,000 posters of Franklin Mills flour—and led to New York State requiring written consent to use a person’s likeness in ads. It also leans on a far newer law: New York’s first-in-the-nation rule signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in Dec. 2025 that requires ads to disclose when they use an AI-generated “synthetic performer.”  The Bron ad carried no such disclosure, the complaint says.   “The integrity of NBA competition—and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play—is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans,” the complaint stated. The Bron app and ad Gupta posted the ad to his X account on Nov. 2 with the caption “Where is Bron?”—and the AI figure, shown mostly from behind, copies James’ build and tattoos. It speaks in what the suit says is a synthesized version of his voice. Another scene shows a rider in a Bron cap on a New York City subway car stopped at 14 Street. The complaint says James’ betting deals, first with DraftKings and now with Polymarket, have focused on football, not basketball, because the NBA bars players from betting on NBA games. By showing him scrolling NBA player props and naming Kalshi, the suit argues, the ad “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player performance.” “The Ad catapulted the Bron App from obscurity to controversy, with the Ad gaining a million views within a day—exactly as Defendants intended,” the complaint read. “But Mr. James has no affiliation with Defendants or their product. Defendants’ intentional use of artificial intelligence to steal Mr. James’s name and likeness was instead an unlawful effort to trade on Mr. James’s identity to enrich Defendants.” The suit alleges the founders built the ad to provoke James. “Defendants calculated that the value of that attention would exceed the cost of any legal consequences, and they treated the violation of Mr. James’s rights as a marketing expense,” it reads. PlayVision, a California- based company founded in 2025 by Gupta and Zoghby, initially developed AI software designed to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. Describing itself as “AI moneyball for sports,” the company later launched Bron as an app that marketed itself as a sports analytics and betting research platform—but by spring 2026, it pivoted to consumer betting. The Bron app pulls recommended wagers from more than 150 sportsbooks and prediction markets. It is free to download: Bron Pro costs $29.99 a month or $249.99 a year. PlayVision and the Bron app did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune . Garnering attention from controversy And according to the complaint, Gupta responded to a cease and desist letter from James’ team on Nov. 5 by suggesting the app would adopt a new name. However, the company had not announced a replacement name when James filed the suit. On Nov. 16, he wrote on X: “We found Bron. Apparently, the lawyers found it too. Find out our new name Wednesday. 10 AM PT.” “They continue to use the Bron name to this day, prolonging the controversy for as long as it continues to generate attention for the Bron App and violating Mr. James’s rights to serve their marketing goals,” the filing read. “And even a belated name change now would not remedy the exploitation of Mr. James’s brand and goodwill that allowed Defendants to garner these millions of views and attention in the first place.” The suit also identifies fellow NBA star and former James’ teammate Luka Doncic as another player whose likeness appeared in the app’s campaign. Doncic separately sent the company a cease-and-desist letter, according to the filing. But that hasn’t intruded on the app’s stride. In response to the suits sent their way, Gupta posted on X—this time, an AI image of the two cofounders sitting in an empty courtroom with the caption: “Taking this to another court. We ain’t done yet.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Feds say soldier in $400,000 Polymarket case repeatedly photographed classified docs
events.summary: Gannon Van Dyke, shown here leaving federal court in April, wants to block evidence that has emerged weeks before his trial. David Dee Delgado/Bloomberg via Getty Images The feds say they plan to introduce new evidence against Gannon Van Dyke. His lawyers called the revelation an "unfair surprise" sprung too close to the trial date. Van Dyke is accused of using military secrets to make bets about Nicolás Maduro on Polymarket. The US soldier charged with using military secrets to place profitable trades on Polymarket says federal prosecutors have dropped a bombshell weeks before trial, revealing they have evidence he repeatedly photographed classified material with his personal cellphone. Gannon Van Dyke , a Special Forces master sergeant who worked out of Fort Bragg in North Carolina, is asking a federal judge to stop a jury from hearing the evidence, arguing it was raised too late. Van Dyke, 37, was arrested in April and accused of winning more than $400,000 by wagering on Polymarket on the question of whether the US would take action in Venezuela or against its then-president Nicolás Maduro. Prosecutors have said Van Dyke was involved in the planning and execution of the operation to depose Maduro and had access to classified information about it. A November 11 letter from the prosecutors to Van Dyke's legal team said new evidence would show that "between at least in or about 2024 and in or about October 2025, Van Dyke photographed information marked classified from U.S. Government systems using his personal cellphone." "The evidence is admissible to show the defendant's opportunity to access classified information, his knowledge of the fact that information obtained by virtue of his employment may be classified, and to demonstrate an absence of mistake or accident in the use of classified information," they wrote. Prosecutors cited Rule 404(b), which allows evidence unrelated to the specific acts alleged in the indictment to be brought up at trial under certain circumstances. In their motion, Van Dyke's lawyers argued the prosecution didn't meet the bar for that and accused the government of "an attempt at unfair surprise." "The prosecution seeks only to muddy Mr. Van Dyke's reputation by alleging he committed another purported bad act, not charged, involving classified information," they wrote. Van Dyke, who pled not guilty and is out on bail , is set to face trial December 7, but that could be delayed by last-minute matters. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Nvidia interim CEO Kress tells employees ‘let’s move forward’ at first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang exit
events.summary: Nvidia executives addressed employees Wednesday at the first all-hands meeting since Jensen Huang resigned. “Let’s move forward,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress told the room, according to a person in the room who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity. Kress also mentioned pay raises for employees, according to the source. Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress told employees "let's move forward" on Wednesday during the company's first all-hands meeting since founder Jensen Huang resigned, according to an attendee who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity. Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones and hyperscale and high-performance computing head Ian Buck. Several other senior members of Nvidia's executive team spoke, including long-time company veteran Jeff Fisher, senior vice president of GPU engineering Jonah Alben, executive vice president in charge of Operations Debora Shoquist and co-founder Chris Malachowsky, according to a person familiar with the matter. Kress opened with the message about moving forward, and also brought up pay raises for employees, according to the attendee. Jones then pivoted to a discussion about the search for the next CEO, the attendee added. The meeting lasted about an hour and was in person as well as streamed on Microsoft Teams. The general sentiment swirling in the room, according to the attendee, is that employees want Huang to come back . Employees have spoken up on X in recent days to call for the return of Huang as CEO, and one senior employee reportedly sent a letter to the board warning Nvidia would lose "irreplaceable talent" if it doesn't consider reinstating Huang. But another person familiar with the matter disagreed, saying that employees welcomed the remarks from leadership as well as the visibility into company leadership. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Jones said during the earnings call on Tuesday. Despite recent turmoil, Wednesday's meeting was not out of the ordinary. Nvidia typically holds all-hands the morning after quarterly earnings reports, according to a former employee who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity. Kress recapped Tuesday's earnings report, calling it a "great quarter," according to one person familiar with the matter. In past meetings, Huang took time to answer questions submitted by employees, according to the former employee. On Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honored to answer these calls and return as CEO." Nvidia shares were down 2% on Wednesday, a day after the company reported third-quarter earnings that topped Wall Street expectations and gave no signal that the company was going to slow its growth. Still, Nvidia faced several downgrades from Wall Street on Wednesday, including from Bernstein and Evercore. WATCH: The rise, reinvention and uncertain future of Nvidia without Jensen Huang

events.title: Vance scraps schedule to address tech outages as Trump admin insists incidents aren't linked
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance abruptly canceled his scheduled DealBook Summit appearance to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages. There is no indication that those outages are the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action, a senior Trump administration official said. The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days. Those incidents include a nationwide ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network. Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages . The cancellation was announced shortly after a senior Trump administration official insisted that the outages, which have affected a wide range of industries and have been felt across the country and around the world, are not the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action. "We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the result of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied" or other "disparate" events, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the government's intelligence assessments. The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network. Jensen Huang slated to appear before House panels Dec. 1; Nvidia lawyer due to testify Dec. 2 Republicans outspent Democrats in record 2026 midterm ad blitz Lisa Cook lawyer signals Fed governor won't attend Trump committee's hearing Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase , an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple . On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack and "not a coordinated effort by a nation-state." He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee. "We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor." But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame. The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported." Sen. Mark Warner , D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC on Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety. "I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm." His comments came hours before before Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering for the first major AI industry IPO. Warner advocated for a "pre-testing regime" for new AI models that establishes guardrails and helps ensure a "culture of safety built in" to the industry." He said the U.S. is "lucky" that it has so far avoided a major AI-generated cyberattack or a crisis with a rogue agent that goes beyond incidents like the Hugging Face breach earlier this year. — CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

events.title: Chris Christie says Jensen Huang shouldn’t come back to Nvidia. Hours later, the board agreed
events.summary: On Tuesday morning, Jensen Huang said he’d return as Nvidia’s CEO if the board asked. By that afternoon, a possible 2028 Republican presidential candidate said he shouldn’t. A few hours later, Nvidia’s board said the same. “No,” former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie said when Fortune’s Diane Brady asked at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum whether Huang should return. Christie lumped the former Nvidia CEO in with President Trump as an example of “people in positions of power without any character.” Speaking onstage with former Democratic Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum Tuesday, Christie, who is a Republican, railed against Huang’s behavior.  “We have gone on a character holiday for 10 years,” he said. “We have said—because we have a leader in the White House and leaders throughout business like Jensen Huang who have said all that matters is the bottom line, and character doesn’t matter anymore.” The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment. Huang steps down Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia last week after admitting he was unfaithful to his wife, amid reports of more than one extramarital relationship. The New York Times previously reported on his close relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence services suspected was a Chinese spy. China has denied the allegation. Huang’s behavior, Christie implied Tuesday, was an example of the degradation of ethics that has taken over America during the past decade. President Trump was first elected president in 2016. Trump, who has forged a close relationship with Huang over the past year, defended the former tech executive, saying in response to a question from ABC Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO. The president has repeatedly expressed sympathy for the former Nvidia CEO, calling him a “tremendous talent” following his resignation. Notable business figures like Elon Musk have backed Huang’s return to the CEO position. Huang in his first public statement since he stepped down said he had received an “outpouring of calls” to return as CEO after he resigned, including from Nvidia’s employees and customers.  “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote in a post on X. Nvidia’s board, however, has remained steadfast. On Tuesday afternoon, interim CEO Colette Kress and Nvidia’s new chairman of the board Harvey Jones oversaw the company’s first earnings call without Huang, and made it clear he would not return. “The board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said on the call. The company on Tuesday reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the three months ended Oct. 25, which was more than double what it reported during the same period last year and was above the $109 billion analysts expected .  “We’ve got this,” Kress said during the call.  Falling public trust Both Christie and Emanuel are weighing runs for the White House. In an interview with Politico earlier this month, Christie said he is still considering whether to run for President in 2028. He previously sought the Republican nomination for President in 2016 and 2024. Emanuel said during the WBUR festival in May that he was contemplating a presidential run in 2028. Political parties aside, the two split on Huang. Christie said Huang’s recent behavior fits in with the decline in ethics that, in his opinion, has taken hold in America over the past decade. “America is no longer being seen around the world as a leader you want to emulate, and I think that is tragic, but it can be fixed with new leadership in Washington at the White House that can do that,” Christie added. But Emanuel, who shared the stage with Christie Tuesday, took a more pragmatic view of Nvidia’s recent leadership shakeup. “Look, Nvidia is a separate issue, and I think the technology is what’s valuable,” Emanuel said. “There are other CEOs. The technology is what’s valuable,” he said. Still, Emanuel agreed with Christie that the loss of public trust goes beyond Washington to the private sector, and especially tech.  “Don’t underestimate the lack of trust that CEOs in America have, the tech bros have,” he said. “This is not restricted just to the public sector.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The AI bubble is cracking. Wall Street is nervous
events.summary: The AI gold rush as we knew it is over. The technology will keep advancing, but unlimited spending and unquestioned valuations is finished. The biggest threat to the AI boom sits in the financing that holds the ecosystem together. The trend line is heading precipitously down. Global AI funding was $239.1 billion in Q1 of 2026, $153.1 billion in Q2 and $103.3 billion in Q3. Is this the bottom? The company at the core of the AI industry may be key to finding that answer. The great repricing has begun Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market value since its October 6 record, over 30% of what was the most valuable company on earth, gone in under six weeks. On Nov. 12, Jensen Huang resigned after 33 years. The CFO is interim CEO and Congress has called Huang to testify. The company at the center of the AI economy now carries succession risk and national security exposure at the same time. Recent earnings reports may have softened the sting, but questions still must be answered. Having great technology does not justify every valuation. The people behind the tech must be able to responsibly steward a company and its mission. The $570 billion question Bloomberg’s chart of circular AI financing puts Nvidia at the center of a global web that includes Microsoft , Google, Amazon , OpenAI, Anthropic, Oracle and CoreWeave. Billions move between them as equity stakes, chip purchases, cloud contracts and guarantees. But, how much of this demand is organic and how much is financed by the companies that benefit from it? Chipmakers invest in AI companies, which buy their chips. Cloud providers invest in AI developers, which commit billions back to cloud. Lenders then finance data centers against those commitments. Nvidia has guaranteed up to $105 billion in lease obligations on an Ohio data center campus built for OpenAI, Nvidia’s own customer. Capital circulates and valuations rise. This loop can power real growth, but also make independent demand look stronger than it is. When suppliers finance their customers and both valuations rest on the same revenue, one default travels fast. Calling the whole system a Ponzi scheme would be irresponsible, but calling it safe would be worse. Morgan Stanley projects nearly $570 billion in global AI-related debt issuance in 2026, more than double last year. Nearly $236 billion was issued by the end of May alone. Someone has to pay for all that capacity. The credit market’s verdict In October, the yield on CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds passed 16%, a level traditionally signaling distress. According to Reuters there is a nearly 63% chance of default within five years. This happened even with an Nvidia agreement in place to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through 2032. Lenders are now asking for higher yields and tighter covenants. Credit investors have started to separate financial strength from AI enthusiasm. With tighter credit we have to begin to ask who in this circle is going to absorb all the loss that is sure to come? Proof wins, speculation loses in the world of data centers Yes, Nvidia remains highly profitable. Microsoft, Google and Amazon still have extremely deep pockets. But, debt-heavy neoclouds and data center developers live in a world of power shortages, construction delays, rising borrowing costs, and local opposition. Billions have been committed to AI campuses before demand and profitability are proven. Data centers are here to stay, but the speculative ones are in trouble. I expect a wave of distressed and underused projects between 2028 and 2031. The survivors will have cheap power and creditworthy customers on long contracts. A gigawatt announced is not a dollar earned. AI politics are changing The EU AI Act is already reshaping compliance. Individual US states are drafting and passing different legislation, and after the recent midterm elections Washington will press harder on safety, energy costs, competition and national security. The idea of building first and answering questions later no longer exists. Regulation will decide who can scale and who cannot. An encore of the fiber build-out The fiber buildout of the late 1990s produced real technological progress, but destroyed vast amounts of investor capital. The internet survived, but many of the companies that financed it did not. AI is real and demand for compute is large. Technological inevitability does not guarantee financial sustainability, but I remain bullish on what AI will do for economies and industries over the long run. I am far less bullish on the financial engineering around it. Today falls short of a debt crisis. But, what we are watching is the first serious stress test of the financial system behind AI. The risk is that financing assumptions break before the technology delivers its economic returns. The winners of the next phase will be the companies that earn sustainable returns on invested capital. GPU counts and gigawatt announcements will matter less. As time passes on this current test, the most interconnected players may find that their biggest customers and their biggest creditors sit in the same circle. events.title: JD Vance says Americans don’t need to stock up. The Pentagon and U.S. allies are preparing for the worst
events.summary: Vice President JD Vance has a message for Americans wondering whether a week of cascading outages signals worse to come: Skip the bunker. “A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,” Vance told Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday, in an interview covered by the New York Post . “My answer to that is no. We don’t see a crisis coming down. But you have to be prepared for everything.” That advice puts Washington at odds with several close allies, which are telling their citizens the opposite. And it lands on a public that, after six days in which Microsoft, the nation’s air traffic system, major banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency all stumbled, has good reason to wonder whom to believe. Six days, five failures The run began November 12 with a massive Exchange Online outage that rippled across Microsoft 365 services. The next afternoon, the FAA halted flights across U.S. airspace for nearly five hours after data flooded its legacy telecom network, and the agency says it has no indication of a cyberattack . On November 16, customers of JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Capital One, and other banks couldn’t get to their money . Chase told Time the cause was “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems” and that “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” A day later, Apple said a faulty internal update knocked out iCloud and other customer services, and the NSA said its classified internal network suffered a “temporary degradation” during routine maintenance. Officials insist the failures are unrelated. “We are not under systemic attack,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila on Wednesday, saying there was “zero evidence whatsoever” that the disruptions were connected. Still, each was a calamity in its own right, and with the events essentially overlapping, it’s no surprise that many Americans began to fear the worst . The backdrop was already grim: In January, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists set its Doomsday Clock at 85 seconds to midnight , which it called “the closest it has ever been to catastrophe.” U.S. allies are telling citizens to prepare Even as Vance spoke, the U.K. government was pushing its “Be Ready” campaign , launched October 22, which urges households to manage on their own for three days if severe weather, outages, or other emergencies cut off power, water, phone, or internet service. In Japan, a new National Disaster Management Agency began operating November 2 with an emergency request that residents keep at least three days of food and water on hand, and ideally a week’s worth. Germany’s federal civil protection office recommends a 10-day supply . Closer to home, Vance’s own administration is planning for prolonged disruption. On Sept. 30, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled a Pentagon initiative called FORTRESS , which, according to internal planning documents, would require every major military installation in the continental U.S. to sustain essential operations on its own for at least 90 days. Does every American need to return to the fallout-shelter mentality of the peak Cold War years? Surely not. But Vance framed the administration’s readiness as an accomplishment, not a warning. “In part, what the president has been so successful at is ensuring we are reinvesting in the United States of America and we are better prepared for crises,” he said. “That doesn’t mean a crisis is around the corner, that just means you’ve got a government who is actually preparing for it.” That reassurance comes from a party voters just moved to check. In this month’s midterms, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate and flipped five governorships, giving them a majority of governors’ mansions for the first time since 2010. Advice is only as good as the messenger The “we” in Vance’s answer is the federal government, and Americans’ trust in it, like any citizen’s trust in their own government, is far from guaranteed right now, says Baruch Fischhoff , Howard Heinz University Professor in Carnegie Mellon’s Department of Engineering and Public Policy. Confidence in government safety messages often follows party lines, which can lull some people into a false sense of security while leaving others with an overinflated sense of dread. “It makes sense to follow advice when you trust the source,” Fischhoff told Fortune . “That means believing that they are honest and that they know what they are talking about.” “People may disagree about how honest a politician is,” he added. “They should not imagine that a politician knows anything about technical matters. All they can do is relay what their experts tell them.” Asked about Vance’s comments, Fischhoff applied the same test. “People who believe that Mr. Vance is honest and that his experts are doing a good job of managing our country’s risks should follow his advice. Other people will see recent problems with the FAA, NSA, and banks as blips with well-managed risks; some people will wonder whether they are being run by people who are in over their heads.” For Fischhoff, being candid about what officials don’t know is part of the job. “The public deserves clear, timely, useful, trustworthy information from honest sources who know what they are talking about,” he said. “That may mean admitting that the experts don’t know what’s happening. For questions affecting the nation, the federal government has a duty to provide that information. If the public is confused, the government is not doing its job.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
