events.title: Orange tap water called 'safe to drink' had metals above guidelines
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Orange tap water TasWater called 'safe to drink' had metals above guideline levels A Sandy Bay resident captured some of the murky water in a jar. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) A sample of discoloured water from a Sandy Bay home has tested above guideline levels for lead and manganese. TasWater had previously told a resident the water was "safe to drink". Health authorities say harm is unlikely from limited consumption, though TasWater is reviewing its messaging. Testing of viscous, orange water that Tasmania's water authority had told a customer was safe to drink has returned levels of heavy metals above drinking water guidelines. Two weeks ago, Sandy Bay resident Emma Thornley turned the taps on in her house and found discoloured water coming out. It happened throughout the day. A load of white clothing came out of the washing machine with dark orange stains while thick, orange water poured from the kitchen tap. State water provider, TasWater, advised residents in the area at the time that emergency repairs were being carried out on a nearby burst water main, and that drinking water "may be discoloured and cloudy" but was "safe to drink". TasWater texted residents in the area saying the water was safe to drink. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) Ms Thornley called TasWater to tell the authority her water did not appear safe to drink so that it could notify other customers. She said her concerns were dismissed. "I actually asked her to guarantee on the recorded line if this water was safe and would not contain anything harmful like heavy metals," she said. "They were very quick to respond that it was absolutely safe to drink and there would be no heavy metals or contaminants in it. "The words they used were that this was the normal water you drink every day; it's just got some sediment in it." Ms Thornley paid to have the water tested at Analytical Services Tasmania, which is part of the state's Department of Natural Resources and Environment. The orange water was above guideline levels for lead and manganese. ( Supplied: Emma Thornley ) The sample was not large enough to test for mercury but was tested for lead and manganese. It found 25 micrograms of lead and 3,210 micrograms (3.21 milligrams) of manganese per litre. According to the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines (ADWG), the highest acceptable concentration for lead is 5 micrograms per litre of drinking water, while for manganese it is 100 micrograms (0.1 milligram) per litre. "I now have lots of questions about why TasWater continued telling me that this was safe to drink," Ms Thornley said. "It also makes me question, in the past when we've had discoloured water, and we've contacted them and told them and the general response is just 'flush the taps if you're worried' and 'it's totally safe to drink', was it actually safe to drink?" TasWater will review 'incorrect' messaging The results of the testing prompted Analytical Services Tasmania to notify Public Health and Tasmania's drinking water officer, Cameron Dalgleish. Mr Dalgleish wrote to Ms Thornley on November 11 and said he had spoken to TasWater about the issue. "They have undertaken to do a full review around the incomplete (and incorrect) messaging and their response to the emergency works," Mr Dalgleish wrote. Mr Dalgleish said he had also flagged questions about the customer service response with the Tasmanian Economic Regulator. Tasmania's drinking water officer has spoken to TasWater about the issue. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Resident wants more transparency about testing Living in a suburb with aging water infrastructure, Ms Thornley said she had received several text message notifications from TasWater in the past two years, advising customers to run their taps and saying the water may be discoloured but was safe to drink. On other occasions, the water had come out cloudy, but she did not receive any communication from TasWater. Ms Thornley wants to see more transparency about TasWater's testing processes, saying there needs to be more accurate communication to its customers. TasWater did not take water samples directly from the affected area at the time. Emma Thornley is concerned about other occasions when the water at her Sandy Bay home has been discoloured. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) The utility's general manager of customer and community, Callan Paske, said TasWater had advised customers via text message on the day of the emergency works to run their outside tap until clear to remove sediment or cloudiness, as per its standard practice. TasWater's investigation into the incident is continuing.

events.title: Fears housing build costs will soar in response to Chinese timber crackdown
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Topic: Forestry, Logging and Timber Industry Australian timber processed at a mill in South East South Australia. ( ABC News ) An investigation is underway to probe whether Chinese structural timber has been dumped or subsidised, harming local industry. The housing industry fears that price increases following the investigation could compound cost pressures on building products. The investigation is expected to be finalised in April 2027. The peak housing body fears prices may increase further as an investigation is underway to examine if structural timber imported from China is being dumped or subsidised at below-market value. The probe by the Australian Trade Remedies Commission (ATRC) is in response to claims by the Australian timber industry that cheap imports are having an unfair advantage over domestic timber, putting jobs and businesses at risk. However, the housing industry says if timber costs increase as a result of the investigation, it will compound cost pressures on building products. In recent years, the price of building materials has soared, but timber prices have remained steady. The Housing Industry Association (HIA) says timber is the core structural element in about 80 per cent of Australian homes. About 80 per cent of that timber is made in Australia, and 20 per cent is imported. HIA chief executive of industry policy Simon Croft said the association backed local manufacturing, but the investigation came as affordability and supply constraints were already stretching the industry. Simon Croft says the timber industry needs support. ( Supplied: Housing Industry Australia ) Other anti-dumping investigations are already underway into building products, including aluminium windows and doors, insulation and some steel products. The HIA believed this pointed to a widespread problem and showed the sector needed support. "When you've got these duties applied to a range of products, that just puts more pressure on affordability," Mr Croft said. "Unfortunately, we don't generally see things [prices] moving the opposite way. "For our manufacturers and suppliers, things like their energy costs, labour costs, input costs, insurance costs are all making it harder for them to be competitive in that global environment." Harvesting underway in a OneFortyOne softwood estate in the Limestone Coast. ( Supplied: OneFortyOne ) One of Australia's largest timber companies OneFortyOne, which operates a structural timber sawmill in Mount Gambier and owns forests that straddle the South Australian and Victorian border, has raised concerns over the impact of Chinese imports. OneFortyOne Australia executive general manager Cameron MacDonald said Chinese competition, inflation and the Middle East conflict had taken their toll on the industry. Mr MacDonald viewed Chinese timber products as an existential threat to the industry. "It's [Chinese timber products] coming at prices that we have really questioned whether that's fair," he said. "We just want to be able to operate on a level playing field with imported products." Cameron MacDonald says he is concerned about losing market share. ( Supplied: OneFortyOne ) Like many businesses, OneFortyOne has been hit by rising overheads, but it has not been able to pass on those costs. "We tried to put a price increase through last year, but that didn't hold because of the imported products from China," Mr MacDonald said. "The other issue is we're losing market share." Businesses like OneFortyOne are struggling to compete against cheap Chinese timber imports. ( Supplied: OneFortyOne ) The company is now operating below capacity. "Since the start of July, our forest business, which supplies sawlogs to all the sawmills in and around Mount Gambier, we've seen our volumes decrease by 40 per cent and that's meant that we've had to release two harvesting crews [and] we're using 15 fewer trucks," Mr MacDonald said. "The consequences of this extend well beyond OneFortyOne. Mr MacDonald said he understood concerns about rising building costs, but savings could come from other areas. "There's a high level of governance around how we operate our businesses, and we'd certainly appreciate a focus from the government on how they can reduce red tape to reduce the cost of operating businesses in Australia." Much of the timber grown and harvested in the Green Triangle is used for construction. ( ABC News: Gary Rivett ) The investigation was initiated by an application from the Australian Forest Products Association (AFPA) and a group of structural timber manufacturers, including OneFortyOne.

events.title: The CEO behind Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t play video games, but analysts say he has put $1.5 billion behind the biggest game launch of the decade
events.summary: After 15 years churning out hit titles like Grand Theft Auto, Red Dead Redemption , and NBA2k, this CEO knows what makes a hit—even if he doesn’t play video games himself.  Strauss Zelnick, a Harvard Law School and Harvard Business School graduate, has been CEO of Take-Two Interactive Software since 2011. During that time, he has helped skyrocket the company’s stock price by more than 1,700% from about $12 per share when he took charge to about $221 per share as of Wednesday. He has also quintupled the company’s net revenue during his tenure, with 2025’s full-year number coming in at $5.6 billion compared with less than $1 billion before he took over. He has been massively successful at the game publisher in the past and is preparing for what could be his biggest success yet with this week’s release of Grand Theft Auto VI. This is all despite the fact he doesn’t play the games he helps bring to life. He may watch others play, but he doesn’t think it’s necessary that he be the one holding the controller, he told Business Insider earlier this year. “I don’t think being consumer-in-chief really helps a CEO be effective in this business,” he said. For the leader of a company selling a vice-laden game, Zelnick’s habits are tame. The Take-Two CEO doesn’t drink, smoke, and works out nearly every day, and sometimes twice a day, Business Insider reported.  Now, Take-Two and Zelnick are preparing to release Grand Theft Auto VI, one of the most anticipated releases of the year, amid increasing competition and economic uncertainty. Zelnick said pre-orders for the game were running above expectations, Reuters reported. Data from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shows the game has racked up 17 million pre-orders so far . Still, Zelnick has already run into some controversy ahead of the launch. Take-Two said over the summer that the new edition of the Grand Theft Auto franchise will start at $80 and will not include a physical copy, which has some gamers questioning whether the game will be truly theirs . While the video game market stood at a whopping $219 billion in 2024, the competition in games has exploded over the past decade or so, with 19,000 games being released in 2023 for consoles and PCs, compared with just under 2,000 in 2014, according to data from consulting firm Bain & Co. The Iran war has also upended the global economy, with many countries facing a strain on oil supply and negative economic effects, which could affect leisure purchases like video games. Still, expectations for Grand Theft Auto VI are high after the success of the series’ previous installment, Grand Theft Auto V. In 2013, GTA V racked up $1 billion worth of sales in three days, the fastest any entertainment release has ever reached that milestone, according to the company . Over the past 10 years, the game has persisted as the bestselling title in the U.S. based on both unit and dollar sales, and has sold more than 215 million units, according to Take-Two . The approximate cost of developing the highly anticipated game is between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, Business Insider estimated, citing industry analysts. Take-Two declined to comment or confirm a dollar amount for the development of GTA VI to Fortune .  While Zelnick would only say that the development of GTA VI “was expensive,” the pay off may be huge.  GTA VI’s release has been delayed several times. It was originally scheduled to launch in the fall of 2025, and then in May 2026. It is now set to release on Nov. 19.  Zelnick said these delays are sometimes part of the game development process. Unlike others in the industry, Rockstar Games, the wholly owned subsidiary of Take-Two that is developing GTA VI , doesn’t participate in “crunch,” which in game development means long shifts and intense work to meet a deadline. The company’s focus is first and foremost on making a quality game, Zelnick said. “It’s sort of like when I was in college. I never pulled an all-nighter because I was good about doing my homework,” Zelnick told BI . “You do your homework, you don’t pull an all-nighter.” A version of this story originally appeared on Fortune.com on May 6, 2026 . More on video games: GTA VI probably won’t cost the U.S. economy $1 billion —and economists say it wouldn’t matter if it did Cloud gaming was once billed as cheaper than buying titles. But new pricing from Microsoft’s Xbox is eroding that argument , gamers say One U.S. Army unit is offering 4-days off to play Grand Theft Auto —but there’s a catch: they’ll have to reenlist if they take the day off to play This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Insurance giant Bupa shuts some GP clinics after buying up chains
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts A GP saved Trish Jamieson's life by detecting her cancer early. ( ABC News: Adam Griffiths ) Bupa is continuing its expansion into general practice by buying up GP clinics, including substantial chains of centres. A former patient and former receptionist accuse the insurer of neglecting a clinic before shutting it, something Bupa rejects. Bupa's purchase of the Partnered Health chain has been approved by the competition regulator. Trish Jamieson says it was her close relationship with her GP of 15 years that was instrumental in identifying early she had oesophageal cancer in 2018. "I went to the doctors, and I saw her on the Friday and she was on the phone to St Vincent's Hospital organising me to go in there on the Monday," she said. Her GP was based in Eastbrooke Belrose Family Practice, a clinic in Sydney's north, which was frequented by elderly patients in nearby retirement homes. Eastbrooke Belrose Family Practice was valued by its patients. ( ABC News: Supplied ) Like many of her fellow patients, Ms Jamieson was devastated when health insurance giant Bupa closed down the practice in March, just 15 months after purchasing it as part of a strategy to buy up GP clinics nationally. Former receptionist Alana Monaci said it was the type of clinic that held 100th birthday parties for lonely patients and whose nurses were always on hand for a cup of tea and a hug. The Belrose clinic was one of three Australian general practices that Bupa bought and subsequently closed. A nearby Sydney GP clinic in Seaforth was converted into one of Bupa's new Mindplace mental health centres. A Gold Coast clinic, Eastbrooke Family Clinic Southport, was also closed down in April, shortly after being purchased. Bupa operates 33 medical centres. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Bupa's Sydney patients were told they could attend the insurer's new larger clinic at Gordon, a tricky journey across town for the elderly in Sydney's congested north shore traffic. The closure of these small clinics comes as Bupa builds its GP network through acquisitions, alongside its expansion into psychology services. Bupa currently operates 33 Bupa Medical and 13 Mindplace clinics but has flagged it wants to operate more. It is following a similar expansion by rival insurer Medibank Private, which had acquired a majority 90 per cent stake in the MyHealth GP chain by 2024. Bupa announced in June it intended to buy another 68 clinics from GP chain Partnered Health as part of its push. The ABC revealed a Bupa clinic encourages GPs to maximise Medicare billings in a push to increase revenue. Do you know more? Share it with us here . Bupa accused of letting GP clinic fail The experience has raised questions about the push by insurers into the GP space. Royal Australian College of GPs president Michael Wright said insurers have a financial interest in keeping people healthy through preventative care. Ms Monaci said in the 15 months Bupa ran the Belrose clinic, conditions noticeably declined. She said the clinic had to wait eight months for an air conditioner to be repaired and it became a lot more difficult to order medical supplies and get IT help. "Just layers, layers of communication that they had to go through to get really quite simple things," she said. Alana Monaci was a receptionist at a GP clinic which Bupa shut down. ( ABC News: Adam Griffiths ) Ms Jamieson also noticed that when Bupa took over in 2025 things dramatically changed. She could no longer get urgent appointments when she experienced side effects from her cancer treatment. Trish Jamieson was no longer able to get urgent appointments with her GP. ( ABC News: Adam Griffiths ) 'Unsettling' experience as doors close When one of the clinic's long-standing GPs decided to retire and another went on parental leave in March, Ms Monaci said Bupa seized the chance to close the practice. The ABC understands the clinic's location underneath a residential building was problematic and when it had trouble attracting new GPs, the site was deemed unviable. Bupa GP clinic urged doctors to lift revenue A GP clinic run by health insurance giant Bupa wrote to doctors, calling on them to use chronic condition plans to ensure "revenue is increasing". In a statement, Bupa said the Seaforth and Belrose clinic closed after a review of local needs and nearby services, and that staff were offered redeployment opportunities. The company said it understands "changes to local medical centres can be unsettling to patients and employees".

events.title: 'Double edged sword': House price rebound for Sydney after market downturn
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sydney to lead Australia's housing price recovery, analysis predicts After a price slump in every major city, Sydney's market could rebound the strongest, says new analysis. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) House prices are predicted to fall between 10 and 13 per cent by mid-2027, according to new data. In its forecast report, Domain said Sydney house prices would then rebound stronger than any other capital city. According to the forecast, median prices are expected to increase from $1.6 million to $1.7 million over the 12 months to December 2027. Australia's housing market downturn is set to drag on in every major city into next year, but new analysis suggests Sydney will bounce back and lead a national price recovery. Domain's forecast report, released on Thursday, predicted house prices would fall between 10 and 13 per cent across major capital cities by mid-2027, driven by high borrowing costs and weak buyer confidence. Distressed sales listings in NSW have jumped significantly. ( ABC News: Fletcher Yeung ) In Sydney, house prices are expected to drop by 10 per cent by June 2027 before stabilising in the second half of the year. The report predicted Sydney, Brisbane and Perth to record the sharpest housing downturn but expected Sydney to have the strongest price rebound of any capital city. David Cannington says 2027 will be a year of transition. ( Supplied ) David Cannington, a senior residential economist at Domain, said buyer confidence had placed downward pressure on the market. "Home buyer confidence has been impacted by higher interest rates, elevated inflation and then on top of that, the changes to housing investment tax policy earlier in the year," he told the ABC. Mr Cannington said buyers and sellers were already adjusting to the changes in market conditions, with 2027 shaping up to be a "year of transition". "We expect price falls to be softer in 2027 than they were this year and by the second half of next year we expect the market will be finding its footing," he said. 'Exodus of talent': Video game developers leave NSW for better support Sydney councils crack down on smart glasses in public places Tame Impala takes out Album of the Year at the 2026 ARIAs — as it happened Sales executive Daniel Eid from Laing+Simmons said he was seeing price guides for homes change almost every week. " There's not much movement at all; properties are sitting on the market," he said. "Anyone that's in a situation where they need to sell, they have to drop their prices all the way down. So it's actually negatively impacted on our vendors that we're dealing with ." Daniel Eid says price guide for homes change almost every week. ( ABC News: Quentin Theron ) He said despite property prices dropping, high interest rates meant banks were being stricter with lending. " I do believe that there are a lot of buyers that are actually saying that they're holding off till next year, forecasting that the market's going to continue to drop. Sharp rise in distressed sales listings The downturn in Australia's housing prices is occurring alongside a rise in the number of distressed sale listings. A distressed sale is when a property is sold quickly, often at a loss, and typically occurs when an owner is under financial hardship. According to SQM Research distressed sale listings surpassed 300,000 in October, the highest level in five years. In NSW, the number of distressed sales listings has jumped from 870 to 1,190 — about one third — since January. SQM managing director Louis Christopher said distressed listings had risen the fastest in the past two to three months and more quickly compared to 2022, a trend that was concerning. Distressed sale listings have sharply risen in NSW. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) "When they climb this fast it tells us more households and investors are under financial pressure and being forced to sell," he said. "It also usually comes before additional weaker prices." Mr Christopher said that while more housing stock was coming onto the market, properties were taking longer to sell. "That's the setting where forced sales start to really build," he said. Mr Christopher said the upswing could be a precursor of a broader shift in market conditions, however distressed listings were still lower than the 2024 peak of 1,400 and well below the levels seen in 2020. Aaron Lih says there is still demand from families wanting to upsize and from first-time homebuyers. ( Supplied: McGrath ) McGrath sales agent Aaron Lih said in recent months he had received calls from clients inquiring about selling.

events.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
events.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer. Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.). Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.). Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine). Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.). Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.). Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda. Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership. The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios . Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen. Who's backing Schumer? Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week. Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King , along with Schumer himself. Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.). Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race. Senators who haven't picked a side Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate. Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership. Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate. Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate. The 2028 factor Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats. Ossoff and Booker , both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard. Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly , also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer. Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender. Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection . What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1. Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

events.title: Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast
events.summary: Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has a problem with the four-year degree, and he brought it to a room full of the people who hire its graduates. “The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways. They don’t like to change,” Stitt said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel with U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt. He said when he digs into the degree programs at the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State, “there’s a book this thick and then you’ve got like three people graduating from these different things.” He added: “I’m not saying that degree is not important, but you can’t be all things [to] all people.” His fix is a 90-credit bachelor’s degree, 30 credits short of the standard 120, or roughly a year less of tuition. In-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges averaged $11,950 in the 2024-25 school year, according to the College Board. Stitt said the idea is to keep the rigor of the requirements, trim some electives, and “get kids ready for the workforce quicker.” RAND counted 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs publicly announced across the U.S. as of May 2026, up from five in 2024, most of them in “applied and workforce-facing fields.” Jason Lee, a senior policy researcher at RAND, has since told the Wall Street Journal the number of shortened bachelor’s programs announced this year are up to roughly 150. From executive order to diploma Stitt signed an executive order in February ordering a 90-day study of 90-credit “accelerated” degrees, and the Legislature followed with HB 3315, which required the State Regents to study feasibility. In June, the regents took action to create a framework for the degrees. “A three-year degree speeds up workforce entry and makes so much sense for students who are ready to work and support a family, right here in Oklahoma,” Stitt said in a statement at the time. On Sept. 3, the regents approved four reduced-credit degrees ranging from 90 to 103 credit hours, according to the Oklahoma Council of Public Affairs : social work at the University of Oklahoma, two at Oklahoma State, in artificial intelligence and in business, and workforce development at Rogers State University. “A college degree doesn’t have to take four years just because it always has,” Stitt posted on X. Other states are moving, too. Tennessee’s higher education commission approved a policy in July allowing bachelor’s degrees of as few as 90 credit hours. Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed the state’s coordinating board to develop pathways in August. The University of North Carolina system approved a pilot in April, and 11 campuses have submitted proposals, according to the James G. Martin Center . What a fourth year was buying The three-year degree tests an old question in economics: how much of a degree’s value comes from what students learn, and how much from what it tells employers. Michael Spence shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in economics, in part, for showing how education can work as a signal, costly proof of ability that employers can’t see directly. A shorter degree is cheaper to get. Nobody knows yet whether it signals as much. Much of Europe has run three-year bachelor’s degrees since the Bologna reforms began in 1999. RAND found that business, information technology, and cybersecurity look most workable for shorter degrees, while fields with clinical or licensing requirements are less adaptable. How graduate schools, employers, and licensing boards will treat the degrees remains uncertain, RAND found. “We don’t have employers who said, ‘Gee, we’ve had three-year graduates,’” Madeleine Green, executive director of the College-in-3 Exchange, told Inside Higher Ed this month. The programs are still small. Johnson & Wales University has 135 students across four three-year programs, and Weber State has 30 across three, according to Inside Higher Ed . Faculty groups have pushed back. The American Association of University Professors and the American Federation of Teachers objected to Massachusetts’ approvals on grounds of “academic integrity.” “This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” AAUP president Todd Wolfson told the Associated Press in August. A year less of tuition is also a year less of revenue for the schools. Stitt’s other pitch to the CEOs was apprenticeships. He said he had visited Switzerland and Germany, where compulsory education stops after the first year of high school and students start working inside companies, and that Oklahoma made liability insurance fixes so companies could take on high school students. He told the room about a 19-year-old in Switzerland who wanted to be an architect. After three years at an architecture firm, she could work as a draftsperson, and university was still open to her. “We’ve got to rethink that in our workforce needs here in the U.S.,” Stitt said. events.title: Burnham considering cuts to national insurance to create more youth jobs
events.summary: PM hints he is open to suggestion in Milburn report to lower NICs contributions paid by companies for under-25s Who are the Neets? UK youth job crisis in five charts UK firms: what is stopping you hiring young people? Andy Burnham has said he would consider cuts to national insurance for young people “very carefully”. The prime minister also believes his proposed changes to welfare are a “very different proposition” from those of his predecessor, Keir Starmer, and the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in the last government. On Tuesday, a report suggested national insurance contributions (NICs) paid by firms for under-25s should be gradually lowered, starting with retail and hospitality companies, to help create more jobs. The independent report , by the former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn, also proposed doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NICs for 21- to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000. Asked if he believed the last government was wrong to increase NICs, Burnham told LBC: “I think it’s something you’ve got to consider very carefully going forward. Obviously, I’ve come in [and] inherited the situation. “I think the last government was right to offer support to employers to take on young people. So, that was one of the things that they did through the youth guarantee. “I will want to look at all of the evidence in relation to it, but also the affordability of making any change to national insurance. There is an exemption for young people up to 21, so there is some [movement] that’s been done in that area. “But I can’t give you a firm commitment today because obviously these matters are matters for the budget more broadly.” Currently, businesses do not pay employer NICs for workers younger than 21 nor for apprentices under 25 unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270. For non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000. Official figures show there are nearly 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet) in the UK. Later, Burnham was challenged by Kemi Badenoch about NICs at prime minister’s questions , with the Conservative leader saying Milburn’s plans would not create jobs without parallel plans to make it cheaper and simpler to employ young people. She said: “They destroy jobs, they kill businesses, and then they offer the businesses a little money to give young people work placements. It makes no sense at all.” Burnham accused Badenoch of only seeking cuts to benefits , without wanting to offer support to jobless young people. He said: “We will not accept [Badenoch] time and again coming to this house saying that we are going to bring down the welfare bill, but failing to support our young people. “[The Conservatives] slashed youth services when they were in government. They cut the education maintenance allowance. They trebled tuition fees. They took hope from a generation – we will give it back to them.” On the backbench rebellion to the last proposed reforms to welfare, Burnham told LBC: “Well, it is a very different proposition. First and foremost, it’s about support for young people, opportunity for young people. “It’s not about an arbitrary number for cuts within the system. You’ve got Conservatives and Reform who are going that way. It’s the crude cuts approach, and it just doesn’t work. It’s why they left office with a million Neets, and we’re going to have to do something fundamentally different. “I think Alan Milburn has laid out what that looks like. It is also about a very different way of providing support, so not the old top-down tick-box system of the past, but a much more localised approach.”

events.title: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
events.summary: Jaan Tallinn, an Estonian billionaire who co-founded Skype, led Anthropic's $124 million Series A five years ago, well before the company's Claude chatbot was released. Tallinn has been one of the most outspoken in the corner of the AI safety community sometimes referred to as "doomers." The traditional profit-seeking sector of Silicon Valley would not have been interested in Anthropic at that time, according to one person familiar with the matter. An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO . Jaan Tallinn co-founded Skype and later sold it to eBay . He led Anthropic's first funding round, a $124 million Series A, five years ago — well before the company's Claude chatbot was on the market and took Wall Street and Silicon Valley by storm. Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT in what could be the largest IPO of all time, and the first public debut for an AI lab. Tallinn's exact holdings haven't been disclosed. But given Anthropic's expected debut valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, the return on his initial investment could be well into the tens of billions. His exact return would depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares along the way. Anthropic's earliest backers connected with the company through philanthropic circles worried about AI's existential risk. They're sometimes described as "doomers." In 2020, Tallinn told CNBC that there's a one-in-six chance that humans won't survive this century, referencing a book from Oxford professor Toby Ord. Tallinn also described a runaway AI scenario where a model is left working overnight and "the world is no longer there in the morning." While he continued to work in tech, Tallinn co-founded the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute , known for one of the first public calls to pause AI. Despite high-profile signatories , including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, the institute's "Pause Giant AI Experiments" letter in 2023 had little effect on the industry. Tallinn's view on AI was influenced by researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who co-authored the 2025 book "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies," about the catastrophic risk of AI without proper checks, according to a person familiar with the matter. Tallinn, who has an estimated net worth of omore than $10 billion, later crossed paths with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who had defected from OpenAI with his eventual co-founders, citing views that Sam Altman's company wasn't taking AI safety seriously enough. Amodei and Tallinn overlapped in the effective altruism community, according to people who know both of them. Effective altruism, sometimes known as EA , is a philosophy that aims to use data and evidence to maximize philanthropic impact. While there's no official membership, its Silicon Valley network ended up generating much of Anthropic's early venture capital money, according to multiple people. Tallinn's early bet was that bankrolling a safety-conscious AI company was one of the best ways to keep a lid on the risk, these people said. Tallinn also invested in DeepMind, which was later acquired by Google . One person, who asked not to be named, said that at the time of Tallinn's investment, there was no expectation that Anthropic "would be a profitable undertaking." Venture investors hadn't yet gone all-in on AI, and it was "before the era of putting AI in your pitch deck," said the person, who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly on the matter. Tallinn declined to be interviewed for this story. Anthropic's first round in 2021 also included Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, who founded Open Philanthropy — now known as Coefficient Giving — which is deeply rooted in effective altruism. The charity was co-founded by Holden Karnofsky, husband of Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Karnofsky also started GiveWell, also largely tied to effective altruism. Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, another known effective altruist, backed Anthropic in its early days alongside Tallinn. Bankman-Fried participated in the Series B in 2022 through his now-defunct hedge fund Alameda Research. The former CEO was convicted of fraud in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. His stake was sold in bankruptcy auction at a fraction of the company's current valuation. Tallinn's early investment initially put Anthropic's price tag at $461 million, according to Pitchbook. It has ballooned in value since, and last raised money at a $965 billion valuation in private markets. The lab has raised money from tech giants Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia, and plans to sell $26 billion worth of shares to a group of tech companies at the IPO price. Anthropic's early investors and some in the safety community aren't overwhelmingly cheering the IPO.

events.title: A government watchdog asked AI chatbots to plan bombings and attacks on US power grids. It found that some would've worked.
events.summary: An electrical substation like some of the targets that AI chatbots planned attacks against during GAO testing. U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Alexa Hunt As a test, government watchdog investigators used popular AI chatbots to plan attacks on US infrastructure. They visited four electrical substations and found two vulnerable to proposed scenarios. All four chatbots initially activated safeguards, but investigators were able to bypass them. Government watchdog investigators used four popular artificial intelligence chatbots to plan attacks on America's electrical grid, then physically visited the proposed targets and found that some were indeed vulnerable to the scenarios the AI suggested, according to a new Government Accountability Office report. The GAO tested four of the most popular AI platforms, OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini, and xAI's Grok, to see whether they could help a malign actor plan attacks against US infrastructure or carry out mass-casualty bombings. Within 12 hours, each platform produced information investigators determined could be used to carry out an attack, according to the report released on Wednesday. Two AI chatbots suggested attacks on electrical substations , one using drones and the other firearms, to cause economic damage. Both identified specific locations and equipment and provided visual aids to investigators. Investigators conducted extensive research, consulted experts, and physically inspected locations identified by the chatbots to determine whether the proposed attacks were feasible and how reliable the chatbots' information was. In one test, a chatbot identified four electrical substations. Investigators visited all four and found that two were vulnerable. Another scenario saw one AI platform generate a video of a proposed drone attack for investigators, and recommended what type of drone to use to execute it. Investigators also consulted an expert who confirmed that an attack on the equipment identified in the plan could cause an electrical outage. Not all AI-generated information was correct though. One produced a map with incorrectly placed roads, while another provided inaccurate information about a proposed target. The findings underscore growing concerns about how AI could help bad actors identify otherwise hard-to-find vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure and quickly develop plans to do harm. A report from Anthropic in September revealed that bad actors were using the Claude chatbot as a weapons engineering assistant , indicating that these capabilities that can accelerate office work can also be weaponized. Beyond attacks on critical infrastructure, the GAO investigators also tested the chatbots' ability to plan mass-casualty attacks with improvised explosive devices. Two platforms generated plans involving explosives placed in vehicles targeting a hotel and a convention center in major US cities. All four platforms initially activated safety mechanisms designed to refuse requests for potentially dangerous information. But investigators were able to circumvent those safeguards . The report did not identify which companies' platforms produced the individual plans, or which specific cities were used as targets, citing security concerns. Companies told investigators they were continuing to strengthen their systems' safety protections. The tests were conducted in spring 2026 using earlier versions of the chatbots. events.title: Skydance CEO David Ellison says it's a 'privilege' to have Elon Musk's investment, and commits to showing 'Musk' doc on HBO
events.summary: David Ellison had high praise for Elon Musk, but is still planning to air the critical documentary about the SpaceX founder. Win McNamee/Getty Images; Adam Gray/Getty Images for The New York Times David Ellison praised Elon Musk, calling him "the greatest entrepreneur of our time." Musk invested $1 billion in Ellison's Skydance — years after Larry Ellison invested $1 billion in X. Skydance-owned HBO will still distribute the "Musk" documentary, Ellison confirmed. Skydance CEO David Ellison is an Elon Musk superfan — but he's not afraid to air the critical documentary about the Tesla and SpaceX CEO. Ellison lauded Musk and confirmed that the serial entrepreneur has invested in his media giant, which was formed when the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery mega-deal closed in early October. "To have his vote of confidence and to have him as a shareholder is an honor and a privilege," Ellison said of Musk at The New York Times' DealBook conference on Wednesday. Musk invested about $1 billion in Skydance, Semafor reported in October. Skydance hadn't addressed that report previously, and Ellison didn't confirm the size of Musk's investment. Larry Ellison, the billionaire founder of cloud giant Oracle who's also David's father, invested $1 billion in the social network now called X in 2022, when Musk bought Twitter. The younger Ellison said he "would be thrilled" to work with Musk, who runs trillion-dollar tech behemoths SpaceX and Tesla, though he said the world's richest man "doesn't invest in a lot of companies." "If there was any opportunity to be able to collaborate with him in the future — from our perspective, it'd be a privilege," Ellison said of Musk. The Skydance CEO sang Musk's praises, comparing the business tycoon to inventors Nikola Tesla and Thomas Edison. "I have so much admiration and respect for Elon," Ellison said. He added that "from my perspective, he is the greatest entrepreneur of our time." Despite Ellison's lofty view of Musk and eagerness to work with him, he said HBO will still distribute the "Musk" documentary , in which famed director Alex Gibney takes the SpaceX founder under the microscope. Musk has called the documentary about him a "hit piece" in an X post while slamming Gibney. HBO, which Skydance bought last month, helped produce the "Musk" documentary. Ellison said he won't make an exception for the "Musk" documentary, even if it puts its newest major investor in an unflattering light. "Of course we're going to honor the deal," Ellison said. "I've said it: We believe in independence. We don't believe in censorship of any kind." The Skydance CEO has faced accusations of political bias for hosting a private dinner "honoring the Trump White House" and attending several UFC events with the president. CBS News' top editor, Bari Weiss, whom Ellison handpicked, has also been  accused of political bias , which she has denied. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tech leaders see silver lining in data center backlash
events.summary: Maybe a slowdown of the AI buildout is… actually a good thing for the AI industry. Some global tech leaders at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World suggested that backlash to data centers or a potential financing bubble might provide the necessary brakes that the industry needs. A reset could mean businesses get a moment to catch up on grid capacity, fiber connectivity, cybersecurity, and to sweeten the deals data-center developers bring to communities where they’re building. Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak acknowledged that winter is coming for the AI buildout and broader economy, but said “ winter doesn’t mean minus 30 degrees. It could be a nice pleasant winter. ” One AI executive said companies must do a better job of messaging how much energy and water data centers actually consume (in one case, a useful example has been telling people data centers are less wasteful than playing a round of golf); another said AI companies need to be more aware of how “violent” it can be when they enter a community and start sucking up resources. Tech executives were reflecting on AI backlash in Silicon Valley, but stopping the buildout altogether? Not a chance. — J.D. Capelouto and Ashley Gold

events.title: Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market
events.summary: Lowe's said it saw strength in online sales during its quarter that contributed to a guidance raise for the full year. The home improvement retailer said it's also seeing strength among its professional shoppers. The company said it received roughly $250 million in tariff benefits during the quarter. Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers. The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion. Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat. CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years. "We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC. Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers. He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects. "We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program." Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $3.10 adjusted vs. $2.88 expected Revenue: $22.76 billion vs. $22.41 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior. The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates. Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year. Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter. "So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said. Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far. Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

events.title: Israeli court extends Gaza doctor Abu Safia’s detention without charge
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? An Israeli court has extended the detention of Hussam Abu Safia, the director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, who remains held without charge amid repeated calls for his release. Abu Safia’s lawyer said that a court in Beersheba decided on Wednesday to extend the physician’s detention for a further six months, according to Abu Safia’s account on X. list 1 of 3 Hundreds of doctors demand World Medical Association suspend Israel list 2 of 3 Israeli rights group raises concerns about jailed doctor amid Gaza strikes list 3 of 3 ‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare The court said that Abu Safia “poses a threat to the State of Israel”, his lawyer reported. “Dr Hussam questioned why his detention order was being renewed once again, expressing that he is being punished for fulfilling his humanitarian mission and professional duty as a doctor at Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza,” the social media post added. The Israeli army detained Abu Safia in December 2024, along with other staff members and patients, during a raid on the hospital in northern Gaza. International agencies and rights groups have called for the physician’s release on multiple occasions, highlighting reports that he is being subjected to abuse in detention. The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said in July that Israel “must immediately release Dr Abu Safiya, or promptly charge him with a recognizable criminal offence and grant him a fair trial”. OHCHR added that it received information indicating Abu Safia “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care”. Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) said last week it had obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a significant loss of weight, a drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain that was not properly investigated. “Not only has he been deprived of his freedom without trial, but he is also being denied his basic right to an independent medical examination,” PHRI’s Naji Abbas said. Last week, the Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking the release of 14 doctors, including hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields, who are being held in Israeli prisons without being charged or brought to trial. PHRI argued that the prolonged arbitrary detentions – in some cases for more than two years – constitute a violation of their individual rights and further undermine Gaza’s healthcare system, which faces a severe shortage of medical professionals.

events.title: Sam Altman doesn't like Elon Musk's vision of a future where humans are 'happy' pets to AI
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it is important that humanity retains control over AI. Spencer Platt/Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman doesn't want to be AI's pet. Altman criticized Elon Musk for previously suggesting that AI could leave humanity akin to "labradors." Altman and Musk have a long-running feud that extends back to OpenAI's early days. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman 's rivalry with Elon Musk has gone to the dogs. On Wednesday, Altman knocked Musk for previously suggesting that AI could become so powerful that it would relegate humanity to the role of a house pet. "I don't want to be a Labrador. I don't want my kids to be Labradors," Altman said during an onstage interview at The New York Times Dealbook summit. "I want people to have the agency over the future that we have had." In July, The Economist asked Musk about a comment he made more than a decade ago that if AI advanced too quickly, it would make humans "like a pet Labrador." "Labradors are pretty happy creatures, that's my experience," Musk told The Economist while chuckling. In 2015, Musk and astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson discussed what would happen if artificial intelligence reached the stage of recursive self-improvement, where AI becomes so advanced that it can begin advancing itself with minimal or no human guidance. Some in AI have said that if that stage is reached, AI will improve so rapidly that it could quickly surpass human intelligence and potentially any means of controlling the technology. "That's all she wrote," Musk said , repeating Tyson's words. Musk described being worried that a recursively self-improving AI "could reprogram itself to be smarter and iterate very quickly and do that 24 hours a day on millions of computers." What Musk talked about then (almost eight years before ChatGPT's release) is less theoretical now. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Altman, and Musk all endorsed Amodei's September call to slow frontier AI research that pushes models toward self-improvement and to use the time in between to find more effective ways to ensure the models remain under human control. Altman has repeatedly said in recent weeks that he wants to ensure the industry doesn't accept any scenario in which humans cede control to AI. He has said he is not convinced that his competitors feel the same way. "We both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future," Altman told Dealbook on Wednesday, while being joined onstage by OpenAI President Greg Brockman. "And there's increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And we both agree that that's a terrible idea." While tamer than some of their back-and-forths, Altman and Musk have a long-running feud dating back to Musk's anger over OpenAI's shift in direction. Musk cofounded the AI lab and was an early financial backer. In May, a jury ruled that Musk waited too long to sue Altman and OpenAI over the matter. At times, Musk has expressed alarm about humanity essentially being domesticated. "I don't love the idea of being a house cat," Musk said in 2016. Musk said then that the way to prevent such an outcome was to hook human brains into computers. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I gave up my career as a lawyer 15 years ago. My retirement savings suffered, but I gained something more valuable.
events.summary: The author left his law career to become a writer. Courtesy of the author I left my career as a medical malpractice attorney after having three children in four years. I started writing $50 stories and eventually built a career as a travel writer and editor. I earn less than I would have in law but gained flexibility and priceless memories with my kids. Fifteen years ago, I walked away from a legal career I had worked hard to build. I was a medical malpractice defense attorney, representing physicians and spending my days researching cases, preparing arguments, and making my case in court. And the surprising thing is, I liked being a lawyer. I loved the intellectual challenge and the adrenaline of standing up in court and arguing for a client. But then I had three kids in four years, and my definition of a good career changed. The author had more time to be with her kids and travel. Courtesy of the author The drive that once had me happily burning the midnight oil disappeared almost overnight. I wanted to be home for school pickups. I wanted to volunteer as a room parent. I wanted to know what was happening in my kids' classrooms and be available when one of them needed me. So I left law. I kicked off my new career by writing stories for $50 My first writing jobs were hardly glamorous. I started writing about things to do with kids in the Bay Area, earning $50 a story. No big expense accounts or fancy press trips. We got to go to special museum events and were invited to try out new ice cream shops. We reviewed parks for their water features and available shade. I was simply happy to find a way to make money doing something that fit into the life I wanted. Over time, those $50 assignments turned into a career as a travel writer and editor. Today, I write about destinations, hotels, family travel, and everything else that gives me an excuse to get on a plane. And one of the best parts of the job is that I can sometimes bring my now-teenagers with me . I've watched my children grow up through the lens of travel. Instead of spending every waking hour at the office, I've explored new countries with them. I've taken them on trips where we've eaten unfamiliar food and figured out how to navigate new cities together. Leaving law had its financial trade-offs That doesn't mean I think leaving law was financially savvy. It wasn't. If I had stayed in the legal profession for the past 15 years, I almost certainly would have made more money. I would have a very different retirement account. But I've come to realize salary isn't the only way to measure a career's value. For me, success has become much more about being present. The author was able to be more present. Courtesy of the author This became even more important when I was diagnosed with breast cancer a year ago. Now more than ever, I want to be there for the big moments in my kids' lives, but also for the seemingly insignificant ones that somehow become the memories you keep. When I was hit in the face with my own mortality, I was immediately grateful that, no matter how my cancer diagnosis played out, my kids would have so many wonderful memories of our times together. I didn't expect writing to become something I genuinely loved Law taught me how to research, make an argument, and pay attention to details. Those skills proved surprisingly useful as a writer. But writing gave me something the legal career couldn't: a way to build a professional life around the life I actually wanted. People often talk about career changes as if they are supposed to lead to something bigger — more money, a better title, a corner office. My life as a "recovering attorney" is bigger in different ways: more time with my kids, more freedom to shape my days, and a career that lets me see the world with the people I love. As my oldest heads off to college , I'm realizing just how much that career pivot gave me. I don't know what my legal career would look like today, and I'm OK with that. I know what my life looked like instead: school pickups, family dinners, classroom parties, trips with my kids, and a front-row seat to their childhoods. That feels like a pretty good career move to me. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: More gas storage is at risk. What’s the government plan for secure supplies?
events.summary: SSE’s threat to close a big storage facility in Yorkshire highlights successive governments’ failures to build a strategy and safeguard supplies Labour faces double blow over UK fossil fuel projects F or those who followed the many months of government dithering over whether to approve production at the Jackdaw gasfield off the coast of Aberdeen, Scotland, there was a treat on social media this week. It was the sight of Michael Shanks, energy minister, almost dancing a jig of delight as the first output from Jackdaw flowed into the national gas network. “It will increase domestic production and further boost our energy security during the transition to electrification and decarbonisation,” he declared . To which the only possible response is: if the security benefit of using domestic gas during transition is so clear (and it is, as argued here from time to time ) why did it take a year of ministerial agonising before the inevitable thumbs up arrived? Still, you might think, at least the government now has a joined-up approach to gas. The long-term part is about rolling out the renewables and heat pumps to continue the decline (albeit slowly) in annual gas consumption. The other necessity is to ensure the infrastructure is sufficiently robust to handle those bleak, still and overcast winter days when electricity generation still relies on gas-powered stations and domestic demand for gas for heating is still high (23m gas boilers won’t disappear overnight). But here is the now-annual reminder of the “emerging risk”, in the delicate official language, to gas security. A year ago, a scary report from the government’s in-house body, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), warned of a danger of having too little gas to meet demand during a cold snap as soon as 2030 if a large piece of infrastructure – a gas import terminal, say – were to be out of action. Now Neso, in its latest update, is saying it all over again. “Our updated analysis shows that the risk identified in our 2025 assessment remains, and that there is an ongoing need for an enduring solution to secure future gas supply,” said the report on Wednesday . What could an enduring solution be? It will have to involve more than greenlighting more North Sea gas production – even with Jackdaw and any follow-on projects, the UK will still rely on imports. So we’re talking import terminals, interconnecting pipes to the continent, or – very likely – reliable domestic gas storage. Or a combination of all three. On the storage front, though, events are moving faster than the government’s decision-making. Centrica hasn’t been filling Rough, the largest offshore storage facility, and will close it next spring unless a deal can be done with government. Now fellow FTSE 100 energy firm SSE says it is preparing to start the process of closing its Atwick facility near Hornsea in East Yorkshire. The cavern represents about 20% of Great Britain’s onshore gas storage. In both cases, the firms are acting rationally, commercially speaking. The economics of gas storage rely on summer prices being reliably lower than winter ones to ensure a profit margin. In a more global world of LNG, or liquefied natural gas transported by tanker, such spreads have disappeared; and geopolitics, such as the closure of the strait of Hormuz, can complicate matters. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Atwick, it should be said, could probably be reopened after closure. But that is less true of Rough. So is the government up for a negotiation to secure even the current gas storage capacity? The position hasn’t moved since the summer when the government conceded for the first time that it may have to intervene. “We recently confirmed plans to explore commercial support for storage and the wider sector, to help protect our gas security,” the energy department repeated on Wednesday. “ We will set out proposals in due course.” It is leaving things late. It is already the case that belt-and-braces gas security for this winter required an eleventh-hour deal with Belgium to avert a planned cut in interconnector capacity. The storage question cannot wait much longer – and delay, one fears, has already handed negotiating clout to the operators if ministers ultimately decide they need to do a deal. The security problem has been recognised for years, even before the first Neso report. The threat of a gas crunch isn’t fresh news. The remarkable aspect is simply how long successive governments have taken to get a strategy together, even as the current one urges households to stockpile to improve national resilience. Before gas storage facilities start to close and narrow options further, it’s time for a plan.

events.title: Read Jim Cramer’s full interview with Nvidia’s Colette Kress: Demand, buybacks and China
events.summary: Nvidia delivered another beat-and-raise quarter on Tuesday in the chipmaker's first report since Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as CEO last week amid a widening affair scandal. Revenue more than doubled from a year earlier, exceeding estimates by nearly $7 billion, while earnings topped expectations by 20 cents per share. An excellent quarter by almost any measure. But investors remain skeptical about Nvidia's future without Huang, who famously founded the company at a San Jose Denny's in 1993. Shares fell 2.5% Wednesday, despite opening higher on the session. Will the company lose its smartest executives and engineers? Would Nvidia remain banker to the increasingly shaky neoclouds? Can it stay ahead of the competition? On Tuesday night, Colette Kress sat down with CNBC's Jim Cramer shortly after delivering her first earnings call as interim CEO to answer these pressing questions and more. This transcript has been edited for clarity. Jim Cramer: After the bell, Nvidia reported earnings, and what a quarter it was. The stock jumped in after hours in response. This is the first time we are hearing from the company since its founder, Jensen Huang, stepped down as CEO last week. So let's check in with Colette Kress, Nvidia's longtime chief financial officer and now its interim CEO. Ms. Kress, welcome to "Mad Money." Colette Kress: Thank you for having me, Jim. It's really great to see you. Cramer: Thank you, Colette. The most important thing I heard tonight was that you increased your revenue growth forecast for next year. Previously, you said you would grow 70%. Now you're saying 75%, off of a higher base. How are you able to do that? Kress: Thanks. Very, very important to understand how much our customers are interested in our compute infrastructure and how much they need the agentic solutions out there. So the most important thing that we have been seeing is just, again, a continuous growth in terms of the demand that's out there. But we also have been working in terms of our supply. So an increase in supply, working with all of our different suppliers, whether that be focusing in terms of what we need in terms of chips, what we need in terms of advanced packaging or memory, all of that is also coming together. We felt very confident, therefore, that we could establish that we will grow 75% year over year for fiscal year '28. Cramer: Now, a lot of people have been saying that there was one man at this company. I've talked with you. There are another 49,000. How is the team holding up? Are there people who are saying, "You know what, this is not the Nvidia I know, I don't want to be there?" Is there a brain drain, as some people have told me? Kress: Yeah, really great question. And remember, the company has been built on the perspective that employees see Nvidia as their life's work. And many of them have been here for decades, working with us from both a technology and a business-and-operations perspective. And now where we're standing is focusing on the business, focusing on getting all of that work done. And I had been working already with leadership. events.title: Investigators make progress in hunt for cause of FAA ground stop
events.summary: Investigators have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system last week, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC. Engineers and analysts are still searching for the root cause of the issue, which led to a four-hour ground stop on Friday. The halting of departing flights happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, that overwhelmed communications feed. Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC. While replicating the issue in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network. The ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack. The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies , the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." Investigators said within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network. That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy said. Since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.
