events.title: Nvidia’s Kress faces a divided workforce as some employees push for Huang’s return
events.summary: Colette Kress is addressed the whole company at the first Nvidia all-hands meeting since the public chaos over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and other reported relationships. Kress will be tasked with filling the leadership vacuum created by Huang's departure and dealing with public calls for his return. One former Nvidia employee who was at the company for more than 15 years told CNBC that Kress will be "eager to demonstrate there's a new sheriff in town." The day before Colette Kress led her first earnings call as Nvidia's interim CEO, she did not want to talk about her predecessor, Jensen Huang . "This is a new era for Nvidia," she told employees in an internal meeting on Monday, according to a person present, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. When someone brought up Huang, Kress quickly changed the subject, according to the person. On Wednesday, Kress addressed the whole company at the first Nvidia all-hands meeting since the public chaos over Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy and other reported relationships. And while Kress will be tasked with filling the leadership vacuum created by Huang's departure, she is also tamping down public calls to bring him back. Huang himself weighed in with his first public statement Tuesday saying he would be "honored" to return to Nvidia. Nvidia's staff split over Jensen Huang return as Kress takes over PRO: Here's what every major Wall Street analyst is saying about Nvidia after its earnings report Kress tells Jim Cramer that 'customers continue to be with us' Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China access: Sources Exclusive: How Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmaker Kress, who has served as the company's CFO since 2013, must steady employees and convince customers and investors that Nvidia can execute on its ambitious targets without the man who made them. At Wednesday's meeting with staffers, Kress was joined by newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones as well as Ian Buck, who oversees Nvidia's hyperscale and high performance computing business, according to an attendee. Kress' message was, "Let's move forward," said the person, who asked not to be named because the event was private. Nvidia's leaders have made clear that the board does not plan to bring Huang back. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen," Kress said in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer on Tuesday. "We want to grow in terms of everything that we need to do with our employees, our customers, our shareholders, and that is where we are going to focus moving forward." Jones echoed the sentiment on Tuesday's earnings call. "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said in opening remarks. Nvidia declined to comment for this story. Kress stressed on the earnings call that the company was focused on the workers who remain, who she said are "committed to doing their life's work at Nvidia." The company also reported better-than-expected earnings and seemed to calm investors' nerves , at least for the moment. Some employees are telling a different story. Support for Huang's return is growing inside Nvidia, sources tell CNBC. An online petition circulating since the weekend has nearly 200,000 signatures, with more than 10,000 of them claiming to be current Nvidia employees. Nvidia currently has roughly 42,000 employees. Outside Nvidia, Huang's reinstatement has been called for by at least two major investors and tech heavyweights such as Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said he "would not mind" seeing Huang return as CEO. Several employees posted on X over the last few days, voicing support for Huang and calling for his return. One robotics engineer said the founder's departure led to his own decision to leave. Another senior Nvidia employee, Nader Khalil, sent a letter to the company's board and top executives warning that failing to reinstate Huang could lead to a loss of "irreplaceable talent," according to The Wall Street Journal. Huang was known for his deep day-to-day involvement in his company's operations, often responding directly to engineers and chiming in personally on technical projects. Engineering employees, in particular, were "extremely devoted to him, almost like a demigod," according to a former Nvidia employee who was at the company for more than 15 years and spoke to CNBC on condition of anonymity. Wednesday's all-hands is a standard meeting: Nvidia traditionally holds one on the morning after each quarterly earnings call, according to the former employee. Still, the meeting is unlike anything the company has experienced. Employees told CNBC that they plan to share their grievances at the all-hands, though it wasn't clear ahead of time if they would be allowed to ask questions.

events.title: Is Apple the safe haven investors think it is? Here's a way to trade it with less risk
events.summary: Apple's forward multiple is rich by historical standards. Now might be a good time to hedge holdings, says Mike Khouw. For months, Apple has been the undisputed haven of the technology sector. As the industry grappled with the brutal reality of Nvidia's post-Huang future, investors blindly rotated into Apple, comforting themselves with the narrative that the Cupertino giant was uniquely immune to speculative overspending on artificial intelligence. While peers bled capital into server farms and data centers. At almost 37x forward earnings estimates, the stock is now priced for perfection, fully valued at precisely the moment the rest of the market is beginning to see multiples contract aggressively. Investors tend to huddle in the shelter of perceived safe havens, but that perceived safety can crack quickly in an adverse news cycle, as Nvidia shareholders recently learned. One part of the news cycle finally caught up to Apple. We've recently witnessed a bizarre parade of catastrophic system failures: the massive Microsoft outage, the FAA grounding flights, and cascading disruptions across major banking networks. Through it all, Apple was immune. Until today, when a widespread outage struck, knocking out iCloud, Apple Pay, and core support systems. The official explanation? Yet another internal update gone wrong. It's undeniably odd how all these major tech infrastructure failures are being chalked up to routine upgrades, all clustering around the exact same narrow timeframe. Without venturing too far into the conspiratorial, the sheer coincidence of these cascading digital blackouts suggests more systemic fragility than we may have realized. That's one thing at less than 10x forward earnings, as Nvidia is, or even at a market multiple. But Apple is twice as expensive as the S&P. Technically, Apple is balancing on a knife's edge. Shares have been relentlessly hugging the upper end of several channel-based technical indicators, such as the Bollinger Band. Apple has been priced at a steep premium for being immune to what ails other struggling stocks, but is now demonstrating similar vulnerabilities. Investors should ask themselves: what's the upside? That Apple trades at more than 40x forward earnings? 45x? Even at that rich multiple, that would represent only 18-19% upside from here. If the market suddenly decided that Apple's premium to the market would be just 50%, instead of 100%, that would be less than 28x forward earnings, a nearly 27% haircut to the current share price. Despite the high multiple, options prices are low versus the market. Market implied volatility is well above average (around the 93rd percentile). Apple implied volatility is actually just below the 1-year average. The price of index options is in the 98th percentile relative to Apple options. Because the stock is nominally expensive (translation? The share price is high in dollar terms), buying outright naked puts is highly capital-intensive. This is exactly where a put spread makes sense. By buying an at-the-money or slightly out-of-the-money put and simultaneously selling a lower-strike put, traders can dramatically reduce the upfront capital cost. More importantly, this structure blunts the negative impact of theta, or time decay, ensuring you don't bleed premium while waiting for the technical breakdown to materialize. Furthermore, taking advantage of the natural put skew—where further out-of-the-money puts trade at relatively higher implied volatility—lets you finance your bearish bet efficiently by selling that inflated premium. Apple's historic premium is built on a foundation of immunity to the chaos infecting the rest of the market. Today's outage proved the company may be more vulnerable than investors appreciate. events.title: Home Depot’s incoming CEO says homeowners are ‘feeling pressure.’ A quarter can’t cover a $5,000 repair
events.summary: Richard McPhail, a 21-year Home Depot veteran who was named the retailer’s next CEO on Tuesday, has been watching financial pressure build among American homeowners. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call the same day, he acknowledged that “a rising interest rate environment puts pressure on our customer and our business.” McPhail, Home Depot’s CFO since 2019, takes over as CEO on Nov. 23. Ted Decker, who recently returned from a medical leave, will step down as CEO and remain chair of the board. That’s a problem for a retailer that booked $164.7 billion in revenue last fiscal year, the bulk of it from people fixing up homes they already own. Homeowners are “one of the most resilient customer cohorts in the economy,” McPhail told Yahoo Finance in a February interview. “But they’re feeling pressure like everyone else.” “If you look at housing turnover, that’s actually been frozen for three years,” he said, adding that turnover has sat at historical lows three years running. He also pointed to customers’ “concerns around housing affordability, general affordability” and “broader concerns over uncertainty and job loss.” Wealthy on paper, stretched in practice Owning a home has long been considered a path to financial security in America. But even homeowners with considerable housing wealth feel squeezed by the rising cost of living, and some struggle to afford the upkeep of their biggest asset. Nearly two-thirds of homeowners (63%) say owning a home causes them at least moderate financial stress, up from 55% in June 2025, according to an October survey of 1,000 homeowners conducted for Hometap, a home equity financing company. That stress comes even as Americans sit on a record $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity as of the second quarter of 2026, according to First American Data & Analytics . That’s the amount owners could borrow against while keeping their combined loan-to-value at 80% or below. But housing wealth isn’t disposable income. Even owners who locked in rock-bottom pandemic-era mortgage rates aren’t immune to rising property taxes and insurance premiums or climbing utility bills . The typical homeowner now spends $16,566 a year on costs beyond the mortgage, about two-thirds of it on upkeep, according to Zillow . Job worries are adding to the strain. In the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s October Survey of Consumer Expectations , released last week, consumers put the odds of higher unemployment a year from now at 45.3%, the highest reading since April 2020. Their perceived chance of losing their own job also ticked up to 13.9%. Delayed repairs are getting more expensive A LendingTree survey conducted in September found that 34% of homeowners had postponed at least one necessary repair or maintenance task over the past two years. Among those with outstanding repairs, 32% said they simply couldn’t afford the work. A surprise $5,000 repair would be entirely out of reach for a quarter of homeowners surveyed. Another 30% could cover it only by substantially draining their savings. Among homeowners who needed repairs over the past two years, 37% dipped into emergency savings, and 33% cut spending on essentials such as groceries, healthcare, or childcare to pay for the work. Waiting tends to cost more. Among respondents whose homes currently need repairs, 34% said delaying the work drove up the price, and a quarter said it caused damage elsewhere in the house. Home Depot is growing anyway Decker sounded a similar alarm in February, telling analysts that “our customers are telling us that they’re not investing” in bigger projects, citing affordability, the jobs picture, and weak consumer confidence. Even so, the business has grown this year. Home Depot reported third-quarter sales of $43.4 billion on Tuesday, up 4.9% from a year earlier, with comparable sales up 2.2%. “Third quarter results exceeded our expectations,” McPhail said. Homeowners may be shelving kitchen remodels, but smaller repairs and maintenance jobs have kept customers coming in. In August, McPhail, then CFO, credited “broad-based demand across the business as customers continued to engage in smaller projects.” Tight budgets are also pushing homeowners to pick up the tools themselves. Among LendingTree respondents who completed at least some repairs, 60% did some of the work themselves because they couldn’t afford a professional. Among millennials, that figure reached 72%. At the other end of the market, Home Depot has been courting professional contractors, builders, and remodelers. SRS, the building-materials distributor it acquired for $18.25 billion in June 2024 , delivered “almost $5 billion in sales in the quarter,” McPhail said. Executives said on the call that cross-selling between Home Depot and SRS is on track to generate $400 million in sales this year, a figure the company aims to double in 2027. The company has also been investing in AI and digital tools that help pros plan projects, manage material lists, and track orders. Its express delivery service now reaches customers within two hours from virtually all of its stores, incoming president and COO Ann-Marie Campbell said on the call. Home Depot now expects total sales to grow about 4.5% in fiscal 2026, with comparable sales up roughly 1.4%. McPhail is betting that speed will keep winning over a cautious customer: “Our investments in express delivery and in AI customer and associate enablement are making a meaningful difference.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Google’s AI feature in Search gets its own incognito mode
events.summary: Google’s search engine has long offered an incognito mode for all those search queries you don’t want logged or associated with your account. Now, Google’s AI Mode in Search is getting a similar feature. In a blog post , the company announced a new feature that brings “temporary threads” to AI Mode, where the conversations you have won’t be resurfaced later in areas like your search history or recommendations. Many leading AI chatbots already offer the option for temporary chats, Google Gemini included. However, there was not yet an option to have a temporary chat when you’re searching Google and are dropped into its conversational interface, known as AI Mode. Google says that users won’t have to adjust their settings to take advantage of the new option. Instead, they’ll be able to click a temporary threads icon in the upper right corner of AI Mode to engage in a temporary chat. This essentially works the same as a temporary chat would in the stand-alone Gemini chatbot. The option could be convenient to use at those times when you start digging deeper into a particular topic via AI Mode and realize that you don’t want the discussion to become a part of your search history because of its personal nature. Once the temporary thread is started, the session becomes detached from your account, Google says. This means that the responses the AI provides won’t be informed by past preferences, nor will they impact future personalization. That could also be useful for those times when you want to learn about something as more of a one-off, but don’t want Google to start to think of the topic as one of your main interests. When you close out of the thread, you will return to searching as usual. The company says the option to engage in temporary chats in AI Mode is rolling out globally on desktop and mobile across all supported languages. events.title: Early data suggests transparent auction pricing is working
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Homes selling for close to published auction reserve prices, early data from Victoria shows In Victoria you must publish the reserve price — the number a seller is willing to sell for — a week ahead of auctions. ( ABC News: Michael Coggan ) Analysis of 2,164 residential auctions in Victoria between October 16 and November 14 shows properties are selling for close to the published reserve prices. NSW recently scrapped underquoting reforms, as the property market downturn leads some sellers to lower their price expectations. Analysts say longer-term data is needed to determine the success of the Victorian reforms. A closely watched change to real estate laws appears to be working to reduce underquoting and help buyers know what a property will sell for, based on early data. Home sellers in Victoria must now publish the price they are willing to sell at — the "reserve" price — a week before an auction. Property platform Homer has compiled the data for the first month since the practice became law in Victoria, for sales from October 16. "The short version is yes, the data does suggest transparency is working," Homer chief executive Henry Pedersen told ABC News. Henry Pederesen is the co-founder and CEO of property platform HOMER. ( Supplied ) Mr Pedersen said properties that sold at auction went for a median of 0.9 per cent above the published reserve price. Sellers in the state were already required to supply a price "range" of no more than 10 per cent, for example, between $600,000 and $660,000. After examining 2,164 residential auctions between October 16 and November 14, more than three-quarters of homes sold had a reserve within that range. Properties that had a reserve above the range were passed in at a higher rate (50 per cent) than those within the range (41 per cent). "The data points one way," Mr Pedersen said. "A guide that matches the reserve gives a home its best chance of selling on the day." ABC News wants to hear your housing journey to better understand how the changing market is affecting your decisions. Tight market makes comparisons difficult Independent property economist Cameron Kusher welcomed the data, but cautioned that longer-term analysis would be needed. "It's hard to read too much into five weeks of data, in a down market, but it's about what you'd expect," he told ABC News "A reserve price, within a guide [range] is more likely to be successful if it's within or below." Cameron Kusher is an independent property economist, based in Victoria. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) What complicates the discussion is the lower level of properties currently being offered for sale. With prices falling , sellers who can wait to sell appear to be doing so. "People are being a lot more selective about what they're taking to auction," he notes. "People with more urgency to sell are the ones taking things to auction right now. They know the price they want and they're being transparent about that". The shift in Victoria is being keenly watched nationwide, as governments grapple with frustrated buyers missing out on homes they never really had a chance at. Underquoting happens when a property is advertised below the actual price that a real estate agent expects it to sell for, or below the price the seller would accept. National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality. It's frustrating for buyers, who spend time and money — in building reports and inspections — on houses and units they were never going to be able to secure. But it is difficult to legislate against. The highly individual nature of property sales means it is difficult to estimate interest and demand to a high degree of accuracy. The New South Wales government just scrapped laws to target underquoting because of the falling market. Under the NSW reforms, agents could be banned from advertising a price that was lower than a written offer rejected by the seller — but that could be problematic in an environment where properties are not worth what they were valued at some months ago, and sellers may have to lower their expectations. " It's not the seller or the agent's fault if the price of real estate is dropping," NSW Premier Chris Minns said. Price falls were a factor in Victoria too, where the first month of the data has coincided with a cooling market. Real estate agents who spoke at the time of the law change expected more sellers to opt for a "private sale" without a set date, because those sales do not have to publish a reserve price.

events.title: Target shares rise 7% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance
events.summary: Target beat third-quarter sales expectations and raised its guidance as it continues a turnaround effort. The retailer is undergoing a turnaround under CEO Michael Fiddelke. Target said changes to its stores and assortment are resonating with shoppers. Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold. The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added. "[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters. Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter. Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds. The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90. "The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time." Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $2.65 vs. $2.07 expected Revenue: $27.07 billion vs. $26.56 billion expected For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier. This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year. On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives. The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season. Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround. As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter. The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories. It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter. Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

events.title: AI was probably involved in recent tech outages — just not in the way you expect
events.summary: Microsoft365 and Chase both experienced tech outages in the past week. Getty Images Efforts to patch cyber vulnerabilities found by AI might be behind the recent string of tech outages. Companies are attempting to fix software issues faster than ever, which may overwhelm their systems. Some politicians and tech executives have said they expect more outages. A spate of high-profile tech outages has people wondering if AI is to blame. They might be on the right track. Organizations have been using AI to discover software vulnerabilities in their systems, then rolling out a higher-than-normal volume of fixes that may have overwhelmed them, politicians and tech executives have said. "We're updating to withstand and be more resilient, and sometimes you do that at a speed where you couldn't test all the potential outcomes of the update," Kevin Mandia, the CEO of cybersecurity company Armadin, told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday. In the last five days, tech outages at Microsoft , JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have caused major disruption for businesses and consumers. A temporary ground stop at every airport in America also caused mass chaos, though Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed aging air traffic control infrastructure for the issue. While tech outages have long occurred periodically, the proximity of recent incidents has led many to speculate whether they were a coordinated cyberattack , rogue AI, or a combination of the two. AI can discover cyber vulnerabilities that have remained undetected for years in human-made, occasionally sloppy software. There are also concerns that the technology could be used to exploit security flaws more quickly than humans ever could. Both these fears appear to have prompted companies to patch things more than usual, which in some cases may have caused things to break. That will, in turn, probably lead to more tech outages, he added. "Nobody wants an outage," he said. "Everybody's going to get operationally better at updating in the AI age. Mark Warner, the vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, reiterated assurances from other government officials that the tech outages weren't the result of a coordinated cyberattack by another country or malicious actor. "When that happens, careless things happen, the system can't absorb those patches as quickly, and you have these series of outages that have taken place. I think we will see more," Warner said. Nicole Perlroth, a former cybersecurity reporter and founder of a cybersecurity-focused venture capital fund, said in an X post that new pressure to patch issues and update software faster means those fixes are more likely to "break things in unexpected, cascading ways." The widespread cybersecurity horrors picked up steam last month, after AI discovered huge flaws in a programming language that up to 70% of websites use. events.title: Meet 4 engineering leaders whose budgets explain how Anthropic has gotten so rich
events.summary: A poster at Anthropic's developer conference in San Francisco advertises its Claude product. Don Feria/AP Content Services for Anthropic Claude Code is the juggernaut product behind Anthropic's pre-IPO growth. It's earned Anthropic billions of dollars, with tech startups among the most excited customers. Four engineering leaders explain their firms' eye-popping Claude budgets. Anthropic is targeting a $1.4 trillion valuation in its initial public offering this week, and that's possible because of some very spendy customers. Anthropic's thousands of business customers and the popularity of  Claude Code  are funneling huge sums into its coffers. Months after the so-called "token-maxxing" craze , some engineering leaders told Business Insider they're still racking up Claude bills worth tens of thousands of dollars on individual projects. Others have come to expect that some of their engineers will occasionally spend more on tokens , the units of AI's output, than they make in salary. Customers who didn't use Claude Code on their business accounts spent less than $75 a month on average, Anthropic's IPO prospectus said, while the top 5% of users using the coding tool averaged around $1,500 a month. All told, Anthropic reported having 11,900 business customers that'd spent $100,000 over the previous year, and 250 that'd spent $10 million or more. Business Insider spoke with several big Anthropic spenders : engineering leaders at companies that have embraced AI for coding and largely favored Claude over its competitors. Tom Wilkie, Chief Technology Officer at Grafana Labs Grafana Labs, an observability startup last valued at $9 billion, has no problem with pouring cash into AI coding tools. Its chief technology officer, Tom Wilkie, told Business Insider that the company's token bills have jumped into the tens of millions-a-year range. It spends about two-thirds on Claude, with the rest mostly going to OpenAI's Codex, he said. "We're not worried about the spend," Wilkie said. "We're not worried about controlling it, just yet." Tom Wilkie, the chief technology officer of Grafana Labs. Grafana Labs One of Wilkie's teams spent tens of thousands of dollars on tokens in a single month to improve the performance of one of Grafana's services — resulting in a six-figure cut to the company's Amazon Web Services bill. He also saw a non-engineer route customer feedback to Anthropic's Fable model, spend more than $30,000 dollars on tokens, and get a cluster of successful changes into the product. Engineers have gotten more comfortable switching projects because the coding language barrier feels lower now, Wilkie said. After a data analyst accidentally racked up tens of thousands of dollars in token spend by leaving a model running, Wilkie said Grafana now gives access to the most powerful AI models in 24-hour increments. Still, it's "no questions asked," he said. "We really want to be careful with the chilling effect of budgets and access control to models because you just don't know where the next big piece of innovation is going to come from," Wilkie said. Bryan Bischof, Head of AI at Theory Ventures Bryan Bischof, who runs AI at Theory Ventures, leads a team of six engineers who build custom software for investors, heads of talent and relationships, and intelligence leads at the San Francisco venture firm. He has personally racked up six figures of token spend in one month, mostly on Claude, and said he could easily crack $1 million if he spent more time running simulations. Bryan Bischof, the head of AI at Theory Ventures. Theory Ventures He and his engineers sometimes use open-weight models, which are far cheaper than Anthropic's top-end options. Bischof said that since time is so valuable, he's often happy for his team to spend on premium tools. "If a very intelligent model is going to dramatically reduce the cycle time, then that's absolutely worth it," he said. Bischof says his firm may also invest in their own always-running AI agents, similar to Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots. Chris Yang, Cofounder and Chief AI Officer of Menos AI At Menos AI, a startup running an AI-powered research software for investors, the engineering team uses Claude Code or Claude models through the coding tool Cursor, cofounder Chris Yang told Business Insider. "Because Claude has been evolving so, so well in terms of coding capabilities, I don't even have much opportunity or willingness to try out Codex," he said. The company's investor software consumes around 90% of its token costs, Yang said, as it routes users' inquiries to different models depending on their difficulty. Yang called himself one of the company's "hero users," since he spends $3,000 to $4,000 on Claude tokens in a month running several AI agents at a time. "We do spend a lot of expenses on the Claude Code use, but when we compare it to a human resources hire, it's still a big benefit," Yang said. "It's still much cheaper than human labor." Kiran Gangadharappa, Senior Director of Software Engineering at Harness Harness, a software development startup worth $5.5 billion, has more than 500 engineers. Kiran Gangadharappa, a senior director of software engineering, told Business Insider that in a recent week, his staff used 265 billion AI tokens, with Claude Code and Cursor being the most popular tools among his engineers. "We definitely see it improving and taking a bigger and bigger chunk of the manual work of writing code," he said. Kiran Gangadharappa, senior director of software engineering at Harness. Harness The biggest token-guzzlers, Gangadharappa said, are gigantic one-off tasks like rebuilding an existing software architecture or conducting security research. He said that using Sonnet, one of Anthropic's cheaper models, helped the company cut spending, as did creating a soft $125-a-week budget for engineers. He expects the company has reached a "steady" level of AI expenses. "Agents never get tired," Gangadharappa said. Have a tip? events.title: Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Senate banking committee, Chairman Scott says
events.summary: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, panel Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said on CNBC's "Squawk Box." Scott said he hopes Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who he said has also agreed to appear, will do so "before Christmas." Scott had asked Huang to appear at a public hearing rather than for a closed-door interview. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee, panel Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also agreed to testify, Scott said. The agreements to appear voluntarily come as pressure builds on Capitol Hill to investigate Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy, which led to his ouster at the chipmaker he founded. "They both have agreed," Scott said. "We will hopefully have this done before Christmas." Huang reached an agreement on Tuesday with the chairmen of three House committees for a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1 jointly before the three panels. Scott had asked Huang to appear publicly in the Senate. A spokesperson for the banking committee did not immediately respond to questions about when Huang and Lutnick would testify. In initial letters to the pair, Scott requested Huang appear on Dec. 3 and Lutnick appear on Dec. 10. "Nvidia seemed to have fairly lax controls, and I want to know how much of the relationship with Alice [Huang] impacted Nvidia's unwillingness or inability, or frankly, just blindness to Megaspeed's providing access to China of the most advanced chipset," Scott said of Jensen Huang's testimony. The details of Huang's appearance before the three House panels on Dec. 1 are still being determined, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told reporters at the Capitol on Wednesday. He said the people who will likely conduct the closed-door interview will be the top Republican and top Democrat on his panel and the Select Committee on China and Select Committee on Intelligence along with their attorneys. The location is still being worked out, Mast said. A date for an appearance before the committees by Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce official who oversees export controls, is not yet set, Mast said. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2. Scott, in his CNBC appearance, also homed in on Lutnick, calling for answers as to why the commerce secretary did not act after being warned about Megaspeed — the Singaporean company where the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, was an executive. Nvidia sold its chips to Megaspeed, which U.S. investigators suspect of diverting them to China. "They were warned as early as March of this year, several months ago, that Megaspeed should be on the 'entity list,'" Scott said, referring to a Commerce Department list of companies the U.S. views as national security risks. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security "didn't do it, Howard didn't do it, we want to know why." Nvidia's staff split over Jensen Huang return as Kress takes over PRO: Here's what every major Wall Street analyst is saying about Nvidia after its earnings report Kress tells Jim Cramer that 'customers continue to be with us' Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China access: Sources Exclusive: How Trump traded Nvidia stock as he championed the chipmaker Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have been embroiled in an intra-administration battle as the fallout from the Huang affair grows. Bessent on CNBC on Friday appeared to blame Lutnick for a lack of action on Megaspeed. "You will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said, referring to Commerce and noting his department has long supported imposing restrictions on Megaspeed. A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on Scott's announcement that he has agreed to appear. Huang's upcoming appearances are likely just the start of the embattled former CEO's problems on Capitol Hill. Democrats will take control of Congress in January and have demanded sweeping investigations into the affair and Huang's cozy relationship with President Donald Trump . The House Energy and Commerce Committee asked interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress for a briefing no later than Dec. 2 on the company's chip exports and information about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. The panel also asked Lutnick and a top deputy to appear to discuss chip export controls. The Wall Street Journal first reported the letters to Kress and Lutnick, and a committee spokesperson confirmed the report to CNBC. — Megan Cassella and Ashlee Trujillo contributed to this report.

events.title: Prince Harry: I'd rejoin the military to fight Russia
events.summary: Prince Harry talks to The Telegraph. The Telegraph Prince Harry sat down with The Telegraph for a new interview. The Duke of Sussex said he would be willing to serve in the military again "100%" and fight against Russia if needed. Prince Harry also plans to announce a new global project that he will head up with the aim of helping military veterans into work. The Duke of Sussex has said he is ready to serve in the Armed Forces again, warning that the threat from Russia means "we should all be nervous." Prince Harry spoke exclusively to The Telegraph's Ukraine: The Latest podcast during an unannounced visit to Lviv — his first major interview with a UK media organization since his return to Britain. He issued a damning assessment of Donald Trump's approach to the war in Ukraine, which he said did not reflect the views of the broader US population. The Duke also suggested that Britain had been in conflict with Russia for the past decade, saying: "Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war." He added that he believed Europe had "woken up to the threat" from Russia, but said his "biggest concern" was that the Continent could "turn on itself." The Duke said he would be willing to serve in the military again if needed, adding: "There is a lot that we can learn from Ukraine. I think there's a lot that the whole world can learn from Ukraine." "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel," he said. Nato leaders are increasingly concerned about a possible conflict, with spy chiefs suggesting in September that Russia could be gearing up for an attack in "months, not years." The UK Government has told households to stockpile tinned food and water in order to be prepared for an emergency. The British military has a strategic reserve of 95,000 retired regular and reserve personnel who can be called up again to fight in a crisis. Some will be mobilised next year for a major Ministry of Defence exercise testing the country's resilience for war. Asked whether he was concerned about the current geopolitical situation, Prince Harry said: "I think we should all be nervous, absolutely. And I think we should be prepared, and I think that those of us that have served should be ready to serve again." The Duke spent a decade in the Army and completed two tours of Afghanistan as an Apache helicopter pilot before ending his military career in 2015. Last weekend, he made his fourth visit to Ukraine since the current conflict began — his third in just over 18 months — as he attended the country's team trials for Invictus 2027, which will be held in Birmingham. Harry will take centre stage at the event, potentially alongside his father, the King, who joined his younger son for the inaugural ceremony in London in 2014. The return of the Duke and Duchess from California in August prompted Mr Trump, the US president, to say he was "glad" the couple had left the country as he criticized their treatment of the Royal family. While Prince Harry did not name Mr Trump, he issued a thinly veiled criticism of the president's approach to the conflict. "I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group — or in this case an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," he told the podcast. Discussing the November midterm elections and the Democrats' forthcoming takeover of the House of Representatives and the Senate, he added: "As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that." "Europe has a united front, and it would be fantastic to have more American support for that as well," he said. The Duke has established a good professional rapport with Volodymyr Zelensky and his team, although did not meet the Ukrainian president on this occasion. He said he believed, based on his four visits to the country and his regular updates from a range of political and military figures on the ground, that Ukraine was winning the war but added: "There needs to be some form of exit strategy for Russia." Prince Harry warned that it was important not to get complacent, insisting that now was the time to "double our support" rather than step back. The new year will bring a new role for him, The Telegraph can reveal. He plans to announce a new global project that he will head up with the aim of helping military veterans into work. The Duke, who travelled to New York earlier this month for a series of meetings about "new business opportunities and partnerships," said it would aim to transform attitudes towards veterans so they are viewed not through the lens of "pity and sympathy" but as "pure talent" to be harnessed. "When they take their uniform off, so much of their experience and expertise and training just doesn't get carried forward," he said. "That is certainly an aspect that I've been focused on, which I hope will help change the perception and ultimately be able to insert elite operators from the veteran community into some of the key areas, which will ultimately help from a defense standpoint, national resilience and also really, uplift communities." "So much of what these guys have been through and who they've been trained to be is underpriced and undervalued, and that needs to change," he said. The Duke said he believed one of the catalysts for broader misinformation about the Russia-Ukraine conflict was social media, which he said was being used to pump out "propaganda." Rather than "playing a leadership role to contain the chaos", social media platforms and other "very powerful players across the world, specifically in America" were "stoking a fire, which is incredibly dangerous," he said, adding: "Some people are incentivized for that, and that does worry me." Prince Harry and Meghan's Archewell Foundation founded the Parents' Network, a support system for parents of children affected by online harm, and the couple have become vocal campaigners against the harm caused by powerful tech companies through social media. The Duke acknowledged that his own military service had triggered post-traumatic stress connected to childhood trauma rather than his experiences on the battlefield. He also said there should be more opportunities for young people to serve, in order to provide opportunities, while creating confidence and resilience. "That doesn't mean that you have to wear a uniform and serve overseas," he added. "But I think the fundamental mechanics and the values and the principles that you can gain from service, military service set you up for life 100%." events.title: What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza?
events.summary: Will Israel’s election change life in Gaza? Billions have been pledged for Gaza since an October 2025 ‘ceasefire’, but rebuilding has not begun, and Israeli attacks continue. Donors have pledged about $18bn for Gaza through US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. But more than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, reconstruction has yet to begin, and nearly 1.4 million Palestinians are still living in makeshift shelters. Even preliminary reconstruction efforts have stalled. The board had asked for $280m to fund the initial building phase, but in September it said most of that money remained unspent. list 1 of 3 Board of Peace warns Gaza ceasefire faces imminent collapse without action list 2 of 3 Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way list 3 of 3 Palestinians find refuge in ancient caves after Israel demolishes homes In its latest report, submitted on Tuesday, the board warned that the truce between Israel and Hamas could collapse unless immediate steps are taken to carry out the ceasefire deal, according to The Associated Press. The next day, on Wednesday, Israel began its first major military ground operation in the Gaza Strip since the ceasefire began, attacking refugee camps in the central part of the enclave. Since the ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,658 Palestinians and injured 6,000, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. Israel continues to block the entry of 60,000 mobile homes promised under the ceasefire deal and to severely restrict food and medical aid into the besieged enclave. It has also yet to allow the Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza to enter the Strip. United States President Trump proposed the board in September 2025 as part of his 20-point plan for Gaza. On November 17, 2025, the United Nations Security Council adopted Resolution 2803, which recognised the board as a transitional administration responsible for setting the framework and coordinating funding for Gaza’s redevelopment. The resolution authorises its role in Gaza until December 31, 2027, unless the UN Security Council decides otherwise. The board’s charter also allows it to work in other areas affected by conflict. Trump chairs the board and can only be replaced if he resigns or is unable to serve. He also represents the US. He appoints its executive board, whose members are Ajay Banga, Tony Blair, Martin Edelman, Robert Gabriel Jr, Jared Kushner, Marc Rowan, Marco Rubio, Steve Witkoff, and Susie Wiles. Each member state has one vote. Decisions need a majority of those present and voting, and Trump’s approval. He can also veto executive board decisions. Under the plan, Palestinian technocrats would run Gaza’s day-to-day affairs through the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, led by Ali Shaath. The committee reports to the board, but Israel has not allowed it to enter Gaza, and it operates from Cairo. The board has 28 members: Albania, Argentina, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Belarus, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Egypt, El Salvador, Hungary, Indonesia, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kuwait, Mongolia, Morocco, Pakistan, Paraguay, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam. Germany, India, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the European Union also attended the inaugural meeting as observers. Countries join by invitation from Trump and normally serve up to three years. Countries that pay more than $1bn in cash in the charter’s first year are exempt from that limit. Which countries have pledged money? At the board’s first meeting in Washington, DC, on February 19, Trump announced about $7bn in pledges from nine countries, plus a $10bn US pledge. He did not say what the US money would be used for. The UAE pledged $1.2bn. Kuwait, Qatar and Saudi Arabia pledged $1bn each, with Saudi Arabia saying it would pay over several years. Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Kazakhstan, Morocco, and Uzbekistan also pledged. What happened to the funding earmarked for Gaza? At a briefing in New York on September 23, the board said donors had made about $18bn [ pdf ] in early funding commitments. It said it had called in $280m from donors for the building phase so far, and that most of it remained unspent. Board of Peace officials previously told the Washington Post that the money couldn’t be spent on projects until Israel allowed international troops or newly-trained Palestinian police to enter Gaza and begin the process of disarming Hamas. The board puts the cost of rebuilding Gaza at about $71bn, close to the UN ’s estimate of $71.5bn, a figure that could rise as more damage is recorded. The board has identified $6bn in projects. It says its six-month recovery plan needs $2.45bn for 66 programmes, plus about $200m in in-kind support. What does the six-month recovery programme cover?

California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide. The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel. Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety." A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater . A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US. "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. events.title: Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices
events.summary: When Chipotle overhauled its rewards program in April , it made perks like free chips and guac easier to snag and added half-off entrées, as diners started to balk at high prices. For the burrito chain, the program helps it weather inflation and keep customers in the Chipotle habit. It now counts more than 24 million active members, and they drove a third of sales in the third quarter, the highest share Chipotle has reported . “I think in this modern world, you have to be really up to speed on what’s going on with your loyalty consumer because arguably it’s the most valuable consumer within your ecosystem,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit , on a panel moderated by this reporter. Loyalty programs have become a front line in the fight for market share. The freebies get people in the door, but the bigger prize is the data: a detailed record of what customers buy and when, which lets brands tailor offers and makes it harder for shoppers to stray. Boatwright, Macy’s CEO Tony Spring, and Ally Financial CEO Michael Rhodes run very different businesses: Macy’s is No. 192 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , Ally is No. 275, and Chipotle is No. 351. All three are leaning on that math. Chipotle won’t shrink the rewards Boatwright said the pull to trim perks is real. As a rewards database grows and inflation squeezes margins, he said, “The gravity pulls brands toward, ‘ How do I capture some margin here.” His own team brought him ideas for cutting rewards. “We are unwilling as a brand to do that,” he said. “I said, come back to me with 10 ideas on how to increase value for the consumer and let’s have a conversation.” That stance tracks with Chipotle’s refusal to chase traffic with deep discounts. In February, Boatwright said he didn’t want to “devalue our core offering” with McDonald’s-style deals and planned price increases below the rate of inflation . Loyalty perks let the chain hand its most frequent diners more value without cutting menu prices for everyone. The same logic shaped Chipotle’s answer to GLP-1 weight-loss drugs: a high-protein menu with low-priced add-ons rather than markdowns. “You’ve got to have innovation that doesn’t discount the core offering, but meets a consumer need state,” Boatwright said. Macy’s wants rewards in your wallet before you pick a store Spring, who took over as CEO of Macy’s Inc. in February 2024, has been steering the 168-year-old department store operator’s turnaround . He said a loyalty program only works if shoppers believe it does. “Loyalty is integral, I think, to the relationships people have with brands,” Spring said. “And we are constantly striving at Macy’s, Bloomingdale’s, and Bluemercury to make sure that the loyalty program has value in the eyes of the consumer, not in our eyes.” The payoff comes when a shopper decides where to look first, at the mall or online. “If the Macy’s app or the Bloomingdale’s app is there and I already have rewards in my wallet, it’s going to encourage me to go there maybe and complete my activity,” he said. Macy’s program is built to be easy to join, Spring said, with rewards that don’t depend on how a customer pays and bigger ones for Macy’s credit card holders. The most committed shoppers can earn perks like free merchandise, free delivery, and after-hours shopping. “If you are more committed to us, we want to provide that value to you,” he said. Spring is also thinking about what happens to those perks when an AI agent does the shopping. Macy’s has started working with Google’s Gemini on agentic commerce, he said, and the priority is making sure reward points, gift cards, and delivery promises still work when a bot places the order. A bank tries to win devotion Food, clothes, and home goods offer sensory experiences that financial services can’t match, and few people feel much affection for their bank. Ally Financial , which bills itself as the largest all-digital bank in the U.S., is trying anyway. In May, it rolled out Loyally, a fee-free rewards program open to customers regardless of their account balance. “The question really is how can we add some real value for customers that gives them reasons they want to keep on coming back to our site and engaging with us,” Rhodes said. “We’ve literally had it for like six months now, but the early results are really encouraging.” Ally is starting from a strong base, by Rhodes’ account. He said customer retention runs well over 90%, about 15% of new account volume comes through referrals, and 70% of customers are Gen Z or millennials. Rhodes argued that AI search is raising the stakes on every customer interaction, because what customers and employees say about a brand feeds the engines that make recommendations. “There are people who spend 10 times what we spend,” he said of Ally’s marketing budget. “Yet in the AI search engines and unbranded inquiries in consumer banking, we show up number one.” Rewarding regulars without shutting out newcomers The harder balance is rewarding regulars while still persuading new customers to try a brand. Spring said that’s where a retailer’s customer data comes in: breaking shoppers into cohorts and targeting each one, both to drive new traffic and to “create extraordinary value for your highest, most loyal consumers.” “It’s not a one-size-fits-all approach,” Spring said. “It needs to be very bespoke. And you have to leverage tools like, dare I say, AI.” Boatwright said every change to Chipotle’s program aims to draw more users in at the top of the funnel, then “make it much more sticky within the funnel and get those consumers coming back more often.” The next test may come when the customer isn’t the one searching. Boatwright said agentic AI ordering is coming whether brands are ready or not, and Chipotle has to make sure it shows up “when you ask your agent, tell me the best burrito in town.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Nvidia sinks after earnings, dragging down neoclouds CoreWeave, Iren
events.summary: Nvidia beat on earnings and revenue Tuesday after the bell. The chip giant's earnings came at a tumultuous time for the company, following former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation last week. Chair of the board Harvey Jones said on the earnings call Huang would not return as CEO. Nvidia shares sank around 2% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang . Trading in the neocloud companies was volatile, as CoreWeave sank about 3%, Iren fell about 2% and Nebius whipsawed. Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG. The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures . But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO. ″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money." "This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers." The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers. In a letter Wednesday, the House Energy and Commerce Committee asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear to discuss chip export controls, and requested a briefing from interim CEO Colette Kress by Dec. 2. Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country. Huang is slated to appear before several Congressional committees in the coming weeks. Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday, Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Huang and Lutnick have agreed to appear before the committee in December. It's slated to be Huang's second appearance on Capitol Hill in December, after the former Nvidia CEO reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for closed-door interviews on Dec. 1. events.title: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
events.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent. You can read this as a polite way of saying, “ I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored. Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand. But what does that actually mean? Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market. A personal brand is a discovery mechanism Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up? You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn. Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find. You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs. Don’t write AI slop LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.” Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.) And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text. Hot takes, with caution Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.” You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends. A routine you can follow Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know. Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast. Write for the people a few steps behind you The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions. It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could. The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you. —Brian IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant To help researchers search through the millions of peer-review publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, IEEE has released a custom AI suite optimized for STEM literature. The suit allows users to search with natural-language queries and provides overviews with reference links. Read more here . Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything. Read more here . events.title: Inside Nvidia’s First Post-Jensen All-Hands: Pay Raises and More Equity
events.summary: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress made her first address to the staff on Wednesday and just minutes into the meeting told employees that they can expect pay raises and more equity in December, months ahead of schedule, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. “So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” she said. Questions about compensation were the most common among the 700 submitted ahead of the meeting, Kress said. She said the next-most common request was for transparency from the board. Kress’ comments came during the first companywide meeting following the resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO last week. Huang had led the computer graphics chip maker since cofounding it 33 years ago, and his presentations during the quarterly town halls internally had become a much-anticipated and memorable spectacle for some of the company’s nearly 49,000 employees. Information rarely leaked from the meetings in the past. But now Nvidia is facing an extraordinary leadership crisis . Huang resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including potentially with a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board chair Harvey Jones said on Tuesday that Huang disclosed “personal behavior” contrary to the company’s policies and norms and wouldn’t be invited back. During the companywide meeting on Wednesday, Jones reiterated the board accepted Huang’s resignation due to his personal conduct and “lack of candor.” He said the company wouldn’t find a “Jensen clone,” but that there are “dynamic leaders out there, with demonstrated intellect, high tech engineering experience, strategic thinking, cultural compatibility, and a track record of success.” He added, “We will not compromise our requirements for the sake of expediency” and that the board would accept employee suggestions on the CEO search. Thousands of employees have apparently lobbied for Huang’s reinstatement. Several well-known tech executives signed a public petition, with about 200,000 purported backers urging the same. Instead, the board is searching internally and externally for a replacement at one of the world’s most valuable companies and one of the biggest drivers of the generative AI boom. Huang’s departures and a slew of government investigations into him and Nvidia have rattled investors. But on Tuesday, Nvidia reported better than expected financial results and forecast growing sales in the years to come. Shares were up about 5 percent on Wednesday. One concern investors have expressed is whether Nvidia might see a brain drain of top talent. Many employees have stayed at Nvidia for Huang and his vision. Nvidia could also be perceived as a less desirable place for new and emerging talent to work with its leadership in flux, during an especially critical time as competition in the AI chips market grows. On Tuesday’s third-quarter earnings call, an analyst from Bank of America Securities asked Kress directly about her “message” to Nvidia investors about talent retention, as well as the company’s overall durability and financial strategy through this major upheaval. Kress replied that “probably the most important thing” company leaders are thinking through right now is stabilizing its employee ranks. “We are always thinking about our employees. Like every community out there, there are diverse opinions,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure they are safe and make sure the work can be done in the current environment.” In a brief question-and-answer session with Kress during the all-hands meeting Wednesday, Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky addressed how the company could maintain its prized culture going forward. He recalled how he, Huang, and other cofounders thought it was “nonsense” to put cultural values up on posters. Instead, they want it instilled in “the way you behave, the way you work together and the way you work,” and he believes that will stand the test of time. “We’re going to be fine,” he said. Kress ended the meeting, which lasted about 50 minutes, by comparing Nvidia’s employees to “90,000 people packed into the sweatiest, hottest” University of Florida football game. In the third quarter, “every single person sings,” she said. “It is impressive to see them all together, all in harmony singing that song… Do you know what? We’re gonna hear that song, guys. And I believe in all of you that you will help sing it. Nvidia, we’ve got this.” Updated: 11/18/2026 1:26 p.m. EST: Updated with new details on comments made during the Nvidia all-hands meeting. events.title: Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and the curious case of the silent CEO candidate
events.summary: Jensen Huang speaking at the Fireworks AI conference in San Francisco. Alistair Barr/Business Insider Nvidia raised its forecast, but the stock kept falling on Wednesday. Potential CEO successor Ian Buck joined the earnings call but didn't say a word. Huang's powerful supporters aren't giving up on their push to bring him back. Nvidia 's board and interim CEO did just about enough late Tuesday to keep the growing army of Jensen Huang supporters at bay. At least for a few hours. "A clean quarter and guide strengthen the board's hand but do not close the question," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note to investors after the AI chip giant reported results. I listened to Nvidia's earnings conference call, and I thought interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones performed well under extraordinary circumstances. Jones came out swinging. He said the board had no intention of reinstating Huang and made it clear that questions about the ousted CEO were off-limits. Nvidia shares fell after those comments. Then Kress quickly delivered some welcome news. Nvidia raised its revenue growth forecast for fiscal 2028. She also pushed back against concerns that the company might have to cut prices to compete, and said profit margins would recover after dipping in the current quarter. The stock rebounded in after-hours trading. But on Wednesday, Nvidia shares continued to fall. That's not good for Nvidia board and the interim leadership. "I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties," billionaire activist investor Bill Ackman said on X on Wednesday. The curious case of Ian Buck Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia. David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images Jones, the board chair, said Nvidia would consider internal and external candidates for its next CEO. That brings me to the most intriguing moment of the call. As the question-and-answer session began, Nvidia announced that Ian Buck, VP of hyperscale and high-performance computing, would join Kress to answer analysts' questions. This was a big deal. Buck is a serious technologist who helped invent CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia's chips so useful for AI. He's also spent more than two decades at the company and has close relationships with its biggest customers. Business Insider has a great profile of Buck , who has emerged as a potential successor to Huang. "His hat is in the ring," Ives said when asked about Buck's appearance on the call. Now Nvidia appeared to have an almost perfect setup. The board had ruled out Huang's return, Kress had reassured Wall Street about the business, and a respected internal technical leader was being introduced to investors. Awesome. Except Buck proceeded to say absolutely nothing. Not a word. I kept waiting for an analyst to ask him a question. Nobody did. And Buck never volunteered anything. That was soooo weird. If you're being floated as a possible CEO of one of the world's most important companies, and you get a chance to address Wall Street during a leadership crisis, surely you say something? Maybe Nvidia wants the strong, silent type as its next CEO. (Huang, as we've learned recently, hasn't exactly been the silent type ). Joking aside, if I were a serious Nvidia investor, I would have wanted to hear from Buck. "It was odd, but then again this situation is all odd," Ives told me after the call. The Jensen comeback campaign Meanwhile, Huang still has powerful, wealthy supporters who aren't going away. With continued declines on Wednesday, Nvidia shares are well below their pre-Huang level — not a great look for the board. "His return to Nvidia is in all of our best interest," Shopify CEO Tobi Lutke wrote on X after Tuesday's results. He added that there could never be a true replacement for a founder like Huang. Ives agrees. "The 15% special meeting threshold, activist pressure, and the Commerce Department's position on the export investigation remain the next steps in the saga," he wrote. Ackman has already explained how shareholders could pressure Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Under Nvidia's bylaws, shareholders representing at least 15% of the company's voting power can demand a special shareholder meeting, provided they've held their shares for at least a year. They could then seek to replace directors with people who support Huang's reinstatement. A new board could then reappoint him CEO. That's a formidable challenge. Removing directors without cause requires support from two-thirds of Nvidia's outstanding voting shares, according to the company's bylaws . And 15% of Nvidia, at current valuations, represents more than $500 billion in stock. Huang owns roughly 3.5%, leaving supporters needing another 11.5 percentage points. Who has that much money? Only some of the world's largest investment funds and sovereign wealth funds. Oh, and Elon Musk. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . events.title: More banks say customers using AI agents are on their own — even if they get hacked
events.summary: Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked. AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments. But financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants. “As third-party AI tools become more widely available, we want customers to understand the risks associated with sharing banking credentials or authorizing those tools to access their accounts,” a Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch. “We recently updated our Online User Agreement to provide greater clarity about those risks and to reinforce that customers who choose to grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activities conducted through those agents.” JPMorgan and Bank of America , the two largest banks in the country, announced similar policies last month. And PNC, the eighth largest bank, changed its terms today. Citi’s update goes beyond telling customers that they are responsible for anything their agents may do; it also informs them that if the AI tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer will be responsible for anything hackers do with their account. Banking giant Citizens similarly emailed its customers this week, warning that they are also on the hook for anything their AI assistant does, according to an email seen by TechCrunch. As AI startups look for more revenue, breaking into personal finance presents an attractive opportunity for companies to add value for customers and wet their beaks in the stream of fees generated by the sector. But if consumers are already leery of sharing their email or chat records with an AI agent, bank and brokerage accounts offer a new trust challenge. Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.” Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat. Markets shuddered briefly in reaction to the prospect of AI tools making it easier for consumers to avoid unnecessary fees or low-interest deposit accounts that pad bank margins. But if AI agents become an important way to interact with financial decisions, banks will fight to control that pathway. Citi’s terms note that AI agents it provides can be used by customers without worrying about additional liability. The reaction by banks is part of a broader trend among businesses of all stripes: AI labs promise that their agents will revolutionize the way people engage with a variety of service providers, then the service providers say “hold on a minute.” We’ve seen it in everything from car-hailing to food service , and how these relationships play out will help determine which AI investments pay off.
