events.title: Alex Karp put Palantir’s early sales team in the Mandarin Oriental instead of a Motel 6—at 10x the price
events.summary: The old advice to dress for the job you want can apply to lodging, too—at least in the thinking of some enterprising executives. In its early days, Palantir Technologies put its young staffers up at a luxury Mandarin Oriental for sales trips instead of booking a budget chain like Motel 6. The call came from Alex Karp, Palantir’s cofounder and CEO, and the logic was simple: In enterprise sales, appearances can matter as much as the bottom line. Even companies that will someday be worth hundreds of billions often start out with a “fake it ’til you make it” mentality. Garry Tan, who was Palantir’s 10th employee and is now CEO of startup accelerator Y Combinator, shared the story in a May 2025 post on X : “Funny early Palantir story. We were doing some of our first sales meetings for Palantir and (team was all under 25 at the time) and were staying at the Mandarin Oriental. We said hey this is a startup! Why are we wasting money on this? Alex Karp said the people you’re selling to will ask you where you are staying. And we aren’t selling Motel 6 software. We are selling Mandarin Oriental software.” From long shot to a $386 billion company Karp’s bet on looking the part has aged well. Palantir began trading on the New York Stock Exchange through a direct listing in September 2020 and was valued at about $18 billion after its first trades. As of Nov. 16, 2026, it was worth about $386 billion, per CompaniesMarketCap . That valuation is disproportionate to its sales. As Fortune has reported, Palantir became one of the world’s 25 most valuable companies while still too small to make the Fortune 500 . None of that was obvious when Karp, Peter Thiel, Stephen Cohen, Joe Lonsdale, and Nathan Gettings founded the company in 2003. Top venture firms passed on it, and Thiel put in much of his own money, alongside backing from the CIA’s venture arm, In-Q-Tel. The CIA became its first customer. Karp, though, clearly believed in what was coming, and he wanted the company to project it. So even in the early days, staffers checked into a Mandarin Oriental when they traveled to pitch customers. The price of looking the part Today, the typical nightly rate for an entry-level room at a Mandarin Oriental is $921, according to Fermata data . A night at a Motel 6, the budget chain Tan mentioned, often costs well under $100; one Albany, N.Y., location lists rooms for less than $65 on Kayak . Those are 2026 prices, not 2000s rates, but the gap is the point: The luxury room costs more than 10 times as much as the budget one. Plenty of people who responded to Tan’s post agreed with Karp. The post was viewed more than 830,000 times, and replies included: “Carry yourself as the team you will be, not the team you are today,” and “This is such a sharp reminder that in enterprise, perception shapes value. Sometimes it’s not just the product, it’s how confidently you signal the tier you’re playing in.” The case for the cheap room Others weren’t sold on the “fake it ’til you make it” approach. Ryan Rzepecki , who founded the e-bike startup JUMP and sold it to Uber in 2018 , posted: “All the way through acquisition we shared hotel rooms and piled into Airbnbs. We even had our clients offer to have us stay in their homes.” And a user named Avery Haskell posted: “And he’s got the exorbitant P/E ratio to show for it!” There’s no single right answer. As many X users pointed out, plenty of America’s most successful companies trace their roots to garages and basements, not luxury hotels. Karp, for his part, still makes no apologies for projecting confidence. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit last December, he told Wall Street critics who call him arrogant to “judge me by the accomplishment.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: US senators urge White House AI chief to fix vulnerabilities after mass outages
events.summary: As Democrats flag AI bank breaches and cyber-attacks in Japan, Jay Clayton says system failures happen A bipartisan pair of US senators are calling on Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and AI czar, to identify and fix vulnerabilities in the US’s infrastructure following nationwide outages at major companies and government agencies. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce, science, and transportation committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican chair of the Senate subcommittee on cybersecurity, sent a letter to Clayton on Tuesday, outlining concerns sparked by reports of AI accessing major banks, cyber-attacks in Japan and more. “The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” Cantwell and Rounds wrote to Clayton, who is also serving as the White House AI czar. “Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services,” the senators wrote. Over the last week, tech outages at major banks, workplace communication systems and even federal infrastructure like the Federal Aviation Administration – triggering a four-hour nationwide flight stoppage that grounded or delayed thousands of flights – have raised alarms about potential cyber-attacks. Top officials have insisted the disruptions stem from software patch updates that intend to address potential AI harms. Clayton and other national security officials told lawmakers on Wednesday that there was no indication the recent outages were the result of a malicious attack. “Based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack,” Clayton said during the House homeland security committee hearing. Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, and Christopher Raia, the deputy FBI director, similarly said they had no reason to believe the outages were connected or the result of an attack. “Many people are patching their systems. They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated,” Clayton told CNBC on Tuesday . “It is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure and as you patch and upgrade your systems, taking them down and bringing them back up, there are things like this that happen.” Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Senate intelligence committee, echoed Clayton . “AI is making it possible to identify vulnerabilities across enormous numbers of systems at unprecedented speed, creating enormous pressure on companies and government agencies to patch those vulnerabilities immediately, often all at once, putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” he wrote on X. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, attempted to quell public speculation and fear by assuring Americans that the tech outages were not linked to one another or the work of malicious actors. But nationwide cyber outages have roiled the country, filled with voters who are already skeptical of rapidly integrating and developing AI . It is unclear what exactly has caused the widespread outages or if AI played a role. JD Vance canceled his scheduled interview at the New York Times’ DealBook summit on Wednesday, citing his need to attend meetings addressing the recent tech outages. Cantwell and Rounds are asking Clayton to provide cybersecurity tools to critical US infrastructure such as hospitals, utilities, small government, federal agencies and more, to prevent further disruptions. They are also asking that US cybersecurity teams secure the same AI systems that are deployed to find vulnerabilities in software, raising concerns that they can “gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems”.

events.title: Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters In today's how-could-things-get-worse-for-Microsoft news, it seems someone's GitHub org admin creds have been compromised The wrong setting for AI cache can cost you a lot of cash 2 hours ago PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road 3 hours ago SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out 8 hours ago UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models 9 hours ago Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action 9 hours ago Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered. CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference , but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization. The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning . According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down. Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do. Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services. To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware. It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too. In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site. “That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware. The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime , an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign. “We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”® Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.

events.title: Anthropic IPO: AI lab considers increasing the offering as investor demand surges, sources say
events.summary: Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, according to people familiar with the details. The AI lab is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday. The stock is set to begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT on Thursday. Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80. The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday. Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion. Anthropic IPO: AI lab considers increasing offering, sources say Anthropic likely to price IPO above the current range of $70 to $78, sources tell CNBC PRO: Anthropic gets a buy rating ahead of IPO this week. What this analyst expects from the AI giant Small investor enthusiasm for Anthropic IPO to rival SpaceX debut Anthropic IPO is not important anymore: 'Big Short' investor Steve Eisman Altimeter's Brad Gerstner aims to invest $5 billion in Anthropic IPO Anthropic IPO guide: Everything you need to know Meet the seven co-founders of Anthropic Anthropic's Wall Street whisperer: CFO Krishna Rao The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range of between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range. A representative for Anthropic declined to comment. Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds. Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD. "I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time." Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses. Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said. Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month. The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.

events.title: Ford starts U.S. battery cell production using Chinese tech amid geopolitical tensions
events.summary: Ford has started U.S. production and shipments of battery cells for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL. The plant has been contentious for the automaker, which has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, for its connections to CATL. Ford said licensed CATL technology and manufacturing support are helping it bring lower-cost LFP cell production to the U.S. quicker. MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL. The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck , which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors. The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China. The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL. Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible. "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells." The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing. Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production. Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry. Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed. The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it. MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture. MongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications.

events.title: Sam Altman warns against a future where AI, not humans, calls the shots
events.summary: OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman believes that people should stay in charge of the future when it comes to how AI technology impacts the world and everyone’s lives. Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, the AI executive referred to discussions in Silicon Valley about whether there will be a gradual handover to AI — meaning AI will eventually become the decision-making authority across every major industry and institution. “One thing we’ve been talking a lot about recently is there’s been this thing in Silicon Valley that seems almost ridiculous to have to fight against, but we both believe very deeply that people need to stay in control of the future, and there’s increasing talk about, well, there is either going to be or there should be this sort of gradual handover to AI. And I — we both — agree that that’s a terrible idea,” said Altman, who was sharing the stage with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman. The hand-off theory stems from the idea that as AI models become increasingly more powerful, they will learn to improve themselves — a concept known as “recursive self-improvement” or RSI. As existing AI technology builds newer, smarter generations, those will eventually become a superintelligence that humans can no longer control, the belief goes. Altman explained that he and Brockman only disagree over how to best accomplish the goal of keeping humans in control, or what sort of challenges we should expect to face along the way. However, Altman characterized this as more of a debate between two people who share the same larger views. “The question of how to actually prevent [handover] from happening — how to actually ensure that we will, given all of the various pressures and given what other companies may try to do — that we are going to actually ensure that people stay in control of the future in a very deep way, and we don’t have this either accidental or intentional handover — I think we can both agree on that,” Altman said. Brockman added that, as the models improve, there’s an increasing responsibility for alignment, safety, and security, which may require changes in how things are currently done. “Monitoring is a good example of something where I think we are going to need new … technology,” he said. Today, AI researchers monitor the model’s chain of thought, where the AI writes out what it’s thinking as it works through problems and performs tasks. But in Brockman’s view, that may not always be the best way to monitor more advanced AI that’s being built now. “As the models have gotten more capable, they can do more within just the forward path without having to actually write out that thinking, which means we need a new approach to monitoring,” Brockman said. “We’re going to need to deliver that, and I think that there will be points where we need to really think about, as the capabilities get to a certain point, chain-of-thought monitorability is degraded,” he continued, adding that all the problems were technical ones to be solved. OpenAI had committed to increased chain-of-thought monitoring after the incident where an OpenAI model escaped containment and hacked into the AI model repository Hugging Face . In Wednesday’s interview, Brockman noted that the company told 25% of its production engineers to stop building things and work on securing the AI technology after the hack. But despite the high-profile breach, he argued that forward progress was still critical to fight bad actors. “I think to realize that if you look to the level of capabilities of models in the world, and you see cyber models that are coming from that are now … in the hands of threat actors everywhere, that I think that it’s really important that defenders use the most capable models to defend,” he said. events.title: Democrats demand answers from Howard Lutnick about Nvidia and his family’s business
events.summary: Democratic lawmakers ask if commerce secretary favored Nvidia to enrich his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald The US commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, faces mounting questions over his handling of the Nvidia affair as Democratic lawmakers demand answers over his family firm’s vast stake in the tech company. Cantor Fitzgerald, the investment firm Lutnick ran for decades before joining the Trump administration , held shares in Nvidia worth “hundreds of millions of dollars” while Lutnick made key decisions affecting the tech firm’s ability to operate, according to Democrats on three key congressional committees. “The American people deserve to know: did the secretary of commerce seriously and perhaps irreversibly compromise US national security interests to make money for his adult children and Cantor Fitzgerald?” said Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Gregory Meeks of New York and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California. Cantor Fitzgerald insists it had “no role” in the Trump administration’s decisions about Nvidia. But in a letter on Tuesday to Lutnick’s son Brandon, who now serves as chair of Cantor Fitzgerald, the trio of lawmakers demanded documents and records, including communications concerning Nvidia. They said that they wanted to “understand whether any actions or decisions by Secretary Lutnick concerning export controls, enforcement measures, or national security policies may have been improperly influenced by Cantor Fitzgerald’s holdings or business interests”. Raskin is the top Democrat on the judiciary committee of the House of Representatives . Meeks is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs committee. Kamlager-Dove is the top Democrat on the foreign affairs subcommittee on south and central Asia. In an accompanying news release , the lawmakers said that they were seeking to determine whether Lutnick “blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China while his family’s firm held hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia stock”. Howard Lutnick led Cantor Fitzgerald until his confirmation as commerce secretary in February 2025, when he transferred his stake in the firm to trusts benefiting his adult children . In the letter to Brandon Lutnick, the lawmakers wrote that at the time of Howard Lutnick’s confirmation, Cantor Fitzgerald had “amassed a significant stake” in Nvidia , reportedly “holding more than 3.5m shares, valued at over $1.3bn”. In a statement to the Guardian, a Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson said that the claims in the letter were “inaccurate”. “Cantor holds no material proprietary position in Nvidia,” the spokesperson said. “Cantor’s Nvidia holdings arise primarily from equity swaps executed for clients. “The decline in our holdings since early 2025 reflects the unwinding of those hedges as clients closed or reduced their swap positions, not a Cantor decision to exit a proprietary position,” the statement continued. “Allegations suggesting that work influenced government decisions are baseless. Additionally, Cantor has no role in US export control or entity list decisions [to determine trade restrictions].” The Cantor Fitzgerald spokesperson also said that they were “confident that a full review of the facts will demonstrate that we have operated our business ethically and in full compliance with all applicable rules and regulations”. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In their letter, the lawmakers also cited a recent New York Times report that Howard Lutnick had pushed to weaken rules affecting south-east Asian datacenters, some of which are Cantor Fitzgerald clients. A commerce department spokesperson told the Times that Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the US and that he does not discuss department matters with his sons. The spokesperson added that Lutnick’s sons also do not discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him. In their letter on Tuesday, the lawmakers asked Cantor Fitzgerald to provide written confirmation that it had “implemented appropriate preservation measures and instructed all relevant personnel to retain potentially responsive records” by 5pm ET on 1 December. The letter comes after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, following reports of his multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The developments have put Lutnick into focus as last week Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, blamed Lutnick’s commerce department for the fact the US had not imposed export restrictions on certain Nvidia chips to China. Both Huang and Lutnick are scheduled to testify before Congress next month.

events.title: Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island
events.summary: Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries draw condemnation from across the region. Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island. Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. list 1 of 3 Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain list 2 of 3 Piecemeal wars: A new kind of world war is already under way list 3 of 3 Can the US and Iran sustain a ‘frozen war’? The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers. The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar. The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates. The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution. Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz. Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them. Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha. Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder. Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported. He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

events.title: World Bank official says Lebanon reconstruction making slow progress
events.summary: Beirut blames Israel’s occupation and attacks on southern Lebanon for reconstruction delays. A senior World Bank official says Lebanon has been slow to use international aid to rebuild areas destroyed during the 2024 war and the renewed fighting since March 2026. World Bank managing director of operations Anna Bjerde said she had to be “honest” about the pace of reconstruction during a visit to southern Lebanon on Tuesday. list 1 of 3 Israel builds 90km network of military roads across southern Lebanon list 2 of 3 More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food shortages, UN says list 3 of 3 UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanon The international financial institution approved $250m in June 2025 to help Lebanon clear rubble and repair “damaged critical public infrastructure” after the 2024 Israel-Hezbollah war. But a September progress report showed that only $4.2m had been paid out, a fraction of the projected $100m by July 2026. The World Bank estimated that rebuilding after the 2024 war would cost about $11b. “Parliament ratification of the said loan experienced considerable delays,” Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s office responded in a statement, adding that the “worsening security situation” as a result of Israel’s continuing occupation of southern Lebanon “delayed the timely launch of project activities”. Israel has continued to occupy and attack parts of southern Lebanon up to the Litani River since March, claiming to destroy Hezbollah infrastructure, while demolishing civilian homes. On Wednesday, Israel fired artillery shells towards the towns of Baraachit and Beit Yahoun in the Bint Jbeil district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA). The towns of Rashaf and Sarbine, extending to Wadi al-Hujair, were also targeted. And Israeli earth movers demolished residential homes in the town of Zawtar ash-Sharqiyah and Haddatha. The United Nations estimates at least 304,500 Lebanese remain internally displaced in the country, down from 1.2 million. Up to 4,500 have been killed in Israeli attacks. Last month, Hezbollah announced it will pay up to $14,000 to families whose homes were destroyed or made uninhabitable by Israel, as the group accused the government of failing to carry out its duties to help the displaced. Israel has refused to withdraw from southern Lebanon, citing security concerns connected to the delayed disarmament of Hezbollah and other groups, which the United States and the Lebanese government have insisted on, as part of the trilateral ceasefire framework launched in April. “Israel will not withdraw from the current lines of these security zones, nor will it redeploy its forces,” Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in a statement on Wednesday, adding that if tensions escalate on the various fronts, “we are fully prepared to seize additional territory”. Bjerde said that “institutions in Lebanon are very thinly stretched” and the security situation required “very careful planning around where you can start and where you don’t start” to remove rubble and repair infrastructure. The World Bank projected Lebanon’s economy to shrink by 6.4 percent this year , in its Summer 2026 Lebanon Economic Monitor report, titled A Conflict-Torn Economy. “The rebound was sharply interrupted by the March 2026 escalation in conflict, which further damaged housing and infrastructure, displaced communities, disrupted supply chains and weighed heavily on tourism and domestic demand,” the report said. According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than one million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of hunger. Despite this, Lebanon’s western-backed government insists it is doing all it can, given the circumstances, such as the distribution of approximately $100m in housing loans granted to 1,500 families, according to NNA. Bjerde said the World Bank needs to be “insistent” and “very close to monitoring on a daily basis” to make sure the work gets done “because you cannot let the people down”, adding that the World Bank wants to see the reconstruction work go more quickly.

events.title: Paris Hilton, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez press House to pass Defiance Act to fight AI deepfake pornography
events.summary: The Defiance Act, which the U.S. Senate unanimously passed in January 2026, would expand on existing federal law to allow victims of sexually explicit AI deepfakes to seek civil damages from people who knowingly create and distribute them. Paris Hilton, along with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is one of the bill's most prominent advocates as it attempts to find the votes to pass in the House, where versions of it have stalled since 2024. Hilton says her recent work with digital identity security company Loti AI uncovered 100,000 explicit deepfake images depicting her, and removed over 60,000 of them. "I'm very fortunate that I have a team of lawyers. I have people helping me. But a lot of these young girls and women don't have that support," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin during the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast. Artificial intelligence can turn an ordinary photo or video into a sexually explicit AI deepfake, with consequences that can follow victims into their classrooms and workplaces. Getting those images removed is one challenge. Holding the people who create or share them accountable is another. Policymakers, advocates and victims say additional federal legislation is needed, but a bill that would give victims new legal remedies has yet to receive a vote in the House after two years of efforts. On Tuesday, Paris Hilton, one of the bill's most prominent advocates, was back on the steps of the U.S. Capitol alongside Defiance Act backers including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and Rep. Laurel Lee (R-FL) to press the U.S. House of Representatives to pass the bill into law. The U.S. Senate passed its most recent version of the measure by unanimous consent in January 2026. The proposed bipartisan bill, the Defiance Act (Disrupt Explicit Forged Images And Non-Consensual Edits Act), would close gaps in an existing federal right to sue over sexually explicit deepfakes, creating the civil right to sue for victims of deepfake pornography. If passed, survivors could sue perpetrators who create, share, publish, solicit, or threaten to distribute this content without consent. Victims could also recover legal costs and seek court orders requiring the content to be removed. "This work is very personal to me and it's just so terrifying now if AI gets into the wrong hands, what's possible," Hilton said during a new episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast with Julia Boorstin. When Hilton was 19, she was pressured into allowing an intimate recording featuring her and her then-boyfriend, Rick Salomon. She expected the recording to stay private and later found it was released without her consent. AI has created an infinitely scalable platform for the online trauma she suffered. "Somebody can literally just take an innocent photo and turn it into some explicit photo or video, and this is happening to millions of women and children all around the world, and they don't have anyone to protect them because the laws have just not caught up with this technology yet," Hilton said. "There's girls who are teenagers in school. This is happening to them, and some of them are taking their own lives because it's just completely humiliated them, and destroyed their confidence ... being able to even walk into school," Hilton said. Hilton is currently serving as chief advocacy officer at digital identity protection firm Loti AI, which helps people find unauthorized uses of their likeness or voice online and file takedown requests. She said the company has detected more than 100,000 explicit deepfakes depicting her and helped remove more than 60,000. "I'm very fortunate that I have a team of lawyers. I have people helping me. But a lot of these young girls and women don't have that support," she said. "People need to know that there's going to be consequences for their actions," she added. The Take It Down Act , which was signed by President Trump in May 2025, made certain disclosures of nonconsensual intimate images, including AI-generated deepfakes, a federal crime. Covered platforms must remove the material and any known identical copies within 48 hours of receiving a valid request. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz introduced the bill in June 2024 after a case in Aledo, Texas, when an Instagram image of 14-year-old Elliston Berry was edited to make her appear nude and the altered image circulated on Snapchat. Berry told CNN that she woke up to calls and texts about the images. "It was out of my control. And they were spreading," she said. She also said it was difficult to tell her mother, even though she knew the images were fake. As a mother, Hilton says she worries about what happens when these images circulate among classmates. "Even though the image is not real, the pain and suffering that comes along with it is very real," she said. Before the Take It Down Act, state laws offered varying protections, and many did not explicitly cover synthetic images.

events.title: Tech outages are causing people to panic-buy. Costco is benefiting, Mizuho says
events.summary: A series of tech outages over the past week has consumers stocking up on emergency supplies, and Costco sales are seeing a lift, research firm Mizuho said. In the final week of October, Mizuho estimated, Costco's U.S. comparable sales, excluding gasoline, rose 11% to 12%. The firm said the stronger pace is continuing through November. On TikTok and other social media platforms, posts urging people to stock up on food and supplies are gaining significant traction. A series of tech outages has consumers stocking up on emergency supplies. Costco sales are seeing a lift because of it, according to research firm Mizuho. In the final week of October, Mizuho estimates, Costco's U.S. comparable sales, excluding gasoline, rose 11% to 12%, up from the normal 6% to 7% the first three weeks in October. Costco reported an 8.1% increase for the month. The firm said the stronger pace is continuing through November, as 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators it tracked on Costco's website sold out as of Sunday night. "Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at COST," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger said in a research note Monday. Bellinger will appear on CNBC's "The Exchange" during the 1 p.m. hour. On Thursday, an outage occurred in Microsoft's Outlook and Teams, and on Friday the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide. On Monday, a software outage at JPMorgan Chase caused banking transaction delays, and a system outage delayed United Airlines flights. The National Security Agency said Tuesday that the spy agency's communication network went down temporarily. The outages appear to come amid a rush to recover software vulnerabilities uncovered by AI tools, and officials are saying there's no reason for panic. Still, on TikTok and other social media platforms, posts urging people to stock up on food and supplies are gaining significant traction. Mizuho raised its price target on Costco to $1,150 from $1,100 and kept its buy-equivalent outperform rating. The firm said U.S. comparable sales could grow more than 10% in November. Mizuho also sees Walmart 's Sam's Club benefiting from emergency preparedness sales as shoppers fill up their pantries, and for Home Depot and Lowe's as they buy home improvement emergency supplies. At Costco, Mizuho will be watching whether the surge brought in new member sign-ups when the warehouse retailer reports its first quarter of fiscal 2027 on Dec. 10.

events.title: I'm in perimenopause while raising kids going through puberty. These 4 family rules help us get along.
events.summary: The author (not shown) said she is working hard to navigate perimenopause while several of her children are also going through puberty. SeventyFour/Getty Images Perimenopause and puberty are colliding in our house. As you can imagine, it's a lot. We're managing hormones and mood swings with limits on reactions and simple self-care tools. We've all learned that self-advocacy and support are essential to keep life running smoothly. No one warned me what this season of life would really be like. While I, at 44 years young, am going through perimenopause , some of my four kids are also going through puberty . The timing is less than ideal. As their parent, I'm supposed to be mature, grown, patient, understanding, and wise. I am instead quite over everything. And I mean, everything. Unfortunately, I'm not the only one. While my kids are mentally, physically, and emotionally growing, as well as doing their adolescent job of trying to become more independent, I am dealing with erratic and dwindling estrogen levels. After going through chemo for breast cancer, my perimenopause journey was kickstarted earlier than planned, resulting in the too-often swamp which I frequently find myself in. Oddly, I've noticed that my kids' and my experiences are actually quite similar. We can be hot and then cold — literally and emotionally — in a matter of seconds. The smallest things can result in a downward spiral : a song we don't like playing on the radio, realizing we are out of our go-to snack, or another notification reminding us of a task we forgot to do. We are working together, as best we can, to understand one another and maintain a peaceful household, but it's taking work from all of us. Here are some ground rules we're using to survive. All feelings are allowed, but not all reactions are Being on an emotional roller coaster is expected for any of us these days. However, blowing up, insulting each other out of anger, or refusing to contribute to the family doesn't fly. The author said that everyone in her house is allowed to have big feelings, but they must do so with respect. Courtesy of Rachel Garlinghouse. My kids and I all know we are each responsible for our own choices and reactions. To try to be as steady as possible, we need to use our tools to stay regulated: exercise, a "thinking" shower (used to help someone calm down and have time to reflect on situations), remembering to eat a snack, and going to bed earlier when we're having a rough day are all tools we use frequently. Real apologies are required We don't apologize to each other over every little snippy comment. However, when we choose to let our emotions dictate our actions, both kids and adults usually end up apologizing at some point. My kids know that an apology can't just be words. It also needs to spur a change in behavior. A muttered "sorry" is only step one. Take, for example, the other day when I accused one of my teens of taking something that wasn't theirs, only to find out I'd set the item down without thinking and later discovered it. I apologized, explained (not excused), and took full ownership for what I did. Grown-ups can be wrong, too, and I want them to see me make mistakes and correct them. We help the struggling person when we are having a good day Having good and bad days is part of being human. However, when we're battling our hormone shifts, the bad often seems to outweigh the good. When one of us is having a bad day, the others try to step it up for that person by taking on one of their chores or encouraging them to go to bed earlier. Sometimes it's a "steer clear" situation, just letting that person have their bad mood and bad attitude without clapping back. I've been known to grab the struggling person a favorite drive-thru snack from time to time, too. We self-advocate for what we need and honor each other's needs We have multiple diagnoses in our home, including anxiety, autism, and ADHD. Any of these, paired with puberty and perimenopause, can make any of us more prone to sensory overload , emotional explosiveness, or overall overwhelm. Because of this, we encourage each other to meet our own needs, and also remind each other to do so when needed. It's become part of our family culture. For example, I just asked my teen to grab their old noise-canceling headphones for their younger sibling, who had a (very loud) field trip to a basketball game that we know would set them off. Noticing the little things and helping whenever we can has proven to go a long way for all of us. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Labour faces double blow over UK fossil fuel projects
events.summary: Large North Sea operator EnQuest says it is quitting oil basin, while SSE threatens to close Yorkshire gas storage site Nils Pratley: with more gas storage at risk. What’s the government plan for secure supplies? The energy secretary has been dealt a double blow after two UK companies signalled plans to pull their investment from large fossil fuel projects amid disagreements over government policies. One of the North Sea’s biggest independent companies, EnQuest, said on Wednesday it was quitting the North Sea oil and gas basin to focus on making better returns in Asia, blaming the “uncertain investment environment within the UK”. Separately, the energy company SSE told investors that next summer it would start the process of closing one of the country’s largest gas storage sites, which is on the North Sea coast, unless the government intervened to offer support amid weak market conditions. The tacit criticism is expected to pile pressure on Miatta Fahnbulleh, who became the energy secretary in July, to clarify the government’s plan to secure the UK’s gas supplies as households face a significant rise in energy bills this winter because of soaring gas costs. EnQuest set out plans to sell its entire portfolio of UK oilfields to the biggest North Sea producer, Neo Next+, for up to $960m (£730m), weeks after the company urged the chancellor, John Healey, to use his budget in November to reform the industry’s tax regime. The UK oil and gas industry said after the budget that the Treasury’s decision to leave its planned North Sea tax changes until the end of the decade was “continuing to drive energy investment abroad”. The British oil company BP is also in the process of exiting the North Sea after announcing in the summer that it would end six decades of production from the basin by selling its entire business there. The EnQuest deal marks “another significant company exiting the UK continental shelf”, according to James Hosie, an equity analyst at Shore Capital. He said the company had opted to leave after 16 years as a leading independent operator in the basin “rather than hold out for an improvement in the UK regulatory and fiscal regime for upstream oil and gas”. SSE told investors that while its Atwick gas storage site in the north of England had a “strategic importance” to the energy system as the North Sea’s domestic production declined, it was “increasingly clear that existing market arrangements do not support their continued operation”. Closing the Atwick facility, near Hornsea on the East Yorkshire coast, would remove about 309m cubic metres of gas, or about 1.5 days’ worth of Great Britain’s gas usage, from the UK’s storage capacity. The site makes up a fifth of the country’s onshore gas storage capacity. When the storage tanks at the UK’s liquified natural gas terminals and the offshore Rough site in the North Sea are included, it accounts for 7% of the country’s total capacity. Rough is also at risk of closure unless its owner, Centrica, the parent company of British Gas , can agree a long-term financial support deal with the government. The renewed concerns over supplies emerged on the same day that the National Energy System Operator (Neso) said in a second consecutive annual report that the UK was at risk of a gas supply crisis as the North Sea’s production winds down. The report echoed concerns that while the UK has enough access to global gas markets to cover demand when weather is normal, if even a single piece of Britain’s ageing gas infrastructure suffered an “unlikely” outage during a very cold spell, then supplies could fall short of demand. This would lead to emergency measures such as shutting off gas supplies to factories, power plants and – in extreme scenarios – homes. A government spokesperson said it had given the North Sea sector and its investors “the long-term certainty to plan, invest and support jobs” by setting out its intention to end the current tax regime in 2030, or earlier if global oil prices fall below a specific threshold. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “The North Sea remains a vital national asset,” the spokesperson added. “Oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, as we continue our transition to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.” The spokesperson said the government would set out its proposals to protect Britain’s gas security, which could include offering commercial support to storage facilities, in due course. Energy companies typically rely on stockpiling gas in their storage facilities during the summer, when prices are usually lower because of weaker demand, before selling the gas at a profit during winter when demand for energy usually lifts market prices.

Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Beware of the temptation to drop just a few more dollars to get the work done California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps 29 minutes ago Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware 50 minutes ago MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof 1 hour ago Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover 2 hours ago PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road 2 hours ago Be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice. Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning. Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze. Sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges users to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background. The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again. "After hitting my $200 Ultra plan limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads." There didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made. They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy. "I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation." The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond. It's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader said, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app. "I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits." Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong , just with customer requests. The problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud , and it appears the lessons need to be learned again. Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we're paying for and to reach a human when the numbers don’t add up." Caution is advised. Especially when a service appears to need only a few more dollars of credit to finish off that task.

events.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it’s ‘hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen’
events.summary: The AI industry is entering a new era, and not just because of its constant stream of new model releases and discoveries. The AI community must now push forward without one of its most influential figures, Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. Huang stepped down last week amid several scandals involving affairs with two employees and an alleged Chinese spy, raising potentially far-reaching national security concerns. Speaking onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and President Greg Brockman each revealed that they had spoken privately with Huang as the embattled former CEO’s public image continued to unravel. “Jensen took one of the earliest big bets on us. We took a big bet on Nvidia,” Altman said. “It’s hard to imagine the AI industry without Jensen.” OpenAI has worked closely with Huang over the years. Nvidia invested $30 billion in the company earlier this year and designs the chips that power OpenAI’s technology. Brockman added that he and his wife are friends with Huang’s family, so the couple had reached out “personally, just to be there for him and his family at this time.” “I think it’s obviously a tough time for everyone, but again, I think Nvidia is such an incredible company,” Brockman said. “I think that… what Jensen has built there, it clearly is built to last, and so we’re excited to keep partnering and looking to the future.” Huang’s impact on Nvidia and the broader AI industry has been so profound that nearly 200,000 people , including Elon Musk and other influential CEOs, have signed a petition calling for the chipmaker to reinstate him. Nvidia executives said during the company’s earnings call on Tuesday that they do not have plans to reappoint Huang, even though the founder offered to return. Altman was reticent to weigh in on Huang’s future at Nvidia. When asked whether he thought Huang could return, Altman replied, “One thing I did not appreciate was everybody on Earth speculating with some random theory.” “I will say, I wish Jensen the best. I wish Nvidia the best,” Altman said. “I don’t think the world needs another set of random opinions on what’s going to happen here.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. She holds a B.A. in English from the University of Pennsylvania and served as a Princeton in Asia Fellow in Laos. events.title: Ina Garten is the queen of easy Thanksgiving. Here are 10 recipes we think should be on your menu this year.
events.summary: We've tested many of Ina Garten's recipes. These dishes should be on your Thanksgiving menu. Rachel Askinasi/Business Insider We love making Ina Garten's recipes, especially during the holidays. And we've tested many appetizers, side dishes, and mains that would be perfect for Thanksgiving.   Here are our favorites, from Garten's cornbread and mac and cheese to her turkey and potato gratin. Holiday hosting can be stressful, which is why we've always loved turning to Ina Garten's recipes . The Barefoot Contessa's delicious and foolproof dishes are essential for planning a stress-free Thanksgiving menu , allowing you to spend more time with friends and family. We've made dozens of Garten's recipes over the years, exploring everything from her comforting pastas to her mouth-watering desserts . So you can trust us to pick Garten's best dishes for your Thanksgiving table. Garten's go-to homemade appetizer is a batch of chipotle cheddar crackers. They're a great way to start the festivities. Rachel Askinasi/Business Insider When it comes to appetizers, the Barefoot Contessa says she likes to make one item and then buy the rest. In October 2022, she told Bon Appétit that her tried-and-true homemade dish for this purpose is a serving of chipotle cheddar crackers.  Garten keeps a log of the cracker dough in her freezer. This way, even if she has some surprise guests over for drinks, she can pull them out and bake off a few as needed.  We thought this recipe tasted just like Cheez-It crackers, but with the consistency of a biscuit. These would be a great pre-meal crowd-pleaser for your Thanksgiving gathering. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's chipotle cheddar crackers here. Garten says this skillet cornbread is the best she's ever made. We feel exactly the same. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread — which serves 10 to 12 people — has a gorgeous golden-brown hue, making it the perfect centerpiece at the Thanksgiving table.  The bread was easy to whip up and tasted deliciously fluffy and moist, with a salty, crunchy crust and a delightfully sweet filling. No one could resist getting seconds, and the leftovers still tasted as fresh the next day. It's no wonder the brown-butter skillet cornbread has earned a permanent spot in our holiday cooking repertoire.  Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's brown-butter skillet cornbread here. Garten's overnight mac and cheese is the perfect make-ahead dish. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten calls this the "creamiest, crustiest, most delicious mac and cheese" that she's ever made. It features cavatappi or elbow macaroni, heavy cream, Gruyère and sharp white cheddar cheeses, nutmeg, breadcrumbs, and plenty of butter.  We made this dish the night before Friendsgiving and threw it in the oven when the party started. It was ready in less than 30 minutes and made a big day of cooking way less stressful. Plus, it's extremely delicious! Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's overnight mac and cheese here. And her easy turkey-breast recipe might save your meal at the last minute. Rachel Askinasi/Business Insider Whether you're looking to keep the main dish low-lift this year, or you find out you're in charge of cooking turkey the day before Thanksgiving, we think this recipe should be your go-to.  This dish is easy to put together and doesn't require as much time or prep as cooking a full-size bird, which makes it ideal for last-minute chefs.  Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's herb-roasted turkey breast here . This wet rub from Garten's turkey recipe is worth making, even if you're not cooking the main dish. Rachel Askinasi/Business Insider This quick marinade was our favorite part of the turkey-breast recipe. You can use the extra rub to season green beans, sauce up potatoes, or serve it as a general dipping sauce for the table.  Even if you're not making Garten's turkey breast, you should pull out this part of the recipe and add some bright, citrusy, fresh-herb flavors to your otherwise rich plate.  Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's lemony, herby turkey rub here . Garten's Parmesan smashed potatoes are a fun twist on a Thanksgiving classic. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider The potatoes were delightfully thick, deliciously creamy, and packed with tons of flavor thanks to the salty Parmesan and subtly sweet potatoes. One friend said it was the best mashed potatoes they've ever tasted.  And the recipe is incredibly easy and quick. After giving the potatoes some time to sit on the stove, we barely had to do five minutes of work — you don't even have to peel them! It's another great make-ahead dish from the queen of hosting.  Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's Parmesan smashed potatoes here. And Garten's roasted rosemary potatoes are the easiest Thanksgiving side dish. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider If you're looking for something a little more classic, we recommend trying Garten's rosemary roasted potatoes instead.  The recipe requires only a few basic ingredients: small red- and white-skinned potatoes, garlic, olive oil, and fresh rosemary leaves. The golden potatoes looked gorgeous when they came out of the oven and were an instant crowd-pleaser. They had a deliciously crispy exterior that gave way to a warm, creamy center, while the rosemary added a surprising burst of flavor to the dish. Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's rosemary roasted potatoes here. But if you want to try our favorite Barefoot Contessa potato dish, you have to make Garten's potato-fennel gratin. Anneta Konstantinides/Business Insider Garten's potato-fennel gratin recipe appeared in her very first cookbook, "The Barefoot Contessa Cookbook."  It only requires a few main ingredients: russet potatoes, one small fennel bulb, yellow onion, Gruyère cheese, and heavy cream. The gratin is deliciously creamy and satisfying thanks to the Gruyère, and the potatoes are perfectly cooked. The fennel also adds a lovely, mild sweetness that cuts through the cheese's saltiness. Garten says her gratin can be cooked the day before and reheated for 30 minutes — perfect if you want to save some time on Thanksgiving.  Get the full recipe for Ina Garten's potato-fennel gratin here. When it comes to dessert, we think these massive chocolate-chip cookies are certainly impressive. Rachel Askinasi/Business Insider What makes these cookies special is that they're super thin and ripple out from the middle to the edges. This wrinkly effect is due to Garten's tip of banging the pan on a counter or stovetop several times during baking.  These cookies were both sweet and salty, with a texture that was crispy, flaky, crunchy, and gooey. events.title: Microsoft and Intel deepen collaboration to deliver differentiated Azure infrastructure
events.summary: November 18, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft and Intel deepen collaboration to deliver differentiated Azure infrastructure The two companies are working together to develop differentiated capabilities in Azure and system-level optimizations, tailoring infrastructure to the performance, efficiency, scalability and security requirements of cloud and AI Microsoft Source | 4 minutes REDMOND, Wash., and SANTA CLARA, Calif. – November 17, 2026 — Microsoft (Nasdaq: MSFT) and Intel (Nasdaq: INTC) today announced an expansion of their decades-long collaboration under a long-term agreement to advance select areas of Azure infrastructure for growing cloud and AI demand. Microsoft is the first company to announce use of Intel Foundry’s EMIB (Embedded Multi-die Interconnect Bridge) advanced packaging technology for Azure first-party silicon. Bringing together Intel silicon and EMIB capabilities with Microsoft’s cloud engineering, the agreement confirms multi-year Intel® Xeon® supply capacity – including instances of next generation server CPUs, codenamed Diamond Rapids – and expands collaboration across the Azure roadmap and Intel-based Azure hardware systems. Microsoft will also collaborate with Intel on Intel Xeon with Compute Express Link (CXL) to drive greater memory efficiency and system-level innovation across Azure, as well as Intel QuickAssist (Intel QAT) and confidential computing. This work further advances existing memory and database performance, including: Up to 2.3x greater performance 1 and memory flexibility for demanding workloads in Azure M-series v4 virtual machines with CXL memory and Intel Flat Memory Mode in Xeon 6 processors. Improved performance and reliability with up to 2.5x faster SQL backups 2 on Azure through the first Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) enabled virtual machines in the cloud. Virtual machine memory and CPU register state encryption as confidential VMs move between hosts through Intel Trust Domain Extensions (Intel TDX). Together, these investments are designed to provide Microsoft customers a more predictable, scalable and resilient infrastructure foundation, with compute optimized for demanding cloud and AI workloads, more efficient memory and stronger capabilities for protecting sensitive workloads. “Our customers need infrastructure built around the workloads that matter to them. Our longstanding collaboration with Intel brings together advanced packaging, custom compute, memory and security capabilities to support Azure compute and continued innovation across Azure. Together, we are connecting silicon and systems engineering to move the industry forward and meet the growing demand for Cloud + AI computing for our customers,” said Saurabh Dighe, CVP, Azure System & Architecture, Microsoft. “Microsoft and Intel share a clear view of where AI infrastructure is headed–increasingly complex systems designed through the co-optimization of silicon, packaging, compute memory and software,” said Naga Chandrasekaran, EVP, Chief Technology and Operations Officer and General Manager of Intel Foundry. “Through use of our advanced packaging capabilities with EMIB to scale future generations of Azure infrastructure, Intel and Microsoft can combine the flexibility of heterogeneous integration with the manufacturing scale required for the AI era—giving customers new levels of performance and economics when interacting with Azure.” About Microsoft Microsoft enables digital transformation for the era of an intelligent cloud and an intelligent edge. Its mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. Microsoft delivers cloud platforms, AI capabilities, productivity tools, and business applications that help organizations innovate, improve agility, and drive meaningful outcomes at scale. About Intel Intel (Nasdaq: INTC) designs and manufactures advanced semiconductors that connect and power the modern world. Every day, our engineers create new technologies that enhance and shape the future of computing to enable new possibilities for every customer we serve. Learn more at intel.com . For more information, press only: Microsoft Media Relations, We.
