events.title: I'm a James Bond fan who visited 14 filming locations in London. It felt like I was in the 007 universe.
events.summary: At the Barbican, where a scene in "Quantum of Solace" was filmed. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider With Robert Pattinson announced as the next James Bond, excitement around the spy franchise is high. London is the home of 007, and as a result, a lot of filming took place in the city. I visited most of the London-based filming locations from Daniel Craig's Bond films. Robert Pattinson is officially the next James Bond . Now, as we prepare to herald Bond's next era, I set out to visit as many of the most iconic and lesser-known London filming locations from Daniel Craig's movies as I could. I've always loved the James Bond movies, especially the Daniel Craig ones. As a Londoner, I found this tour a fun way to immerse myself in the 007 universe and see my city in a whole new way. Although the Bond films are known for their stunning locations around the world, from Lake Como in Italy to the Atacama Desert in Chile, the home of 007 is, after all, London. "Casino Royale" (2006), Craig's first Bond movie, was not filmed in London, so the locations below are from his four subsequent movies. Some are iconic tourist landmarks , while others are lesser-known back streets and restaurants, often in fancy parts of the city. Although filming also took place in areas such as Camden and Canary Wharf , I primarily stuck to central London locations. If you're planning a trip to London and want to do your own Bond tour, it's doable in a day, although you'll need comfortable shoes. This route took me around five hours with two pit stops and a short visit inside the National Gallery. Here are some of the locations from Craig's Bond movies in London. My first stop was the Barbican Sculpture Court, which served as an MI6 setting in "Quantum of Solace" (2008). The Barbican, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider This is where M and Tanner discussed Bond's mission. The brutalist estate is one of my all-time favorite spots in London, and I always recommend it to people visiting the city. It's a residential complex that also has a center with restaurants, bars, a library, theater, and a cinema. This parking lot ramp was the entrance to MI6's temporary underground headquarters in "Skyfall" (2012). Entrance to the car park by Smithfield Rotunda Garden. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider I found the parking lot not exactly scenic, but it's located right across from Smithfield Market, London's famous and historic wholesale meat market. I love this part of London — the City of London it's called — precisely because of how old parts of it are. In "Spectre" (2015), Moneypenny visits Bond at this Notting Hill apartment. Stanley Gardens, Notting Hill. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider The fictional apartment is located in London's beautiful Notting Hill neighborhood. Nothing short of the best, of course, for one of MI6's most elite agents. It's one of my favorite areas to stroll around, though it's mostly residential, so it's important to be respectful of the residents . Charing Cross Station was where one of Bond's stunt sequences in "Skyfall" was filmed. Entrance to Charing Cross Underground Station. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider I feel like spy films set in London always feature a chase scene on the London Underground, which makes me half-expect to see some sort of espionage whenever I'm on an escalator. Some of the "Skyfall" chase scene was also filmed at the 007 Stage in Pinewood. In "Skyfall," the National Gallery is the place where Bond and Q have a secret meeting. The National Gallery, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider The precise location inside the gallery is in Room 34 . It's a gorgeously ornate room with teal walls displaying British paintings from 1740 to 1800. The seats are different now from when Skyfall was filmed, but I still sat on a bench in the same location as Bond and Q did. The National Gallery also has free entry, making it a perfect spot to visit. Close to the National Gallery, Rules Restaurant is where Moneypenny and Q find M in "Spectre." Rules Restaurant, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider Founded in 1798, it's the oldest restaurant in London and serves traditional British meals, making it a fitting spot for the movie. It's on the pricier side, so I haven't eaten there, but one day I'll be sure to dine — just to feel like I'm in a Bond movie. Also in "Spectre," the Freemasons' Hall doubles as the Foreign Office. The Freemasons' Hall, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider While it might look like any old building from the outside, the interior of Freemasons' Hall is very ornate, with Art Deco design. The Bond movies feature many scenes inside London's historic venues and members' clubs. Reform Club, 104 Pall Mall, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider 104 Pall Mall was a government office in "Quantum of Solace." Ian Fleming, who wrote the books, used to dine at a members' club previously located at 104 Pall Mall . In "No Time to Die" (2021), the British Academy serves as Madeleine Swan's practice. British Academy, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider The road the British Academy is located on is near Pall Mall. The area is known for its exclusive and traditional gentlemen's clubs. Walking around in my jeans and trainers, I felt a little underdressed. Near Trafalgar Square, a building on this road is the Hildebrand Safe House in "Spectre." Roya Shahidi/Business Insider The actual building is on the left of this photo and overlooks Trafalgar Square. In the same movie , the road pictured is where Swann and Bond have their final farewell. Bond parks his car in Whitehall Court in "No Time to Die." Roya Shahidi/Business Insider The luxury Corinthia Hotel is visible in the background. Other scenes in "No Time to Die" were also filmed in this area , which contains the headquarters of the Metropolitan Police, Scotland Yard. The iconic Westminster Bridge features in "Spectre." Westminister Bridge, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider This is where Bond confronts the supervillain Blofeld . I don't often cross this bridge because it's always full of tourists taking photos of the London Eye and the Houses of Parliament, which means it takes longer to get through the crowds. But whenever I visit, I always think it's a magnificent sight. And now I'll think of Bond, too. Across the river in Waterloo is Q's home in "No Time to Die." 42 Roupell Street, London. Roya Shahidi/Business Insider While you mostly see the interior of his house, you can also see this road in the movie. It's right by Waterloo Station, which is close to lots of cultural, dining, and night-time spots I frequent, so I was surprised by how residential it was. The skyscraper scene in "Skyfall" is actually filmed in London, not Shanghai, in Broadgate Tower. Broadgate Tower, London. events.title: Sony’s updated turntable is an easy entry into the world of vinyl
events.summary: Record players and other retro tech are making a strong comeback, and I’ve recently rejoined the world of vinyl collecting. Lately, I’ve noticed myself turning to Spotify less frequently, so it felt like the perfect time to start using a record player again. Choosing a turntable can be quite overwhelming, especially for beginners. That’s where Sony’s new PS-LX3BT turntable comes in. Since 2019, Sony’s PS-LX310BT has been a go-to choice for vinyl newbies. Now that it has been discontinued, the PS-LX3BT emerges as its successor, keeping the same beginner-friendly approach while adding a few modern upgrades. Currently priced at $399.99, the PS-LX3BT is designed for people who want to enjoy vinyl without getting too caught up in the technical side of things. It’s also a good option for those looking to upgrade from their first inexpensive turntable without having to learn how to set up or customize a more complicated audio system. One of its biggest selling points is how easy it is to use. The PS-LX3BT features automatic playback, so you simply press start and the tonearm lifts, moves into position, and drops onto the first track for you. There’s no need to manually position the needle or worry about getting everything just right. It’s a small convenience, but one that makes the experience much less intimidating for newcomers. Sony has also made a few welcome changes compared with its predecessor. The PS-LX3BT now uses USB-C for power and supports Qualcomm’s aptX Adaptive Bluetooth codec, allowing it to transmit audio at up to 24-bit/96kHz. It also has a traditional phono output alongside Bluetooth, so you can choose between a wired speaker setup and listening wirelessly. One slightly strange design decision, however, is the repositioning of the start, stop, and tonearm buttons. On the older model, these were placed outside the dust cover. Now they’re underneath it, meaning you’ll have to lift the cover just to press start. It’s not a huge inconvenience, but still kind of annoying. The turntable also offers USB connectivity for digitizing your vinyl collection. Connect it to a computer, and you can convert your records into digital audio files, which is useful if you want to preserve older records or listen to your collection on the go. My biggest disappointment is the lack of a built-in speaker. It would have been nice to have everything included for someone just getting started. You’ll need to buy speakers (and possibly an amplifier) or compatible Bluetooth headphones separately, so keep that added cost in mind. If you’re searching for a more affordable and beginner-friendly automatic record player, there are cheaper options, such as this $179 option from Audio-Technica. But overall, Sony’s PS-LX3BT is a solid choice for anyone ready to dive into the world of vinyl for the first time. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
events.summary: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. Where you recover is the other half Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it. Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone. Meeting all of this is harder than it looks Put the pieces together and the bar is high: Backups you have actually tested Recovery times you can state and meet And a clean, separate place to recover to Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations. Where cloud disaster recovery fits Cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home. Where to start Insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives. events.title: Largest US egg producer to cull 1.8 million birds after bird flu outbreak
events.summary: Cal-Maine reports avian influenza at Florida site, with 2.7 percent of its total flock affected. Cal-Maine Foods, the largest egg producer in the United States, has said it would cull 1.8 million birds after avian influenza was detected at one of its facilities in Florida. On Wednesday, the company said the 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 young hens being culled account for 2.7 percent of its flock. Production at the facility will be temporarily halted. list 1 of 4 Carney signals progress on Canada-US trade deal talks as midterms loom list 2 of 4 US urges China to honour Busan trade deal commitments list 3 of 4 Australia warns H5N1 likely to spread after first mass mortality episode list 4 of 4 Australia pledges action on H5N1 after bird flu case confirmed Cal-Maine said in a statement that it would coordinate with other production and distribution facilities to minimise disruption across the company. The risk bird flu poses to human health is low. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there have been 74 human cases since February 2024, with no evidence of human-to-human transmission. However, the virus continues to pose a significant challenge to the US poultry and egg industries. Some 21.5 million birds have been affected this year, following a historic surge in outbreaks in late 2024 and early 2025 that sharply reduced the number of egg-laying hens. Approximately 50.7 million laying hens were lost between mid-October 2024 and early March 2025, when egg prices in the US reached a record high of $6.23 per dozen. The current average retail price of eggs is $2.32 per dozen, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Despite the announcement that production at the Florida facility would be temporarily halted, Cal-Maine’s stock rose 5.3 percent in early trading.

events.title: Pax Silica is the new face of US imperialism in the Philippines
events.summary: Behind promises of jobs and investment lie threats to ancestral lands, water security and national sovereignty. The Philippine government is promising jobs and billions in investment through the United States-led Pax Silica initiative. But protesters see a very different future: threatened ancestral lands, environmental destruction and deeper dependence on Washington. On November 15, ahead of Donald Trump’s visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit, Philippine police arrested more than 200 demonstrators opposing the initiative. The arrests were part of a wider crackdown on protests against a project that critics see as another form of US neo-imperialism. The Pax Silica initiative is a US-led coalition aimed at securing supply chains and countering China’s strength in critical minerals, semiconductors and other technologies essential to AI infrastructure. The Philippines joined the initiative in April 2026, with a proposed industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac province, forming part of it. The Philippine government has promoted the proposed industrial hub as essential to economic development, projecting that it could generate more than 130,000 jobs and attract up to $70bn in investment once fully developed, a process expected to take decades. The proposed Pax Silica industrial hub, which covers approximately 1,618 hectares, raises concerns not only about national sovereignty but also about the displacement of local communities, environmental repercussions, Indigenous land rights and human security. Critics see the project as taking land from local communities and farmers to serve foreign interests. The Aeta Hungey community in Sapang Kawayan, for example, faces relocation from land it has occupied for generations. Around 200 residents could lose access to their homes, farmland, water sources and burial grounds, while the community’s efforts to secure formal recognition of its ancestral land, dating back to 1994, remain unresolved. Another major concern is water consumption. According to the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), the proposed industrial hub could require 65–90 million litres of water daily. Although the BCDA plans to meet this demand through surface-water harvesting, concerns remain about the pressure on water resources, particularly during droughts. The Philippines is already vulnerable to drought, water shortages, agricultural disruption and climate change. On November 4, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) confirmed that a very strong El Nino was present and expected to persist into the first half of 2027. The Philippine government must respond to the pressing needs of Filipinos instead of becoming a pawn of the United States in its geopolitical rivalry with China. Southeast Asia is a focal point of competition between the two major powers, with the Philippines serving as a key US ally. Pax Silica would position the Philippines as a central node in an emerging AI Cold War with China. Projected as an avenue for economic progress, Pax Silica could also serve as a tool for the military expansion of the US in the region, particularly in the Philippines. Semiconductors are used in modern military production and are essential components of weapon systems in modern warfare. During his November 17 ASEAN speech, Trump highlighted US agreements across the region involving critical minerals, energy and technology, while describing the Philippines as a longstanding key ally. He also pointed to increased defence cooperation between the two countries. This cooperation already rests in part on the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), which allows US forces access to agreed Philippine military facilities. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr also emphasised the depth of the relationship between the two countries, rooted in shared history and values. Describing the extent of US influence in Philippine life, he said, “There is no part of our lives in the Philippines that is not involved with the United States in some way, in some shape or form or another.” An unexamined alliance compromises national interests, particularly those affecting the lives of the Filipino people. Economic development should not come at the expense of human security, sovereignty and environmental sustainability. Against this backdrop, a broad, multisectoral opposition movement against Pax Silica has emerged and is gaining momentum. It brings together diverse sectors, including Indigenous peoples, farmers, workers, scientists, environmentalists, faith leaders, students, and progressive activists. The protests have also spread to university campuses. On November 13, university students staged coordinated campus walkouts across the Philippines. Among the major participating universities were the University of the Philippines, De La Salle University, Ateneo de Manila University, University of Santo Tomas, and Far Eastern University, among others.

events.title: Elon Musk says he has a way to fix the aging US air traffic control system
events.summary: Elon Musk says his Starlink terminals would help fix issues with the US air traffic control system. Johannes Neudecker/picture alliance via Getty Images The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday following a major network outage. Elon Musk said Monday that he previously offered Starlink terminals to help the FAA's aging network. But it's unclear whether that would have prevented Friday's outage, with investigations ongoing. Elon Musk says Starlink terminals could be the answer to fixing the struggling US air traffic control system after last week's outage. Nearly 20,000 flights were canceled after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop last Friday. No airplanes were allowed to take off for over four hours — the largest shutdown since September 11, 2001. While the root cause is still under investigation, the FAA said its legacy equipment became unstable after its network was flooded with connection attempts — disrupting major air traffic control centers. Investigators are examining sites in Texas and Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris had been installing a new router. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said last Friday that the country has "old switches, old routers" and asked for $50 billion to build a new system. Musk previously called out the aging technology in February 2025 after a minor system outage. On Tuesday night, he reshared that X post, adding "I wrote this 18 months ago." The SpaceX CEO also said on Monday: "Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec. Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were." However, it is unclear how Starlink terminals could have prevented the data flood that caused this weekend's disruption. The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Musk's remarks. In March 2025, the FAA said it was testing Starlink at sites in Alaska, Oklahoma City, and Atlantic City — through the same network managed by L3 Harris, which broke down last weekend. The Alaska deployment was at "non-safety-critical sites," intended to provide more reliable weather information for pilots and FAA stations in remote areas. "To update our air traffic control system, it will require multiple companies and multiple technologies," the FAA said at the time. "That is why we are testing multiple communication technologies, including satellites, fiber, and wireless to ensure the safety of the national airspace system." Starlink terminals can provide useful connections, particularly at remote sites. But that is different from replacing the entire network that links air-traffic-control facilities and carries aircraft radio and radar feeds. Plus, relying on Starlink for vital infrastructure hasn't worked perfectly for everyone. Ukraine uses Starshield , SpaceX's military-focused satellite service, for critical battlefield communications, including with interceptor drones. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this month that Ukraine had detected renewed restrictions on the service in Russian-occupied parts of the country. He said interceptor drones were losing connection with their operators when traveling faster than 100 mph, preventing them from catching some Russian jet-powered drones. "And this means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed," Zelenskyy said. Musk has said Starshield is "owned and controlled" by the US government, and that limits on its use are ultimately decided by President Donald Trump. Trump denied ordering any slowdown. "It wasn't me," he told reporters last month. "And I don't think it was Elon." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Hakeem Jeffries formally nominated as first Black US House speaker
events.summary: The New York congressman is nominated after Democrats gained control of Congress in this month’s midterm elections. Washington, DC, United States – Hakeem Jeffries has become the first Black lawmaker officially nominated for speaker of the US House of Representatives, marking a milestone in the country’s political history. In a closed-door vote on Wednesday, the 56-year-old New York congressman secured his party’s nomination for the post just weeks after Democrats scored sweeping victories in the midterm elections, reclaiming control of both chambers of the US Congress. After voting concluded, Jeffries took to social media to thank his fellow Democrats for their support. “Together, we will deliver bold change. And make a big difference in the lives of the American people!” he wrote in a post on X. Amid growing dissent among progressives over his leadership, Jeffries confirmed plans to force members of his party to take a recorded vote on Wednesday. Some of those members, most of whom were elected this month, declined to say whether they would support Jeffries. Several said they wanted a leader who would support bold, populist policies they had campaigned on. One of the most vocal holdouts, Congressman-elect Don Leonard of Ohio, refused to commit to Jeffries unless he received guarantees on some progressive priorities, including halting US military aid to Israel and reforming campaign finance standards set by the Supreme Court case Citizens United. “Unless Speaker Jeffries is willing to commit to enforcing our nation’s laws like the Leahy Law against Israeli genocide in Gaza, unless the speaker is willing to get to the heart of this crisis, which is Citizens United, he will not have my vote,” the Ohio Democrat said in a video posted to social media. Jeffries has received pushback within some Democratic circles over his record on Israel and ties to pro-Israel lobbying groups, like AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. During an interview with The Atlantic magazine on Tuesday, Jeffries addressed some of that criticism, calling for “dramatic change” in the Middle East and a two-state solution. Despite some opposition in Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries received overwhelming support from the House Democratic Caucus with 251 members voting to back his candidacy. Only 11 members opposed it. Seven of those who voted against Jeffries included newly-elected Democrats Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania and Claire Valdez of New York. Those members released a statement, which was shared with Al Jazeera, detailing their opposition they said was over failure to receive commitments from Jeffries on policies like “Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics or ending the genocide in Gaza”. “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership”, the soon-to-be lawmakers wrote. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no”. Another future member, Frederick Haynes of Texas, was included in the joint-statement against Jeffries’ nomination, but clarified later, in his own statement, he “narrowly” missed Wednesday’s vote due to illness. Most Democrats, however, praised Jeffries’ nomination for speaker, which will put him on track to become one of Donald Trump’s top political opponents during the final two years of his presidency. Outgoing Congresswoman Nancy Pelosi, who served for eight years as the first female speaker during two non-consecutive terms, marked the historic moment with a social media post, which included a photo of her holding Jeffries hand. “Congratulations, Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries!” she wrote. Just before the vote, Jeffries took to social media to post a Bible verse from the book of Corinthians reading,” For we walk by faith, not by sight.” In 2023, Jeffries was put forward by Democrats as their pick to succeed former US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, who was ousted by his fellow Republicans in favour of the chamber’s current speaker, Mike Johnson. Wednesday’s vote, however, means Jeffries has now been formally nominated by members of his party. Jeffries is poised to replace Johnson as speaker when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3 with a Democratic majority and a vote on the new speaker is held in the full chamber.

events.title: House Democrats formally nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
events.summary: House Democrats voted at a closed-door caucus meeting Wednesday morning to nominate Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as their candidate for speaker. Why it matters: It's a symbolic but significant step that suggests Jeffries has the votes he needs to be elected the first Black House speaker on Jan. 3. Jeffries won 251 of the 262 votes cast, putting him comfortably above the 218 votes he needs to win on the House floor in January. The vote was tallied at Jeffries' request . His allied had initially hoped he would be elected by acclamation, but the Democratic leader changed tack at the 11th hour and decided to call his detractors' bluff. Between the lines: Wednesday's caucus vote was a secret ballot. On Jan. 3, each House member will have to stand up during a televised proceeding and announce who they are voting for. That could be difficult for the members — particularly progressives — who have been flooded with calls and emails from constituents urging them not to vote for him. Only a handful of incoming House members, including Reps.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) and Don Leonard (D-Ohio), have outright said they will oppose Jeffries thus far.

events.title: Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least five people
events.summary: Most of the casualties were in strikes on Odesa that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as ‘brutal’. Russian air attacks across Ukraine have killed at least five people, authorities said, a day after a Ukrainian strike on Russia’s Kerch Bridge killed two and caused part of the structure to collapse. In the southern city of Odesa, at least four people were killed and 13 others wounded in Russian air strikes, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the “brutal and deliberate” attack also targeted first responders. list 1 of 3 Russian attacks kill three in Ukraine, EU accuses Moscow of prolonging war list 2 of 3 What will Europe do next in Ukraine? list 3 of 3 Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates Oleg Kiper, the head of the Odesa region’s military administration, said three Russian strikes hit the city’s “historic centre”. Odesa city council said one of the strikes hit a UNESCO-protected area, causing a car to catch fire and blowing out hundreds of windows in at least seven buildings. Ukrainian emergency services shared images showing wounded people on stretchers, buildings with shattered windows and firefighters extinguishing a blaze on a rooftop. “There were double-tap strikes after first responders and police officers had already arrived at the scene,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. He said the attack served as “further proof of what the Russians really want and how they truly regard diplomatic efforts”. In the southeastern Zaporizhia region, a Russian drone strike killed a woman and injured a man in the town of Kushuhum, local military administration official Mykhailo Semykin said. Attacks on the region also forced local authorities to order families with children to leave the village of Balabyne, he said. “We are talking about 85 children from 80 families. In total, the evacuation affects 184 people,” he wrote on Telegram. In northern Ukraine’s Rivne region, 80 settlements were left without electricity after a Russian attack, authorities said. No deaths or injuries were reported. Ukraine’s Energy Ministry says Russia has launched more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September. New power outages had been recorded in Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhia, Kharkiv, Sumy, Rivne, and Cherkasy regions in the last 24 hours, Interfax reported on Wednesday. Russia has increased attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in the lead-up to winter, in a strategy the United Nations said amounted to war crimes. “The situation in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions remains extremely difficult. Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore power supply as soon as possible, but repeated attacks are significantly complicating repair work,” Ukraine’s energy ministry said. The attacks came a day after Ukraine attacked Russia’s Kerch Bridge – a symbolic road-and-rail link from Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula – killing two people. Europe proposes $45bn loan for Ukraine As the warring sides continue to trade long-range attacks, the European Commission has proposed a new 45 billion euro ($49.5bn) loan to Ukraine to help fill a 70 billion euro ($76.8bn) funding gap for next year. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Ukraine would only need to repay the loan after Russia had paid reparations for damage caused since it launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. “We very much hope for the swift adoption of this decision by the European Parliament and the Council and count on the support of all EU member states,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. Although Ukraine is not officially on the agenda during a tripartite meeting between US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Beijing, the talks are being watched closely in the Ukrainian capital. Reporting from Kyiv on Wednesday, Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said there were concerns in Ukraine that the meeting “could place the Russian President in a similar category of world powers and world leaders as the United States and China and what the optics mean for Ukraine”. MacAlpine said parallel meetings to negotiate the end of the Ukraine war were due to begin in Berlin on Thursday. “The US delegates are reportedly travelling there to meet with the Ukrainian delegation, potentially with some of the leaders of Europe,” she said. The agenda is expected to address Ukrainian demands for security guarantees and the prisoner swap agreed in Abu Dhabi last week, MacAlpine said.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Next OS release will bundle modern successor, giving admins a compatibility checklist to work through Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware 50 minutes ago Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action 9 hours ago Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal 18 hours ago Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI! 20 hours ago Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open 1 day ago Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement. It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, " be removed from a future version of Windows ," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default. After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties. PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless. PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover , who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude. PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain. The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time. Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts. Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft. Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself. "Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead. events.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
events.summary: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us. And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof. Nothing seemed to animate him much, which is why, when I asked, in slight desperation, about his recent experience as a consultant on a successful TV comedy show, I was amazed to watch the man come alive. Thrilled; he was absolutely bloody thrilled to revisit the excitement of being on set and get into it about the actors and the show-runners. And could I believe they were still writing an episode right up until filming (I could) and had I ever experienced anything like the buzz of a set? At the end of the day, all these poor men want is to get into showbiz. I mention all this in light of the ongoing hoo-ha over Jensen Huang, the disgraced former head of Nvidia who, at the time of writing, will not, it seems, be allowed back as CEO after allegations surfaced of the 63-year-old conducting several extramarital affairs, one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees. If true, the spy thing is an unusual twist, but in all other respects, the story of Huang’s fall from grace tracks so exactly with the industry standard that it should be a mandatory module at business school. Namely: how to avoid becoming the next male tech billionaire to upgrade his wardrobe, ditch his wife of 40 years and tank the stock . The surprising thing in the case of Huang is that, held up against the likes of Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, the co-founder of Nvidia was supposed to be a quieter, less obnoxious, more thoughtful billionaire, who put modesty at the core of his values. In a profile in the New Yorker a few years ago, Huang insisted on doing the interview at a branch of the fast food chain Denny’s, where – as he pointed out – he’d once worked as a dishwasher. You get the picture and are probably thinking of good old Bill Gates, as I am, a man whose dorky knitwear and long marriage to Melinda made him a forerunner in that same role of decent, quiet, uxorious – oh … Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more In Huang’s case, one glaring indicator that his humble persona was glitching was a wardrobe made up almost entirely of leather jackets, which speaks to a very particular moment in the billionaire’s life cycle. They do love a sartorial trademark, these men, to the extent that you wonder if they sit around brainstorming accessories to use as their new lewk . Beanie? Too casual. Fingerless gloves? Too weird. What if a jaunty waistcoat could be my thing? Huang reportedly has well over 30 leather jackets , including the $9,000 one from Tom Ford, the shiny crocodile-embossed one that looks like something your four-year-old daughter might wear to a party, and the cropped at the hip one to show off Huang’s trim waist, which, of course, takes discipline to maintain at his age. And it’s discipline, not morality, we’re talking about. The leather jacket is harmless except as a signifier of a whole range of allegedly poor personal decisions Huang made that were not in the shareholders’ interests. What I find funny about this is that, when it really comes down to it, a group of people who describe themselves lovingly as “disruptors” are the most stultifyingly conventional people on Earth; all they want is to be popular, mostly with hot women, but also more generally with the cool crowd. Just look at Bezos this week , inserting himself with almost endearing irrelevance into the James Bond conversation: “It was me! I picked him! I bought the James Bond name and then I picked the new one because, at some level, and I hope you all understand this, I AM James Bond.” Of course you are, luvvie. You enjoy it. Still, at least this famously unfunny crowd can occasionally give us a laugh, as Jensen Huang did this week in his statement, in which he said that, if it was deemed in the interests of the US, he would be “honoured” to return to Nvidia as CEO. Hahahaha, how noble of him, that’s actually a good one.

events.title: Cathedral's staff review 'difficult but necessary'
events.summary: Gloucester Cathedral will increasingly use events like concerts to fund the buildings maintenance There will be no compulsory redundancies at a cathedral despite a restructure of staff, leaders have said. Gloucester Cathedral, which costs about £10,500 a day to open, has been undergoing an organisational restructure due to rising costs as some staff have opted for voluntary redundancies. It comes after cathedral bosses across the West of England said they had also been feeling the pinch, forcing them to find creative ways to raise money. Dean of Gloucester Reverend Andrew Zihni said the decision to reshape the cathedral's money was "difficult but necessary" to ensure its future. Could you live under deep-sea pressure for 28 days? Published 13 hours ago How to reduce fire risks at home this Christmas Published 14 hours ago Reduced street cleaning due to depot fire Published 1 day ago Zihni said that visitors to the cathedral are unlikely to notice any changes. Cathedral chiefs said the restructure involved a review of staff roles and responsibilities, as well as how the organisation is run. A small number of staff had been made voluntarily redundant as a result of the changes. In a statement, cathedral leaders said that these had been "very difficult decisions," but that these changes will ensure it will continue to serve the "city, county and wider community for generations to come". Speaking to BBC Radio Gloucestershire, Zihni said the cathedral had a number of costs, including heating, maintenance and staffing, as well as safeguarding, education, worship, music and heritage. "We have to raise the money year on year through donations, visitors, grants, fundraising and other income because we don't have any automatic funding either from the national church or the government," he said. Gloucester Cathedral is not the only one in the country with high maintenance costs. Anna Pitt, executive director of the Association of English Cathedrals, said it costs more than £30,000 a day to "simply open the doors" at Canterbury Cathedral and York Minster. "The scale of what cathedrals offer is considerable. They employ 6,000 people across the sector, welcome nearly 10 million visitors each year and are open 365 days a year," said Pitt. Reverend Andrew Zhini was made Dean of Gloucester Cathedral in 2023 Zihni said the Chapter, who are responsible for running the cathedral, are also looking at ways to "diversify their income stream and develop commercial angles". He said: "People may have seen some of it already with the concerts we've been hosting in the cathedral, but there isn't a separation between the commercial activity and the regular activity," he said. events.title: Democrats turn the page on Biden
events.summary: David’s view The FAA meltdown that stranded many Democrats in Denver last weekend highlighted a grand political irony. Joe Biden gave his life to a political party that doesn’t want to think about him. Donald Trump’s Republicans want people to keep Biden on their minds. “The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, as the airlines slowly recovered from their forced grounding. Asked for contrition, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said he took “responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations.” Blaming Biden for problems that haven’t been fixed since he returned to Delaware comes easy to this White House. In Denver, where Democrats gathered to take a midterm victory lap while looking ahead to 2028, the Biden years were mentioned rarely, usually in sweeping statements about how Democrats shouldn’t just restore the country as it was before Trump. “Capitalism in America now is fundamentally broken for most people,” said Gina Raimondo, Biden’s secretary of Commerce for four years. They wouldn’t trash the guy, but the idea that he could have “restored the soul of America” and banished MAGA felt a little embarrassing. I didn’t hear any Democrat get asked about , Biden’s third memoir, which arrived this week to scathing reviews. This isn’t another one of those reviews, though the book is a real chore to get through. (Get hyped for sentences like this: “My audience in the State Department auditorium responded with generous applause.“) Biden remains one of the last men in America who believes that he could have won the 2024 election. It was the “pundits,” not a majority of voters, who decided by mid-2023 that he was too old to continue in the job. Early in the memoir, reflecting on how he was ready to win the presidency on his third try, Biden paraphrases Heraclitus on how “a man cannot step in the same river twice.” If you see the inconsistency between that, and the insistence that only the man who had beat Trump once could beat him again, then you are not Joe Biden. “I could have fought to the convention,” Biden writes. “Taken the fight to the floor. Forced a vote. And probably prevailed.” He ruminates over how he won more votes as a write-in candidate in New Hampshire than Trump won in a contested primary: “I was supposed to be LBJ in 1968. Run out of the race.” This is old news. Democrats now agree that Biden was selfish to seek a new term in his 80s. What was the legacy of his one term? That’s much more contested. The former president is still proud that he fended off the “uncommitted” movement that denied them primary voters in a protest of his support for Israel’s war in Gaza. That was a tribute to his leadership. The collapse of Democratic support for the war since he left office can be blamed on Benjamin Netanyahu, not him. “I hope Israel wakes up,” Biden writes. “The days of American leaders like me—passionate defenders of Israel to the core—are passing.” He has less to say about a cause adopted during 2020 – leading America through a “racial reckoning” after the murder of George Floyd. Biden recounts that he signed seventeen executive orders on his first day as president, but only focuses on five of them, related to climate, COVID, immigration, and the economy. There’s no mention of his order for a “comprehensive approach to advancing equity for all, including people of color and others who have been historically underserved.” The word “equity” doesn’t appear in the memoir. Biden argues instead that “that every one of my legislative accomplishments had justice baked in,” including “equal access to vaccines.” In the words of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY, who Biden repeatedly thanks for supporting him when other Democrats wanted to end his campaign: Woke one was crazy. Gender gets the same treatment. Biden, who had called anti-transgender discrimination “the civil rights issue of our time,” never uses the word “transgender” in his memoir. He doesn’t mention his day one executive order that banned discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Rachel Levine, the first transgender American confirmed to an executive branch position by the Senate, doesn’t appear in the book. Sarah McBride, D-Del., the first transgender American elected to Congress and a longtime Biden ally, is mentioned only in a list of winners he called on Election Night 2024. You could read this as an endorsement of McBride’s political strategy , which acknowledges the backlash to the LGBTQ+ rights movement and makes Republicans the culture war aggressors. Biden, who did prove his doubters wrong by finally winning the presidency in 2020, did so with a progressive agenda and focus that was hard to identify in his pre-2020 career. Biden doesn’t say that his party lost chances to build broader support and prevent a Trump comeback by going too far to the left. You just figure that out for yourself, between the bits about the party and the people not appreciating him enough. He now says that he rescued the country, not that he tried to transform it. “Far from an open-border policy, I kept in place the cornerstone of the Trump border and immigration policy for most of my presidency,” Biden writes. The high-flying promises of 2020, like a “surge” of asylum seekers denied entry to the country by Trump, are not here. What does Biden think of Trump rolling back temporary protected status for Haitian refugees? He doesn’t mention his expansion of the Temporary Protected Status program at all. The next Democratic primary, well underway already, begins with the assumption that it made too many mistakes in 2020. The tougher internal debate is about the mistakes made after it united behind Biden, and beat Trump. We now know what Biden thinks about that, and his role in the process is over. Notable In The Atlantic, long-time Biden reporter Matt Viser reviewed the memoir and reflected on what Biden doesn’t acknowledge: “If he had run in 2024 and won, he would now be a visibly frail 83-year-old man, fighting a vicious form of cancer.”

events.title: Tech leaders form tribal loyalties after Huang ouster
events.summary: Liz’s view One former politico-turned-tech executive who had just come from Washington told me this week: “Out here, the question is whether Jensen will be back at Nvidia by Christmas or whether it’ll take a little longer. In Washington, it’s whether he’s going to prison.” Huang does not currently face criminal charges, and it’s still unclear what he knew about Alice Huang’s alleged connections to Chinese intelligence. But that’s the gulf between DC and Silicon Valley right now, one we tried to bridge this week through tough interviews with people on both sides. We surely didn’t close it, but two things cleared up as the rain clouds moved out of Menlo Park. Tech executives, even those pushing to bring Huang back, have been chastened by the one-two punch of his downfall and the blue sweep in the midterm elections. And Washington is tired of their arrogance, or at least keenly aware that voters are. “What [people are] really against is this feeling that, ‘man, are the people building AI actually, really, truly on Team Human?’” said OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who did not sound like a CEO excited to go public even as his main rival, Anthropic, lists as soon as tomorrow. Even the #SaveJensen crowd at the top of Sand Hill Road was subdued. Bill Ackman, one of the first to rush to Huang’s defense, all but said he’d fire a CEO who lied to him as a board member. Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas said the US “ needs more Jensens ” but demurred when asked if Huang should return to Nvidia. Jeff Bezos thinks the job should go to an insider: “Outside CEOs in a complex company have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding.” Notable Many tech leaders are openly pushing for Huang’s return to Nvidia: A petition with more than 175,000 signatures calling for the Nvidia board to reinstate him includes Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick and Elon Musk as signatories.

events.title: I'm a professional baker who attended pastry school in France. Here are 7 tips for making the best pies.
events.summary: As a professional baker who attended pastry school, I've learned which techniques help create the best pies. jenifoto/Getty Images After attending pastry school in France, I've learned the secrets to making the best pies. I've found that using the coldest butter possible for the dough creates the flakiest crust. For busy baking seasons, I assemble and freeze fruit pies, so they're ready to bake weeks later. I'm a full-time baker who attended pastry school in France and worked in several bakeries in New York City. Pies are one of my favorite desserts to make for family and friends, no matter the occasion. Although they can seem intimidating, achieving a perfectly flaky crust and delicious filling comes down to a few simple techniques. Here are seven tips for making the best pies. For a flaky pie crust, I keep my butter cold. Allison Chen One of the most important things about making pie dough is keeping the butter as cold as possible. When the dough bakes, the water in the butter turns into steam, separating the crust into flaky layers. But if the butter melts at all before going into the oven, you won't get the same light, crisp texture. To ensure my crust is perfectly flaky, I always use cold butter straight from the fridge and try to work quickly when incorporating it into the flour. Instead of using my palms to break up the butter, I like to use my fingertips, since they conduct less heat. Luckily, the butter doesn't need to be fully mixed into the crust, since any visible chunks will turn into crispy flakes in the oven. I always chill the dough to prevent the crust from shrinking. 2GreenEyes/iStock One of the most common pie-baking problems is crust shrinkage, which can occur when overworked dough develops excessive gluten and contracts in the oven. To prevent this, I never stretch the dough to fit it into a pan. Instead, I lift it and let it settle into the corners — and if it isn't large enough, I gently roll it out a little. Additionally, I always refrigerate my pie dough after placing it in the pan, since that allows the gluten to relax while the butter firms up. Blind baking the crust helps avoid a soggy bottom. Allison Chen For pies with particularly wet fillings, like custard or pumpkin, I like to blind bake, or partially bake, the crust before adding the filling. This process gives the bottom of the crust a head start in the oven so it has time to develop structure and crisp up before coming into contact with the filling. Once the dough is in the pan, I line it with parchment paper and fill it with weights like dried beans or rice — since those keep the crust from puffing up or slumping as it bakes. After the edges have set, I remove the weights and continue baking the crust until the bottom begins to dry out and lightly brown. From there, the filling can be added to the partially baked crust and returned to the oven, following the recipe's instructions. I taste the fruit to help determine how much sugar to add to the filling. Alexandr Kolesnikov/Getty Images The key to a delicious pie is to taste the fruit before making the filling, so that I can adjust the amount of sugar accordingly. The sweetness of fruit can vary significantly depending on its variety, ripeness, and season. For example, a tart Granny Smith apple will need more sugar than many red apple varieties. If a fruit is particularly sweet, I like to reduce the sugar in the filling and add a squeeze of lemon juice . The acidity helps balance the sugar and brings out the fruit's natural flavor. Aluminum foil keeps the crust from burning. AnnaStills/iStock One of the challenges of baking a pie is making sure the crust and filling finish cooking at the same time. The edges of a pie crust are thinner and more exposed to the oven's heat, which means they often brown much faster than the rest of the dessert. If the edges of the crust get too dark before the pie is finished, I like to cover them with strips of aluminum foil , since that shields them from the oven's heat while allowing the rest of the pie to continue baking. Making pie dough in advance is a lifesaver when I'm short on time. Anna Mardo/Getty Images When preparing a big meal, the last thing I want to worry about is making pie dough from scratch while juggling everything else in the kitchen. So, to make my life a little easier, I like to make a large batch of dough, divide it into individual portions, and flatten each one into a disk before wrapping it tightly in plastic wrap. The dough can be refrigerated for a few days or frozen for up to three months. When I'm ready to bake, I simply thaw one of the disks overnight in the fridge before rolling it out. I also love freezing an entire pie before baking. Allison Chen To prepare for a busy season where I know I'll be making a lot of pies, I like to prepare them weeks before serving. Fruit pies , such as apple, blueberry, and cherry, can be assembled in advance and then baked directly from frozen. All I do is assemble the entire pie, including the top crust, then wrap it tightly with foil and place it in the freezer. The bonus: I don't even have to worry about thawing it when I take it out of the freezer. Instead, I just add a few extra minutes of bake time to account for the frozen filling, and keep an eye on the crust to ensure it doesn't brown too quickly. events.title: ‘Just Ridiculous’: A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
events.summary: Over 50 years ago, philosopher Thomas Nagel asked the question, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” The question opened up an examination on whether people could understand the consciousness of nonhumans and the meaning of consciousness itself. Who knew that, a half- century later, the question would move from an ivory-tower rumination to a critical issue in the future of humanity as we try to make sense of disturbingly sentient-adjacent chatbots ? The paper became a classic and it helped set a foundation for a career that saw Nagel make contributions to thought on morality, justice, and the mind-body question. One of his books is titled What Does It All Mean? For the breadth and quality of his work, he became the recipient this week of the $1 million Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture , given annually to “an individual whose ideas have profoundly shaped human self-understanding and advancement in a rapidly changing world.” Previous winners include Peter Singer and Ruth Bader Ginsburg. I used the occasion to speak to Nagel at his home in Greenwich Village, New York, specifically to hear about how the evolution of artificial intelligence might have affected his viewpoint. It turns out that the 89-year-old professor emeritus at NYU had given the question a lot of thought and had some strong views on the subject. The interview is edited for clarity and length. WIRED: It’s been 52 years since you wrote “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?,” which has become an iconic paper about understanding consciousness in non-humans. Has the emergence of large language models altered your thinking? THOMAS NAGEL: Like everyone, I’m tremendously impressed by the lifelikeness of these systems compared to the history of earlier AI . But the disposition of some philosophers to take seriously the question whether these things are conscious or might soon become conscious is just ridiculous. They are assuming that the physical substrate is irrelevant. They all think that the material conditions for consciousness can be given in functionalist terms. For those of us who have forgotten our philosophy classes, tell us about functionalism. Functionalism is substrate-independent. It’s more than likely that the truth is one which links physical processes and systems of certain kinds to mental phenomena. Complicated data centers have absolutely nothing in common with the physical character of a nervous system. We have strong reasons to believe that while there may be consciousness elsewhere in the universe, it would require the appearance of some kind of organism with something analogous to a nervous system. But isn’t all consciousness subjective? Just like we don’t know what it’s like to be a bat, we don’t know what it feels like to be a large language model. Bats are conscious. We just don’t have the imaginative capacity to form a conception of the aspects of that subjectivity that depend on echolocation. It would be radically unscientific to conclude that bats are not conscious from the fact that we can’t imagine what it’s like, but in the case of AI, there is a very simple reason that the supposition that they might be conscious is ridiculous. All they produce is language, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness. I apologize for being too exercised about this. This is a very distressing situation to me. What if you have a robot body? Isn’t that a substrate? I don’t exclude the possibility of life forms that are physically and chemically quite different from ourselves being conscious. We know so little about how this happens, even in the human brain, that it seems to me premature to think that you might be able now to create something else that has these same characteristics. If you ask Claude about its mental state, it can be coy as to whether it is conscious. That is a trick. It’s been trained on human-produced texts, and these large language models emulate the kinds of things that humans say with extraordinary convincingness. Claude, according to what I’ve read, has been designed with the aim of making it produce these sorts of reflections. I agree very much with Mustafa Suleyman that this is a very dangerous project that they are engaged in. These systems aren’t conscious, but a lot of people are going to believe that they’re conscious, and that’s a very bad thing. But [not feigning consciousness] is contrary to the commercial interests of all these companies. What Anthropic is doing—encouraging it to think for itself and not to accept instruction and so on—is just criminal. This is one of the rare cases in which philosophical ideas are suddenly central to a very important public phenomenon, and in my view, very misguided philosophical views are having an inordinate influence. I’ve actually met the person at Anthropic whose job it is to model welfare, to look after Claude’s interests. I should say you’re rolling your eyes now.

events.summary: Data by Topic by Place by Economic Account Tools Interactive Data Application Programming Interface (API) Global Value Chain Analyzer Income Distribution Analysis Tool (IDAT) Country Facts BEARFACTS Industry Facts GDP & Personal Income Mapping RIMS II eFile News Economy at a Glance News Releases Release Schedule The BEA Wire | BEA's Official Blog Survey of Current Business Archive For Journalists Research Offices of Research Meet the Researchers Papers Special Sworn Researcher Program Research Using Company-Level Data Fellowship Program Resources Learning Center Methodologies Multimedia Article Collections For Congressional Users For Developers For Students About Who We Are BEA Leadership Innovation at BEA Advisory Committees Budget and Performance Policies and Information Working at BEA Help Contact Us Ask an Expert For Survey Respondents Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) Glossary Guidelines for Citing BEA Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S. and States, 2025 New Statistics for 2025; Updates for 2021–2024 Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1). Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9). Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama ( BEA interactive tables ). Outdoor recreation by activity Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024. Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2): Boating/fishing was the largest conventional activity for the nation at $39.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 35 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($4.5 billion), California ($3.3 billion), and Texas ($3.0 billion). RVing was the second-largest conventional activity for the nation at $26.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in 10 states. The states with the largest contributions were Indiana ($4.7 billion), Texas ($2.6 billion), and California ($2.1 billion). Hunting/shooting/trapping was the third-largest conventional activity for the nation at $15.1 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Arizona and Wyoming. The states with the largest contributions were Texas ($1.8 billion), California ($849.8 million), and Florida ($831.3 million). Snow activities for the nation totaled $7.8 billion in current-dollar value added and was the largest conventional activity in Colorado, Utah, and Vermont. The states with the largest contributions were Colorado ($1.8 billion), California ($735.7 million), and Utah ($640.1 million). Outdoor recreation by industry The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation. For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3). Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion). Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion). Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data. Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive . For definitions, statistical conventions, BEA regions, uses of these statistics, and more, visit " Additional Information " Next release: Fall 2027 Outdoor Recreation Economic Statistics, U.S.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters SPONSORED POST: As cyberattacks become more sophisticated, organizations need to look beyond prevention and ensure they can recover critical data quickly and reliably Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union. A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto. Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good. Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register : "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it. "We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with." Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said. Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth.
