events.title: British hackers face prison for GTA 6 data breach and crypto thefts
events.summary: Two British hackers are facing lengthy prison sentences for separate hacks as part of their roles in long-running, prolific cybercriminal hacking groups. The two are accused of hacks that stole millions of dollars in cryptocurrency and leaked pre-release footage from Grand Theft Auto VI. Tyler Buchanan, 24, from Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years by a U.S. court after he was extradited to the United States in 2025. Buchanan was accused of stealing at least $11 million in cryptocurrency from dozens of companies as part of a phishing scheme. The attacks would impersonate IT helpdesks and call up unsuspecting employees and trick them into giving over their credentials, which the hackers would use to break in and steal cryptocurrency. Meanwhile, Arion Kurtaj, 21, from Oxford, England, has pleaded guilty to several cyberattacks that he carried out while a teenager. One hack included the theft of data and extortion of Rockstar Games, the maker of Grand Theft Auto VI, which was released Wednesday after several delays . Kurtaj was previously ordered by a U.K. court to be detained indefinitely after deeming him unable to stand trial due to his autism diagnosis and his perceived high hacking risk to the public. But U.K. authorities, tasked with charging Kurtaj with cybercrime offenses, confirmed Monday that he had admitted to several hacks, including leaking footage of the long-awaited video game, and would subsequently face a public trial. U.K. authorities confirmed earlier reporting that Kurtaj hacked several companies, including while he was confined to a hotel amid police protection from rival criminal gangs. The authorities said Kurtaj used an Amazon Fire TV stick to hack the companies, which breached his bail conditions. Both Buchanan and Kurtaj were members of overlapping cybercriminal groups, dubbed 0ktapus, Lapsus$, and later Scattered Spider . These prolific hacking gangs mostly consist of teenagers and young male adults, lending to the term “advanced persistent teenagers,” whose focus and motivations were to steal as much money as possible through various cyberattacks. Over the years, the hackers were collectively responsible for hundreds of cyberattacks targeting big companies, including Coinbase , DoorDash , Mailchimp , and Nvidia . By late 2024, both U.K. and U.S. authorities say they had indicted five of the hackers whom they believed were key members of the hacking groups, including Buchanan. The U.S. Department of Justice said this week that Buchanan is the fifth and final defendant to be sentenced in this case. The company said it detected "unauthorized access to certain systems" on its platform between late October and early November. Customer notification emails seen by The Register list potentially affected information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and country or regional settings. StubHub International, operated by Ticketbis S.L., apologized for the intrusion and offered the usual promise to implement security enhancements after the fact. The company said it had addressed "certain vulnerabilities" while containing the incident and was continuing to monitor for suspicious activity. Outside cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation. The company warned that any exposed information could be used to make subsequent scams more convincing. "To date, we have found no evidence of unauthorised access to account passwords , banking information or payment card details," the email stated. "We also have no evidence that the compromised information has been used fraudulently. "However, there is a risk that third parties could use this information to attempt fraud, identity theft or phishing through emails, messages or calls that appear to come from StubHub International or other trusted organizations." The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond. Digital Fuel Capital bought StubHub International from Viagogo in 2021 after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required the international business to be sold to address competition concerns. In June, the CMA fined Ticketbis £889,200 and ordered refunds exceeding £590,000 after finding that mandatory fees were omitted from upfront ticket prices. events.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
events.summary: MIT Technology Review ’s highly subjective take on the latest buzz about AI Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home. Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Don’t be fooled by this summer of AI hype Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. events.title: Tencent says new US chip curbs won’t hurt cloud revenue, may slow model training
events.summary: The comments came after Tencent reported 8% growth in third-quarter revenue on Nov 18, missing expectations and slowing from the previous quarter. Tencent said new US chip curbs will not badly hurt cloud revenue because its cloud business mainly runs inference on domestic chips. The rules may slow training of Tencent’s next AI model, which Martin Lau called “unfortunate”, and push Chinese firms to rely more on local chip supply. Tencent’s third-quarter revenue rose 8% to 207.3 billion yuan, below forecasts, as gaming cooled; AI cloud demand grew, and net profit beat estimates. BEIJING – China’s Tencent Holdings said on Nov 18 that new US restrictions on remote access to advanced AI chips would not substantially hurt its cloud revenue, though they would likely slow development of its next AI model. Washington this week unveiled rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips through overseas data centres. “We actually don’t see an impact, because our cloud business today is primarily running inference,” chief strategy officer James Mitchell told analysts on a post-earnings call. Mitchell said Tencent’s more efficient models could now be run on a “surprisingly limited number” of domestic chips. “We think that our cloud revenue will not be substantially adversely affected by the changes,” he said. President Martin Lau called the tighter restrictions “unfortunate” and said they left Chinese companies with less advanced computing power. Lau said the measures would affect AI model training and likely slow development of Tencent’s next model in the near term. Over the longer run, Chinese companies would have to rely on domestic supply chains and chips, he said, adding that the latest restrictions were likely to accelerate their development. The comments came after Tencent reported 8% growth in third-quarter revenue on Nov 18 , missing expectations and slowing from the previous quarter as momentum in its gaming business cooled. Demand for artificial intelligence services continued to boost Tencent’s cloud business, a key focus for investors assessing whether the company’s heavy AI spending is beginning to generate returns. The tech giant reported revenue of 207.3 billion yuan (S$40.1 billion) for the three months ended September, below an LSEG consensus estimate of 210.8 billion yuan. Revenue grew 11% in the previous quarter. Revenue from fintech and business services, which includes the cloud unit, rose 9% to 63.7 billion yuan, with demand for AI-related cloud services a key driver. Chinese technology companies have struggled to secure advanced Nvidia chips because of longstanding US export restrictions, leaving them at a disadvantage to some US rivals. Tencent said in 2025 that chip shortages were constraining cloud growth as it prioritised using AI chips internally over renting computing power to external clients. Revenue from value-added services, which includes gaming, rose 3% to 98.3 billion yuan in the quarter. Domestic gaming revenue increased 11%, while international gaming revenue slid 9%. Net profit rose 0.8% to 63.61 billion yuan, beating analysts’ expectations of 59.46 billion yuan. Capital expenditure totalled 81.4 billion yuan in the September quarter, up from 52.8 billion yuan in the June quarter. Tencent spent 84.7 billion yuan in the first half of 2026 , exceeding the roughly 79 billion yuan it spent in all of 2025. REUTERS

events.title: I'm a travel advisor who plans luxury trips to Italy. Here are 5 mistakes I see travelers make again and again.
events.summary: As a travel advisor, I know there are a few things you should never do when traveling to Italy. Vanessa Kromer I've worked as a travel advisor for 16 years and have sent clients on luxury Italian vacations. As someone who also loves traveling to Italy, I've seen my fair share of common tourist mistakes . In my experience, overpacking or changing hotels too many times can ruin a trip. As a luxury travel advisor, I've sent hundreds of clients to Italy over the past 16 years. Plus, as someone who loves traveling there myself (I typically take two or three trips to Italy each year), I've seen many tourists make the same mistakes repeatedly. Here are the things I always tell clients to avoid when traveling to Italy. Changing hotels too many times can ruin a trip. Vanessa Kromer Many travelers I work with want to visit three to five Italian cities in nine days, changing hotels every two nights or less. In my opinion, though, the only souvenirs these travelers will come home with are extreme sleep deprivation and zero memory of what they actually did or saw. Instead, I recommend two or three hotel changes at the most. This way, they're not living out of a suitcase for the entire trip and can really enjoy each destination. Many travelers feel obligated to visit famous attractions, regardless of their personal interests. Vanessa Kromer I find that many travelers add popular tourist destinations to their itineraries just to check them off their travel bucket lists. In my opinion, though, this is a waste of valuable vacation time. For example, if you have zero desire to see The Vatican or the Colosseum, you can fill that time with something totally amazing in Rome that piques your interest. Or, if you don't drink wine, I recommend spending free time in smaller Tuscan cities like Siena or Lucca instead of at a winery. At the end of the day, it's important to craft your Italian vacation itinerary around your desires. Because trust me — there's something for everyone. Overpacking makes travel less convenient. Vanessa Kromer Less is always more when it comes to packing for an international trip , and Italy is no exception. Far too many times, I've gone to Venice and seen people with large checked bags trying to drag them up and over hundreds of steps to their hotels. Plus, there are sometimes luggage limits on taxis, trains, and ferries. That's why I always aim to travel with just a carry-on. To do this, I alway recommend packing layers and a combination of mix-and-match wardrobe staples. Relying only on AI-generated itineraries can ruin a trip. Vanessa Kromer Lately, I've seen a lot of clients coming to me with AI-generated itineraries . However, AI doesn't have the expertise of someone who's actually been to Italy. For example, a long train ride may seem OK on paper, but it's not always fun in the July heat. Plus, I've seen these bots create difficult-to-navigate agendas to remote areas that no travel advisor would ever suggest to first-time travelers. AI can work as a starting point, but it's always worth having someone who's been to Italy review the itinerary, too. Overscheduling each day leaves no time to enjoy Italian spontaneously. Vanessa Kromer In my opinion, Italy is best enjoyed slowly: savoring a glass of wine at a rooftop bar in Florence, lingering over a long dinner with incredible views in Positano, or having a morning espresso and cornetto at a café while people-watching in Milan. That's why I never recommend planning more than one tour a day. Plus, I always suggest leaving either mornings or afternoons free to explore a destination at your leisure. events.title: LeBron James sues sports betting app Bron for using nickname and likeness without permission
events.summary: NBA star’s lawsuit alleges ‘previously unknown app’ acted illegally ‘to gain notoriety’ by seeming affiliated with James LeBron James sued the sports betting research app Bron on Tuesday, accusing it of trademark infringement for using his nickname ⁠and an artificial intelligence-generated ⁠likeness of him in ​a recent ad campaign without permission. In a complaint filed in New York City federal court, the Philadelphia 76ers star, whose nickname is Bron, said he carefully protects his image and chooses who to endorse, reflecting his ⁠status as “one of the most recognizable identities in the world”, and commands tens of millions of dollars for endorsing products or ventures. James’s endorsement is “uniquely valuable”, the complaint said. “And that is why defendants decided to ⁠steal it all for themselves.“ The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James’s name, to give up any money they have already made and to award damages – including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. “Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app,” the lawsuit states. “They intentionally created the false impression that Mr James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions.” Bron did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc, is based in California. It was launched by the chief executive, Anish Gupta, and chief technology officer, Marc Zoghby, in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James – down to his tattoos, voice and No 23 jersey – sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app. James’s lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports . The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1m times, the lawsuit alleged. Gupta responded to the attorneys’ demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James’s legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name would be announced on Wednesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket . It alleges that the app’s marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. “The integrity of NBA competition – and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play – is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views.” James, 41, is the NBA’s all-time leading ‌scorer, with four MVP ‌awards and four league championships. He also has three Olympic gold medals.

events.title: Jensen Huang won't make Steve Jobs-style comeback, Apple chief's biographer says
events.summary: Supporters of Jensen Huang are insisting that parallels exist between Nvidia's former chief executive and the late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs . They are arguing that, just as was the case when Mr Jobs left Apple in the 1980s, Nvidia will not be as prosperous without Mr Huang. “This would be an Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy from Nvidia's board if they did that, and a grievous harm to the United States of America,” posted Epic Games founder and chief executive Tim Sweeney on X, a day before Mr Huang resigned . But while both Mr Huang and Mr Jobs were forced out of the companies they co-founded, the similarities do not seem to go much further. In 1985, Steve Jobs had major disagreements with Apple’s board as Macintosh sales fell far below expectations and there were complaints about his management style. They voted him out of the company. People have been asking me if Jensen Huang might make a comeback -- similar to how Steve Jobs was driven out of Apple and then returned and saved it from near-bankruptcy 12 years later. The answer is no, Jensen won't mount a comeback like Steve Jobs. The two have almost nothing… pic.twitter.com/MQP0JuVDup — Geoffrey Cain (@geoffrey_cain) November 13, 2026 Mr Huang, however lied to his board about his initial affair with a woman US officials suspect is a Chinese spy, and then told his board that there were no other infidelities. A subsequent affair came to light, and Mr Huang was accused of violating US technology export laws in his dealings with companies linked to China. Journalist Geoffrey Cain, author of Steve Jobs in Exile, which looks at the Apple co-founder's years after his removal from the company, disagreed that Mr Huang's situation was similar. “Steve Jobs was pushed out for being horrible to work with, no spies involved – though he did visit the USSR and pitched the Mac,” Mr Cain posted on X. “Simply put, Steve was too immature at 30 years old to stay at Apple, and many engineers refused to work with him.” Unlike Mr Huang at Nvidia, Mr Jobs was not Apple's chief executive when he was fired from the company in 1985, he added. “He was the head of the Macintosh division, he reported to John Sculley, the CEO, who asked the board to remove him,” Mr Cain said. Instead, Mr Jobs' departure from Apple in 1985 suggests it is possible for Nvidia to survive and be successful without its co-founder. Although Mr Sculley stepped down as Apple's chief executive in 1993 amid disappointing sales, between 1985 and 1992, he led the company through some prosperous years and introduced products that that were critically acclaimed and consumer hits. He also prompted Apple to make an investment in ARM, which later proved to be critical in providing processors that were later used in the iPhone. His tenure was far from perfect and Apple's market share suffered towards the end of Mr Sculley's time at the company, but its profits grew and status expanded on his watch. Apple struggled from 1993 until 1998, following Mr Sculley' departure. Mr Jobs's return in 1997 and his eventual appointment as chief executive proved a pivotal moment that led Apple to a renaissance, but Nvidia is a completely different company in vastly different circumstances. After Apple's co-founder died in 2011, chief executive Tim Cook increased Apple's revenue, sales and market share in an unprecedented manner. After Mr Jobs' initially ousting from Apple, his new company, NeXT, failed despite having momentum and ample investment. Lacklustre sales prompted Mr Jobs to discontinue the company's hardware in 1993 and focus on software, but he learnt from that. “Those years were failure upon failure, and they taught him,” Mr Cain wrote . "People have been asking me if Jensen Huang might make a comeback - similar to how Steve Jobs was driven out of Apple and then returned and saved it ... The answer is no," Mr Cain wrote on X On Tuesday, Mr Huang said he was willing to return as chief executive at Nvidia if the company's board of directors ask him to do so. Nvidia's board is not said to be pursuing the idea of allowing him back.

events.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
events.summary: New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device — from isolating a subject and defining its motion to generating the finished video. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and animations for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark. Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark. Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting. GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables. Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters. Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required. Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark. Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate lighting and materials with near-final-quality ray-traced previews as they work. The practical difference is immediate: instead of navigating a noisy, resolving preview, Ray Reconstruction delivers near-final-quality lighting, reflections and materials in the interactive viewport in real time. DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction support requires Blender 5.3 and the latest NVIDIA Game Ready Driver or NVIDIA Studio Driver. Download the NVIDIA App to get automatic notifications when the latest drivers are available, optimize games and applications from a unified GPU control center, and discover the latest NVIDIA tools and software. Windows Server 2028 Coming to DGX Station for Windows Announced at Microsoft Ignite, Windows Server is evolving for organizations that need to run AI closer to their enterprise applications and data. Microsoft is expanding hardware choice through support for the latest AI silicon, helping customers take advantage of accelerated inference and increasingly capable models in their own environments. NVIDIA DGX Station for Windows platform powered by the GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip is expanding to include support for Windows Server 2028.

events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report and Natural Gas Monthly Note: Five-year average=2021–2025 Working natural gas in storage in the Lower 48 states ended the natural gas injection season at 3,810 billion cubic feet (Bcf), exceeding the five-year average by almost 2%, according to estimates based on data from our Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report released on November 12. Injection season runs April 1–October 31, the months of typically lower natural gas demand. While net injections were 2 Bcf less than the five-year average this injection season, working gas stocks are higher than usual because they started the 2026 season 3% (63 Bcf) above the five-year average at 1,878 Bcf. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Natural Gas Storage Report Higher than average inventories at the start of the summer injection season allowed storage operators to reach their end-of-season targets with smaller incremental natural gas injections. Although total dry natural gas production during the 2026 refill season was 3% higher than the same period in 2025, according to S&P Global Energy, most of the increased production during this period was used to meet rising demand from liquefied natural gas export terminals . Mild spring temperatures during the first several weeks of the refill season mitigated seasonal residential and commercial natural gas demand, allowing the surplus to the five-year average to grow, peaking at 198 Bcf (7%) for the week ending August 7, before declining for the next 10 consecutive weeks, as warmer-than-normal temperatures during the summer months increased power generation demand for natural gas. Mild temperatures returned during the final weeks of the injection season, which led to above-normal injections. Weekly injections ranged from 108 Bcf in early June to 15 Bcf in late August. In our November Short-Term Energy Outlook , we forecast natural gas withdrawals during the 2026–2027 heating season (November 1–March 31) will total 1,900 Bcf and that inventories will be 4% above the five-year (2022–2026) average at the end of March 2027 because of a relatively mild winter and increases in natural gas production. events.title: Why France is sending soldiers into Ukraine and how Russia is responding
events.summary: Russia is responding forcefully to France's confirmation that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine for training and maintenance help with supplied weaponry PARIS -- Russia is responding forcefully to confirmation from France that it periodically sends military personnel into Ukraine to provide training and maintenance help with some of the weaponry it has supplied for the war . Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said: “This is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,' but direct participation in the war.” France says the soldiers and weapons specialists are noncombatants. “Since we are not at war with Russia, these, in fact, are not combat units,” French Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said. Speaking on Wednesday to French broadcaster RMC, Rufo said French personnel are “a very long way from the front line. They come to carry out occasional missions.” She didn't specify their numbers, but said that they are “a few soldiers, specialists, including armaments engineers, who work — or can come to work — on an occasional basis to maintain complex equipment, such as Mirage aircraft or Caesar howitzers, and provide targeted training on certain equipment.” France first delivered Mirage 2000-5 fighters last year to Ukraine and trained pilots and mechanics for them. The French Defense Ministry says the aircraft have helped fend off missile and drone attacks. It also says that with donations from allies and purchases, Ukraine's force of high-precision French-made Caesar howitzers has grown to become the largest in the world. France has also supplied precision bombs, cruise missiles, air defense systems, light tanks and other equipment. Rufo told French lawmakers on Tuesday that France is “accelerating” its support in light of Russia's air campaign against Ukrainian targets. She spoke of a “complete absence of any intention to engage in combat” and described as “absurd” Lavrov's accusation that France is directly participating in the war. JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Only a “very limited" number of French personnel are engaged in “the extremely limited” missions, Rufo said. Her comments came after French media, including broadcaster RFI and Le Monde newspaper, reported that small contingents of French military officers stay in Ukraine for short rotations as part of the so-called Operation Volia, since at least this summer. French military personnel have been operating in Ukraine for more than six months and France isn't alone in providing such support, Lavrov said Tuesday at a news conference in Manila, Philippines, where he was attending a summit of Southeast Asian nations. “We have conveyed our concern through the available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer ‘support for Ukraine,’ but direct participation in the war,” he said, without naming the countries. “This is just like the assistance with target designation, the provision of satellite data and much else,” he said. Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said that Moscow will regard any foreign troops in Ukraine as legitimate targets and it will be up to the Russian military to determine a response. The United Kingdom has soldiers in Ukraine, but officials haven't disclosed how many or what their role is. The U.K. Defense Ministry confirmed two deaths of British soldiers in Ukraine in the past year, in both cases in accidents. Since Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, dozens of countries have trained more than 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers, at locations outside the country — in France , the U.K. , the United States, Poland, Germany and elsewhere — including on Patriot missile batteries, F-16 combat jets and other equipment. They have also trained recruits, officers, medics and other specialists for combat. Jill Lawless in London, Sylvie Corbet and Catherine Gaschka in Paris, and Lorne Cook in Brussels, contributed to this report. events.title: US futures point higher led by rebound for Nvidia
events.summary: Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang HONG KONG -- Tech stocks are leading U.S. futures higher Wednesday after Nvidia easily exceeded Wall Street expectations as it deals with the abrupt departure of CEO Jensen Huang. Futures for the S & P 500 rose 0.6%, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.2%. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq advanced 1%. Oil prices are continuing on a downward trajectory despite new attacks by Iran that threaten to disrupt the shipment of Middle East crude through the crucial Strait of Hormuz. Prices declined after the American Petroleum Institute said that U.S. crude inventories rose by 5.3% last week, a boost that far exceeded projections from energy analysts. Chipmakers are surging early after Nvidia reported that its revenue doubled from last year to $116 billion. Nvidia shares are up 4% in premarket trading. Broadcom, Arm Holdings and Advanced Micro Devices are following closely behind. Retail stocks are mixed after Target raised its outlook for the year following its strongest sales growth in nearly five years. Despite the strong performance, shares dipped 3% and Walmart, which reports quarterly earnings Thursday, fell more than 1%. President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday with trade likely to be the focus of talks with China's leader, Xi Jinping , but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public. Later on Wednesday, the U.S. Federal Reserve will release minutes from its most recent meeting, with new indications that it has yet to tame inflation . The persistence of elevated inflation makes it highly likely that the Fed will raise benchmark interest rates at its next meeting in December. It kept rates unchanged late last month , after raising them in September. The Fed increases borrowing costs in an effort to cool spending and bring down inflation. events.title: After a 13-year wait, 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations
events.summary: “Grand Theft Auto VI” has begun rolling out worldwide, bringing players back to Rockstar Games’ Vice City LOS ANGELES -- After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here. “Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon. The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, meaning players in Asia and other regions can start playing hours before its U.S. release. New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached. “The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.” In the capital, Wellington, players stayed up to be among the first to try “Grand Theft Auto VI.” Among them was Adam Simmons, 50, a director of photography who launched the game in his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low to avoid waking his wife and daughters. “The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive,” he said after half an hour of shooting, car theft and jokes about Florida. “You really feel like you are in a world,” he added. “The places and how they’re put together feel right.” Simmons moved to New Zealand from Portland, Oregon, five months ago — a decision he joked had been influenced by the prospect of playing “Grand Theft Auto” before his friends. He praised the game’s emotional connection with its characters and said he expected its expansive world to offer hours of play long after he finished the story. By 1 a.m., he reluctantly admitted he should go to bed, though he expected to put in plenty of hours in the coming days. “I have my own company that I have to run,” he said. “So I’m the boss, but also I’m just going to lose sales because a video game came out.” The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida. Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida. Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity. Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release. The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity. Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight. In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack. Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation.

events.title: How three leaders donated the $20 million Melinda French Gates gave them with no strings attached
events.summary: Philanthropist Melinda French Gates launched a $240 million Global Leaders program in 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries without warning or requirements other than donating the money b... Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble says she was shocked when philanthropist Melinda French Gates picked her to receive $20 million to donate however she wanted. The psychologist, author and founder of The AAKOMA Project, a nonprofit supporting the mental health of young people of color, has long admired French Gates’ work, especially in the diversity of her support initiatives. Breland-Noble just never expected to be the focus of one of those initiatives. “It really was shock and awe,” she said. “My mom just had a knack and a penchant for finding people that nobody else was helping and she would help them. And so for me, the excitement was I get to honor my mother’s legacy by doing the same thing.” In 2024, through her philanthropic organization Pivotal, French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, where she gave $20 million each to 12 luminaries, including Breland-Noble, without warning or requirements other than donating the money by the end of 2026. It was part of her plan to donate $1 billion to support women and girls at a time when nonprofits focusing on their issues receive only about 2% of all U.S. philanthropic funding . Now, with nearly all the money donated, Pivotal has seen enough to call the trust-based philanthropy initiative a “huge success” and is looking for ways to replicate it and encourage other donors to do the same. “There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” French Gates said in a statement to The Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.” According to Pivotal, the average grant the Global Leaders handed out was approximately $240,000, with 91% of the donations going to organizations that had not received funding from Pivotal before. Haven Ley, Pivotal’s chief strategy officer, said a final report on the Global Leaders program will come next year, but that the organization is already looking for ways to build on it. “We did this not just for the impact," Ley said, “but because it was a model that was intriguing to us.” French Gates said the different vantage points on the world’s challenges have made Pivotal more responsive and helped the Global Leaders be more impactful. “For me, this is as much about expanding who gets to make decisions about funding as it is about where funding goes,” she said. For Breland-Noble, being able to donate to others on a grand scale was a meaningful new experience. Though she has been working in the mental health field for decades, she is relatively new to running her own nonprofit. Breland-Noble established The AAKOMA Project, which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents, in 1999 as an academic research lab, only turning it into a nonprofit in 2018 so that it could put its research findings into action. To donate the $20 million that French Gates had given her, Breland-Noble created The MATTIE Fund – short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity, but also named for, and inspired by, her mother Mattie McLeod Breland. The MATTIE Fund donated to well-established groups like Asian Mental Health Collective. But Breland-Noble made a point of expanding her donations to groups outside her network, searching Google and LinkedIn to find ideas. She asked her Instagram community for recommendations, as well as audiences at her speaking engagements. Those searches led to her support of BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina, which trains young people to use their creativity, and Daddy Stroller Social Club, which helps new fathers deal with postpartum depression. Breland-Noble said she was thankful to French Gates for the opportunity to give. events.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
events.summary: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars. The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least. Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at between $70 - $78 each. If they go for the highest price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn each. So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy? In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT. He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him. Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track , and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity. Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences. Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI. But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship. Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious". Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic. She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian. Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright. She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations. The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work. Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture. He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project. Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends. He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity". Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources. Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America. Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg. He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director. Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank. Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University. His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic. Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other. But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI. He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain. The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute. Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance. Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones. Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with : revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion. "We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year. Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company. The bigger risk is not near-term demand but operations, maintaining employee confidence, retaining talent, and preserving Nvidia's innovation culture." Forrester principal analyst Naveen Chhabra Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent. When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated. But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with." Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year. Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there. Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of Hopper kit to China during Q3 after being given the go-ahead from the Trump administration to sell products like its H200 accelerators in China.

events.title: Rwanda in deportation deal with European countries
events.summary: Five European countries aim to start deporting failed asylum seekers to Rwanda, which has long been criticized for its human rights record, by next year. Many EU nations are tightening immigration rules in response to far-right electoral pressure. The removals are seen as a means to “confront the massive challenges of illegal migration ,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said. Austria, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands are also involved. Rights group Amnesty International described the deal with Rwanda as “ disgraceful ,” highlighting the country’s “track record” of silencing political opponents and critics, allegations Kigali has consistently denied. Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said “we need to go beyond the existing cliche ,” adding that refugee rights were respected in the country. A previous UK-Rwanda deportation plan — which differed as it targeted anyone who had come without permission, rather than those who had failed the asylum process — was abandoned in 2024 after a change in government. — Damian Zane

events.title: U.S. drivers are just absorbing high gasoline prices
events.summary: Pain at the pump may have changed some votes, but it's apparently not prompting big changes in how much Americans drive. Why it matters: Most driving isn't especially optional, so people are absorbing the cost. This year Americans have paid an additional $88 billion for gasoline relative to a no-war baseline, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab. The Energy Policy Research Foundation finds that U.S. households paid between $300 and $730 more on gasoline in March-August compared to the prior year. State of play: Gasoline demand from the beginning of March, right after the Iran war started, through early November is very similar to the same stretch last year, per federal data. There's "no discernible evidence of a decline in gasoline consumption," UC-Berkeley energy economist Lucas Davis writes in a new post on the topic. That's despite gasoline prices being 31% higher since the war began compared to the same period last year. The intrigue: Davis points out that the stubborn demand comes despite polling that shows Americans say high prices are changing their habits. He flags an April Washington Post-ABC News survey that showed 44% of respondents saying they had cut back on driving. Multiple polls show some version of this. For instance, 57% of respondents in a June Gallup survey said high prices were causing them to drive less. How it works: Davis' post and the chart above rely on the federal Energy Information Administration's measure of gasoline product supplied. EIA calls it a proxy for demand, and measures gasoline leaving the supply chain, including refineries and bulk terminals. There's no perfect measurement. The Transportation Department tracks miles traveled, though there's a lag. The most recent data, for August, does not show a drop-off this year. The bottom line: "[T]his is a valuable reminder of the gap between what people say and what they do," Davis writes. "Drivers may talk about cutting back, but studies in the economics literature consistently find that gasoline demand is inelastic in the short run," he writes.

events.title: Ministers to drop foie gras imports ban to help seal EU food trade deal
events.summary: Animal welfare charities criticise ‘backwards step’ on foie gras, production of which has been banned in UK since 2007 Ministers will drop plans to ban foie gras imports into the UK in order to smooth a trade deal with the EU that will be announced this week. As first reported by the Financial Times, the proposed ban will be officially dropped on Friday when the government announces its sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) trade deal with the EU to reduce checks and paperwork on imports and exports of food and drink with the bloc. Labour promised before coming to power that it would ban foie gras imports. Before the election, Steve Reed, the then shadow environment secretary, said Labour would “ban the commercial import of foie gras, where ducks and geese are aggressively force-fed”. He labelled the practice “beyond disgusting”. Foie gras is made by force-feeding ducks and geese grain through a funnel or tube that has been thrust down the bird’s neck – a process known as gavage that swells the animal’s liver to many times its normal size. The livers are then harvested. Banning it has proved difficult as EU countries including France produce and export the product and are against other members putting in place an import ban. The Guardian reported earlier this year that ministers were preparing to drop the ban in order to secure concessions. Sustainability chefs and animal welfare charities have criticised the U-turn. Boris Johnson’s government promised to use the powers granted by Brexit to ban the “cruel” product, which still appears on menus across the country almost seven years after the UK officially left the EU. Some restaurants still sell foie gras but many shops have removed it from sale, including the king’s grocer, Fortnum & Mason, which took it off shelves in 2021. The production of foie gras has been banned in the UK since 2007. The French chef Alexis Gauthier used to sell more foie gras than any other restaurant in London before converting to a vegan diet and menu. He now sells a mushroom-based “faux gras” to customers of his Soho restaurant, who include the former Beatle Paul McCartney. Gauthier said the ban being dropped was “terrible news”. “I find it very sad our government capitulates so easily,” he said. “The cruelty of foie gras belongs firmly in the history books, not in a progressive society in 2026.” Will Murray, a co-founder of the sustainable British restaurant Fallow, also based in London, serves a mushroom parfait rather than foie gras. He said: “This feels like a step in the wrong direction with regards to animal welfare. I think London diners aren’t really asking for a big return of foie gras on menus.” David Bowles, the head of public affairs at the RSPCA, said: “We are extremely disappointed that farm animal welfare laws have been put on the chopping block as part of this new deal. Any suggestions plans to act on foie gras are being shelved to ease EU realignment are deeply concerning for animals and would be a clear backwards step.” A spokesperson for the charity Four Paws said: “The UK prohibited the production of foie gras nearly 20 years ago because of the serious animal welfare concerns associated with force-feeding ducks and geese. Yet foie gras produced using these same methods can still be imported and sold here. As the UK strengthens its relationship with the EU, animal welfare must not become a casualty of closer trade ties.” Government insiders indicated that the ban would be dropped but noted that the method of production was banned in the UK. A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the method raises welfare concerns. They said: “We are negotiating a food and drink deal that will slash red tape and costly paperwork, make it easier and cheaper to export seafood, boost the British economy by up to £5bn a year, and back British businesses and jobs. We are working closely with businesses to ensure a smooth transition so they can make the most of the benefits this deal unlocks.”

events.title: States where people spend the most on college education, ranked
events.summary: Rhode Island has the highest cost of attending college in the US, when measured by the share of household income. Wolterk/Getty Images On average, a college education in the US accounts for more than half of a year's household income. Several US colleges have annual costs of attendance of over $100,000 in 2026. Rhode Island has the highest cost of education as a share of income, while Utah has the lowest. The cost of higher education is rising across the board, but in some states, getting a college degree is more expensive than in others. A recent WalletHub study examined how the cost of an in-state college education compares across US states and ranked them on affordability. The study examined each state's average cost of attending an in-state public college full-time and compared it to the state's median annual household income , using data from the US Census Bureau and the National Center for Education Statistics. The study doesn't include Alaska and Wyoming due to data limitations. In states like Rhode Island, which was ranked as the state with the highest college education costs, a $79,194-a-year undergraduate degree can cost up to 90.2% of the median household income. Meanwhile, in Utah, which has the lowest cost of education as a percentage of median income , a degree costs only 27.58% of an annual household income. Even in the most affordable state, a college education costs more than a quarter of a year's income, and in 21 states, it costs more than half a year's income. events.title: Dangote eyes Ghana cocoa and sugar deals
events.summary: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote is in talks with Ghana’s government to establish sugar and cocoa manufacturing plants in the West African country, he said at an event in Accra. Africa’s richest man, who originally built up his conglomerate in cement and sugar before developing the continent’s largest oil refinery, said the proposed partnership with the government had the potential to create more than 50,000 jobs in Ghana, the world’s second-largest cocoa producer. In a separate development, the Dangote Refinery said it plans to increase its initial public offering by nearly a third, to $2.1 billion, after it was heavily oversubscribed, Reuters reported. Africa’s largest-ever IPO attracted orders worth nearly $4.5 billion — around three times the shares originally on offer. The industrialist’s conglomerate has embarked on a continent-wide expansion drive in recent months that has included breaking ground on an oil refinery project in Kenya and signing an agreement with Zimbabwe targeting projects in cement and power generation . — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: Cruises sound pretty awful. People are still booking them more than ever.
events.summary: Headlines may seem like they're scaring away potential cruisers, but a lot of people are still setting sail. Britt Erlanson/Getty Images Before 2019, the last place you'd see Mark Jessup was on a cruise ship. As the long-standing stereotype goes, "I thought it was just for old people," the 47-year-old skincare company owner recalled thinking. The fear of seasickness certainly didn't entice him either. Actually, nothing did — until his coworkers dragged him, then an unwilling 39-year-old post-office worker, on his first vacation at sea in late 2019 aboard Carnival Sunshine. "The rest was history," Jessup, who's now a travel content creator known on social media as Mark J, told Business Insider. Since then (and even following an industry-wide pause amid the COVID-19 pandemic), the cynic-turned-fan has been on 56 floating resorts. Jessup cruises every month, usually on four- to seven-day voyages, and even relocated from Massachusetts to Florida three years ago, both for the weather and to be closer to cruise ports. He enjoys the convenience of the onboard gym and food, as well as the ability to unplug from his phone. "I like traveling, and I realized it was just so much easier for me to go on a cruise," Jessup said. "My sons were getting older, and I was wanting to do something more for me. Cruising was my escape to figure out who I was and what I wanted." Meanwhile, the vacation-at-sea industry seems to be facing a perpetual public-relations crisis. Earlier this month, the "never-ending cruise" Villa Vie's Odyssey abruptly suspended operations, leaving more than 200 passengers stranded in Cambodia. A few months before that, there was a deadly multi-country hantavirus outbreak linked to a cruise ship. Just last year, the 2025 Netflix documentary "Trainwreck: Poop Cruise" dove into what happened aboard the Carnival Triumph after an engine fire left about 4,000 people stranded in 2013. The title speaks for itself. In a statement, Carnival called the incident a "teachable moment for the entire cruise industry" and said it spent millions upgrading its fleet after investigating the issues that led to the disaster. Then, of course, there are the seemingly annual nightmarish "man overboard" headlines and reports about norovirus outbreaks on cruises. Yet, the cruise industry sustains . To understand the cruise boom amid its challenges, you have to understand how social media, product innovation, and affordability have built a travel-industry fortress so formidable, even a federally mandated, industry-wide shutdown during a pandemic couldn't shutter it for good. I've spent several years sailing on cruises for work. Brittany Chang It's no secret that I, a seasoned cruise reporter, have had my apprehensions about cruising , for reasons quite similar to Jessup's. Yet, throughout my career, I've become especially partial to the behemoth ships of companies like Royal Caribbean and Norwegian, topped with extras like splashy waterparks, exciting Cirque du Soleil-like productions, and wine bars with a cool downtown panache — all bait for younger cruisers that might've thought we were "above" cruising. "People would say that cruising was for old people, but the innovation that's come out … I think is why it's capturing the attention of the people," Austin Maxwell, a 31-year-old cruise content creator who's been on 43 unique ships across 16 cruise lines, told Business Insider. Unsurprisingly, these flashy amenities have become irresistible to travelers, and it's part of what's keeping the industry afloat despite the negative headlines. The Villa Vie Odyssey abruptly halted operations shortly into its "never-ending" sailing. Suy SE / AFP via Getty Images The success story of cruises The cruise industry is seeing a historic boom in popularity. AAA estimates that a record 22.4 million Americans will cruise in 2027, a 3.6% increase from the year prior — and the fifth year in a row AAA has projected a record increase. By comparison, 14.2 million Americans cruised in 2019. Much of this growth can be attributed to newcomers: According to a 2025 Cruise Lines International Association report, 31% of cruisers globally over the prior two years were first-timers — up from 24% in 2019. For cruise giants like Royal Caribbean Group, this surge means about 60% of its travelers are now either new to cruising or to the brand, Naftali Holtz, the company's CFO, told investors in mid-2025. "I have a lot of people that have always done land trips, and they're resistant to the idea of going on a cruise," Bitsy Clayton, a 63-year-old luxury travel agent of almost 24 years, told Business Insider. "Once people decide to do it, I think they're surprised at how much they like it." Clayton's clients, most of whom are between the ages of 50 and 70, gravitate toward the likes of Silversea, Regent Seven Seas, Crystal, and Seabourn — smaller ultra-luxury ships with high-touch service. The vast majority of her clients are repeat cruisers, including some who've spent $250,000 on a single at-sea vacation . Are cruise lovers just ignoring the risks and potential horrors at sea? Maybe — but headlines only tell a small part of the story. Clayton said it's "pretty rare" for her clients to bring up these types of nightmare incidents. "It can happen on any vessel, but I think on the smaller ships, you've got more staff, a lot more attention to detail, and more things that could curtail something escalating," she said. I can have amazing food, be treated like royalty by these amazing team members, and I don't have to hotel change every other day. Carly Caramanna, a 40-year-old travel writer "Cruising could be like 10% bad and 90% good, but everybody's only going to focus on the 10%," Jessup said, explaining why the negative headlines don't affect his decision to keep cruising. Instead, he focuses on what he can control at sea, like decreasing his chances of getting sick aboard by avoiding touching stairwell railings or the tongs at the buffet. He also has an extensive cabin-cleaning routine , which includes bed-bug checks, sanitizing all high-touch surfaces with cleaning wipes, and bringing his own bed sheets and pillowcases. Cruises have protective measures in place to prevent sickness, too. Hand-sanitizer bottles have become a fixture on floating resorts, luxury or not. Go on a giant Royal Caribbean cruise , and you'll likely see crew in fast food-shaped costumes singing "Washy washy!" on repeat by the buffet entrance. The World Health Organization also has global standards around health screenings and sanitation requirements that cruise lines are expected to follow to further help control disease and other hazards at sea. Of course, safety and health concerns will remain. Likely no amount of public relations work can make the world forget its norovirus- and COVID-19-era "floating petri dish" reputation. events.title: Adnoc sees sulphur output doubling as Hormuz disruption sends prices to record highs
events.summary: Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's sour gas unit expects its sulphur output to double or even triple over the next decade, betting that a by-product it once paid to get rid of has become a core business after the Iran war pushed prices to record highs . “Sulphur will be the future gold,” Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive of Adnoc Sour Gas, said at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai on Wednesday. He said Adnoc produces about 7 million tonnes a year, and that could rise to between 14 million and 20 million tonnes as the company increases gas output. Most of the gain would come between 2030 and 2035, he added, and the final figure depends on which projects are sanctioned. Sulphur will be the future gold Adel Al Jaberi, chief executive, Adnoc Sour Gas The plan shows how the closure of the Strait of Hormuz turned an overlooked commodity into a strategic one. The Gulf accounts for about 47 per cent of global seaborne sulphur exports , according to S&P Global, and the disruption pushed free-on-board benchmarks above $1,000 a tonne and delivered prices to about $1,200 to $1,300 by July. Sulphur is a key input for phosphate fertiliser and for the sulphuric acid used to process nickel and copper. When Adnoc started developing its Shah field 10 to 15 years ago, sulphur traded at minus $8 a tonne because producers had to pay buyers to take it away, Mr Al Jaberi said. “Nobody was thinking about applications at that time,” he said. During the crisis, it hit record prices. “That's the journey of sulphur.” Prices climbed from an average of about $500 a tonne before the conflict to $1,100 to $1,200 in late June, according to CRU. Adnoc set its own July official selling price for the Indian subcontinent at a record $1,000 a tonne free on board Ruwais, $180 to $200 above the previous high set in 2008, according to Argus. Prices have eased since then as buyers pulled back. Adnoc cut its October price by $70 to $890 a tonne, and spot Middle East prices fell to $740 to $790 a tonne by mid-October, according to Kpler data. Adnoc ships its sulphur mainly to China and Morocco for fertiliser. Mr Al Jaberi said the company is working with the Adnoc Research Centre and Khalifa University on new uses, including solid-state batteries, new types of fertiliser, cosmetics, cement and soil improvement. The extra sulphur will come from a push into harder-to-produce gas. Mr Al Jaberi said Adnoc's upstream unit produces about 12.5 billion cubic feet a day and aims for about 17.7 billion in the coming years, which means developing marginal and sour fields. Shah gasfield, which was suspended after a drone attack caused a fire in March, now produces 1.45 billion cubic feet a day, and Adnoc plans to raise that to 1.85 billion or possibly 2 billion. Earlier this month, Adnoc took a final investment decision on the Ruwais Diyab unconventional gas development, its first large-scale unconventional gas project. Mr Al Jaberi said a single sour gas well once cost as much as $50 million. AI-driven reservoir modelling, drones and robots have since cut costs and inspection times. Demand is also coming from data centres. “Out of 5 megawatts, 1 megawatt at least will go for AI,” he said. Iman Nasseri, senior vice president of Middle East and Asia at FGE NexantECA, told the panel that the region's LNG exports will double to 200 million tonnes within a decade. He warned it would be “naive” to treat every announced data centre as new gas demand.
