events.title: Your favorite Thanksgiving dishes won’t cost substantially more this year – here’s why
events.summary: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on Unsplash Inflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute . That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022 , the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began . I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report , published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time . As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data . Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive . Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5% , and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data . But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak , which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more . Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data . Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers . Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35 , Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people . Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. Elizabeth Canales receives funding from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

events.title: Jeffries nears historic speakership as power shifts in Congress
events.summary: Hakeem Jeffries could soon become America's first Black House speaker, even as Black lawmakers confront rising threats to their power in D.C. Why it matters: Proposed committee term limits and another round of redistricting could weaken Black lawmakers' influence they spent decades building. By the numbers: The number of Black lawmakers in the 120th Congress will be stable from the 119th, based on results so far. The House will likely seat 59 Black voting members, down from 61, according to the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies . All four Black House Republicans are departing, while Black Democrats have gained two seats. Black membership in the U.S. Senate will rise from five to a record seven, including Sens.-elect Scott Colom of Mississippi and Juliana Stratton of Illinois . Zoom in: Democrats are in the middle of a sometimes messy generational power transfer, with younger lawmakers challenging more senior members for committee chairmanships. Those chairmanships have long helped Congressional Black Caucus members exercise power beyond their numbers. "For CBC members, the power is seniority," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) told Politico in 2014. "I've been around a while. ... Some wisdom, at least, is important to what we're going through right now," Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, 81, (D-N.J.) told Axios in 2025. Sticking point: Democrats are considering a four-term limit for committee leaders , starting after the 2028 elections, that could eventually force three veteran Black Democrats to step aside as committee leaders. Bennie Thompson, 78, of Mississippi, leads Democrats on Homeland Security. Bobby Scott, 79, of Virginia, leads Democrats on Education and Workforce. He faces a challenge from Connecticut Rep. Jahana Hayes, 53. Maxine Waters, 88, of California, leads Democrats on Financial Services. She faces a challenge from Illinois Rep. Sean Casten, 54. Zoom out: A Democratic wave helped Black incumbents survive redistricting this year, but that level of support may not be repeated in future elections. The Supreme Court's April ruling in Louisiana v. Callais narrowed protections against maps that watered down the Voting Rights Act, potentially exposing more Black-held districts to redistricting. Texas' new maps pushed veteran Democrat Al Green into a primary against another Black incumbent. Green lost. His heavily redrawn former district elected Latina Democrat Leticia Gutierrez. Black Democrats Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina won in redrawn districts. Louisiana's 6th District heads to a December runoff. Between the lines: Hispanic Democrats are also gaining influence, with their numbers in Congress reaching new highs. California Rep. Pete Aguilar, a Hispanic Democrat, appears headed for majority whip, a top party leadership job. The Congressional Hispanic Caucus expects 55 members, including senators and Puerto Rico's nonvoting resident commissioner — its largest membership since its 1976 founding. Yes, but: Hispanic gains don't necessarily come at Black lawmakers' expense. Hispanic Democrats on Financial Services have backed Waters , showing how the two groups can work together as their members seek more influence. Younger lawmakers say term limits could open doors for the next generation of Black and Hispanic leaders.

events.title: My husband and I chose to pursue career opportunities in different cities. We each lived with one child and reunited on weekends.
events.summary: The author and her husband (not pictured) took jobs in different cities in Texas. SolStock/Getty Images My husband and I received lucrative career opportunities in Austin and Dallas in 2019. We decided to live separately with one child each and reunite as a family every weekend. The pandemic brought us back together and helped us realize that family time mattered most. Throughout Summer 2019, our family — two kids, a rescue dog, my husband, and me — lived in Austin. I was a mom with a few contract jobs while my husband worked full time. That pivotal year, I got what Vito Corleone would call "an offer I could not refuse," and so did my husband. By Fall 2019, my husband and I were living in two different cities , each with one kid, while still married. We both had jobs in Austin My husband was a young professional working for a tech startup. Pay was reasonable. Culture was great. He felt valued and satisfied with his work. After working in downtown Austin, he'd come home to our elementary-aged son, toddler daughter, dog (Chester), and me. I had an extensive background in fitness. I had served in campus recreation at a few Texas universities in the early '00s when glamorous rec centers were a competitive recruiting tool for colleges. From 2005 to 2010, I played an integral role in the construction of the Dedman Center for Recreational Sports at Southern Methodist University. The author was offered a job in Dallas and her husband stayed behind in Austin. Courtesy of the author By the mid-2000s, lavish recreation facilities weren't just value-enhancers for schools. They became highly desirable in the multifamily market. My work with SMU's fitness center was noticed by a nearby apartment community, The Village Dallas. I got an offer in Dallas Mention The Village Dallas to anyone who lived in Dallas in the 1970s, and they'll get a grin like a Cheshire cat, recalling the iconic property. The Village is a community of apartment complexes that share central amenities. It attracted young singles. The Village had aged. Lincoln Property Company was ready to restore The Village Dallas to its old glory days. Village Main Street would be a $350M hospitality addition to The Village Dallas. It would include a boutique hotel, restaurants, bars, a country club, a pool that would rival Las Vegas resort pools, sports fields, and a recreation center. I was invited to serve as a consultant on the rec center. From 2015 to 2019, I worked from Austin as the project's fitness consultant. I marked up renderings, allocated dedicated space for programming, selected equipment, tendered bids, and procured CAD drawings. I would meet with stakeholders occasionally in Dallas but handled most of my obligations remotely. In 2019, I received an offer to transition into a full-time role as Executive Director of Wellness. The Village presented me with a six-figure salary, bonus structure, and housing allowance. Acceptance would mean relocation to Dallas. With my husband's support , I took the job. We split up our family My husband notified his employer that he would need to tender his resignation to move to Dallas , citing my job offer. He had worked for the tech company for seven years by then, and it was no longer a startup. These were high times for Austin tech businesses, and my husband was valued in his role as senior manager. His supervisor asked that he hold off on giving his letter. The next day, he was presented with a sizable salary increase to stay put. We had options. I could revoke my acceptance, and we could maintain the status quo in Austin. He could decline the offer and move to Dallas for my job. Or we could lean into both. We chose the latter. On weekends, the family would come together. Either the boys would drive up to Dallas or the girls down to Austin. We kept our 6-year-old son in his established school in Austin. Our 2-year-old daughter and I moved into a Village apartment in Dallas. We connected over FaceTime nightly and in person on Saturday and Sunday. Our plan was to give it a year, then revisit our situation. We decided the family needed to be together Then the pandemic changed everything. My daughter and I drove home to Austin for what we thought would be a week. It ended up being three months. The pandemic was a tragic time for the world. Conversely, for our family, it bound us back together under the same roof . We felt immense gratitude. We were glad that we took agency and tried something difficult. Our sacrifices translated to financial security. My husband and I modeled for our son and daughter that our family supports ambitious women. We agreed that togetherness was our top priority. We had to choose between Austin and Dallas. I resigned from my job in June 2020, although my husband was willing to be the one to do so. He loved his work, and my squirrely heart preferred outdoor adventures over business meetings. Now, the kids and I go on hikes, jump off cliffs, and ride a Vespa scooter. I became a wellness writer. I've authored three books, created content, and emboldened other women to get outside and be active. I still model ambition. It just looks different now. events.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
events.summary: Published 18 November 2026, 07:15 GMT Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year. A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week. Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget. Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show. Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel. In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%. Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved. Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings. Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs. VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January. But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East". Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power." Sophie, who manages a cafe in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk". "I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said. "I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa." Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you Published 7 hours ago Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs". Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October. Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs. Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins. But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively." Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022. Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October. But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels. And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years. Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates. It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028. In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested. A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there". events.title: Bahrain's war-hit Sitra refinery weeks away from full capacity, Bapco Energies CEO says
events.summary: Bahrain's Sitra refinery, hit six times by Iranian strikes since the regional war began in late February, is still weeks away from returning to full capacity, the chief executive of energy company Bapco Energies said on Wednesday. The 415,000 barrels-per-day plant is now running at more than 80 per cent of capacity and will hit 100 per cent by the end of the year, Mark Thomas said on a panel at the Middle East Gas Conference in Dubai. The refinery is “near returning to its design capacity”, Mr Thomas said. “If you give us a few more weeks, hopefully we'll get to that point.” The final step is restarting conversion units such as the hydrocrackers, which come last in the sequence after the crude and distillation units. The recovery is a turnaround for Bahrain's only refinery, which was in the last stage of commissioning, with 27 of 32 units running, when the attacks began. It was targeted daily for about six months. “There was a moment in time that I actually felt we could be offline for one, two years,” Mr Thomas said. With the Strait of Hormuz still largely closed to normal traffic, the war has also upended where Bapco sells its fuel. Before the war, about 85 per cent of the refinery's output was exported through Hormuz. Now about 80 per cent is used within the Gulf, because damage to refineries across the region has left neighbours short of fuel. Bapco is selling jet fuel to Qatar and the UAE, diesel to Iraq and fuel to Saudi Arabia. Calling the shift temporary, Mr Thomas said export pressure will build again as rival plants are repaired. Naphtha and liquefied petroleum gas, which have no buyers in the Gulf, still have to be transported through the strait. Moving LPG has been “extremely” difficult because it needs specialised carriers. Charter rates are four times the norm and insuring one vessel for the roughly eight-hour transit costs $17 million, Mr Thomas said. “On a cargo of 300,000 barrels of diesel, it's outrageous.” Bahrain's nuclear future Bapco is also preparing to bring small modular nuclear reactors to the kingdom. The company would like to be “principally an investor, potentially an operator”, Mr Thomas said on the sidelines of the conference. A civil nuclear deal with the US, known as a 123 agreement, is “in final stages”, he said, but he declined to say when it might be signed. Mr Thomas described a 10-year development period. “We won't have anything on the ground till 2035,” he said. Asked about a target of two gigawatts by then, he said Bapco is “incubating the whole concept” for now. Bahrain, which has the Gulf's smallest hydrocarbon reserves, is looking for new sources of power as its main gas reservoir, in production for 42 years, is in decline. Bahrain and the US signed a preliminary agreement in July 2025 that opened the way to talks on a 123 agreement, which US law requires before American nuclear material or equipment can be transferred. Market volatility has helped Bapco's trading arm, which “far exceeded our expectations” this year, Mr Thomas said. It was set up to market the refinery's barrels but has quickly moved into trading third-party cargo. This year Bapco also imported crude by ship for the first time, in addition to its supply through the AB-4 pipeline from Saudi Arabia. Mr Thomas declined to name the source. LNG setback Bahrain's plans to import liquefied natural gas have been set back by the war. Demand collapsed after Aluminium Bahrain, Gulf Petrochemical Industries Company and an iron producer were hit. Bapco bought eight LNG cargoes in 2025, five of them from the US. Mr Thomas said 2027 will be “a transition year” and expects demand to return to prewar plans by 2028 or 2029. At home, Bapco is mapping offshore seismic with US company EOG Resources and expects the prospects to be gas-rich. Results will take about another year and a half, Mr Thomas said.

events.title: Windows Server 2028 won't be compatible by default
events.summary: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI. Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote . "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware." Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings. "For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup." With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote. "Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts." For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world. AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P. Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list. Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints. Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release. Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaults." "Hardening is the right direction," he said, "but it will add work for teams moving to Server 2028." According to Lansweeper’s figures, as of October 2026, Windows Server 2019 ruled the roost with 33 percent. Windows Server 2025 had reached just 7 percent. "From behavior we've seen in the past," said Dochy, "adoption is primarily driven by lifecycle, so until the more used versions start going EOL, I don't expect much adoption, similar to what Server 2025 is experiencing." Windows Server 2025 remains under extended support until 2034, but Microsoft's direction of travel is clear: beefed-up security by default, a home for AI applications, and Intune management for fleets of servers. ®

events.title: Cassava seeks $1B for Nvidia chips
events.summary: Cassava Technologies is seeking as much as $1 billion to buy Nvidia chips, according to Bloomberg, as one of Africa’s biggest tech groups attempts to build computing infrastructure across the continent. The fundraising effort is part of the ambitions of Cassava’s founder, Zimbabwean billionaire Strive Masiyiwa, to build Africa-based computing infrastructure for the AI boom. Most of the money would be used to buy chips for data centers across the continent, and the rest would upgrade the company’s digital infrastructure to handle AI workloads. Cassava last year announced that it had secured investment from the US chipmaker. Africa accounts for a tiny fraction of global data center capacity, according to the Africa Data Centres Association’s 2026 report, leaving companies that are seeking AI compute dependent on limited continental infrastructure . South African President Cyril Ramaphosa is in California this week leading a 300-plus delegation seeking insights and investment around AI. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
events.summary: Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year. Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone. But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how. Energy bills forecast to rise by 26% That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%. Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November. Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels. Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights. How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit. The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support. The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , external , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills. While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%. It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full. There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed. Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then. The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data. But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices. Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater. Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few. If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people. Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again Published 6 hours ago One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings. The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February. Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come. To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure. The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down. The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention. As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay. That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances. events.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
events.summary: Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year. Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone. But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how. Energy bills forecast to rise by 26% That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%. Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November. Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels. Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights. How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit. The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support. The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation , external , as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills. While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%. It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full. There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed. Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then. The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data. But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices. Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater. Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few. If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people. Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again Published 6 hours ago One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings. The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February. Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come. To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure. The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down. The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention. As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay. That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances. How is the rising cost of living affecting your quality of life? events.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver. How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us? —Amit Katwala Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure. Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power . —Casey Crownhart MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century. As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple The agency’s classified communications network has gone down. ( CNBC ) + Marco Rubio says they’re unrelated and not hostile acts. ( Guardian ) + But AI is accelerating the discovery of vulnerabilities. ( Vox ) + And making online crimes easier. ( Nature ) + Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status. ( DW ) + Other infections could be next. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Only nine countries have backed COP31’s AI climate pledge The voluntary pledge doesn’t include binding targets. ( Reuters $) + Plans for carbon removal tech have divided COP31. ( New Scientist $) + For all its flaws, the annual climate meeting still matters. ( Axios ) + What to know about this year’s talks. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Nvidia has delivered blowout results and rejected Huang’s return Revenue more than doubled amid booming AI chip sales. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that. Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease. The technologies could make IVF more effective and accessible. But they’re also raising difficult ethical questions about how far reproductive medicine should go. events.title: Surge in complaints, compensation claims after Telstra outage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Telstra's July network outage drives surge in telco complaints Topic: Telecommunications Services Industry The Telstra outage prompted a spike in complaints. ( ABC News: Glen Armstrong ) Dissatisfied mobile and internet customers are increasingly turning to the industry ombudsman for compensation amid rising network outages. Consumer advocates say telcos should provide automatic compensation to those affected. A woman unable to receive updates about her critically ill mother was among more than 13,000 Australians who lodged official complaints with the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) in the September quarter. The 12-hour Telstra network outage on July 8 fuelled a 72 per cent surge in complaints that mentioned network outages, including domestic violence victim-survivors, people in ill-health and customers in financial hardship. In total, telcos were forced to pay out $1.9 million in compensation to 2,267 complainants in the quarter, via a combination of direct compensation, bill adjustments, refunds and account credits. Network outages are an increasingly common and expensive headache for phone and internet customers, according to the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN). Its chief executive, Carol Bennett, said the ombudsman complaint figures were "only the tip of the iceberg" when it came to customer harm caused by outages. "Since April 1 this year, Optus has had 110 outages, and Telstra has had 334," Ms Bennet said. Modelling by FTI Consulting estimates the July 8 Testra outage cost the Australian economy $552 million and the 2023 Optus outage in the order of $2 billion. Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) Cynthia Gebert said telcos should act swiftly and fairly to address the harm caused by phone or internet outages. Cynthia Gebert is the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman. ( Supplied: Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman ) She added that consumers always had the option to lodge a complaint with the TIO seeking compensation if they were unsatisfied with their provider's response. "Losing service can be much more than an inconvenience," Ms Gerbert said. Overall, complaints about telcos rose 8.4 per cent on the previous quarter, with the top three complaints being disputed charges (4,151 complaints, down 7.3 per cent on the previous quarter), compensation for poor experience or inconvenience (2,032 complaints, up 58 per cent) and complaints about 'no service' (1,311, down 9 per cent). The number of complaints to the ombudsman seeking compensation for a poor customer experience or for being inconvenienced by their telco provider has doubled over the past year. Carol Bennett says the onus should not be on customers to go cap-in-hand to retailers. ( ABC News: Abubakr Sajid ) A spokesperson for Telstra said 99 per cent of consumer and small business customers who had complained directly to the telco about the July 8 outage had had their complaint "resolved and closed". "We encourage anyone that believes they still require assistance to reach out to us." Telstra typically dominates the list of most complained about telcos, in part due to its large customer base and large regional and remote coverage. ACCAN's Ms Bennett said the onus should not be on customers to go cap-in-hand to retailers to prove their damages to get redress. Consumer groups are pushing for telco customers who suffer outages to be awarded compensation automatically, similar to what happens in the energy sector when service disruptions occur. Telstra CEO 'deeply sorry' for outage Telstra chief executive Vicki Brady apologises to the company's customers, saying the telco let them down and that investigations into the cause of Wednesday's Telstra outage are continuing. ACCAN is also calling for enforceable standards to ensure companies invest sufficiently in networks to provide reliable services, along with the implementation of 'domestic mobile roaming' so that customers can connect to another provider in the case their network fails in an outage. This echoes the findings of a Senate inquiry in September that recommended the federal government mandate domestic mobile roaming for both voice calls and text messages. It also recommended the introduction of "substantial" civil penalties for telcos that fail to meet reliability and performance standards, and to introduce "a comprehensive automatic compensation scheme for those directly or indirectly affected by service outages.

events.title: Republicans could expedite bill to make big oil immune to lawsuits, warn experts
events.summary: GOP lawmakers are rushing through high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in Climate groups fear lawmakers could pass a bill by the end of the year that would give fossil fuel companies immunity from lawsuits and legislation that aim to hold them accountable for the climate crisis. After the blue wave election, Republican lawmakers are rushing to pass high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in. Hundreds of elected leaders and climate groups sent a letter to congressional Democratic leadership urging them to reject any proposal that would shield fossil fuel companies from liability for the climate crisis. Iyla Shornstein, political director for the Center for Climate Integrity, said the election results showed voters don’t want this type of legislation. “Voters at the polls sent a clear message about how costs are impacting their everyday lives. Gas prices are skyrocketing, but why would we spend our time giving special treatment to big oil, who are also simultaneously enjoying record profits at our expense? … The elections sent a pretty clear message that our elected leaders need to be spending their time helping working families, not major corporations like big oil.” In April, Republicans introduced the Stop Climate Shakedowns bill that would shield fossil fuel companies from various attempts to hold them accountable. Ted Cruz and Harriet Hageman, two Republican lawmakers, introduced companion Senate and House bills. “Radical environmental groups have waged a coordinated campaign to weaponize our judicial system against American energy producers, including many in Texas,” Cruz said in a statement announcing the Senate bill. “They’re using meritless lawsuits to bankrupt our energy industry, kill good-paying jobs and drive up the cost of electricity and gasoline for hardworking families.” Eleven states, two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities have filed lawsuits against big oil companies to hold them accountable for the climate emergency. The lawsuits are grounded in science that connects climate disasters to emissions from fossil fuel companies and increasing evidence that the companies deceived the public about their own internal science warning them about the dangers of fossil fuels. Another accountability effort has come from states such as New York and Vermont that have passed climate superfund laws to recover costs by shifting the financial burden from climate disasters on to the fossil fuel companies that caused them. Both New York and Vermont’s superfund laws have faced opposition including challenges by the Department of Justice; a judge struck down the New York superfund law in September, the state’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is appealing. The fossil fuel immunity bill has four key parts, said Shornstein: it would dismiss existing climate liability lawsuits against fossil fuel companies, prohibit new lawsuits, void climate superfund laws and assert that the federal government is the sole authority over the regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and the climate crisis, which pre-empts states from acting on it. Stopping climate lawsuits and superfund laws was a top priority for the American Petroleum Institute this year, but the bill stalled in September when the House judiciary committee failed to advance it. Shornstein said Republican lawmakers could still rush through the bill or attach immunity language to other legislation before the end of the current Congress. “We’re at a critical moment, because Trump and the GOP and big oil’s allies want to bail out the fossil fuel industry while they still have power,” she said. “Immunity for big oil has been high on the list of priorities, so this is their last-ditch effort.” “We need to be extremely on our toes and vigilant and ready to mobilize to make sure that Congress rejects this sweeping giveaway to big oil,” said Kathy Mulvey, program director for fossil fuel accountability at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I expect that they would see the lame duck session as a real opportunity to push through the Cruz-Hageman bill.” The bill would block source attribution science, a growing field of science that connects climate disasters to the emissions of specific oil and gas companies. The bill says such scientific efforts “lack scientific credibility and are, therefore, arbitrary”. “The fact that [they] are specifically going after this field of science and the scientists who are playing a leading role indicates really how much they’re threatened by being held accountable for the harms that they’re causing,” Mulvey said. The immunity bill follows a pattern of powerful industries asking Congress to shield them from liability – although not all have succeeded. In the 1990s, when tobacco companies faced dozens of lawsuits seeking to recover costs from smoking-related illnesses, they unsuccessfully lobbied Congress to introduce legislation to shield them.

events.title: Nvidia clarifies when it will — and won’t — keep financing neoclouds
events.summary: One reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it. And Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter , which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter. But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the company aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, announced in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company said. Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking . She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion. Under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she said. “There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress said to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call. She pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before. Kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially new data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future. “The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.” One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products . Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over . events.title: SpaceX $40 billion chip financing to stay off balance sheet
events.summary: The colossal $40 billion financing that Apollo is lining up for SpaceX could hit markets as early as this week, but it won’t be hitting their balance sheet, according to people familiar with the matter. The financing will go into an SPV, or special-purpose vehicle, allowing SpaceX to keep it off its own balance sheet and instead rent GPUs from its subsidiary. Apollo will be lending close to $20 billion of the deal upfront and then syndicating it or selling it to other investors later. Other companies, including Meta, have utilized this kind of financial workarounds to keep debt off their bottom lines. It also allows the companies to keep their ratings elevated. Portions of the seven-part deal could be sold to investors as early as this week. The arrangement includes an array of pricing — the bulk of which, $35.5 billion, will price at 8.3% and 7.75%, Semafor reported earlier . Other, riskier parts of the deal will price even higher, at a blended rate that could exceed 9%, but will account for less than $3 billion of the overall financing. events.title: Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers
events.summary: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the forecast rise next year Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain looks likely to go up by 26% in January . But your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. Providers are offering fixed tariffs that work out up to £407 below the estimated price cap, according to price comparison website uSwitch. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. The easiest way is to use a price comparison website such as Uswitch , GoCompare and The Energy Shop . They typically obtain a lot of information from suppliers so you need to provide very little to get a quote (you might be alarmed by how much data is on there). Once your usage details are in and you have selected which energy you want to compare – probably gas and electricity – and how you pay, you will be presented with a list of tariffs. You will see the price for using the same amount of energy as you do now, what type of deal it is – fixed or variable – and how long it lasts. You will also be shown if there are exit fees. You will have to pay these if you want to move again before the end of the deal, and there is usually one for gas and one for electricity. Some are just £25 each, although some are £100. As a default, comparison sites typically show only the deals from providers that pay them commission when you switch, but a list of all offers should be available; look out for filters that let you see the whole of the market. The cheapest tariffs are often with providers that do not operate via switching sites, so you will only see them if you opt for all deals. If you want to move to one of them, you need to go direct. If you would prefer not to move, call your provider and ask if you are on the best tariff for your usage. If you are not, then it should also be able to help you move to a better deal. Should I move my gas and electricity? It’s up to you, and comparison sites will let you compare dual-fuel deals and separate accounts for each, letting you decide which is cheapest. What if I owe my energy supplier money? You will not be allowed to switch if you are more than 28 days behind with payments to your current supplier. If you’re on a prepayment meter you cannot move if you have a debt of more than £500. What if the supplier owes me money? Your old provider should give you a final bill within six weeks of your switch and it then has 10 working days to refund you anything it owes. For each milestone it misses it has to pay you £40 in compensation. I’m a tenant – does that mean I’m stuck? No. Unless you pay the landlord for your gas and electricity and they manage the accounts, you should be able to switch. Citizens Advice says if your landlord pays your energy provider and you want to switch, you should find a tariff you want and then explain to the landlord why it’s a good deal – but it says they do not have to switch. How long does it take to switch providers? The new supplier must take over your account within five working days, unless you specify a later date for the move – for example if you are switching from an existing contract with exit fees. If there are delays, your new supplier must give you £40 in compensation. Switchers who have problems should complain to the provider in the first instance, but can then approach the energy ombudsman .

events.title: Target will take momentum from strong third quarter into the holiday shopping season
events.summary: Target is reporting its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation NEW YORK -- Target delivered its strong quarterly sales gains in roughly five years, fueled by a revitalized product lineup, expanded same-day deliveries and price cuts that brought in customers battered by inflation. The company raised its annual earnings and sales outlook again on Wednesday after an encouraging third quarter. Target reported a better-than-expected 7.1% increase in net sales, the best performance since the fourth quarter of 2021. The company also posted its third straight quarter of quarterly comparable sales, which include sales from online and its physical stores. Sales made through digital channels operating for at least 12 months increased 9.8% from the same quarter last year, while comparable sales at established stores rose 4.6%. The three-month period that ended Oct. 31 overlapped with back-to-school shopping season. The Minneapolis retailer reported growth in a majority of its six core merchandise categories, led by electronics, gaming equipment, sporting goods, toys, trading cards and collectibles, a category Target refers to as "Fun 101.” It also cited higher sales of beauty products, food and beverages. But Target CEO Michael Fiddelke , a 20-year company veteran who became chief executive in February, told reporters this week that the sales momentum was not limited to certain categories or based on any one initiative. He said Target has seen business pick up across its markets among shoppers of all incomes. “It’s the cumulative impact of changes across our business that is driving this guest preference for Target,” Fiddelke said. The company said November net sales so far are in line with the full-year outlook. Together, comparable store and digital sales in August, September and October increased 5.6% though that figure is being compared to a 2.7% drop in the year-ago period. The retailer also reported a 5.6% gain in the first quarter and a 3.8% uptick in the second quarter of this year. In March, Fiddelke unveiled a multibillion dollar investment plan aimed at reversing a post-pandemic sales slump. The overhaul included a focus on stocking products and brands that would help restore Target's reputation as a place to go for affordable yet stylish items. Target launched a new Target Beauty Studio concept in more than 600 locations in September. The new area, which features upscale beauty products and staff trained to offer advice, partly replaced the Ulta shops that were in some stores before Target and Ulta Beauty ended their partnership in August. With U.S. consumers expressing concerns about the U.S. economy and their own finances, Target also has promoted price reductions this year, including cuts on nearly 2,000 additional items during the third quarter. The company said most of the new items it has for the holiday shopping season cost $20 or less, including thousands priced at $5 and under. Target is one of the first big retailers to report third-quarter earnings. The results could give industry analysts and economists another read on how U.S. consumers responded to ongoing inflation pressure before the end-of-year holidays. Target said it earned $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, including a 50-cent benefit from a government tariff refund. In the third quarter of 2025, the company reported $689 million, or $1.51 per share. Net sales rose 7.1% to $27.07 billion compared to $25.27 billion in the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $2.08 per share on net sales of $26.5 billion, according to FactSet. Target now expects net sales for the full year to be up roughly 6%, one percentage point higher than the guidance it gave in August. The company projected full-year earnings per share of $10.65 to $11.40. That includes a $2.14 tariff refund benefit. In August, the company expected earnings of $9.90 to $10.90 per share. Analysts were projecting profits of $10.25 per share on sales of $110.27 billion. events.title: Inside Google’s push to make AI the new Auto-Tune
events.summary: Google is trying to prove that AI won’t replace artists. The tech giant has rolled out a suite of generative AI music features over the past year, including Flow Music — a tool it acquired in February when it bought the startup ProducerAI — which allows users to create songs from a single prompt, in the same style as AI music giants like Suno and Udio. But the company’s pitch to artists is that its technology can also act like a tool in their creative process, not unlike Auto-Tune or MIDI. To prove it, Google launched Flow Music Sessions earlier this year, an artist residency program for those curious about integrating the technology into their creative processes. Residents work in Spaces, a Flow Music feature carried over from ProducerAI that allows artists to vibe code their own tools and plugins. The fusion of art with artificial intelligence makes some artists queasy, and it has since ChatGPT launched in 2022. But, Google has long found ways into the creator economy from different angles. It grew YouTube, today a juggernaut video-sharing site rivaling cable, largely by giving platforms to independent creators. Now, it’s betting that artists wary of AI can be won over in the same way: on their own terms. For artists in Google’s Flow Music residency, that distinction is important. “I draw creative fuel and energy and joy from making things myself,” Avanti Singh, a sound designer and resident at Flow Music, told Semafor. “I’m not particularly interested in prompting an entire song to be created because the most fun part for me is writing lyrics and singing and collaborating.” Instead, artists in the program vibe code to bolster the creative process, cutting down on the most tedious production steps. Mike Costanzo, a producer in the residency, built a “perfect kick” plugin in Spaces that he says cuts down the time it takes to find an apt kick drum for a song. He picks a genre, taps a musical key to tune the drum, and the plugin handles the rest. Google has come under fire for its AI music generation. A group of independent musicians and songwriters filed a lawsuit against Google in March, alleging the tech giant trained its music model Lyria 3 on copyrighted recordings from YouTube without permission or compensation. Google Flow now runs on newer versions of that model. Google has moved to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that music uploaded to YouTube is already broadly licensed for AI training in accepting the platform’s terms of service.

events.summary: The News The recent dip in AI company valuations isn’t concerning to one of the Gulf’s biggest investors in the space because it could allow stronger businesses to emerge and give the industry time to win over public opinion, Qatar Investment Authority’s CEO said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The $580 billion sovereign wealth fund invests for future generations, a time horizon that can absorb volatility while the industry’s winners emerge. “A quarter of a blip or a year of correction doesn’t really mean much for us as a long-term investor,” Mohammed Al-Sowaidi said. “We have a super cycle of innovation happening now. It’s a big revolution, it has to have its ups and downs.” A possible downturn could deliver productivity gains across industries, according to Al-Sowaidi. Companies that succeed will become more distinct and focused, which makes assessing their business models somewhat easier. The potential of AI in areas such as manufacturing, drug discovery, and other applications that could improve lives and expand the economy as reasons for confidence in the technology. QIA has committed to invest $500 billion in the US over the next decade. That plan hasn’t changed, despite the US-Iran war’s effect on the country: Qatar’s energy infrastructure was struck by Iran, and LNG exports are a fraction of normal flows. Still, QIA has remained acquisitive this year, and Al-Sowaidi said “no dividend has been given out to the government,” which is funding itself with other reserves. Q&A QIA backs Anthropic. Did you seek additional shares in the IPO? We’ve been early backers of Anthropic. We believed back then that this could be a very good, new form of enterprise solution. We did submit and in a couple of days we’ll see how the results are. It can’t be more interesting from a timing perspective. It’s a large business and they’ve demonstrated great execution. Has Qatar been able to secure the advanced AI chips it needs from the US? From a Qatar perspective, we are very well integrated into the United States. Most of the applications we have are US applications from an AI stack point of view. We’re very well integrated with the financial system in the US, with the Treasury Department. So we had no struggle really getting this executed. Do you plan to invest more in US tech? Over the past 12 years, we’ve been doubling down on technology in the US. We have an office in New York, where we doubled the operation to about 40 people, and they’re frequent visitors to the West Coast. A lot of great ideas come from San Francisco and from the leading technology companies. We’ve been focusing on artificial intelligence and applications and frontier labs and infrastructure plays. I think it’s just the beginning of a large cycle of super innovation. The searches resulted in officers seizing cash, drugs, and other high-value items, including a watch worth around £230,000, with the total haul valued at more than £2 million. Police put losses identified so far at £1.5 million and expect that figure to rise as the investigation continues. events.title: A flawed test for African banks
events.summary: Fitch’s downgrade of the Africa Export-Import Bank in June 2025 sparked a furious debate about the assessments of multilateral development banks by global rating agencies. Then in February, Moody’s proposed changes to its methodology for assessing these types of banks. The revisions, applied since July, introduced a potential two-notch downgrade if a bank does not have large, highly rated, and non-borrowing shareholders. This could make it difficult for African-owned development banks to secure higher ratings without bringing in non-African shareholders, effectively forcing these lenders to surrender part of their ownership and control. Credit ratings are intended to provide an independent assessment of an institution’s capacity and willingness to repay its obligations. In the case of assessments of multilateral banks, rating methodologies have a bias towards non-African shareholders. In effect suggesting that African governments, irrespective of their demonstrated financial commitments, cannot provide sufficient capital to the institutions they have established. The nationality of shareholders may be relevant to risk analysis, but it should not become a substitute for examining fundamentals. If the institution has strong risk management and governance structures, adequate capitalization, quality assets, and high liquidity, where the shareholders come from should be less important. Foreign investment and diversity of shareholding are valuable, but they should be a strategic choice for the institutions themselves rather than a condition implicitly imposed by the architecture of credit assessment. A more fundamental issue is the difference between paid-in capital that shareholders have actually contributed and callable capital that they have promised to provide if there is a need. Afreximbank is a good example. Shareholders’ funds stand at approximately $9 billion, while its net income increased by 30% in the first half of 2026. The commitment of African shareholders is also significant. According to the bank’s leadership, African governments contributed approximately $2.6 billion in additional paid-in capital by the end of 2025. A further $526 million had been paid or committed in cash contributions in 2026. In addition, shareholders have committed substantial callable capital. This is another important layer of protection for creditors. But Moody’s new methodology still places more value on callable capital from foreign highly rated shareholders than substantial paid-in capital from African shareholders. A more balanced assessment should recognize capital contributions and other tangible financial commitments regardless of the creditworthiness of shareholders. Today’s rating methodologies characterize geographical concentration and an exclusive focus on the African business environment as indicators of high risk. This creates a further structural disadvantage for African-owned multilateral development banks whose mandates require them to serve African economies. To secure higher credit ratings, these institutions need to reduce lending to the very economies they were established to support. This will diminish their role and purpose. Rating agencies should not be expected to overlook weaknesses in African governance, capital adequacy, liquidity or risk management. Independence and analytical integrity remain essential to the credibility of the ratings industry. To maintain this, three changes are necessary. First, ratings should be accurate and consistent in their assessments. African institutions should not be penalized simply because their shareholders are African and operate in Africa. Nationality should not be a proxy for financial capacity and willingness to pay. Second, African governments must continue to support their institutions with capital and affirm their legal commitments established through their agreements and treaties: This pushes rating agencies to assess multilateral banks based on their legal and operational merits. Lastly, African countries must strengthen cooperation among their multilateral financial institutions, deepen domestic capital markets, and support the development of independent African credit rating capacity. Greater competition and analytical diversity will improve the quality of credit assessments, provided all agencies maintain rigorous standards. Africa cannot build its own strong multilateral financial institutions if the price of recognition is surrendering the ownership and control to foreign shareholders.

events.title: Netflix, Fox and the $2bn bid for the 2030 World Cup that could reshape live sports
events.summary: The battle for the US TV rights to the tournament will pit the traditional broadcaster and the ‘whatever-it-takes’ streamer. It could be a tipping point in the industry T he awarding of broadcast rights in the United States for this year’s World Cup was a cut-price deal to avoid legal action from the existing rights holders, Fox Sports. This week’s tender process for the 2030 tournament will be anything but. Media rights and broadcast experts canvassed by the Guardian in the US and Europe are united in agreement that Fifa will benefit from the most competitive and expensive auction in the competition’s history. It is expected to fetch between $1.5bn (£1.13bn) and $2bn, with some predicting the outcome could be a landmark moment for the sports and entertainment industry. There also appears to be a clear frontrunner. “I would put money on Netflix to win – they will pay whatever it takes,” one experienced media rights buyer told the Guardian. Multiple sources have confirmed that Netflix would submit a bid before Thursday’s deadline for first-round offers, along with their fellow streamers Apple TV, Disney, Amazon, YouTube and Dazn, as well as the traditional broadcasting heavyweights, Fox, ESPN, NBC Universal and Skydance, although the last of these may find itself constrained by the budget cuts being made after its $110bn acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Netflix has already bought exclusive rights in the US for the 2027 and 2031 Women’s World Cups. “There’s a huge range of buyers and therefore a broad range of possible outcomes,” one broadcasting veteran says. “All the media companies and streamers will bid. Fox will find it very challenging to retain the rights.” In a significant change, Fifa is selling the English and Spanish rights together for the first time, a move that indicates it is seeking a single exclusive rights holder, which would suit the streaming companies. With Fox having paid $485m for exclusive English-language rights to the 2026 World Cup, and NBC Universal’s Telemundo paying $600m for the Spanish-language rights, the only certainty is that the 2030 price will be far higher, despite less attractive kick-off times for a US audience as the tournament is in Morocco, Spain and Portugal. The impact of the time difference is hard to price, but may not prove to be that significant given the seemingly insatiable demand. NBC paid about $1.5bn for exclusive rights for the 2024 Paris Olympics and were rewarded with average daily viewing figures of more than 30 million, albeit with far more variation in programming than a World Cup. Fifa awarded non-competitive extensions to Fox and Telemundo in 2015 as compensation for moving the 2022 Qatar World Cup to winter, a perspective that was strengthened on the back of this year’s record-breaking tournament. Fox’s live coverage of Spain’s extra-time victory over Argentina in the final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history, with a peak audience of 51.685 million; five World Cup games brought in average audiences of more than 20 million; and the average viewing figure across all 104 matches was 7.7 million, twice the figure in Qatar four years earlier. Telemundo’s coverage, available through NBC’s streaming platform Peacock, averaged a total audience of 6 million viewers per game, with Spain v Argentina and Mexico v England attracting peak audiences of more than 23 million, the highest-ever for Spanish-language broadcasts in the US. The bumper audiences were extremely lucrative for the broadcasters, with figures from the advertising sales analysts Guideline showing that Fox and Telemundo generated a combined $1.19bn in advertising revenue alone during the tournament, almost three times the figure from Qatar four years earlier and more than their original rights investment. Fox alone brought in $835m from World Cup advertising, with 30-second slots costing between $200,000 and $750,000 according to the Hollywood Reporter, and the six-minute hydration breaks generating between $2m and $9m per game. Having left a considerable amount of money on the table because of the circumstances of the 2026 process, Fifa is determined to cash in this time around. Holding the auction only four months after the US hosted the World Cup appears a clear attempt to capitalise on the success of the previous tournament, which contributed the vast majority of Fifa’s $4bn media revenues over the four-year cycle to 2026. The addition of hydration breaks will give bidders such as Fox more revenue to play with, although Fifa will expect the option for extra adverts to drive up the price and take its own cut this time around, having missed out in the summer. The two three-minute breaks in each half were only finalised last year and did not feature in the 2026 tender documents. “Sports advertising is much more valuable than entertainment programming as it has a broader reach,” says François Godard, an independent media analyst.
