events.title: Felicis leads $7.5M bet on Unsiloed AI to make enterprise documents usable by AI agents
events.summary: As businesses increasingly turn to AI agents to automate work, the vast amounts of information locked in complex documents remain a challenge. Unsiloed AI has raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to tackle that problem, aiming to help enterprises make their documents more accessible to AI agents through specialized technology. Silicon Valley venture capital firm Felicis led the round, with participation from Y Combinator, Orange Collective, and Uncorrelated Ventures. Angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner also participated. Business documents often include tables, charts, and complicated layouts that AI systems can struggle to interpret accurately. But getting the information wrong can lead to costly mistakes for businesses, and the impact could be severe in the case of a bank, hospital, or a law firm, as they rely on these documents for their daily work. Unsiloed aims to solve this problem with software that breaks down complex documents, extracts information from tables, charts, and other elements, and turns it into structured data that AI agents can use. The technology also shows where the extracted information came from in the original document, so businesses can check the results rather than take the AI’s output at face value. “The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic,” said Unsiloed co-founder and CEO Aman Mishra (pictured above, right) in an interview. “There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.” Mishra co-founded Unsiloed with Adnan Abbas (pictured above, left), his former classmate at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur. The two joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 batch after spending some time developing the technology. Unsiloed is already working with customers in finance, legal services, and healthcare, Mishra told TechCrunch. One bank is using its technology to process documents, while a law firm has deployed it on its own servers to handle contracts and old case files, he said, without naming either customer. Mishra, however, named voice AI startup Bolna AI as a customer, saying it uses Unsiloed to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents. The San Francisco-headquartered startup has entered a market that is already crowded and includes specialized document-processing startups such as Reducto and Unstructured, as well as offerings from Microsoft and Amazon. Businesses also sometimes use general-purpose AI models to extract information from documents, giving Unsiloed another set of competitors. Mishra told TechCrunch that Unsiloed’s advantage lies in how it processes complex documents. The startup uses what it calls “dual-stream” vision models, which handle text and image data separately, along with a technique called “heat map-based chunking” that helps identify the most important parts of a document. “In one of the streams you have the text tokens, in the other stream you have the exact image tokens,” Mishra said. “This is something that we have spent a lot of time architecting.” The technology then directs more computing power toward areas such as figures, numbers, and charts. Unsiloed also uses a specialized decoder that takes industry-specific terminology into account, helping it distinguish between terms that can mean different things in different business contexts. Supporting those claims, Mishra pointed to a test involving 542 financial documents supplied by an enterprise customer. Unsiloed achieved 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points, per a technical brief shared by the startup. The test compared Unsiloed with major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence, and the customer’s in-house extraction tool. The results have, however, not been independently verified. Unsiloed also claims to have outperformed competing AI document-processing tools on olmOCR-Bench, a public benchmark developed by Allen AI. In tests conducted by the startup, Unsiloed scored 88.0, compared with 66.0 for Reducto’s agentic system and 39.9 for Unstructured. The benchmark covered 1,403 PDF pages and tested how well the systems handled tables, mathematical expressions, scanned documents, and complex layouts. Unsiloed’s pricing, Mishra said, starts at one cent per page. He asserted that the startup’s approach also helps keep its costs down by directing computing power toward the parts of a document that need the most attention, instead of processing every section in the same way. Currently, Unsiloed has a headcount of seven people. The startup, Mishra said, plans to use the fresh funding to hire more researchers and engineers, expand its sales efforts, and develop proprietary datasets to improve its technology. events.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
events.summary: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs W hen I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI . But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes. Winning union recognition would be a huge step forward in securing a meaningful say over our conditions at Rockstar, but its significance would reach far beyond that. As one of the biggest and most influential game studios in the world, what happens here could open the door for other workers across the UK to imagine an alternative future for the industry – one in which workers’ voices are taken into account more. Sometimes it’s hard to see the impact of these games when you’re working so hard on them. It’s only at times like this that the staggering scale of GTA’s success hits you. GTA V has sold over 230m copies, generating more than $10bn (£7.6bn) in worldwide revenue, surpassing any film in Hollywood’s history. This latest instalment is expected to break those records. Behind these numbers are thousands of people whose talent and hard work make the games possible. With a recognised union, we can ensure everyone, across every department, sees a fair share of the success we contributed to. Our games are industry-leading. Our wages, conditions and bonuses should be too. While the highs of a game release like this can be incredible, game workers have also come to expect other, less welcome side effects: intense overtime in the buildup and mass redundancies in the aftermath. In previous years, Rockstar has faced allegations of “crunch culture” , where game workers are expected to do unhealthy amounts of overtime in the run-up to a launch. With a strong union we could make sure there is no return to this system. We have already seen the introduction of some overtime pay, and now we want to keep on pushing to ensure that every hour worked in our industry is an hour paid. After the big day, we have had no indication that layoffs are coming, but it’s hard not to worry about what the future holds. Studios across the industry have been slashing huge portions of their workforces, with an estimated 24,000 roles axed globally over the last two years. It says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off. But the truth is that workers across the sector are helpless to resist the waves of redundancies crashing around us, until we get organised. There’s another reason this is a pivotal moment for the UK’s biggest game studio to secure union recognition. The rapid emergence of AI is transforming how studios work and raising fundamental questions about the future of our industry. Across the sector, the skills that workers spend years developing risk being devalued as their creative work is replaced by AI. Rockstar has said it is committed to preserving jobs and it has been clear that our games will continue to be made by people. But with recognition we’d have a seat at the table to manage this industry-wide transition together. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more This vote will be many people’s first introduction to unions. It’s only over the past decade that game workers have begun to unionise, realising that to tackle the industry’s mounting challenges we need to come together. The IWGB Game Workers Union – which was first founded by Rockstar workers among others in 2018 – now represents thousands of members, across 300 UK studios. Encountering unions for the first time, people have a lot of questions. We’ve heard from colleagues who are nervous that the union is an outside troublemaking force that will threaten the company. But we’re not outsiders. We are hundreds of studio employees who live for Rockstar, its output, and the players. We want to see it succeed.

events.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?
events.summary: It could protect you and your family in the event of death or accident – and in some cases it costs no more than a TV streaming service N o one wants to spend time imagining the worst thing that could happen, and perhaps that is why about 60% of UK adults have no life insurance, or why more people have pet insurance than have income protection for if they become too sick to work. However, there are certain milestones in life, such as having children or taking on a mortgage, that focus the mind on what might happen if things do go wrong. How would your family manage if you or your partner died? How would you cover the mortgage if you had an accident and couldn’t work? It’s not fun to dwell on these possibilities, but it makes sense to assess what they would mean financially, and what you can put in place to protect you and your family. There are plenty of insurance options and in some cases monthly premiums cost no more than a TV streaming service. Whole-of-life cover With this, sometimes called life assurance, premiums are paid each month and on the death of the policyholder, a set sum is paid to the beneficiaries named in the policy, assuming the claim is valid. If the cover is a joint policy for a couple, it will typically only pay out on the first death. Term life insurance This will also pay a set sum on the death of the policyholder in return for monthly premiums, but the cover ends on a specified date. It is often used to protect children while they are still dependent, or to cover a mortgage. If you buy a policy with a 25-year term offering a £100,000 payout, and the policyholder is alive at the end of that 25-year term, premiums stop, and no payment is made. It is generally cheaper than whole-of-life cover, because the insurer may never have to pay out. Decreasing term life insurance Like term life, but the sum that would be paid decreases over time. It is often used to cover a repayment mortgage, since what you owe the lender reduces as you pay it off. Income protection This will pay out a fixed sum each month for a specific period, often with an end set for the insured person’s retirement date. Premiums can be expensive. Agreeing to start receiving payments six months after you become unable to work, or reducing the monthly income amount, or the period for which you’ll receive it, can cut costs. Critical illness cover This pays a lump sum if you are diagnosed with one of the specified critical illnesses it covers, which typically include heart attack, stroke and some cancers, during the policy term. It won’t cover accidents or injuries. Conditions for payouts vary between providers. This type can be bundled in with life cover. Family income benefit If a parent dies, the family receive a predetermined income for a set number of years. Policies are often designed to pay out until children reach adulthood. For example, you might set up a policy when you have a baby and set an end date for when the child turns 22. The payouts are made for however many years you have left on the policy. It can be difficult to work out which policy is right for you. We took four scenarios and asked experts to suggest the kinds of cover that could provide peace of mind, at the right budget. Sadie, a teacher, earns about £53,000. Jim, who is a type 1 diabetic and insulin dependent, is self-employed and has an irregular income, generally lower than Sadie’s. Both are in their late 30s. They live in a rented flat with their two young children. They plan to buy a home and have built up about £15,000 in savings. Priorities Their budget is important, as they are saving for a deposit, but James Shattock, the managing director, protection, at Legal & General, says: “If one, or both, became ill or couldn’t work then, without cover they may need to eat into their savings.” As she is the main earner, protecting Sadie’s income is wise. But if Jim were to fall seriously ill or die, Sadie’s work patterns might need to change, so factor this in. Options One would be a combined life and critical illness policy to cover Sadie’s salary, Shattock says. One paying a £100,000 lump sum in the event of her death or critical illness, would cost about £45 a month, based on her current age. They could also consider income protection, although it’s more expensive. A policy that pays £2,650 a month until retirement age, deferred to start paying after six months off work, would cost about £70 a month. Kirsty Stone, a certified financial planner at The Private Office, suggests family income benefit to “provide security at a lower cost”. According to Justin Harper of LifeSearch, £30,000 a year of family income benefit for Sadie over 20 years would cost roughly £18 a month. For Jim, taking into account his diabetes, insuring a payout of £15,000 a year over 20 years would cost about £14 a month. Caveats Insurers would require details on Jim’s diabetes, such as blood glucose control, HbA1c readings, and any complications, for underwriting, says Harper.

ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit. The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed . ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight. An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering. Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters , designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch." Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing. The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem. The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV. NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year. ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can." The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. However, it uses Russian RD-180 engines, a dependency the US wishes to remove . ® Updated at 1747 GMT to reflect ULA's statement about the likely cause of the failure.

events.title: India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed US robotics companies the data they need
events.summary: As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments. The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital. Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks , but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups, including Mecka AI , XDOF , and MicroAGI , are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them. Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview. Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN . KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch. Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from. “Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said. Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers. The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized. That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said. Over the last few months, India has emerged as a hub for collecting training data for so-called physical AI, with startups, including Human Archive and BuildAI , tapping into the country’s large workforce to record people performing everyday tasks. However, the practice has also raised questions about privacy and consent, particularly when people are recorded inside their homes. Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated. Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said. events.title: The DRC's Ebola outbreak remains out of control
events.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak is spiralling , with the disease spreading at a record pace despite a surge in funding. Rampant misinformation, widespread violence, and a lack of medical equipment have aided the spread of the Bundibugyo strain, which is now Africa’s biggest-ever Ebola outbreak by geographic reach. A lack of treatments or vaccines has also meant that the current outbreak is more fatal than ever: Around 50% of those who are infected die, the highest-ever mortality rate for Ebola. Although authorities are seeking more funding, more than $700 million remains unaccounted for by the DRC, according to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, while frontline workers have gone unpaid for months. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Easier QR code payments, smoother online checkouts to come with enhanced PayNow
events.summary: Tourists visiting Singapore and Singaporeans travelling overseas can also expect more payment options as links between local and regional QR payment networks are expanded. SINGAPORE – Consumers can look forward to easier QR code payments here and a smoother online shopping checkout process as enhancements to the PayNow instant payments system are rolled out progressively from 2027. Tourists visiting Singapore and Singaporeans travelling overseas can also expect more payment options as links between local and regional QR payment networks are expanded through the enhanced SGQR+. These proposed enhancements and their implementation road map were outlined in the PayNow Generation 2 Phase 2 report released by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) on Nov 18. The first phase examined how PayNow has evolved since its 2017 launch, with findings released in June . The second phase has identified seven enhancements to address gaps identified in the review, to be made between 2027 and 2028. Through the enhanced SGQR+, Singaporeans and tourists will be able to pay with their preferred apps without having to check which QR schemes are accepted by the merchant, as Singapore connects to more major regional QR networks through SGQR+. This will also enable more Singapore merchants to accept payments from tourists through a wider pool of foreign payment networks and Singaporeans to pay through local apps in more countries. Development of the SGQR+ switch, which will provide an additional connection between participating schemes rather than require merchants or payment providers to replace their existing arrangements, is already under way. A limited roll-out in 2027 will connect an initial group of participating schemes and test live payment journeys before expanding in scope in 2028. Another key enhancement is deep-linking. Already live in Lazada checkouts via the OCBC app, it seamlessly opens shoppers’ preferred payment app when they select PayNow when checking out on an e-commerce platform. This eliminates the need to screenshot or download QR codes and retrieve them in the payment app from their phone gallery. Higher PayNow limits will also allow Singaporeans to make and receive larger government payments with instant confirmation. The enhancement will first be introduced in late 2027 with one government agency, which has not been identified, before being progressively rolled out to other agencies from 2028. Singapore currently applies a $200,000 limit for PayNow, which constrains its use for some high-value payments, such as property down payment or full payments for cars, above this threshold. Clearer and more consistent rules will also be developed to address payment disputes, refunds, fraud and scams that may arise from individuals’ PayNow transactions to merchants. This could offer customers and merchants a more consistent dispute resolution experience, with clearer processes and potentially faster resolution in certain cases, particularly those involving technical issues. Such safeguards will be introduced in stages over 2028 by the Singapore Payments Network ( SPaN), which was set up in 2025 by MAS and ABS to oversee Singapore’s national and cross-border payment schemes. MAS will bring together SPaN, Banking Computer Services and other key partners to innovate new payment capabilities for emerging use cases, including AI agent-initiated payments. Industry participants, including ABS, banks and payment service providers, will also test ways to process very large numbers of frequent micro-payments more cheaply. OCBC said it has already enabled PayNow deep-linking with platforms such as Lazada, Pinduoduo, AXS, Frasers Mall and AnyWheel, as well as government agencies like the CPF Board for a more seamless checkout experience. UOB said it is working with industry partners to explore some of the capabilities envisioned under the plans to enhance PayNow Generation 2, including how deep-linking and account-to-account payments can be more seamlessly integrated into online shopping jour neys. Sheila Chiang is a business correspondent at The Straits Times.

According to a notice published last week , Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments." CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government. The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice . The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested. Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP). PNC tech team slammed: 'Inadequate' tests of code contributed to loss of 413k records A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022. The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date. The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence . The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London. events.title: David Beckham's perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink | Arwa Mahdawi
events.summary: David Beckham’s perfume, Poundland – and a mighty, mighty stink The Beckhams have made an art of monetising their every move. But apparently there are limits to where they’re prepared to sell their wares T houghts and half-price prayers with Poundland, please. The discount chain has been on the verge of collapse for a while , and its future looks bleak. Now, to add to the ignominy, David Beckham is kicking it while it’s down. Not literally, by the way: I suppose I should spell that out since we’re dealing with a litigious billionaire . I did not mean to imply or cause a reasonable person to infer that Sir David is standing on Brixton high street kicking a Poundland. Rather, DB Ventures, the licensor of the David Beckham brand, is causing a bit of a stink about the fact that the football legend’s fragrance range was found on sale in the discount store as well as at other purveyors of budget goods. It is now suing the perfume company , Coty, which it further accuses of under reporting sales, for $41m (£31m). “DB Ventures … ensures that all of its brand licensing partnerships maintain the lifestyle and luxury image of the brand that Sir David has carefully cultivated for decades,” court filings stated. “Imagine, then, the shock and dismay experienced when DB Ventures discovered that David Beckham products were being offered for sale in a gas station. How could this possibly have happened? Desperation and greed.” Coty has denied that it had ever sold the fragrances in Poundland. Either way, the lawyer who wrote this exquisite paragraph is wasted in the legal profession and should really think about a marketing career. They’ve managed to distill the essence of the Beckham brand in just a few words: desperation and greed. I’m not saying that Victoria and David Beckham, who are now worth an estimated £1.2bn, aren’t talented and hardworking, etc. But at a certain point monetising every second of your life, and wringing every possible penny out of your famous name, gets a bit naff, doesn’t it? While celebrity-backed businesses and endorsements are obviously commonplace, the Beckhams have taken things to an extreme, slapping their name or image on everything from whisky to Walkers crisps to AliExpress. Even 15-year-old Harper Beckham is launching a skincare brand . They’ve become the British Kardashian-Jenners. Not everyone in the Beckham family seems quite so keen on the family business, however. “My family values public promotion and endorsements above all else,” Brooklyn Peltz Beckham, who has been in a bitter feud with his parents, lamented in a statement published in January . “Brand Beckham comes first.” You’d think that a public feud with their son would have taught Posh ‘n’ Becks that there are certain things money can’t buy. For everything else, there’s Poundland. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: China dominates battery graphite, but this startup could break the monopoly
events.summary: Electric vehicle sales in the U.S. may have leveled off, but the market for batteries inside them isn’t slowing down, quintupling in the last five years. Many of those are made in the U.S., but they’re largely dependent on China for key ingredients, including graphite. Graphite is a key ingredient in lithium-ion batteries, where it forms the anode, the part that stores the battery’s charge. Chinese companies control about three-quarters of the graphite anode supply chain and 97% of synthetic (human-made) graphite anode production, according to Benchmark Mineral Intelligence . One five-year-old startup, Molten Industries , is working to break that dominance. Molten Industries has started operating a demonstration plant in Oakland meant to prove the technology works, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. The plant is will pave the way for U.S.-made graphite to win a share of the market. “The new plant will be producing graphite that’s at cost parity with China plus tariffs,” Caleb Boyd, co-founder and CTO of Molten Industries, told TechCrunch. In other words, once U.S. import taxes are added to Chinese graphite, Molten’s price would match it. He said future plants should match China’s cost even without tariffs, which he called a built-in advantage of the technology. Molten’s Oakland plant will make about 300 metric tons of graphite annually, which is enough for 300 megawatt-hours of batteries. That’s enough for about 4,300 EVs. The bulk of the output will go to undisclosed customers that are testing it in their battery cells. The next facility, which Molten has yet to announce, will take the same template used in the Oakland plant and replicate it several times over, said Boyd. The startup’s technology began in a Silicon Valley garage . It uses electrical resistive heating, which passes electricity through a material to heat it, to split methane (the main ingredient in natural gas) into pure carbon and hydrogen. “You can think of it almost like a massive toaster,” Boyd said. The company says the system uses three times less electricity than existing methods, and it runs on natural gas, which is cheap and plentiful in the U.S. “We think it’s very hard to compete with China if you’re just copying their processes and trying to compete on cost,” said Kevin Bush, who co-founded Molten Industries with Boyd and is the company’s CEO. “So we are using a resource in the United States that’s abundant in natural gas, and we’ve brought some innovation to actually be able to drive down the cost of graphite production globally.” Here’s how the chemistry works: When methane (CH4) is heated without oxygen, each molecule breaks into one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. The hydrogen atoms pair up into hydrogen gas (H2), which Molten sells at market prices to a customer next door. The carbon is then processed to meet battery makers’ requirements. The basic idea of using heat to separate methane has been around for over a century, but early attempts to commercialize it ran into trouble. Carbon built up and clogged the reactor, and Boyd said no company before Molten had been able to produce high-quality graphite this way. Solving that problem changed the company’s direction. Boyd and Bush — both materials science PhDs from Stanford — originally set out to make clean hydrogen from natural gas. Most hydrogen today comes from steam reforming, a cheap but polluting process. The two wanted to reap the benefits of a low-cost feedstock like natural gas without the pollution, and they expected to sell the leftover carbon as a by-product. But as they experimented with ways to keep the reactor clean, “we actually started making this really high-quality graphite,” Boyd said, which “changed the entire economics of what we were doing.” Molten went from a hydrogen company that happened to sell graphite to a battery-grade graphite company that happens to sell hydrogen. The company says both businesses could bring in billions of dollars. If Molten supplied the entire U.S. battery market, it could also provide about a third of the hydrogen used in the country, the company claims. Other uses for high-quality graphite, like thermal batteries that store energy as heat, could expand both markets further. The new factory, Boyd said, “is really a milestone, not just for the company, we think, but globally.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism.

If the pilot works, Nets plans a nationwide roll-out. Chief executive Lawrence Chan said the aim is to make QR payments “more accessible for everyone, including visitors to Singapore”. The updated Nets app also helps tourists and families. It supports more visitors through SGQR and adds a family wallet with spending limits and transaction alerts for dependants. SINGAPORE – Consumers can soon use smartphones to complete purchases at NETS payment points – without scanning a QR code. This was among the enhancements to the N ets app announced on Nov 18. Nets is the first to pilot the tap QR facility to pay via SGQR. This feature enables consumers to make payments simply by tapping their near-field communication (NFC)-enabled smartphones at participating N ets SGQR points, without first opening the app. It offers a convenient alternative to the existing scan-to-pay method. This initiative, to run for two months will be piloted in phases, starting in Toa Payoh in December. There are plans for a nationwide roll-out if the pilot is successful. Tapping to pay via QR will initially be available through the N ets app, with support for other participating banking apps and wallets expected over time. N ets ’ chief executive Lawrence Chan said: “As usage expands, our priority is to make QR payments more accessible for everyone, including visitors to Singapore, while advancing interoperability across the payments ecosystem.” The other new features on the app will also benefit groups such as tourists, said the payments services group. From now, those whose home-country payment apps are not linked to Singapore’s single, standardised QR code, or SGQR, can also use the local payment ecosystem through the N ets app. Visitors from countries with established QR cross-border linkages with Singapore, such as China, India and Indonesia, can continue to pay directly through their local bank or wallet apps. The other enhancements include a family wallet, through which users can use sub-wallets to support the spending needs of their dependants. The primary user can set a spending limit and be notified of the transactions in their sub-wallets. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: They Were Just Admitted to the Bar. Now They’re Federal Prosecutors. Meet Trump’s New DOJ.
events.summary: Michelle Urra for ProPublica In early October, a recent law school graduate shared a post on LinkedIn that would have been unheard of before the second Trump administration. After passing the bar exam, 29-year-old Preston Bigley wrote, “With this milestone complete, I will begin serving as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Criminal Division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Texas.” It was a remarkable achievement, considering Bigley had graduated from Texas A&M’s law school in May and had been hired by the Justice Department in August to be, as his resume notes, an “incoming” assistant U.S. attorney. That unusual title was followed by an unusual caveat: “pending bar admission.” Once officially licensed to practice the law, he updated his profile to show he had become a bona fide federal criminal prosecutor. Bigley is one of a growing cohort of inexperienced attorneys, many of them fresh out of law school, who are being fast-tracked to fill the shoes of seasoned career prosecutors who fled or were purged from the DOJ in President Donald Trump’s second term. That brain drain, amounting to thousands of years of experience, comes as prosecutions of fraud and drugs have fallen in key districts to make way for Trump’s immigration agenda, ProPublica found. Across the country, ProPublica identified more than 50 new assistant U.S. attorneys with less than three years of experience who traditionally wouldn’t have been considered for such vital positions, legal experts said. Some were hired with the intent to anoint them as prosecutors — once they pass the bar exam, public disclosures show. That figure is likely a fraction of the actual total, as a comprehensive analysis is impossible because DOJ staff identities are redacted in government personnel data . But of those ProPublica identified through bar membership records and social media, about 20 passed the bar within the last year. At least seven were in the same May graduating class as Bigley, from a range of schools. “The fact that the DOJ is hiring, and indeed actively recruiting, right out of law school — it’s an astounding break with past practice,” said Juliet Sorensen, a Loyola University Chicago law professor and former assistant U.S. attorney. “It reflects a lowering of standards for a job that is important and requires lawyers who are meticulous, committed to doing the right thing, and bring with them experience beyond just law school.” To understand how Trump transformed the DOJ, ProPublica examined federal court data and records, federal workforce and state bar information, and social media accounts. We also interviewed more than two dozen former assistant U.S. attorneys. More than half of those who left the Justice Department in Trump’s first 18 months boasted nine-plus years of legal experience. Those who left had spent, on average, more than 13 years working for the government, the analysis shows. Those more experienced attorneys were the ones most likely to take on complex cases, such as money laundering, organized crime and drug trafficking, legal experts say and court dockets show. ProPublica shared its analysis and detailed questions with the DOJ; the department did not respond. Previously, the DOJ said it “remains committed to investigating and prosecuting all types of crime.” Under Trump’s Second Administration, Newly Hired Assistant U.S. Attorneys Have Less Experience Than Those Who Departed Note: This analysis of federal pay codes does not include experience ranges for supervisors. We also exclude some special assistant U.S. attorneys for whom we cannot infer experience or supervisory status. Pratheek Rebala/ProPublica The DOJ has long hired recent graduates through its Honors Program, which places graduates into rigorous training through the main office in Washington, but experts say the program was small and not meant to replace prosecutors. Before Trump’s second term, the DOJ typically would not hire new prosecutors unless they had a minimum of three to five years of legal experience, former officials and law professors said. That standard is gone. Earlier this year, Bloomberg Law reported , the DOJ waived a policy requiring at least one year of experience. While private law firms routinely hire promising graduates before they pass the bar exam, typically to begin their training, the DOJ’s hiring of new grads is a striking departure from its once-rigorous hiring process, said University of Michigan law professor Barbara McQuade, a former U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan. “The people who I hired came to us as partners in law firms,” said McQuade, who was appointed by President Barack Obama. “These were superstars who had been very successful at large law firms or in state court prosecutors’ offices.” Trump’s creation of a less experienced DOJ will have longstanding consequences, McQuade said. “It means that some very serious crimes will go unpunished,” she said. “It takes experienced prosecutors at the federal level to bring down corporate fraud, transnational gangs and corrupt public officials.” While experts expressed concern, some of those benefiting from the law school-to-federal prosecutor pathway have voiced excitement on LinkedIn. “I look forward to beginning my DOJ career by serving the Del Rio Division,” wrote Jacquelyn Kilcommons, who graduated from Pace University’s law school in May. “Upon receiving my bar exam results, I will transition into an Assistant United States Attorney (AUSA) position.” As he announced his new role in the district of Washington, D.C., newly graduated assistant U.S. attorney Ellis O’Donnell wrote, “In the past few months I have had the honor to graduate from Vanderbilt University Law School and to sit for and pass the Wisconsin Bar Exam.” None of the recent law school graduates responded to requests for comment. Shifting Personnel, Shifting Caseloads The departure of assistant U.S. attorneys in Trump’s second administration marks the largest number of exits two years into a presidential term in at least two decades. Beyond the personnel turnover, the administration’s priorities have shifted since Trump retook the White House, an analysis of Federal Judicial Center data shows. As immigration cases shot up nationwide, felony fraud prosecutions fell sharply in key districts. Amid an exodus of prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia, for instance, fraud cases fell 66%. Those cases dropped 14% in the Southern District of Florida, a hotbed for white-collar crime, where many prosecutors have left in protest of Trump’s retribution campaign against people deemed political enemies. Nationally, drug prosecutions have fallen about 10% in Trump’s first 18 months and fraud cases are flat. Meanwhile, the number of people facing immigration-related charges skyrocketed by almost 50%, clogging the courts and depleting resources at U.S. attorneys’ offices nationwide. events.title: America's measles return leaves infants vulnerable
events.summary: The loss of the United States' measles elimination status is a particularly worrisome sign for infants in hot spots who are too young to be vaccinated against the disease. Why it matters: Outbreaks still may be concentrated within certain parts of the country. But infants and other unvaccinated people are living with a continuous threat. Driving the news: The Pan American Health Organization announced on Tuesday that it revoked the U.S. status after 26 years, as expected . That's after state reports of 7,700 cases and 10 deaths since measles first began spreading in Texas early last year, according to the New York Times . (The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention currently reports only nine deaths.) Hundreds of people — often unvaccinated children — have been hospitalized. State of play: The measles-mumps-rubella vaccine is highly effective, meaning the vast majority of cases today occur in people who haven't received an immunization against the disease. Just over 1 in 10 of those infected this year were hospitalized, but that jumps to 17% among children under 5 years old, per the CDC . Between the lines: For most of the population, remaining unvaccinated against measles is a choice, albeit one parents make for their children. But for the youngest Americans, receiving a vaccine isn't an option for several months. The earliest an infant can receive an immunization against measles is at 6 months, with the official recommendation for most children being a first dose between 12 and 15 months. Though infants do receive protective antibodies against measles from their mothers, those gradually decline over their first months of life. What they're saying: "Most babies don't receive a first measles vaccine until age 1. With measles endemic again, parents can no longer assume grocery stores, airports, churches, or even pediatricians' offices are safe spaces," Jerome Adams, President Trump's first-term surgeon general, posted on X. "The community protection we took for granted is gone, and U.S. moms now must live in fear that their babies will be harmed by a completely preventable disease, while they do [everyday] tasks." Some experts are raising the prospect of an official three-dose schedule for the MMR vaccine, in which all infants get the earlier dose in addition to the two already recommended. Details: Infants can receive a dose as early as 6 months if they live in or are visiting places with a high risk of exposure or are traveling internationally. "For those under 6 months of age, the best thing we can do is awareness and improve that cocoon and immunity the best that we can," said Elizabeth Murray, a pediatric emergency medicine doctor and a spokesperson for the American Academy of Pediatrics. Parents should "make sure whoever you are around or whoever is around your baby is up to date on all of their vaccines," she added. Zoom in: New research has also documented how measles infections acquired during pregnancy are becoming more common and can have dire consequences. Between January 2025 and the end of September this year, 112 cases of measles during pregnancy — almost entirely among unvaccinated women — and 13 cases of congenital measles (meaning a case in a newborn contracted from its mother) were reported to the CDC, according to research published this week in the New England Journal of Medicine . Nearly a quarter of the pregnant women were hospitalized for reasons other than labor, and adverse outcomes for babies delivered within 14 days of their mothers developing a measles rash included preterm delivery and admission to intensive care. Congenital measles can also result in severe neurologic complications, the report notes. The bottom line: "We will likely be dealing with measles this year, next year, and the year after," Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, wrote on Substack . "And, until immunization rates increase, we will continue to see more suffering, more hospitalizations, and more deaths from this entirely preventable infection."

events.title: Democrats offer Republicans an ‘open door’ on Medicaid cuts
events.summary: The News One of the incoming Democratic Congress’ top priorities next year is reversing the GOP’s Medicaid cuts. The new majority might even get Republican votes to do it. Democrats are already deep in internal discussions about whether to court support across the aisle for delaying the steep Medicaid reductions passed as part of last year’s GOP megabill — which will result in large coverage losses. While they’re ready to pursue a party-line spending bill if Senate Republicans mount a filibuster, Democrats also sense an openness in President Donald Trump’s party to roll back the cuts. “There’s disquiet on the Republican side about implementing these at all,” said Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va. He described an “open door” for bipartisan discussions about changing the Medicaid cuts, which the Trump-backed bill phased in through 2028. The prospect of a bipartisan vote to change the cuts grew more real after the Trump administration announced last week that it would give states an extra six months to enforce the megabill’s Medicaid work requirements. Democrats viewed that as a sign that even Republican-led states are having difficulty complying with the new rules, which require verification of Medicaid beneficiaries’ continued qualifications for the low-income healthcare program. How Democrats approach reversal of the Medicaid cuts will be a crucial early test of whether the party can deliver on a cost-of-living agenda that delivered large blue majorities in both chambers in the midterm elections. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said he has recommended to Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and other top Democrats that the party start off with targeted bills addressing the work requirements and the megabill’s cut to the provider tax, a mechanism states use to finance their Medicaid programs. Booker said he’s had private conversations with Republicans already about the Medicaid changes. “My strategy, advice I’m giving to leadership and others is, the more finite bills we pass, the clearer it makes the issue for the American public. When you pack in these big bills, it makes it easier to give a pass to Republicans,” Booker told Semafor. He also said he’s open to broader negotiations with Republicans: “We’ve got to negotiate with them to get to 60.” Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., who will chair the Finance Committee, said Democrats want to pull out the Medicaid changes “from the roots.” He wants Democrats to use the six-month pause in enforcement of the work requirements to “make sure the country sees what’s going on.” But he declined to commit to a finite approach or a broader package: “I’ve been meeting with my colleagues on and off the committee. I don’t want to front run them.” Battleground-seat Democrats are signaling a particular willingness to negotiate with Republicans over the work requirements, even as the whole party pushes to roll back as many of the Medicaid changes as possible. Even though their sizable House majority would allow Democrats to pass their preferred Medicaid bill, they’ll still have to contend with the Senate filibuster. “I’ve always been willing to compromise on the work stuff,” said Rep. Darren Soto, D-Fla., who just narrowly won his race. “There’s already been a history of work requirements in our state and a lot of these different programs over the years. So I don’t think we get caught in the weeds on that just yet.” But Democratic leaders are doubtful a deal is possible. “We’re going to move forcefully and expeditiously to reverse all of the damage that was in the ‘one big, ugly bill.’ If the Republicans are willing to come to the table, we’ll have that discussion. That hasn’t been the case to date,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters. He’s pledged a multi-pronged health care agenda next year, including an expansion of Medicare eligibility, saying on Tuesday that “a return to the status quo is not acceptable.” Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told Semafor that Democrats won’t get his vote to reverse the work requirements. But he also said he would work with them to protect Medicaid benefits and blunt the pending changes to the provider tax. “When it comes to benefits, when it comes to the provider tax … I not only want to reverse that; I think we ought to provide a new dedicated stream of funding to rural hospital emergency rooms to see that no more of them close,” Hawley said. “We’ve got whole counties now in Missouri, they don’t have hospitals within 50, 60, 70 miles.” Room for Disagreement The majority of Republicans are, at this point, not in favor of delaying or scrapping the work requirements. The crop of swayable GOP votes for most of what Democrats want to do is not large, unless there’s a broader deal or Trump gets involved. “It’s not a Medicaid cut. Medicaid was never designed to say that an able-bodied adult with no kids and no disability should be able to get free healthcare,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who will chair the chamber’s GOP campaign arm next year. Burgess, David, and Nicholas’ View The Trump administration’s decision to give states six months of flexibility to enforce the Medicaid work requirements may be an early sign that further delays could be on the horizon. In fact, the GOP megabill allows the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to grant extensions of up to two years to states that are encountering difficulties implementing and enforcing work requirements — as long as they are making a good-faith effort. Yet even if Democrats are simply going through the motions by talking about courting GOP votes for Medicaid changes, that exercise may be worth the trouble for their purple-district members. A lot of newly elected Democrats, even some progressives, say they’ll start off the 120th Congress willing to work with Trump and across the aisle. Few in Washington see compromise as likely, but it’s not impossible. A Trump veto of party-line legislation to claw back Medicaid cuts could set up a politically disastrous scenario for the GOP if millions of Americans on Medicaid suddenly find themselves without coverage in the middle of the 2028 presidential campaign. Notable Advocacy group Keep Your Care led a group of 400 organizations this week asking Republican and Democratic leaders to include a two-year delay of the Medicaid work requirements in lame duck legislation . Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard Neal, D-Mass., and Energy and Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, D-N.J., are asking the Trump administration for details on the decision to disenroll 750,000 Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollees earlier this year.

events.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
events.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.  Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.  OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.  Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes. But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication. Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.  But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.” In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies . For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.  “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

events.title: The terrifying rise of AI hacking tools
events.summary: A new breed of widely available AI tools is helping hackers launch cyberattacks around the clock , breaching corporate networks in a matter of hours and overwhelming defenders. Why it matters: AI-enabled hacking is still in its infancy, but open-source tools — which are free to download — are fundamentally changing the economics of cybercrime. Hackers can launch self-adjusting attack plans, allowing agents to find vulnerabilities and steal credentials, sometimes before human defenders realize their systems are being probed. Driving the news: Recent cyberattacks involving publicly available "AI agent frameworks" are drawing warnings about how quickly hackers can infiltrate corporate networks. The FBI warned Friday that hackers have used an AI framework called Artex to attack organizations worldwide, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. In a separate report Friday , Amazon said hackers used Artex to steal AI model credentials, then used those stolen resources to power additional attacks. Last week, developer platform Railway and blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack also reported attacks involving Artex. Palo Alto Networks said Thursday that Chinese-speaking hackers used another open-source framework, Cairn, to conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations between August and September. In a separate report Monday, Google said hackers used Cairn during an intrusion into the U.S. aerospace sector. CrowdStrike also saw one group using Artex to target more than 200 organizations worldwide over 11 days last month. Reality check : Cyberattacks are still scary and tech resiliency is still built on a faulty internet foundation, making mishaps possible even without clear evidence of AI-assisted hacks. A litany of popular services — including Microsoft , Apple , Chase , United , Workday , the Federal Aviation Administration , the National Security Agency — have all reported outages in the last week. An unknown group infected about 178 major websites with crypto-stealing malware through the Optimizely Web experimentation platform in less than a day, according to Report URI . Affected websites included Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, Gitlab and Ikea, and AI doesn't seem to be involved as of now. What they're saying: "We're seeing more active attacks than ever right now," Sam Rubin, senior vice president of Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 threat intelligence and consulting unit, told Axios. "The open-weight models are getting close to frontier-level capabilities," and when combined with tools like Artex and Cairn, they are "really hitting organizations hard," he added. Incident response firms worldwide are stretched to capacity, with some turning away cases because they lack resources, John Hultquist, chief analyst at Google's threat intelligence group, told Axios. How it works: Artex and Cairn use AI agents to automate tasks hackers traditionally performed themselves. A hacker gives the framework a target and an objective, such as breaking into a company's network. AI agents develop attack plans, search for vulnerabilities and use hacking tools to test possible entry points. The agents share findings and adjust tactics when something fails, allowing them to operate around the clock without constant human supervision. Between the lines: Hackers are also stealing the computing resources needed to sustain their AI-powered attacks. Amazon's findings show how attackers can steal access to AI models and use that access to find more credentials, expanding their operations without paying for the computing power. The intrigue: These frameworks aren't necessarily good at hiding their activity, but that might not matter. Hultquist said autonomous attacks generate substantial suspicious activity, potentially making them easier to detect. But financially motivated hackers may only need to steal valuable information before defenders stop them. He also warned that state-backed hackers could use these capabilities to disrupt critical systems before defenders can intervene. What to watch: Security teams may need to fundamentally change their defenses to keep pace with automated attacks.

events.title: Egypt raises minimum wage, but workers doubt whether it can be enforced
events.summary: Hisham, 48, sleeps in a cabin in the desert near Ain Sokhna, 200km from his home, guarding a construction site. He earns 10,000 Egyptian pounds ($186) a month, and did so long before the government's latest wage decision. The job is dangerous, he told The National . “They should be paying me much more just because of the amount of snakes I have had to kill on the job.” His pay reflects risk, not fair wage by decree. The same holds for much of Egypt's private sector , where pay often follows its own logic: risk, scarcity of skills and competition from informal work are bigger determinants of pay than government mandates. On Sunday, the National Wages Council, chaired by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, approved a raise in the private-sector minimum wage to 8,500 pounds ($158) a month from January 1, up from 7,000 pounds since March 2025. Unaccounted labour The decision is binding on all of Egypt's about four million private establishments, which employ about 26.5 million people, cabinet spokesman Mohamed Adel said. The private sector accounts for 82.8 per cent of the employed. The Labour Ministry said inspectors would strictly enforce the 2025 labour law, which sets fines of 5,000 pounds to 50,000 pounds that multiply with the number of workers affected, and pointedly warned employers in a statement on Monday against deviating from it. But the state's reach is limited. More than 60 per cent of jobs in Egypt are informal, outside contracts and social insurance, according to International Labour Organisation estimates. In fact, a private-sector minimum was only introduced in 2022, when more than 3,000 companies and 22 sectors applied for exemptions. Labour Ministry inspections of 26,486 private establishments between March 2025 and March 2026 found 6,591 in violation, about one in four, according to a review of the figures by the fact-checking platform Saheeh Masr. For Egypt's biggest employers, the new floor is already out of date. Businessman Naguib Sawiris said earlier this week that none of his companies' staff earn less than 10,000 pounds. Ahmed, 42, has worked as a porter at El Sewedy Electric for five years. He earns 11,000 pounds, about 30 per cent above the new minimum, and gets a raise every year without waiting for a government order. Furthermore, skilled workers are leaving factory jobs “to drive tuk-tuks”, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said during a seminar last month. He described a labour market where factories must outbid the informal economy for workers, rather than simply meeting a legal minimum wage. A tuk-tuk driver answers to no employer, pays no social insurance and keeps his day's earnings in cash. Workers without that leverage have little say over their pay. A teacher at a private school in Cairo told Saheeh Masr he earns 4,500 pounds after eight years. He said he would not ask for more because the management “excludes any teacher who asks for better pay and replaces them with new ones on lower salaries”. A security guard in Cairo's Heliopolis district told The National on Tuesday that his pay has stayed at 6,000 pounds since 2021, and nobody has told him it will rise. A 31-year-old woman who runs a two-year-old service business in Heliopolis said she would probably not raise the 6,000 pounds a month she pays each of her two Sudanese workers, employed by verbal agreement. Stretched by higher taxes and tougher enforcement, she hired Sudanese workers because they accept less than Egyptians. The owner of a small supermarket chain in Nasr City said he had replaced most of his Egyptian delivery staff with Sudanese men because “they work harder, give me less trouble and they accept lower wages than Egyptians”. Others see signs this time may be different. Yasser, 39, who packs vegetables at a wholesale warehouse in New Cairo, has been earning 6,000 pounds and was told he would receive 8,500 starting next month. He received no increase in pay after the last order, so he thinks the government is serious now. He had accepted the low pay because his employer provides transport, saving him about 2,000 pounds a month. “We hope the National Wages Council states that the decision means a net income of 8,500 pounds, and not gross, otherwise we are fooling people,” read one widely shared post online. Eroded by inflation Alaa El Sokky, an employers' representative on the council, said the figure is gross and that workers would take home 7,000 pounds to 7,500 pounds after social insurance and tax. The National 's calculation, based on current tax brackets and the employee's 11 per cent insurance contribution, puts it at about 7,200 pounds. Mr El Sokky said the increase of more than 20 per cent outpaced inflation, which slowed to 12.7 per cent in cities in October. Since the last rise in March 2025, prices nationwide have climbed about 18 per cent, based on official index figures. But that leaves out the earlier economic shock . The pound traded at about 15.7 to the dollar until March 2022 and is now near 54, after a series of devaluations and a float in March 2024. Urban inflation peaked at a record 38 per cent in September 2023. The government has also cut subsidies to ease pressure on its budget, a central part of its International Monetary Fund programme. The increase places the cost of higher wages on private employers rather than the state, which is seeking to contain spending under its IMF programme. Talks on the programme's latest review have ended without an agreement, delaying a potential $2.3 billion disbursement. Egypt quadrupled the price of subsidised bread in June 2024, the first increase since 1988. It also raised electricity tariffs by about 45 per cent, and in March this year raised fuel prices by 14 to 17 per cent. In October, transport inflation stood at 25.8 per cent and housing and utilities at 24.5 per cent. Rent alone can take half the current minimum with the median in Cairo's El Marg district being 3,500 pounds, according to Saheeh Masr. In dollar terms, the floor has barely moved. The first private-sector minimum of 2,400 pounds was worth about $154 in 2022. The new one is worth about $158. So workers have absorbed four years of price rises and subsidy cuts with little change to their purchasing power.

events.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6% after petrol and diesel prices hit record high
events.summary: Increase in October piles pressure on households as Iran war pushes up oil cost and rattles global economy Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October after petrol prices increased and diesel hit a record high amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) show the headline rate of inflation as measured by the consumer prices index rose from 3.5% in September and was in line with City economists’ forecasts. As households brace for the colder winter months with household gas and electricity costs soaring, the latest figures push the headline inflation rate to the highest level in a year. In a reading underscoring the pressure on the Bank of England to raise interest rates, the ONS said fuel prices were the major contributor. Annual costs of raw materials and goods leaving factories also continued to climb, driven by rising energy and crude oil prices amid the Iran war. Fuel prices for motorists rose at an annual rate of 33.2%, the largest increase since July 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine sparked a global surge in energy prices. The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p a litre between September and October to reach 174.7p a litre, the highest level in four years. Diesel prices rose by 7p a litre to 199.5p a litre, the highest price on records dating back to 1996. Andy Burnham’s government has pledged to offer support for households grappling with a fresh cost of living squeeze as the stop-start Iran conflict rattles the global economy and drives up inflation worldwide. At the budget last month the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans for a £100 winter handout for 20m households to cushion the blow from the global economic storm. The latest inflation figures took into account a 4% increase in the Ofgem energy price cap from the start of October. A forecast from the consultancy Cornwall Insight on Wednesday predicted a 26% jump in energy bills in Great Britain from January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year for a typical household. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year. Earlier this month, Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% and warned further increases in the cost of borrowing might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the longer the conflict continued the more likely it was that rate increases would be needed, despite a recent drop in global energy prices since the US midterm elections. Speaking at a conference in London on Tuesday, Bailey said inflation was “probably going to be a bit less” than the 5% forecast made by the Bank earlier this month. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning However, he said that if the war pushed energy prices higher, the “more likely persistent inflationary effects will take hold and the higher the level of interest rates will need to be”. Financial markets anticipate at least two quarter-point increases before the end of next year. Analysts said the Bank could raise borrowing costs from as early as next month. Core inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – was unchanged at 2.8%, matching economists’ forecasts. Services inflation, which the Bank has been monitoring closely for evidence of domestic inflationary pressures becoming entrenched, also held steady at 3.7%, slightly below City predictions for a rate of 3.8%. Air fares rose by 1.8% between September and October amid an increase in long-haul ticket prices – offset by a downward effect from European flights. Prices for alcohol and tobacco also rose, by 4.5%, influenced by the timing of an increase in tobacco duty at the start of the month. Food prices rose at the slowest rate since September 2021, at 0.9%, down from 1.3% in September. Emma Reynolds, the chief secretary to the Treasury, said: “The conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world. “The household energy payment, announced in our budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January, which will help to give families breathing space now. “The budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future.”
