events.title: SAP opens AI to on-prem customers, but cloud commitments could shut smaller firms out
events.summary: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned. Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward. Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access. In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said. However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn . It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway. Henzler told The Reg : "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?' "Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?" The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model. "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said. "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, independent of the commercials." The Register asked SAP to respond to Henzler's concerns. A spokesperson said: "The offering separates a customer's commercial commitment to cloud ERP from the timing of its operational migration. Customers that meet the applicable commercial and technical requirements can use supported AI capabilities with eligible ECC or on-premises SAP S/4HANA systems while modernizing their landscape. Eligibility is not determined by the number of ERP instances and can therefore also extend to single-instance customers." There are thousands of SAP ERP users worldwide, including some of the world's largest businesses. Despite efforts to get them onto the latest iteration – S/4HANA – and in the cloud, where the vendor promised it could gather a greater "share of wallet" from customers , there has been a dogged resistance to these complex and time-consuming migrations. Gartner figures for Q4 2024 showed only 39 percent of worldwide ECC customers – from a total of 35,000 – had bought or subscribed to SAP S/4HANA licenses. More recently, The Reg uncovered that SAP was about €2 billion short of its target for getting customers off on-prem support. Customers still running older ERP systems face pressure to embrace AI-supported automation. Whether SAP's terms help them do that – or simply help move them onto RISE – remains the question. ®

events.title: Alaska Native strongholds push Peltola into Senate history
events.summary: Mary Peltola's path to Senate history ran through four Alaska Native strongholds that delivered more than half of her statewide first-choice lead. Why it matters: The Yup'ik Democrat is the nation's first Alaska Native U.S. senator, powered by communities that endured disenfranchisement, forced displacement and federal violence. The win amplifies their voice on tribal sovereignty and subsistence rights after decades of neglect and discrimination — much as Mississippi Delta Black voters powered Democrat Scott Colom to his surprising Senate victory. By the numbers: Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 12,400 first-choice votes statewide in Alaska's Nov. 17 unofficial count . Four western and northern House districts delivered a combined margin of about 6,700 votes. In Bristol Bay/Aleutians , for example, Peltola led by roughly 1,150 votes. In Bethel/Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and Western Alaska/Norton Sound , she led by roughly 2,300 votes. In North Slope/Northwest Arctic , she led by approximately 900 votes. Stunning stat: Those four districts accounted for just about 5% of Alaska's first-choice Senate votes, but roughly 55% of Peltola's statewide lead. Alaska's 2021 redistricting report identifies Districts 37–40 as Alaska Native-controlled. Alaska Natives, alone or in combination, accounted for 85.8% of the voting-age population in District 38, 85.1% in 39, 62% in 40 and 43.8% in 37, using 2020 census figures. About 22% of Alaska residents identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or in combination with another race, according to the 2020 census . State of play: Peltola carried the 50% margin needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation , where lower-ranked preferences from other candidates' supporters could have tipped the race toward another candidate. Michelle Sparck of the nonpartisan Get Out the Native Vote effort told KNBA that Native groups mounted aggressive outreach, including in Native languages. Organizers saw gains in some rural communities, though definitive statewide turnout comparisons remain pending. Zoom in: In Kwethluk, the Yup'ik village where Peltola grew up, she outpolled Sullivan 136–9. In Savoonga on St. Lawrence Island , she led 157–5. In Tlingit communities Angoon and Kake , she led 109–22 and 140–30, respectively. The Navy apologized in 2024 for destroying Angoon in 1882 and bombarding and burning Kake in 1869 . Flashback: In 1915, Alaska's territorial lawmakers required Native citizenship applicants to abandon tribal ties and customs. In 1925, after Congress extended citizenship to Native Americans, Alaska imposed an English literacy requirement that disenfranchised many Native voters. During World War II, the U.S. removed 881 Unangax̂ people from nine villages to Southeast Alaska camps plagued by disease and poor shelter. The intrigue: In April 1969, Sen. Ted Kennedy traveled 3,600 miles over three days through Native communities, following a poverty tour his slain brother Robert had planned. TIME documented villages with 60% unemployment and homes without plumbing, comparing the trip to Robert's visits to Appalachia and the Mississippi Delta. Partisan accusations over publicity overshadowed the poverty Kennedy sought to expose. Yes, but: Alaska Native voters today don't vote as a bloc. The Alaska Federation of Natives endorsed no one in the Senate race. And district returns can't establish how individual Native voters voted — or prove a statewide turnout surge. Between the lines: In communities covered by the EPA's Alaska Native Villages data, 1,129 homes lacked drinking water, wastewater service or both in 2025, down from 6,892 in 2005, per an EPA report . Native leaders continue pressing Washington on subsistence rights, infrastructure, education and self-determination.

events.summary: House Democrats are all but certain to nominate Hakeem Jeffries for speaker Wednesday morning, setting the stage for a floor vote by the full chamber in January. events.summary: Capitol Hill is grappling with the prospect of the Food and Drug Administration operating without a Senate-confirmed leader indefinitely, after the White House pulled the nomination of Heidi Overton to lead the agency Tuesday night. It’d been unclear whether the embattled White House official could get the necessary votes to be confirmed by the Senate’s health committee from lawmakers skeptical of her positions on vaccines, the abortion pill, and flavored vapes. But Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., asserted after the nomination was dropped that he believed the White House “abandoned a viable confirmation path.” “Pro-life Senators sought final assurances from the Administration regarding the Administration’s commitment to life issues,” Cassidy said. “The Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.” Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, is being weighed as a potential replacement, but there are questions swirling about whether anyone could be confirmed on a compressed timeline before Democrats take power. Chris Meekins, a Raymond James healthcare analyst who worked at HHS during Trump’s first term, predicted the FDA will not have a permanent leader anytime soon, a development that “inevitably creates uncertainty.” “Had the White House heeded warnings by many before and after her nomination, they could have avoided this unfortunate outcome,” Meekins said. — David Lim

events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Supercomputing BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features SC 26 Supercomputing Month 2026 Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 Cybersecurity Month 2026 VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps 29 minutes ago Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware 50 minutes ago Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover 2 hours ago AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery 3 hours ago Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps 13 hours ago UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

events.title: ADGM proposes three months of extra unpaid maternity leave
events.summary: Abu Dhabi's financial free zone ADGM could introduce longer maternity and paternity leave allowances and make it easier to change jobs under new regulations it is considering. The proposed changes, revealed this week , are open to public consultation until December 9. They aim to strengthen protections related to wages and statutory rights, the ADGM Registration Authority said. The proposal includes introducing 65 days of unpaid maternity leave , in addition to the 65 days that new mothers currently have. Currently, the first 33 working days of maternity leave are fully paid, with 50 per cent pay offered during the following 32 days. The amendments also propose extending paid paternity leave allowance from five working days to 15, and introducing an additional unpaid leave entitlement of five working days immediately afterwards. Those allowances would also apply during an employee's probationary period, but the proposal “does not alter the pay arrangements for those leave entitlements, which remain unavailable during the probationary period”, the paper said. The amendments also propose that employment regulations expressly clarify that an employee is entitled to be paid their daily wage while on holiday. The paper proposes clearer time frames and processes for cancellation of work permits and employer-sponsored residency visas. Under the proposal, employers will be required to cancel an employee work permit and a residency visa “as soon as reasonably practicable”, or no later than 30 days, following the termination date, unless otherwise permitted or agreed in writing. The amendments would also enable an employee to apply to the registrar for cancellation of the permit and visa if the employer fails to do so. The Registration Authority is proposing the introduction of a new section to protect employees from “being subjected to any detriment, including dismissal, because the employee has asserted, or indicated an intention to assert, a right conferred by the employment regulations, or has alleged in good faith that the employer has infringed such a right”. This would allow an employee to apply to the court for a declaration and, where appropriate, compensation of up to two years of wages. ADGM, which has been rapidly growing, had a combined workforce across Al Maryah Island and Al Reem Island of 49,027 in the first half of the year, up 34 per cent on the same period last year.

events.title: MP urges council to speed up heating oil payments
events.summary: Labour MP David Smith has urged Northumberland County Council to speed up heating payments Published 18 November 2026, 08:48 GMT An MP has urged a council to speed up the process of heating oil support payments as energy prices soar. About 23,000 Northumberland homes use oil systems as they are not connected to the mains gas supply. Labour's North Northumberland MP David Smith said a freedom of information request from 21 September showed just over a third of households who applied for help with heating oil costs had received funding from Northumberland County Council. However, the Conservative-led local authority said its latest figures showed significantly more applications had now been approved almost two months on. Energy prices have increased due to ongoing conflicts around the world. Unlike gas, oil prices are not protected by the Ofgem Energy Price Cap, and households have experienced huge increases in the cost of filling tanks. Smith said the freedom of information request showed there had been 328 applications for heating oil assistance, but only 112 had been approved with total payments amounting to £36,123. The council said its figures showed more than 160 applicants and 40 venues had been supported, and there was no backlog for residents seeking support with heating oil, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service. "Those not receiving support are applicants who have not been able to demonstrate their household is either vulnerable or struggling to afford heating oil due to a low income," a spokesperson said. The government provided £5m to the county council through its Crisis and Resilience fund in April, including almost £500,000 to support households struggling with the cost of heating oil. Bamburgh Conservative councillor Guy Renner-Thompson has a home which uses a heating oil system. He urged the government to bring in more financial support, saying the council fully expected to spend the entire £498,459 heating oil allocation. events.title: Security flaw found in Java, world's third-largest programming language
events.summary: A tech start-up used AI to uncover a critical software bug in Java that had existed for more than a decade (generic photo) Published 18 November 2026, 04:57 GMT A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java. Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions. Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments. It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw". The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage . On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance". The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug. Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related . With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability it has called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system. In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public. Oracle, the owner of Java, released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes - including for this flaw. At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident. But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system. The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment. What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble? Published 23 October US National Security Agency's classified internal network reportedly goes offline Published 21 hours ago Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java. First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation. One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC. Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program. The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said. In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added. The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online. Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services. The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif. PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web. Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks. At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline. The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java. "It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said. "AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone. Earlier in November, OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands. Are we too reliant on big tech companies? Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Microsoft is asking customers to apply for reimbursement. They should protest Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware 50 minutes ago PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road 2 hours ago Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal 18 hours ago Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI! 20 hours ago Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open 1 day ago I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology. A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage. To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements. Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do. That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes. Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages. I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done. But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements. If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity. events.title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to rise by 26% to £2,166 from January
events.summary: Government under pressure to help households as increase would add £443 to average annual dual-fuel bill Energy price cap rise: how to switch providers Tell us: are you shopping around for a better deal? Energy bills across Great Britain are predicted to reach £2,166 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East conflict piles pressure on the government to offer more support to hard-hit households. The government’s cap on gas and electricity prices is likely to rise by 26% early next year, equivalent to adding £443 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, in one of the biggest quarterly price rises on record, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight. The dire prediction for millions of hard-pressed households marks the final forecast before the industry regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem , sets electricity and gas rates for the coldest months of the year from January through to March via a new energy price cap next Wednesday. The forecast was well above Cornwall’s prediction in late September that the cap would rise by 16% to £1,999 a year from January. Bills are expected to be even higher after an increase in gas market prices through October because of escalating violence in the Middle East and deepening fears over Europe’s gas storage levels. Figures released by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday showed the headline rate of inflation rose to 3.6% in October , up from 3.5% in September, after petrol prices rose and diesel hit a record high. Craig Lowrey, the retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight, said: “After already climbing in October, energy bills look set to rise again in the new year, and the timing could hardly be worse, with colder weather in January pushing up energy use and households already dealing with the cost of living crisis. “Once again, the cause lies thousands of miles away, yet another reminder of how events beyond our control have a very real impact on our energy bills.” The energy price rise will come as a blow to the government after the chancellor, John Healey, promised to set “a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe” in his maiden budget last month. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, said: “I know that the price of energy bills this winter weighs heavily on struggling families up and down the country. Access to energy is an everyday essential and not a luxury, which is why we have taken immediate action to give people breathing space.” The assurance echoes Healey’s budget which promised “breathing space” to struggling households this winter through a one-off payment of £100 in January for 20 million households in council tax bands A to D. The £2.6bn “household energy payment” will go directly into bank accounts to “take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”, according to Healey. The payment will be in addition to the warm home discount, which offers about six million means-tested households in England, Wales and Scotland £150 off winter fuel bills. The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year, which have shaved about £150 a year off costs. The Treasury also promised to keep the 5% VAT levy off electricity bills for 29 million households until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year. Fahnbulleh said: “Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power.”

events.title: Half of David Jones job cuts are casual staff with no entitlements
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts These are the jobs slated to go at individual David Jones stores Internal documents provide a breakdown of where the David Jones job losses are slated. ( ABC News: Loretta Florance ) About half of the David Jones slated job losses are casual staff. Internal documents show the specific breakdown of jobs at the 19 stores set to close. The retail workers' union says it is focused on securing employee entitlements. Half of the 1,689 jobs slated to go at David Jones are permanent roles, while the rest are casuals with no entitlements to be paid out once 19 stores close, internal documents show. A briefing document seen by ABC News shows the specific breakdown of jobs at the stores set to be shut by the end of 2026. There are 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand closing, as last week confirmed by the receiver, FTI Consulting, acting on behalf of David Jones' secured lender, Hilco Capital. Of the 1,689 roles encompassed in the earmarked stores, 843 are casuals while 846 are permanent workers employed on either a full-time or part-time basis. The workforces are larger in urban stores slated for closure, including the Perth flagship store in Hay Street Mall, and Warringah and Hornsby in Sydney's north. The briefing by FTI Consulting sent out this week noted "redeployment options". The retail workers' union believes only 170 jobs will be saved at this stage, with the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association (SDA) giving the ABC more detail this afternoon. "We expect in the coming couple of days, between Thursday and Monday, that people who have got those redeployments will be informed about them," the union's NSW branch secretary Bernie Smith said. Are you a David Jones worker or do you know more? Confidentially contact our journalist on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me What are these workers entitled to now? David Jones was went into voluntary administration earlier this month. ( ABC News: Zahra Anwary ) This week, it was confirmed that the retailer's 6,000-strong workforce was owed $11 million at the time the 188-year-old retailer was put into voluntary administration on November 5. It is understood that figure only includes annual and long service leave entitlements owed to staff, and does not include the extra ballooning debt to permanent workers that will now be owed severance. The SDA said it was working to confirm information about redundancy payouts. In an administration process, workers are paid back their entitlements before other creditors, such as suppliers. However, clawing back cash is contingent on a rescue package or successful sell-off. This means the workers could face a drawn-out process to get what they are due. FTI Consulting and David Jones' administrator McGrathNicol were both contacted for comment about who is responsible for paying various entitlements to workers. There are federal government guarantees in place to help workers when no cash can be recovered; however, these exclude migrant workers. Meanwhile, casuals do not get accrued entitlements like holiday pay, instead receiving a higher hourly rate. The casuals will now just be out of work. Bernie Smith says the union is focused on securing employee entitlements. ( ABC News ) "They don't receive redundancies, and they are very focused on trying to get alternative employment for as many workers as possible outside of David Jones," Mr Smith said. "We think there's a bit of a missed opportunity for David Jones, but I know the cost of doing business is challenging." Mr Smith said the union had been in talks with other retailers about taking on the haemorrhaged David Jones workforce but would not share brand names. "Those are early discussions and [it's a] difficult time of year for hiring," he said. "But we've been pleasantly surprised at the willingness of what could be done. It's a difficult time in retail, but there is a real interest in these experienced salespeople." David Jones creditors owed at least $459 million The retailer owes at least $180 million to suppliers, more than $200 million to lenders and more than $10 million to its own staff. Mr Smith said in the meantime the union was focused on securing employees' entitlements. "There's $11.3 million of accrued entitlements to annual leave, long service leave," he said. "But there's also the redundancy payments on top of that, that isn't available to our members until the administration comes to an end, which could be months away.

events.title: After US$6.3 billion crypto heist, Binance plans foray into 5 Asian markets
events.summary: Binance’s expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion (S$8 billion) being stolen from its platform in October. Binance plans to enter five Asian markets in 2027, with South and South-east Asia as priorities. It has talks in five or six markets, and details are due in early 2027. The plan follows a record US$6.3 billion hack in October, linked by the FBI and Binance to North Korea. Binance has restored most withdrawals and aims to reopen all remaining networks and assets by week’s end. The heist has raised fresh concern over crypto security. Binance says it contacted regulators in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, and talks now focus on wider industry risks. SINGAPORE – Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets in 2027 with South and South-east Asia as key priorities, its regional business head said, not long after the firm was hit with a record US$6.3 billion (S$8.1 billion) digital heist in October. “We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets... three of which are in quite mature stages,” S.B. Seker told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Nov 18. “The others are ongoing conversations.” He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in more than 10 jurisdictions, was looking at, but said details of the planned expansion were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of 2027. Binance’s expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from its platform in October. The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, but Pyongyang has denied that. The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier in November after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said last weekend it aimed to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week. The Binance heist, which has been described by experts as the largest crypto theft ever, has renewed scrutiny of inconsistent security practices in the industry. Seker, the firm’s head of APAC, said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded. “Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present,” he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations. Binance says the Abu Dhabi Global Market’s Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator. Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry. “The conversations now are ‘Well, this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?’ It’s moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation,” he said. “We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore.” REUTERS

events.title: UN says Singapore’s Penguin International broke Libya arms embargo; company disputes panel’s findings
events.summary: Penguin International said the two vessels highlighted by a UN panel were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons. Singapore shipbuilder Penguin International disputes a UN panel’s claim that two vessels it sold later reached Libya in breach of the UN arms embargo. The company says the security vessel and landing craft were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons or ammunition to Dubai-based 2020 Volume Boats. The UN report named Penguin and Penguin Shipyard Asia but did not recommend sanctions. Penguin says the case has not materially hit operations and the chance of UN sanctions is low. SINGAPORE - Singapore-listed shipbuilder Penguin International has disputed a United Nations panel’s finding that its sale of two vessels subsequently shipped to Libya violated an arms embargo, saying the vessels were built for commercial use and delivered without weapons. In a bourse filing on Nov 17, the company said the transaction involved a security vessel and a landing craft sold in December 2024 to Dubai-based 2020 Volume Boats. Both vessels were delivered from Penguin’s yard in Singapore, and then shipped to Benghazi, Libya. On Mar 24, 2026, the UN Panel of Experts on Libya published a report naming Penguin and its wholly owned subsidiary, Penguin Shipyard Asia. The panel classified the security vessel as a naval-type fast patrol vessel and the landing craft as a dual-use vessel, and considered their transfer to Libya a violation of an arms embargo imposed under UN Security Council Resolution 1970. However, the panel did not recommend sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary. Penguin said it disagreed with the panel’s characterisation of the vessels and its conclusion that the transaction breached the arms embargo. The company maintained that both vessels had been designed and built for commercial purposes and were delivered without arms or ammunition on board. Penguin said it had corresponded with the UN panel between January and May in 2025 and provided the information requested in relation to the transaction. It became aware of the panel’s report in September 2026, about six months after its publication, and subsequently engaged Singapore legal counsel and an international sanctions specialist to assess the implications. Based on the advice received, Penguin said being named in the report did not itself constitute a sanctions action or impose any direct penalties. The company also understood that the likelihood of the UN imposing sanctions against Penguin or its subsidiary on the basis of the report was low. Separately, Penguin has been corresponding with Singapore Customs since November 2025 regarding the export of the vessels. The company said the matter had not materially disrupted its operations, and its board was not presently aware of any material financial impact. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: Indonesia resumes rate hikes to defend rupiah, more tightening seen
events.summary: The rupiah is currently the worst-performing among emerging Asian currencies. JAKARTA – Indonesia’s central bank unexpectedly raised its policy rate on Nov 18 , resuming a tightening cycle intended to put a floor under the rupiah after the currency hit multiple record lows in the past week amid domestic political turmoil. Analysts said the move is unlikely to be the last, with persistent external pressures and concerns over Indonesia’s market appeal expected to keep the central bank on a tightening path into 2027. Bank Indonesia (BI) raised the benchmark seven-day reverse repurchase rate to 6%, the highest since January 2025, matching the prediction of 10 of 27 economists polled by Reuters. The rest had expected a hold. Its overnight deposit facility and lending facility rates were also increased by the same amount to 5.25% and 6.75%, respectively. BI has now raised the benchmark rate by 125 basis points since May to defend the rupiah, currently the worst-performing among emerging Asian currencies. The rupiah touched an all-time low of 18,285 per US dollar on Nov 17 and has traded near that level since. Governor Destry Damayanti said the hike was a “pre-emptive” move to ensure the inflation rate stays within BI’s target range and to maintain the attractiveness of rupiah assets in anticipation of a US rate hike in December. “Going forward, BI will continue to consistently direct its monetary policy to strengthen the stability of the rupiah exchange rate in order to keep inflation within target,” Destry said. The rupiah has been under pressure for most of 2026 on concerns over fiscal discipline and political interference in the central bank. It weakened further last week after Indonesia’s Vice-President resigned and four senior police officers implicated in an illegal wiretapping, including of the President’s phone. The rupiah’s depreciation has so far had limited impact on inflation, which eased slightly to 3.23% in October, within BI’s 1.5% to 3.5% target range. The government caps fuel prices through subsidies to keep inflation under control. Senior Deputy Governor Aida Budiman said the rate decision would ensure inflation stays within target in the next two years. The rupiah barely moved after the policy decision. Destry said the central bank’s other measures, including a 200 basis point cut in reserve requirements announced in October , would help offset the impact of higher rates on liquidity, bank lending and economic growth. Some analysts have described BI’s October policy announcement as perplexing. Asked about its policy stance, Destry said BI’s policy mix was innovative, designed to address “problems that are increasingly complex”. Indonesia’s economic growth accelerated in the third quarter to 5.47%, data showed earlier in November , from 5.29% in the previous three months. That, however, remained far slower than President Prabowo Subianto’s 8% target by 2029. Persistent external pressures, concerns about a potential downgrade by MSCI for Indonesia’s stock market and political uncertainty may extend BI’s tightening cycle into 2027, analysts said. Barclays predicted BI would resume tightening to reach a terminal benchmark rate of 6.75% in the middle of 2027. Jakarta-based Bank Permata expected the benchmark at 6.50% by the end of 2027 . Consultancy firm Capital Economics also expected the main rate to be at 6.5% by the end of 2027, with investors monitoring if BI would deliver more hikes, economist Jason Tuvey said. “Investors will be watching closely for any comments from government officials regarding today’s decision by the central bank given their push for faster economic growth,” he said. “The acid test for Bank Indonesia will be how it responds if the rupiah were to come under fresh downward pressure in the coming months,” Tuvey said. events.title: Can AI Agents Really Shift Chip Design Left?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agent orchestration at various stages of design, verification, and validation will require new methodologies and coordination across tools. Engineering expertise remains essential, and proprietary data is still siloed. Cost and complexity could limit adoption, giving larger companies an advantage. Experts at the Table : AI agents are moving into more parts of the chip design flow, but connecting them across different tools and processes remains a challenge. Questions also remain about how to capture decades of engineering expertise, protect proprietary design data, and keep costs manageable. Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss these issues with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: If AI agents are modifying code, and you keep updating AI models and agents, how much can you really shift left? Darbari : This is going to be a new methodology direction the industry will be taking, much like UVM, where you combine these different flows together. How do you combine all the agents together? I don’t get a sense that anybody really knows today how this combination is going to work. From what I have seen in different presentations, they’re still looking at how these things unfold. A lot of agentic AI companies lack the field experience of having seen these problems firsthand, so what they’re building is not what the consumer wants. In many cases, the big consumers are building their own stuff because they know what they want. They have the field experience. They have data from many years. So, where will the big EDA vendors go to streamline this, and how will that shape the end use? I don’t know. Laviv : One of the challenges with emulation is that when running in co-simulation mode, the simulation slows down. Maybe, instead of having UVM or other languages that slow it down, AI will get its own language and get SystemVerilog RTL synthesizable code that you can put in the machine. Then you’ll need less of the software, and you can run faster in emulation. I’m not sure yet if the methodology would change quickly, but UVM might not stay forever. Darbari : That’s what Nvidia’s head of GPU said at DVCon U.S., isn’t it? The formal is replacing simulation, or is going to replace simulation. I’m less interested in how each of these individual technologies works with each other, but I’m very interested in whether all of this adoption will lead to a coherent story. Schirrmeister : You have lifecycle, manufacturing, digital implementation, functional verification, and you have specification engineering. Making sense of it is the light bulb — making sure it works, getting it to layout, getting it into the actual physical silicon and 3D, and then observing it during the lifecycle. Each of these flows has many sub-components. Functional verification to emulation is like one of the five. There is virtual prototyping, formal, simulation, emulation, and prototyping. Everybody gets their own agent. So you have an agent doing something localized. Now you start getting an agent that orchestrates these things together as a functional thing, and then you get an agent that connects to the front end. This is an onion of agents, with more and more layers on top. EDA vendors are all saying we have Level 5 stuff, and there’s truth to that within the scope of the operating domain. Berg : This is very much about hierarchy. Darbari : But who’s going to pay for all this? Do the small companies have the budget to tokenize their banks and run all of this? Schirrmeister : Do you mean the guys building the product, or the guys building the tools? Darbari : The ones running the product. These are the consumers. They would need to pay for the tokens. I have a feeling that only the big companies will be able to afford this. They’ve been running it full-on, saying they haven’t written any code. All of this is agents. But it would get very interesting if the cost of doing all of this could be significantly reduced. Schirrmeister : What’s exciting about this is that all the smaller designs that used to be difficult because you had to go through all of this will benefit. If you want to be an Nvidia competitor, you still cannot do this out of your garage. That still has to be a big company. Berg : You’ve got levels of agents at this point, and a Level 5 orchestrating the whole thing. The industry is going to work on building each of these and then iterating and improving them. That’s the only way in which you’re going to get agents to learn and replace large groups of engineers doing the grunt work that’s necessary here. SE: But that hierarchy needs to start with whatever shifts left to include in each one of these different blocks, right? You need to at least define, in general, what you’re going to be doing. Berg : You’re going to have information being fed back to ensure that when they go to the specification of the functional, there are constraints placed here. That way, you can improve the probability of manufacturability. Schirrmeister : Can I have an agent model and predict that path? Berg : Yes, you can. Schirrmeister : But you want to check, right? You need to make sure early on what the multi-physics effects of what you’re doing will be. Berg : Yes, and without that, it will be dead on arrival in manufacturing. Schirrmeister : So now the question becomes, ‘How much can you really abstract?’ Laviv : AI is doing a great job on, say, 80% of the challenges. But then you have experience from individuals who have been in the industry for 30 years with unique skills that AI doesn’t have. We had a discussion where we talked about 250 different skills for power, emulation, format, and verification. AI doesn’t have those skills today. The industry needs to figure out how to gather those skills in order to really get to a flow where an agent can talk to an agent and has all the decades of experience that is hidden in Apple, Qualcomm, and Intel. Berg : It took 50 years, but in 2024, the Nobel Prize in chemistry was given in part to a software called AlphaFold , which predicted with uncanny certainty how proteins fold. Proteins are much more complicated than the crystalline structures that we deal with on a daily basis. But it took 50 years to get there. That said, it’s a proof of concept. Whether or not you believe it can be done in semiconductors, it’s going to happen.

events.title: Canada’s La Caisse in talks for stake in Bain’s Singapore-based Bridge Data Centres, sources say
events.summary: Workers laying cables outside Bridge Data Centres (BDC) in Johor on May 6. La Caisse is in advanced talks to buy a stake in Bain Capital’s Singapore-based Bridge Data Centres, with a deal possibly signed in weeks, sources said. Bain is selling at least 40% of BDC and may sell up to half, but the talks are not exclusive and the valuation is still disputed. BDC runs data centres in Malaysia, Thailand and India, but faces weaker sector sentiment, debt worries and new US chip export curbs on South-east Asia. HONG KONG – Canadian pension fund La Caisse has emerged as the leading bidder in advanced talks for a stake in Bain Capital’s Bridge Data Centres (BDC), two people with knowledge of the matter said. Bain Capital kicked off a sale process for at least 40% of BDC shares earlier in 2026 , targeting a valuation of US$5 billion (S$6.45 billion), which drew interest from private equity, infrastructure and pension funds, Reuters has reported. The size of the stake La Caisse would buy is still being negotiated, but Bain Capital could be selling up to half of its holdings in the Singapore-based firm, said one of the people. A deal could be signed in the coming weeks, but the talks with La Caisse are not exclusive and terms not finalised, the person added. Some bidders were looking at a valuation of US$4 billion for BDC, said a third person with knowledge of the transaction. Bain Capital, BDC and La Caisse did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. All the people declined to be named due to confidentiality. BDC operates data centres in Malaysia, Thailand and India, one of many companies that have been aggressively building capacity in Asia over the past two years to meet surging demand for cloud computing, AI and digital services. TikTok-owner ByteDance was the anchor tenant at the first phase of BDC’s MY06 hyperscale data centre in Johor, Malaysia, according to a BDC release. But BDC is seeking to diversify its customer base and has signed new contracts with global tech companies, one of the people said. The talks on the sale of a stake in BDC come at a time when sentiment in the sector has soured on concerns about mounting debt-funded AI spending. Worsening the outlook, South-east Asia’s US$100 billion-plus AI industry faces fresh US curbs on advanced chip exports to the region, announced on Nov 16 , aiming to restrict Chinese companies’ access to computing power to train AI models. BDC was founded a decade ago by industry veterans Michael Foust and Kris Kumar in partnership with Bain Capital, which merged the firm into Chinese data centre operator Chindata in 2019 and listed the combined business on the Nasdaq in 2020. The two businesses were separated again under a new entity WinTriX after Bain Capital took Chindata private in 2023 in a US$3.16 billion deal. In January, Bain Capital completed the sale of Chindata to a consortium led by Shenzhen Dongyangguang Industry that valued the business at US$4 billion. REUTERS

events.title: Singlife to phase out Singlife Account insurance savings plan by end-2027
events.summary: The discontinuation of Singlife Account does not affect customers who hold other insurance policies with Singlife. Singlife will stop its Singlife Account savings and insurance product, with no new applications accepted and all remaining accounts closed by Dec 16, 2027. Customers with under $100 will close from Dec 16, 2026; those with $100 or more can keep earning 1.5% a year and use the account until Dec 16, 2027. The bundled insurance cover ends when accounts close, but claims can still be made for insured events that happened while the policy was active. Singlife says the move reflects changing customer needs. SINGAPORE – Home-grown insurer Singlife will discontinue its savings and insurance product Singlife Account, with all remaining accounts to be closed by Dec 16, 2027. Singlife said it generally does not disclose customer numbers for individual products. The decision to discontinue Singlife Account is “part of our ongoing review of our product offerings to ensure they remain relevant to customers’ evolving financial needs”, said a Singlife spokesperson on Nov 18. In an e-mail on Nov 16 at about 5pm, Singlife Account executive director Bernard Low notified customers of the account closure, providing details on what to expect from the changes. Customers also received a pop-up notification on their Singlife app. Singlife will also stop accepting new account applications. The closure date depends on the account value. If an account has remained below $100 for more than 120 days as of Nov 11, 2026, it will be closed on Dec 16, 2026. If the 120-day mark is reached after Nov 11, 2026, the account will be closed in the following month. Accounts with $100 and above will be closed on Dec 16, 2027. Until then, customers with at least $100 in their accounts can continue to make top-ups and withdrawals, earn the base rate of 1.5% per annum, and continue to be covered as long as their policy remains in force. The insurance coverage bundled with the Singlife Account will lapse when the account is closed, but customers can still submit claims for insured events that occurred while the policy was in force. From Dec 16, 2026, customers will no longer be able to make payments to third-party merchants using funds from the Singlife Account via PayNow UEN. Existing customers of Singlife Account received an e-mail on Nov 16 informing them of the account closure. Customers can opt to withdraw their funds earlier, but the account will still be closed on its scheduled date. Singlife urged customers to make sure they have linked and updated their bank account details in the Singlife app so that their remaining funds can be returned to them automatically. If the refund process fails, customers will be contacted. Singlife was founded by former HSBC Insurance Singapore CEO Walter de Oude in 2014. He led Singlife’s acquisition of Aviva Singapore in 2020 and their subsequent integration, before leaving the firm. He launched financial services platform Chocolate Finance in 2024. In several Reddit threads posted on Nov 16, some customers discussed alternatives to switch their cash to, laying out other options in the market, such as MariBank, GXS Bank, Trust Bank, Syfe, Chocolate Finance and SingFinance. The Singlife Account, launched in 2019, is an insurance savings plan that functions much like a savings account, allowing customers to earn returns on their deposits with no lock-in period and fees. It also provides payment features, and death or terminal illness coverage of up to 105% of the account value. In a media release announcing Singlife’s merger with Aviva Singapore in 2020, it reported that the Singlife Account hit 100,000 downloads within the first three months of launch, with customers entrusting almost $500 million through the product. It was also referred to as a “mobile-first” insurance savings plan. The decision to discontinue Singlife Account is “part of our ongoing review of our product offerings to ensure they remain relevant to customers’ evolving financial needs”, said a Singlife spokesperson. PHOTO: SCREENGRAB FROM SINGLIFE APP At the time, customers could earn 2.5% interest per annum on their first $10,000 with an initial contribution of $500. Singlife is now a wholly owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Life , a Japanese insurer based in Osaka. “C ustomer needs have evolved, and we are focusing our efforts on developing solutions that better serve our customers,” said the firm’s spokesperson. As demand for legacy planning solutions grows, the insurer recently introduced newer insurance savings plans, such as Singlife Heritage Income, to help individuals preserve and distribute their wealth. Sharon Salim is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, with a focus on jobs, workplace culture and trends.

events.title: Brief rally for S’pore tech stocks after Nvidia’s strong earnings exceed forecasts
events.summary: Nvidia’s third-quarter revenue more than doubled to US$115.8 billion (S$149.3 billion) from a year ago. SINGAPORE – Singapore tech stocks opened firmer on Nov 18, following Nvidia’s third-quarter earnings call at 6am Singapore time, quickly pared gains in intra-day trading as weaker sentiment in the tech industry persisted, but ended higher when the market closed. Both AEM and Frencken were trading below the previous day’s close at the mid-day break, while UMS’ counter was flat. At the close, UMS was 3% higher at $1.74, Frencken was up 0.6% at $1.71 and AEM gained 3.5% to end at $6.55. The brief rally among the Singapore tech stocks suggests investors are willing to acknowledge strong AI fundamentals, but are not yet ready to overlook the broader risks, said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Singapore. The momentary boost came from Nvidia’s strong earnings for the third quarter ended Oct 25, which exceeded analysts’ expectations. The US chipmaking giant’s revenue for the quarter more than doubled to US$115.8 billion (S$149.3 billion) from a year ago, beating estimates of US$109.1 billion and marking the 17th straight quarter that it has topped Wall Street’s revenue expectations. Meanwhile, its net income also rose 105% year on year to US$65.3 billion. The company expects even higher revenue – about US$130 billion – next quarter and has raised 2027’s growth outlook to about 75%, on the back of strong, broadening AI demand for Vera Rubin, its newest generation of AI processors. This points to sustained spending across the chip supply chain and supports order books for Singapore’s tech and precision engineering firms, said Ritesh Ganeriwal, managing director and group head of investment and advisory at Syfe. He noted that these firms are one step removed from the data centres most directly affected by the new US curbs announced on Nov 16 , which ensure restrictions on access to sensitive US technology are not circumvented through remote computing arrangements, such as involving data centres in third countries including Singapore. “Their shares may still swing with sentiment, but their orders depend on global chip investment, which Nvidia’s results show remains strong,” said Ganeriwal. He added that customer concentration and order visibility will differentiate the winners among semiconductor and precision engineering firms which benefit from sustained AI investment in a selective and potentially volatile recovery towards the year-end. While Nvidia’s earnings were strong enough to challenge concerns about an immediate slowdown in AI demand, they did not resolve questions about the sustainability of AI spending, elevated bond yields, tighter US export restrictions or Nvidia’s future leadership, noted Chanana. “These concerns are particularly relevant for Singapore’s semiconductor companies, which are exposed to global capital spending cycles and have already experienced considerable share-price volatility.” Nvidia’s eyewatering performance comes amid the huge scandal surrounding the company and its co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned following allegations of at least two extramarital affairs – one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with a company executive. Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the call that the company’s board has no intention to reinstate Huang, despite petitions from both employees and industry leaders , and will continue to search for its next permanent chief . Chanana said that Huang’s departure does not undermine Nvidia’s existing technology or demand overnight, but “it raises questions about whether the company can maintain the same pace of innovation and execution over time”. “An internal appointment of a new CEO could offer greater continuity in customer relationships, engineering priorities and supplier coordination, while an external hire might bring fresh perspectives but also greater uncertainty around execution.” In particular, she noted that interim CEO Colette Kress, who has been the company’s chief financial officer for 13 years, delivered a “reassuring” performance on the earnings call, emphasising strategic continuity and the company’s ability to execute its technology roadmap without Huang, whose vision and supply-chain relationships were vital to Nvidia’s success thus far. As the US authorities investigate whether Singapore company Megaspeed International was involved in smuggling Nvidia chips to China, Nvidia also stopped disclosing the scale of its business in Singapore since 2025, according to a report by the Financial Times (FT) on Nov 17. Singapore primarily serves as the company’s global hub, and only a small quantity of its chips ends up in or goes through the Republic . Before the 2025 reporting change, Nvidia said in its financial filing that it booked sales based on the billing locations of its customers, but the end-customer’s location “may be different than our customer’s billing location”.

events.title: Dollar holds near 19-month high as data supports case for US rate hikes
events.summary: The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.06% to 103.67. The dollar stayed near a 19-month high as strong US retail sales and higher import prices backed expectations of further Federal Reserve rate hikes. Traders now see a 95.7% chance of a 25 basis point Fed hike in December, while more US data and Fed speeches may shape the next move. The yen held steady after Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda backed more tightening, while the Australian and New Zealand dollars fell on weak market sentiment. TOKYO – The dollar held steady near a 19-month high on Nov 18 as US economic data and comments from Federal Reserve officials lent support to the case for interest rate hikes. The yen held its ground after Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Kazuo Ueda reiterated the need to tighten policy further . The Australian dollar fell to a 10-month low ahead of a key jobs report on Nov 19 . Data on Nov 17 showed US retail sales increased moderately in October, reinforcing expectations for a rate hike in December . Attention turns to US housing starts data due later on Nov 18 and a series of Fed speakers, ahead of the Nov 19 release of minutes of the central bank’s meeting in October , when it held rates steady . “Overall, the report reinforces our view that further interest rate hikes from the Fed are warranted in order to counter demand-pull inflation,” Henry Russell, a London-based economist for ANZ, said about the US sales data. “The strength of domestic demand in the US, in our view, warrants a decisive monetary policy response from the Fed.” The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.06% to 103.67. It touched 103.78 overnight, its highest level since April 2, 2025. The euro was down 0.14% at US$1.0982, while the yen edged up 0.08% to 159.25 per dollar. Sterling lost 0.13% to US$1.3191. In addition to a 0.2% rise in retail sales that matched expectations, import prices climbed 1.1% in October compared with expectations for a 0.7% increase. More US data is expected with the Census Bureau due to report housing starts data for October. Analysts are projecting an increase to 1.245 million from 1.221 million in September, while building permits likely decreased. New York Fed president John Williams is expected to speak again following comments on Nov 17 when he said the Fed will likely need to raise interest rates further to contend with inflation. Fed Board governor Michael Barr and Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari are also expected to speak at separate events. Traders are pricing in a 95.7% chance that the Fed will raise its key rate by 25 basis points (bps) in December, the CME FedWatch tool showed. The odds of a 50-bp increase have fallen to 4.3%, from 13.5% a month ago. “All Fed speakers are saying that the Fed should raise rates in an incremental way,” said Tapas Strickland, chief market strategist at Moomoo ANZ, on a podcast. “The reduction in the probability of a supersized move has resulted in a bit more stability re-emerging in markets.” Markets got a measure of relief after Nvidia reported after the bell that third-quarter revenue doubled and forecast higher-than-estimated sales for the fourth quarter, boosting shares in Asia The next major test of sentiment will be the market debut of AI bellwether Anthropic on N ov 19. Japanese data on Nov 18 showed exports rose to a record monthly value in October on strong semiconductor-related demand. Also in Tokyo, BOJ governor Ueda said the central bank should continue raising interest rates, while stressing the need to anchor underlying inflation around its 2% target. The Australian dollar sank 0.18% versus the greenback to US$0.6719 and earlier touched US$0.6718, its lowest point since Jan 19. Nov 18 data showed a surprise jump in wages, but labour figures on Nov 19 are considered more crucial to determining if the central bank will need to hike rates again. The New Zealand dollar slid 0.07% to US$0.5488, nearing its 19-month low hit on Nov 17 . REUTERS

events.title: S’pore unveils AI missions to fight financial crime, improve SME financing, enable safe AI payments
events.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said Singapore wants to establish itself as a leading AI innovation centre. Singapore launched three AI plans for finance: fight financial crime, improve SME lending, and let AI agents make safe payments. Gan Kim Yong said the aim is shared tools, testing, and wider use. The Monetary Authority of Singapore is already pooling data from five banks to spot scam patterns, with a design study due in early 2027. It will also test richer data and synthetic data to speed and widen SME financing. Singapore will set rules for AI agents, with safeguards for identity, authority and accountability. It also unveiled PayNow Generation 2 and SGQR+ to make QR payments simpler, while warning firms not to break chip export laws. SINGAPORE – Singapore is launching three national artificial intelligence initiatives to combat financial crime, improve financing for smaller businesses, and enable AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users. Speaking at the Singapore FinTech Festival at Singapore Expo on Nov 18, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said these missions will bring together financial institutions, technology companies, researchers and public agencies to build shared capabilities in a bid to achieve more than any institution could alone. Singapore will also test promising solutions against global best practices and standards, and take those that work well towards wider deployment. To strengthen the country’s ability to detect and disrupt financial crime, Gan, who is also chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), said the Republic must connect information across the financial system while strengthening detection within each institution. “Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank. A victim’s money can pass through several institutions within minutes. We will not be able to mitigate the risk if each institution sees only its part of the transaction chain,” he added. He noted that a proof of value is already under way with five banks, pooling transaction data securely to allow AI models to find patterns that no single bank can see on its own. The MAS will begin a design study in early 2027 to develop the blueprint, including its governance and operating model, he added. Singapore also wants to help businesses, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), gain better access to financing through richer data. Using these data sets, AI can identify information and patterns that traditional approaches may miss, giving lenders a fuller picture of a firm’s creditworthiness, said Gan. It will also support faster, better-informed lending decisions, make it easier to serve smaller businesses and lower the cost of borrowing for lenders. Singapore will invite AI tech companies to develop and test solutions using realistic synthetic data, said Gan. These trials will assess whether AI and richer data can make SME financing more forward-looking and accessible before determining the longer-term data and infrastructure needed to scale them up. The Republic will also look into enabling AI agents to make transactions safely on behalf of users. While AI agents make cash management more efficient and speed up payments, they must operate within defined authority and limits, and institutions and enterprises remain accountable for actions taken on their behalf, with safeguards built in from the start, he said. Singapore will work with the industry to test practical applications in controlled environments – such as embedding conditions into transactions – and examine the safeguards needed for wider use, including common approaches to identity, authority, accountability and interoperability. “We want to establish Singapore as a leading AI innovation centre, with the policies, standards and infrastructure to support trusted use of AI agents in finance.” Gan also unveiled the latest report for PayNow Generation 2, which sets out how Singapore will make payments simpler, safer and more accessible for all users. This includes a new SGQR+ switch, which will enable Singapore residents and tourists to pay with any SGQR+ label using their preferred QR app, as well as other enhancements. Gan also touched on the new US rules requiring companies to have licences to export or re-export advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore. He said the Republic will act against those who do not abide by its laws, amid growing scrutiny of the possible diversion of advanced US AI chips to China. “We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities,” he said. “We will act against those who flout our laws.” In a separate fireside chat, Gan noted that ASEAN countries have varying levels of digital and AI readiness, with some at the forefront of technological development while others are at the start of their digitalisation journey.

events.title: Adnoc L&S ship attacked in Strait of Hormuz with one crew member missing
events.summary: Adnoc Logistics and Services said on Wednesday that a crew member was missing after one of its ships was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday evening. “Search and rescue operations ongoing in co-ordination with the relevant authorities,” the company said. All other crew members have been safely evacuated from the vessel. Eleven were injured and are receiving medical care where required. “Adnoc reiterates the importance of protecting seafarers and safeguarding freedom of navigation and maritime security,” the company said. It added that further updates will be provided as more information becomes available. The latest incident comes after Adnoc L&S last week said one of its vessels was damaged in an attack in UAE territorial waters in the Gulf, without identifying the ship or the extent of the damage. Iran has claimed a series of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and off the coast of Oman and the UAE, often blaming operators for hitting sea mines . Tehran has been condemned for its attacks on non-military vessels. A gas tanker which was struck in the strait on Tuesday was also seen to be engulfed in flames. India’s Foreign Ministry confirmed 21 crew members were safely evacuated from the Panama-flagged Tara Gas, while two were taken to hospital and one is unaccounted for. In July, two crude oil tankers operated by Adnoc L&S were struck by projectiles in the strait, killing one crew member and injuring others. Another company ship was attacked in August, although no injuries were reported. Earlier this month, the UAE National Guard rescued 22 people after a fire broke out aboard a cargo ship in the Sea of Oman. Adnoc L&S, the shipping arm of Abu Dhabi energy giant Adnoc, operates a fleet of between 500 and 800 active managed, owned and chartered vessels. Last week, the Abu Dhabi-listed company raised its full-year profit forecast for the fourth time this year after third-quarter earnings more than quadrupled, as disruption from the Iran war drove up tanker charter rates. Net profit attributable to the equity holders of the company jumped 310 per cent to $842.7 million in the three months to the end of September, from $205.4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 160 per cent to $3.29 billion, while operating profit nearly quadrupled to $898.7 million. It now expects annual net profit of about $4 billion.
