events.title: IMF puts UAE back into growth territory for 2026
events.summary: The International Monetary Fund has upgraded its projection for the UAE’s economy to 0.2 per cent growth this year, amid the easing of Iran war disruption and a recovery in oil production. The IMF had previously said it would shrink by 3.9 per cent. The change marks a major turnaround for the Arab world's second-largest economy. Real gross domestic product is expected to grow by 7.3 per cent next year, slightly lower than the fund's previous projection of 7.7 per cent, the IMF said after a visit to the UAE this month. “The UAE economy has demonstrated strong resilience to regional disruptions, supported by the authorities’ swift policy response,” Said Bakhache, IMF mission chief for the UAE, said. “Substantial public-sector and external buffers, a well-capitalised banking system and targeted fiscal and financial-sector measures helped cushion the impact.” Oil recovery The fund said oil production had also recovered, while some non-oil sectors were showing signs of gradual recovery, supporting the growth of the UAE economy. The Iran war, in its ninth month, has disrupted a number of sectors across the region, with tourism and aviation among the most affected as airlines cancel or reschedule flights. The Strait of Hormuz, the global chokepoint for crude supply, was effectively shut as Iran attacked ships transiting the channel. Inflation stays high However, regional countries including the UAE and Saudi Arabia began to supply crude to global markets through pipelines as well as via ships. UAE Minister of Energy and Infrastructure Suhail Al Mazrouei told Adipec this month that the country’s oil exports surpassed prewar levels “at a certain time” during the conflict. The non-hydrocarbon sector is projected to contract by 0.5 per cent in 2026 and expand by 5.4 per cent in 2027, while hydrocarbon growth is expected at 2.3 per cent in 2026 and 13.3 per cent in 2027, the IMF said. Inflation is projected to average about 5 per cent in 2026 before easing to about 3 per cent in 2027 and converging towards 2 per cent over the medium term as supply pressures and base effects unwind. “The outlook remains subject to significant uncertainty. Escalation of regional tensions and disruptions to trade, tourism and supply chains could delay the recovery and add to inflationary pressures,” Mr Bakhache said. “Global financial volatility and cybersecurity risks also warrant continued attention. On the upside, faster normalisation of regional conflict and stronger investment and productivity gains, including from AI, could support higher growth.” The UAE's financial system remains resilient, underpinned by substantial capital and liquidity buffers, while asset quality has continued to improve. Against the backdrop of elevated inflation and strong credit growth, continued close monitoring of liquidity and funding conditions, asset quality, and sectoral exposures remain important, the IMF said. Developments in real estate and financial innovation also require sustained supervisory vigilance and regulatory co-ordination to further safeguard stability, it added. Real estate activity has moderated from earlier peaks, with conditions varying across emirates and market segments. 'Capacity to adapt' The IMF emphasised greater trade integration and diversification of trade routes to strengthen resilience against future disruptions. It also welcomed comprehensive economic partnership agreements signed by the UAE to expand trade partnerships. “The resilience of the UAE economy and its high capacity to adapt to global developments and sustain growth embody … the effectiveness of the country’s proactive policies, which have reinforced the pillars of financial and monetary stability and solidified the UAE’s standing as a leading global economic and financial centre,” Khaled Balama, Governor of the Central Bank of the UAE and Governor for the UAE at the IMF, said in a separate statement. Total banking assets surpassed Dh5.815 trillion ($1.57 trillion) by the end of the third quarter of 2026, reflecting the “strength, soundness, and high resilience of the banking system in supporting sustainable economic development”, Mr Balama added.

events.title: A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype
events.summary: Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet . Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters. When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe. The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo , who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming. AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool. Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall. Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator . That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed? Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less." What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it. I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA 's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month. My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.” Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation. Not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn't noticed, because having equal numbers of men and women at an engineering conference felt perfectly normal . Yet it's not something I've ever experienced at AI events in Australia or America. Whatever else the Chinese are doing with AI, they've put gender politics aside in AI engineering. To put that in context: not long after leaving Shanghai, Alice Huang became major global news. A Shanghainese woman working in AI might look suspicious to an American who only ever sees men working in the field. Fei-Fei Li , Mira Murati and Daniela Amodei stand out as exceptions that prove the rule, but none of them, despite stellar work, have anywhere near the profiles of their male peers. In China, it's different. It's become commonplace to be dismissive of Chinese progress in AI, ascribing it to copying, " distillation " and outright theft. Yet the Chinese make both the best small models and the best robots, and are moving ever-closer to making them work well together. Chinese labs share their results with their peers and their competitors: nearly every model, closed or open, has benefited from the research done by DeepSeek and Alibaba. Practicality, balance and openness seem to be serving them well. Perhaps, after OpenAI follows Anthropic out to the public markets , and shareholders get a voice, stability, sanity and a bit of quiet will cross the Pacific. Those are some Chinese imports I'm looking forward to. ®

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Prepares to unleash full wrath of Digital Services Act over Chinese e-tailer's alleged sales of illegal products A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype 13 hours ago Nvidia places chip exports under boardroom supervision after Huang's exit 1 day ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 2 days ago Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China 2 days ago Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer 4 days ago Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the company also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations. The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform. Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps. Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including: Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports; Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks; Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety; Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu; When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores; Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores. A Temu spokesperson told The Register the company respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings. "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson said. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns." The EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine. Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods. This announcement of new action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions. Europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retailers. The bloc has tried to make life harder for Chinese e-commerce outfits by charging a temporary €3 customs duty for every shipment sent from outside the EU and valued at under €150. Google recently revealed that new charge saw its advertising revenue from Asian customers fall.

events.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
events.summary: Published 18 November 2026, 06:04 GMT Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom. No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology. That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy. The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure. While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years. The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders. Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market. It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier. But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him. Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending. Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says. "If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says. Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run. That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing". Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly. The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy? That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement. Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back". Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning . Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm. When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped. "I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds. The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms. Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off. Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year. Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.

events.title: New US AI, data centre curbs could slow down AI adoption, investment across South-east Asia
events.summary: The US restrictions on access to computing power can affect data centre investment across South-east Asia. US rules now limit AI chip shipments and overseas data centre access for China, risking a split between US and Chinese tech systems. South-east Asia, especially Malaysia and Singapore, may see slower data centre investment as firms wait for licence rules and face weaker demand from Chinese customers. Analysts warn compute is becoming a strategic resource, with more US controls likely and possible Chinese retaliation that could damage the fragile trade truce. SINGAPORE – The scandal surrounding former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang now risks escalating into the start of a war between the world’s two largest economies for a strategic resource: computing power. The US’ move to curb both indirect AI chip shipments to China and its access to overseas data centres – ahead of a summit between the nations’ presidents – could be the first shot in the much-dreaded fragmentation of the global tech ecosystem. If mounting US-China friction on tech dominance raises the cost of or limits access to AI models and computational capacity, it could slow down the global adoption of artificial intelligence needed for extracting broader economic value from the technology, said analysts. The new measures, which will come into effect 90 days after it is gazetted in the US’ Federal Register, expand US chip export controls to cover Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil, aiming to close routes through which smuggled chips have been reaching China. Licences are now required to export advanced chips to any non-US headquartered firms in these countries. The measures also ban Chinese chip designers from using foreign chip foundries, such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company or South Korea’s Samsung, to manufacture chips. Data centres in third countries are now required to obtain a US licence before supplying significant amounts of AI computing power to Chinese-owned or Chinese-headquartered firms. The US goal is to crack down on companies such as Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which bought billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and built data centres throughout South-east Asia. Megaspeed came into the public eye on Nov 8 after the disclosure of an extramarital affair between Jensen Huang, co-founder of US chipmaker Nvidia, and Megaspeed’s former top executive Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who is suspected by the US of being a Chinese spy. He stepped down as Nvidia chief executive officer on Nov 12, while she has been banned from re-entering Singapore and is believed to be in China. Beyond the impact on China, the US restrictions on access to computing power may affect data centre investment across South-east Asia, including Singapore, which has an estimated 1.6GW of capacity spread across more than 70 facilities. Most analysts believe Malaysia stands to lose the most, given that it has been the biggest beneficiary of the region’s data centre build-out. However, the whole region will still suffer because restrictions on access to overseas cloud facilities would undermine the commercial case for expanding capacity to serve Chinese customers. This could weigh on investment in data centres by both Chinese and US companies. Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle in 2027. Lim Siew Khee, an analyst at brokerage firm CGS International, expects the near-term impact on ASEAN markets to be felt mainly through slower AI-related capital expenditure and investment into 2027, particularly in Malaysia and Thailand, as investors await licensing clarity. However, enterprise cloud, sovereign AI and domestic digitalisation should sustain broader data centre investment. Analysts said these new regulations were clearly rushed through, given that there were several drafting errors in the official document, and loopholes remained. For example, Chinese companies can still lease data centres in the US. However, American hyperscalers are unlikely to take any risks by providing access to Chinese companies, especially those that are direct competitors. Swiss private bank Julius Baer analyst Enrico Chinello said compute – the hardware and the supporting infrastructure used to train AI models and run them – is increasingly being treated as a strategic resource, and access to it is becoming a point of mounting geopolitical friction. “The AI market could be fragmenting into a US-aligned ecosystem and a Chinese one, each building its own chips, models and infrastructure,” he said. London-based research and consultancy firm Capital Economics expects US chip restrictions to tighten further. Its senior China economist Leah Fahy said the US Congress looked set to include a series of even harsher chip restrictions in the National Defence Act, due to be passed in December.

events.title: Malaysia says growth stronger than expected but AI risks loom
events.summary: Gross domestic product rose 5.5% in the three months through September, more than the statistics department’s 5.3% advance estimate. Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% in the third quarter, above the 5.3% estimate, helped by AI demand and strong domestic spending, with firms still upbeat into 2027. Bank Negara Malaysia said growth could stay above 5% in 2026, but warned of risks from Middle East conflict, weak commodity output and any drop in AI returns. US rules now require licences for advanced AI chip buyers in Malaysia and other countries, and the central bank said it is too early to know the impact. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia’s economy expanded faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, supported by demand for artificial intelligence and resilient domestic spending, as officials said they are trying to gauge the impact of new US rules on AI. Growth surged to 6.9% in September, Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) said in a statement. “The Malaysian economy is well-positioned to build on its momentum in 2027,” governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said at a briefing on Nov 18, predicting growth of more than 5% in 2026. “Downside risks include re-escalation of conflict in the Middle East and lower-than-expected commodity production.” Another downside risk is if AI returns disappoint, Rasheed said, though he predicted the tech upcycle “will be sustained into next year, although at a moderate level compared to what we’ve seen”. Malaysia’s status as a net energy exporter has allowed it to maintain some of the world’s lowest fuel costs despite the Iran war, shielding it from the high energy prices that have battered neighbours such as Thailand and the Philippines. But the data underscores its reliance on the AI boom, just as the US examines whether South-east Asian countries are allowing China access to advanced AI chips and servers. Data centre operators in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will need a US government licence to purchase advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers, according to an interim rule released on Nov 16 by the US Commerce Department. The measure seeks to restrict China and other US adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses US-designed processors. “This is an example of the geopolitics that we are all facing,” Rasheed said , noting it is too early to know the impact of the rule change. “In terms of the impact on data centre investment, based on our estimates of the ongoing and planned projects, it is expected to remain strong up to 2028,” he added. Out of the 120 companies in data centres, China accounts for only 13%, according to Rasheed, with the US, Australia and domestic interests accounting for the rest. It was unclear what Rasheed’s statistics referred to. US hyperscalers account for the bulk of announced investment in Malaysia, while more than half of data centre capacity is in co-location facilities, where Chinese workloads may rival or exceed American ones, according to a report on Nov 18 from Gareth Leather, Capital Economics’ senior Asia economist in London. “The restrictions could affect a much larger share of Malaysia’s data centre industry than ownership figures suggest,” Leather wrote. “Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI investment cycle.” While the quarterly expansion was slower than the second-quarter pace of 6%, growth accelerated to 6.9% in September. Rasheed noted the country’s businesses have adapted to supply disruptions even as they face higher costs. Firms remained optimistic on the outlook well into 2027, the central bank said, citing business expansion, tourism activities, electronics demand and commodity prices. Rasheed said electrical and electronic firms’ order books have been solid, showing strong demand. The ringgit extended an earlier decline, weakening 0.6% against the dollar and underperforming other Asian currencies on Nov 18. Kuala Lumpur’s benchmark stock index held earlier losses, declining 0.3%. The third-quarter growth “is bang in line with our forecast and shows not just remarkable resilience, but also the economy powering through multiple external shocks ”, said Nomura Holdings economist Euben Paracuelles. “There is no need for the monetary stance to remain accommodative when growth is above potential for several quarters in a row, and pipeline price pressures are building.” BNM is set to raise its benchmark rate by 25 basis points in the first quarter, Paracuelles added. The central bank kept interest rates unchanged at 2.75% at its final policy meeting of 2026 earlier in November, but signalled it would be ready to act if price pressures grow. The ringgit has declined around 1% against the dollar in 2026, compared with declines of more than 6% for the Indonesian, Philippine and Thai currencies, limiting the impact of imported inflation.

events.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
events.summary: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November , which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938 , which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning . The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw , says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list , expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work. “Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.” Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.” That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure. The rest of Big Red’s flaws Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists. So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition. Big Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue. The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10. By Tenable Security’s count , 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs. Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®

events.title: UOB to use A*STAR’s multilingual AI tool to guide S-E Asia relationship managers on client calls
events.summary: Built on A*STAR’s large language model MERaLiON, the AI solution can understand 11 languages and dialects spoken in South-east Asia, where UOB’s retail customers are concentrated. UOB and A*STAR are testing an AI tool built on MERaLiON to transcribe and translate client calls in real time and help the bank's relationship managers follow regulatory rules. The tool can handle 11 South-east Asian languages and dialects. It flags missed checks, such as identity verification, and suggests questions and scripted lines. UOB hopes to roll it out next year, but there is no fixed date. The bank says it will support staff, not replace them, while improving coaching and customer service. SINGAPORE – UOB and A*STAR have tied up to explore how an artificial intelligence tool can help relationship managers better engage clients, as the bank drives greater deployment of AI across its operations. The tool is designed to transcribe and translate customer calls in real time, and prompt relationship managers with questions to ask and disclosures to make so they comply with regulatory guidelines. “(We) see potential for this solution to help our relationship managers better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance,” said UOB’s group chief financial officer Leong Yung Chee in a statement on Nov 18 on the first day of the Singapore FinTech Festival. In a demonstration to the media on Nov 13, UOB and A*STAR showed a mock customer call in which an early version of the tool could log sentences spoken in a mix of English, Mandarin and Malay. When the relationship manager neglected to properly verify the client’s identity, the tool flagged it in red, prompted her to ask for an NRIC number and suggested a scripted line. Panchai Aroonpairoj, a senior client adviser at UOB Private Bank, said the tool could come in handy when he speaks with older Thai clients, who may sometimes use Teochew phrases during their calls. An early version of the tool could transcribe sentences spoken in a mix of languages. As he does not understand the dialect, he would otherwise have to ask them to repeat themselves in Thai, disrupting the flow of the conversation. UOB believes that the solution could also provide insights for more targeted coaching of relationship managers, complementing existing training methods such as role-playing while a human observer gives feedback. The bank hopes to roll out the AI tool some time in 2027, though there is no fixed timeline yet, said UOB’s head of enterprise AI Alvin Eng. For now, A*STAR and UOB will work on developing the application and tailoring it to the bank’s needs. Angela Chee, a director at A*STAR’s Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing, said this would mark MERaLiON’s first use case in the banking sector. Other banks such as DBS, OCBC and Standard Chartered have also been testing the model and evaluating how they would use it. The model’s existing users include social service agency Lions Befrienders, which has a MERaLiON-powered voice agent to automate check-in calls on seniors, and tech service provider NCS, which uses the model for voice transcription for its in-house chatbot. A*STAR Director Angela Chee (left) and UOB's Head of Enterprise AI Alvin Eng at a demonstration of a new AI-powered tool for relationship managers. “A large part of our work will be doing model adaptation to see how we can teach the model to speak or to think like a financial person, so (it) can transcribe more accurately,” said Chee. A*STAR will have to familiarise MERaLiON with the terminology and acronyms that UOB uses, and incorporate feedback from the bank as it tests the solution. UOB, like many banks, has been stepping up its deployment of AI to streamline workflows and drive value. It has more than 300 AI and data analytics use cases, including a solution that optimises cash replenishment routes and schedules for its ATMs. The MERaLiON solution will not supplant its relationship managers. “That’s not our philosophy,” said Eng, adding that the tool is meant to augment staff. For Aroonpairoj, the value of his team is clear. “You need relationships, which means you need human touch,” he said. “People will trust humans more than machines.” A*Star/Agency for Science, Technology and Research

events.title: Mary Peltola unseats Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska, extending Democratic wave
events.summary: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated two-term Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan , flipping another GOP-held seat in a state President Trump carried comfortably in 2024, the AP projects. Why it matters: Peltola becomes the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska since 2008, extending a historic blue wave in a race marred by controversy. Her victory comes in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, underscoring the extraordinary reach of the Democratic backlash against his second term. It also delivers another blow to Republicans after sweeping Democratic victories in states including Texas, Ohio, Iowa and South Carolina. State of play: The race drew scrutiny after The New York Times reported allegations that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Dan Sullivan to draw votes from the incumbent. Peltola's campaign denied involvement, but the reporting prompted Alaska's Republican governor, Mike Dunleavy, to order an investigation into whether state laws were broken. The Justice Department also launched a criminal investigation and subpoenaed people connected to the alleged effort. No one involved in the race has been charged with a crime. On the campaign trail, the candidates clashed over the cost of living, the Iran war and Alaska's energy industry, with Peltola challenging Sullivan's record in Washington. Peltola campaigned on her signature "fish, family and freedom" message, emphasizing affordability, protecting Alaska's fisheries and putting the state's interests ahead of party politics. Trump traveled to Alaska in October to rally support for Sullivan, whom he praised as one of Washington's most respected senators. Sullivan embraced the president's support , betting it would energize Republican voters despite their party's political headwinds. The big picture: Alaska has long leaned Republican, but Peltola's ability to win crossover support — including votes from Republicans who ranked her above former Gov. Sarah Palin in 2022 — helped put the state in play for Democrats. Peltola made history in that 2022 special election as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She won a full term later that year before losing her House seat to Republican Nick Begich in 2024. Sullivan, a former Alaska attorney general and Marine Corps veteran, has represented Alaska in the Senate since 2015. The two-term Republican campaigned on his record on energy development and national security. Context: Another candidate named Dan Sullivan — a retired teacher from Petersburg, Alaska, listed on the ballot as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. — became a factor in the race. The Trump administration sued Alaska on Oct. 22, seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan lost and votes for the other Dan Sullivan could have changed the outcome. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit on Nov. 1, ruling that the administration lacked standing to bring the case and that its proposed remedy was unworkable. The Justice Department appealed the decision. Sen. Sullivan committed to accepting the results even if he didn't win. How it works: Alaska's ranked-choice voting system added another wrinkle. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate wins a majority of first-choice votes, the last-place candidate is eliminated and votes for that candidate are redistributed according to voters' next available choices. The process repeats until a candidate wins a majority. What's next: Alaska election officials will complete the remaining certification steps, with the Justice Department's appeal potentially affecting the process.

events.title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new Bond
events.summary: Watch: Jeff Bezos on involvement in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond Published 18 November 2026, 02:40 GMT Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous". The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond". This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022. Robert Pattinson: How the Twilight star became 007 Published 2 days ago 'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007 Published 2 days ago "There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday. Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028. In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime." The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced. The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment. Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks. But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands. "We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said. There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob." The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas. Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise. "Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter. The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report. events.title: Woolworths shoppers call for answers over gift card draining issue
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Woolworths says the issue affected a number of digital gift cards. ( ABC News ) Woolworths customers are demanding answers after hundreds of dollars were drained from their digital gift cards. Some fear their personal and financial information may have been compromised. Experts say an automated attack or software vulnerability could be to blame, but Woolworths has declined to explain what happened. Frustrated customers who have lost hundreds of dollars from drained Woolworths gift cards are calling on the supermarket giant to explain what happened and warn others who may be affected. Woolworths apologised to affected customers on Monday, saying it recognised the concern the issue had caused and was investigating reports as a priority. But Woolworths has declined to comment on what caused the issue or disclose how many shoppers lost money, despite earlier acknowledging a problem affecting "a number of customer e-gift cards". Woolworths did not say whether the issue was contained. ( ABC News ) The ABC has heard from more customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards were drained without their knowledge over the past week, reporting losses of up to $500. All had purchased their cards digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app during a promotional period offering 4 per cent off gift cards. Transaction histories seen by the ABC show payments to stores customers say they did not visit. In other cases, transactions are listed against an online store or a generic descriptor without identifying a store or location. Experts say there are several possible explanations for the losses, including an "enumeration attack" or software vulnerability, but they caution there is not enough information so far to determine what happened. Paul Hobbs, from Brisbane, said he was frustrated Woolworths had not been more proactive in communicating about the issue. "If you're serious about customers and you're concerned about some transactions that have happened, whether you can explain it or not, you should be reaching out to customers and alerting us," Mr Hobbs said. Mr Hobbs, who started using gift cards to pay for his groceries because it was more economical, discovered on Monday that his card had been drained without his knowledge. His transaction history showed a payment of $210.16 described as "Woolworths Group Limited Services", but did not specify a store or location. Paul Hobbs says the unauthorised transaction was listed against a generic descriptor of "Woolworths Group Limited Services". ( Supplied ) "Woolworths should have made me aware of this so that I don't stress about where the funds have gone, rather than rely on me finding out elsewhere," he said. "They always tell you the customer is important to them, but they're happy for something strange to happen and stay silent." Mr Hobbs said he had not shared his card details and Woolworths had not warned him about a potential problem. Chris Lang, from Hobart, said he wanted to know whether there had been a data breach after he lost his entire gift card balance to purchases he did not recognise. "Losing up to $500 is no small thing," he said. He said he had emailed the gift card support address provided by the company but had so far received only an automated acknowledgement. "It would be nice for Woolworths to communicate what's going on," he said. "It's hard to know how to react without some indication of what the issue is." Woolworths apologises after customers report gift card draining Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and is investigating, with replacement cards among the possible next steps for affected customers. Sydney man Michael Bennett previously told the ABC his e-gift card had disappeared from his digital wallet after a $400 balance was drained. Mr Bennett said he got in touch with a Woolworths representative who described the problem as an "IT malfunction" and said there had been no security breach. Woolworths has not publicly confirmed that explanation. Debbie Kellie, who also lost $500, previously told the ABC she had deactivated her Visa card as a precaution and that the matter had been referred to Queensland police. All the customers the ABC spoke to insisted they did not share their card details with anyone or accidentally disclose them to a spoof website. Woolworths said on Monday its team would work directly with customers to determine appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards.

events.title: Kakadu tour operator says waterfall closures led to his 'worst' dry season
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mixed results for Kakadu tourism businesses amid site closures, 'horrendous' road damage Topic: Tourism and Leisure Industry Popular Kakadu National Park attractions, including Jim Jim Falls and Twin Falls, are closed to visitors. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) For almost a decade, Sean "Chizo" Chisholm has been showing sightseers around Kakadu National Park's most popular attractions in his four-wheel drive. While many visit the World Heritage-listed park, located about 3 hours south-east of Darwin, to view ancient rock art or take in spectacular sunsets at Ubirr, most of his passengers travel to see its cascading waterfalls. Sean "Chizo" Chisholm has been taking tourists around Kakadu National Park for almost a decade. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) With Jim Jim Falls remaining closed this dry season , the Never Never Tours owner said his company had wrapped up its "worst" season ever, with business down by 45 per cent. "We took out 470 people last year; that was 97 carloads," Mr Chisholm said. Despite still offering day trips to the waterfalls near Jim Jim, Mr Chisholm said he was left out of pocket from $30,000 in customer refunds and had to lay off two staff members. Sean "Chizo" Chisholm says Never Never Tours issued thousands of dollars in refunds this year. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) He also said the state of the outback roads he travelled, including the road to Gunlom Falls, was "horrendous". "We spent a lot of money on cars this year, fixing them up, getting them towed back out to Darwin," he said. Kakadu tourists greeted by closure signs It is known as the jewel in the Northern Territory's tourism crown, but visitors to Kakadu National Park are being greeted by closure signs blocking roads to key waterfall sites. In June, Parks Australia confirmed Jim Jim Falls and Twin Falls would stay shut through the Top End's peak tourism season, while "critical road and infrastructure upgrades" were undertaken to repair flood damage from cyclones earlier this year. "Traditional owners expressed their concerns for the safety of visitors to their country and have requested that the area remain closed until all road upgrade projects are completed," Parks Australia director Ricky Archy said at the time. "Parks Australia respects and supports this decision." The decision prompted a stern warning from the NT's tourism minister and concerns from the sector , with tourism operators holding a roundtable discussion to try to prevent further closures in Kakadu. The wetlands of Kakadu National Park are home to a range of unique birds and wildlife. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Kakadu Tourism, an Indigenous-owned group of local tour operators and accommodation providers, said recent weather coupled with ongoing cost-of-living pressures culminated in a "perfect storm" this peak season. "We were bracing ourselves," director of sales and marketing Samantha Waldron said. "We knew it was going to be a challenging season. We had two cyclones last wet season, and Kakadu National Park was completely inundated with water, so we knew there would be delays to tourist sites opening. "Obviously, we look at the fuel crisis, there's fuel scarcity and then people are concerned about the cost of fuel, so we knew that was then going to impact our drive market as well." Samantha Waldron says the cost of living has affected the local drive market. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) Ms Waldron said Kakadu Tourism's campgrounds had been "severely" affected by the severe weather, with sites sitting at 42 per cent occupancy between June and August. "We were down by 10,000 visitors [to Kakadu National Park] just in the month of June and if we looked at our campground, which is really where we were most impacted, we were down by about 1,500 campsites across those three peak months," she said. On-country experiences still accessible Ms Waldron urged both locals and people from interstate to visit Kakadu for more than just its bucket-listed waterfalls, saying the rock art, Indigenous culture and other natural landscapes within the park were accessible year-round. The cost and availability of fuel discouraged many tourists from driving to Kakadu National Park this dry season. ( ABC News: Dane Hirst ) "We don't want people sitting at home waiting for the waterfalls to open," she said. "People can connect to country, they can go on our cultural tours and they can view the rock art and sit and watch the sunset." Senior custodian Mandy Muir said she believed the site closures pushed more tourists to cultural experiences instead, estimating her campsite's visitor numbers had almost doubled in a year.

events.title: Highlights from my opening of the Ignite keynote this morning on how we’re building a frontier ecosystem to turn advances in AI into real-world impact.
events.summary: People stopped being impressed by AI demos, they just want their work to get easier. ⠀ Microsoft talking about an ecosystem instead of a single model is how that actually happens. Exciting to see GPT-6.2 and Meta's models coming to Foundry, giving businesses more flexibility to build AI solutions around their specific needs. Well said, Sir. A frontier ecosystem only matters when it works on the ground, not just on stage. In my daily work on data centres, I see this gap clearly. AI can show great promise in a demo, but real-world impact comes when power, cooling, connectivity and resilience all hold together under continuous load. When an AI system has to act, decide and execute, there is no room for downtime or latency. That is why this shift from models to real outcomes is so important. The value will not come from how advanced the model is alone, but from how reliably the infrastructure behind it can support it at scale, across different regions, languages and operating conditions like we have in India. Building that dependable layer is what will turn AI advances into actual productivity, and that is where the real work lies. Keeping Humans at the centre. Human in the Room. Human in the Loop. The one thing that struck while looking on this morning was how Microsoft was making itself a one stop shop to better compete. On a micro level, I created an AI Productivity and Workforce Transformation Programme™ with the intent to improve work processes and bridge the gap for those who can't pay or are not as knowledge using AI tools. As such it is also beginner friendly. I have about twelve tools in my Programme that also includes Microsoft Copilot, Excel AI, Word and Microsoft Forms. Looking at the presentation, I was amazed how Microsoft is competing with the Zapier's, Otter AI, Trello, Notion and others - kind of made me feel like I should rewrite the Programne using only Microsoft tools. However, that won't help many because my Programme tells people how to get things done using free AI tools until they can pay/ upgrade to the paid tools for greater, better results and collaboration. I was impressed by Microsoft's presentation today though👍🏼 As Microsoft moves toward more autonomous AI agents, how do you envision measuring success beyond adoption and productivity? Could business outcomes become the primary measure of AI’s value? The move from single-player AI to people working alongside agents is where most mid-size organizations in Latin America will feel Ignite's impact. What we see on the ground is that the technology arrives before the groundwork: identity, permissions and data classification decide whether agents create value or create risk. I'm curious how much of this ecosystem will make that groundwork easier for companies without large security teams. The most consequential takeaway from the keynote isn’t just Copilot evolving into an OS for work-it’s the architectural emphasis on enterprises owning their context layer (Microsoft IQ), tracking unit economics via Agent 365, and enforcing runtime containment through Microsoft Perception and Execution Containers. Scaling autonomous agents in production only works when context governance, FinOps telemetry, and non-human identity boundaries are built into the stack from day one. One of the most impactful speeches of the day! Particularly appreciated the emphasis on ownership and the responsibility every enterprise must take for its intelligence systems. Honestly, nobody is asking for a smarter demo anymore. Everyone just wants their day to get a little easier. And that's why this ecosystem thing matters. It's not one tool doing one trick, it's everything actually fitting together in real work. events.title: Anthropic’s IPO: Will Singapore investors back AI’s promise or help fuel another bubble?
events.summary: Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), according to its latest IPO plans. SINGAPORE – Anthropic’s upcoming listing will put the market’s appetite for artificial intelligence to the test. Do investors still see AI as a lucrative opportunity? Or have concerns over lofty valuations, soaring spending and uncertain returns brought them back down to earth? The Nov 19 Nasdaq listing of the company behind the Claude chatbot comes amid significant volatility in AI-related stocks. Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion), according to its latest initial public offering (IPO) plans. It is offering 825 million shares at between US$70 and US$78 apiece, potentially raising US$64.4 billion, including shares sold by existing shareholders, which could make it the biggest IPO in history. A strong debut would signal that investors still see fortunes to be made from AI. Conversely, a lacklustre one might suggest that investors are becoming more discerning about the prices they are prepared to pay for the stock. A subsequent fall in Anthropic’s share price could signal either a broader loss of confidence in AI or a reassessment of the company’s valuation and prospects. This does not have to be a bad thing, though. Given the transformational potential and benefits of AI, a correction could be an opportunity for more sensible, long-term value investors to enter the market. Founded in 2021, the San Francisco-based company develops the Claude family of AI models used for tasks ranging from writing and software development to research and data analysis. Anthropic plans to use the proceeds from the offering and a concurrent US$26 billion private placement to fund general corporate purposes, including investments in computing infrastructure, research and development, and business expansion. Its prospectus points to the technology’s potential to accelerate scientific discoveries, help researchers tackle diseases such as cancer and improve productivity across both the public and private sectors. In healthcare, for example, AI could help doctors identify diseases earlier and aid researchers in developing new treatments. In education, it could provide personalised learning support, while businesses could use it to improve efficiency and reduce costs. The strategic and national importance of AI is also evident in the lengths to which the US has gone to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors. On Nov 16, Washington announced new restrictions requiring US export licences for shipments of certain advanced AI chips to data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, among other countries, as it seeks to prevent Chinese companies from accessing American computing power through overseas facilities. The rule underscores the urgency with which the Commerce Department is scrambling to crack down on Chinese access to sensitive American technology, following reporting that the agency turned a blind eye to smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China. But Anthropic’s prospectus also lays bare the formidable costs and risks of developing the technology. The company further warned that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if developed or deployed without adequate safeguards. Such risks could arise if AI systems were weaponised, misused or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy, particularly if advances in the technology outpace developers’ ability to evaluate and control them. The prospectus also highlights the possibility that increasingly autonomous systems could take harmful actions without human intervention. Meanwhile, the company is still unprofitable, recording a net loss of US$104 billion for the first nine months of the year, compared with US$25.1 billion in the same period in 2025. Anthropic has also disclosed approximately US$900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, much of it related to computing capacity and infrastructure extending over many years. These levels of expenditure raise questions about whether the company can sustain its growth, maintain its technological advantage and generate sufficient profits to justify investors’ expectations. But even a strong debut could prompt questions about whether speculation is running ahead of economic reality. Investors would do well to remember what happened during the dot.com boom. In the late 1990s, investors poured money into internet companies on the assumption that the new technology would transform commerce and communication. While they were right about the internet’s potential, many were wrong about the companies they backed and the prices they paid. The lesson was that investors could correctly anticipate a technological revolution and still lose fortunes betting on it. The cryptocurrency boom and bust offers another warning.

events.title: Bank of Japan governor says central bank should keep raising rates
events.summary: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said it was important to see underlying inflation anchored around 2% over time. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said the bank should keep raising rates, as financial conditions are still accommodative and inflation must stay near the 2% target. The BOJ left rates at 1.25% on Oct 30, but said policy has entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot. Ueda said a food consumption tax cut could lift growth, while the BOJ will judge its impact and warned bond-buying could make long-term rates more volatile. TOKYO - Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Nov 18 that the central bank should continue raising interest rates, while stressing the need to anchor underlying inflation around its 2% target. Speaking in Parliament, Ueda said it was important to see underlying inflation anchored around 2% over time and conduct monetary policy appropriately to ensure that this could be achieved. “Given that financial conditions are still accommodative, it would be appropriate to continue raising the policy rate and adjust the degree of monetary easing in line with developments in the economy, prices and financial conditions,” Ueda said. The BOJ kept interest rates steady at 1.25% at its Oct 30 meeting but declared victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target and stressed its policy had entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot, reinforcing its hawkish bias. Ueda said the planned consumption tax cut on food would likely support economic growth by boosting households’ real purchasing power, though the size of the impact would depend on factors such as companies’ pricing behaviour and consumer sentiment. Once the details of the measure are finalised, the central bank will assess its impact on underlying inflation and reflect that analysis in future policy decisions, he added. Asked about the possibility of emergency bond-buying operations, Ueda said the BOJ would make a comprehensive assessment based on conditions at the time, including whether serious disruptions to market functioning had emerged and required a policy response. He also cautioned against using such operations to contain long-term yields, saying the move could prove counterproductive if markets perceive the BOJ as helping finance government spending. “In that case, long-term interest rates could become even more volatile,” he said. events.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from all US freeways
events.summary: Published 18 November 2026, 03:07 GMT Waymo has temporarily suspended its driverless vehicles from operating on all US freeways, the company has said. The decision comes after California banned Waymo's driverless taxis from state freeways following a series of recent traffic incidents. California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) cited an "imminent hazard to public safety" for the ban, noting an incident this month in which several driverless Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on US Route 101. Waymo said it was working with state officials "diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations", adding that no injuries or collisions were reported following the incident on US Route 101 south of San Francisco. California's DMV said Waymo's driverless taxis presented a risk "due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present". In another incident earlier this month, footage widely seen on social media appeared to show a Waymo car trying to overtake patrol vehicles that were deliberately slowing the pace of traffic on a San Francisco highway. The California ban, which came into effect on 11 November, would remain in place until Waymo "demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions". A Waymo spokesperson said: "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance." Data on Waymo's website suggests that its cars, compared to human drivers, are involved in 95% fewer crashes resulting in serious injury. Waymo currently operates driverless taxis in 15 US cities, but only offered freeway rides in a handful of those locations, including San Francisco, Los Angeles and Miami. The company's driverless taxis can continue to operate on regular city streets. In May, Waymo recalled thousands of its self-driving cars in the US over a software issue that could allow vehicles to drive into flooded roads. In the same month, multiple Waymo cars were spotted driving around a cul-de-sac in Atlanta, Georgia , in the early hours of the morning. Have you been affected by the issues discussed in this story? events.title: Can Labour end the youth unemployment crisis? – podcast
events.summary: There are about a million young people across the country not in employment, education or training. Could Alan Milburn’s landmark report help change that? Richard Partington reports The UK has one of the worst rates in Europe when it comes to youth unemployment. From the savage cuts to youth services during austerity, to the impacts of the pandemic and now the threat of AI to entry level jobs, young people across the country are feeling that the social contract is broken. But now Alan Milburn, the 68-year-old New Labour veteran, has published a radical review urging the government to spend billions on a new deal for young people. However, it comes at a price. Because at the same time, Milburn is proposing massive changes to the welfare system, with cuts specifically designed to hit those under 25. The answer must be radical, he says. “This cannot be fixed by tweaking the edges of the existing system. The response now has to be full throttle: not another initiative or another round of incremental reform, but transformational change.”

events.title: 'He's a double-down kind of guy': Tina Fordham on Trump, Iran and the hypotheticals of Obama in 2028
events.summary: It is a gorgeous Sunday morning in Dubai, the kind that makes the headlines from the Strait of Hormuz feel a world away. Tina Fordham is not about to let anyone relax. The woman who persuaded Citi to hire Wall Street's first chief global political analyst in 2003 has one message for leaders and investors in the region. Do not bet on this war ending with a handshake and a return to how things were. That, she says, is "what I really caution against". "We're going to go somewhere else." Ms Fordham is the founder of Fordham Global Foresight and author of the Amazon bestseller Mad World: A Geostrategy Survival Guide for Leaders . Trump 2.5 US President Donald Trump's Republican Party was heavily beaten in the midterm elections. Wall Street's overnight verdict was that "surely Trump will back down in Iran". Ms Fordham is having none of it. "That's not the way that he thinks about things. He's a double-down kind of guy," she says. "This is a president in a hurry. He's ageing. He's been dealt a blow in the midterms." Mr Trump's "domestic political capital, and certainly his international political capital, is diminishing, but he's still the most powerful man in the world", she adds. So prepare for Trump 2.5 – episodic, still ready to punish adversaries and reward allies. "He still retains a great deal of power." Parking an armada in the Gulf and waiting for Tehran to fold will not work. "The regime in Iran still thinks that it can outlast him," Ms Fordham says. "Iran is a weaker power, no question about it. Its military capacity is much diminished as a result of this conflict, but it still has the power to inflict damage and costs on the United States, on its allies, on its proxies." And “we haven’t even started to find out about that yet”, she warns. The butterfly effect she writes about is already at work, not least in Israel, where "there's a possibility that we've got a different government in Israel, not just possibly without [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu, but for the first time bringing in the Arab parties". Obama redux Legacy matters to Mr Trump. "He wants to expand the size of the United States on the map." Which brings us to succession. Borrowing from the late Donald Rumsfeld, she calls the elections and leadership transitions stacked up for 2027 and 2028 the "known knowns". On Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, she does not hedge. "I think he's likely to be impeached next year once the new Congress is in." Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance "don't have to go straight into the running for 2028. They can step out," Ms Fordham adds. "They can take four years out. They could take eight years out and wait and keep their powder dry." Then the curveball. "Likewise, if Trump could win again, so could Barack Obama." There is, of course, the small matter of the US Constitution. The 22nd Amendment bars anyone elected president twice from being elected again, ruling out Mr Obama as firmly as Mr Trump. So is this a real risk or just a tail risk? She does not blink. "It is a plausible risk. In my book, I talk about plausible hypotheticals." Her point is less about the law than the taboo. If a third-term push breaks it for one side, it breaks it for both. And Mr Obama's late arrival on the midterm campaign trail, she says, "was electric". "We make the mistake of extrapolating present circumstances out indefinitely as if there aren't all of these twists and turns," she says, before catching herself. "I can't believe I'm quoting Rumsfeld again, but he also said, 'Stuff happens.'" Who holds the cards? As Mr Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin prepare for "an unprecedented three-way meeting, if indeed it transpires", she recalls a line Washington loves. "The phrase that the White House has used many times in the last two years has been, 'Who holds the cards?'" Her answer was that "China holds a lot of cards". Beijing is following an old rule, she says: "Never interrupt your enemy while they're making a mistake. China sees the United States using firepower, depleting its ballistic missile stocks, bogged down in these conflicts." Meanwhile, China has led the clean energy transition and built oil stockpiles that caught markets off guard. "What other surprises does China have up its sleeve?" Born with PQ For the Middle East, the big story is "the withdrawal of the US security and trade guarantee. That is not entirely Trump's doing, but he put the nail in the coffin". She called it a decade ago, in a 2016 paper titled Goodbye, Pax Americana . The Gulf's flurry of deals with European capitals is not a hedge, she says. "It is a strategy." The lowest-hanging fruit, she adds, is doing more with the neighbours. "I advocate, though, that we all develop what I call our PQ, our political quotient." The Gulf has it in spades. "In this part of the world, people got it," she says. "You're born with it." Boardrooms in London and New York are another matter. When 170,000 Russian troops massed in Belarus, almost every leader she spoke to insisted Mr Putin would not invade because it would wreck the Russian economy. "It was groupthink of immense proportions," she says. "They couldn't overcome looking at the world through a commercial lens, and that's the wrong lens for thinking about geopolitics." Wall Street took its time catching on to her, too. She likens herself to the band grinding away in the bar on the corner. "You cut a hit record and they're like, 'Oh,' you know, 'Where have you been?'" Her parting advice is for every executive without a geostrategist on speed dial: "Build your PQ so that when things happen, you know, and you don't have someone like me or General [David] Petraeus in the room with you, you don't say to yourself, 'That won't happen because it'll be bad for the economy.'" IQ, EQ, and now PQ. Consider it the survival kit for a mad world.
