events.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
events.summary: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC , CNN , Equifax , Ledger and Zoom , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content. The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge. According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s. Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “ DarkSword ” and “ Coruna ,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote . “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.” “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.” Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content. One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing. “So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.” Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “ Content Security Policies ” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons. “With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.” How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload. Image: blog.report-uri.com. The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records. Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West. “Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’

events.title: Long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting found in Manhattan closet sells for $4.8M
events.summary: A painting dug out of a New York City closet this year after being stashed away since the 1980s has sold at auction for $4.8 million NEW YORK -- A long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting that had been buried in the closet of a Manhattan apartment for decades sold at auction Tuesday for $4.8 million. The 1930 landscape painting “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” is likely the first in a series of three works depicting Lobo Peak in northern New Mexico, according to Christie’s auction house. Its existence was known from a 1931 photograph, but its whereabouts had been kept secret until recently. A Manhattan woman in her 90s nonchalantly told her niece one day in 2022, “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet.” Her family believes she received the painting as a graduation gift from her mother, who had purchased it in 1963 from a New York gallery for $3,800. The woman, who died recently, displayed it in her East Village apartment for many years until the mid-’80s when she noticed a guest looking at it a little too closely. From then on she kept it in her closet, safely hidden behind coats and boxes. When the family finally unboxed it this year, they discovered it has all the hallmarks of O’Keeffe’s work, including her signature marking on the back: a star with her initials scrawled in the middle. JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The 10-x-24-inch (25.4-x-61-centimeter) oil painting is among O’Keeffe's early love letters to New Mexico, where she settled and lived for decades. The identity of the winning bidder was not disclosed; it sold for $4,878,000. Known as the “mother of American modernism,” O’Keeffe maintained a home and studio in Abiquiu and a nearby summer residence tucked between the red-rock cliffs of Ghost Ranch. She died in 1986 at age 98 and is best known for her paintings of flowers and American Southwest landscapes. The second piece in the “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico” collection is at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the other, for many years, was in the collection of the Rockefeller family. events.title: Asia stocks choppy after Nvidia earnings as Anthropic pricing looms
events.summary: Oil prices also edged down, with Brent crude futures 0.2% lower at US$93 a barrel as Asian trading began. Asia shares fell after Nvidia’s strong forecast, as investors stayed worried about AI spending returns, leadership uncertainty and supply chain risks. Nvidia shares slipped after hours, and the market now watches Anthropic’s share pricing as another test of demand for AI companies. Oil eased, the yen was flat, and Japan’s exports rose for a 14th month, while US rate and inflation worries kept risk sentiment weak. SINGAPORE – Stocks erased early gains in Asia on Nov 18 after Nvidia posted a better-than-expected sales forecast , as investor confidence remained fragile over questions about the company’s future leadership and potential impacts on its regional supply chain. In choppy trade, MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan reversed an initial rally to be down 0.1%, narrowly extending its losing streak into a fifth day. Japan’s Nikkei 225 slid 0.3% , while US S&P 500 e-mini futures clung to gains, up 0.3%. Despite Nvidia’s upbeat earnings, strategists noted that deeper concerns over the sustainability of AI capital expenditure remain. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Bank in Singapore, said: “Nvidia’s results were reassuring and gave investors a reason to refocus on earnings, but they haven’t resolved the broader questions around AI spending returns, financing sustainability and leadership uncertainty. “So we are seeing an initial relief rally, but not necessarily the conviction needed for a sustained recovery.” In oil markets, Brent crude futures were 0.6% lower at US$92.60 a barrel in Asian trade, following data showing an increase in US crude and fuel inventories last week. The ongoing Middle East conflict and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, however, limited losses. Nvidia shares slid 0.5% in after-hours trading, after rising as much as 3.8% following the chipmaker’s third-quarter revenue report and a fourth-quarter forecast that beat market expectations. The tech company’s earnings report was its first since Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure as chief executive officer in November . The Wall Street Journal reported that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is probing Nvidia, citing sources familiar with the matter. The SEC has declined to comment on the matter. “We’re at a point of peak uncertainty because investors still don’t know what Nvidia’s long-term leadership will look like,” said Brian Colello, senior equity analyst at Morningstar. Overnight, stocks on Wall Street sold off again, with the S&P 500 down 1% to log a fourth consecutive session lower prior to Nvidia’s earnings report. “Risk sentiment remained firmly on the defensive overnight, with the tech-led sell-off extending across global markets,” Westpac analysts said in a note. “I’ve looked at this whole week as a referendum on AI,” said Jake Behan, head of capital markets at Direxion in New York. “Nvidia gave us a read on the buildout, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies.” The next health check on the AI industry will come as Anthropic prepares to price its shares later on Nov 18 ahead of its market debut, which could value the company at as much as US$1.4 trillion (S$1.8 trillion). The company has guided its initial public offering price to the top of its range or above, Bloomberg News reported. The yen fluctuated between gains and losses, to trade flat against the US dollar at 159.41 yen. Data showed Japan’s exports rose for a 14th successive month in October, driven by demand for shipments related to semiconductors. The US dollar index, which measures the greenback’s strength against a basket of six currencies, was steady at 103.60 , after reaching its highest level on Nov 17 since April 2, 2025, the date of US President Donald Trump’s Liberation Day tariff announcement . The yield on the US 10-year Treasury bond was down 2.1 basis points at 5.08%. On Nov 17, Alberto Musalem, the St. Louis Fed president who is a non-voter on interest rates in 2026, said that the Federal Reserve may need several rate hikes to bring inflation under control and should act soon to ensure the problem does not get worse. In cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin was up 0.1% at US$64,347.95 , while ether was down 0.1% at US$1,804.06 . REUTERS

events.title: Some Nvidia directors continue push to bring Huang back
events.summary: Despite Nvidia’s proclamation Tuesday that it didn’t plan to bring ousted CEO Jensen Huang back to the chipmaker, a faction of board members is pushing for his return, according to people familiar with the matter. Huang has met with a number of tech executives and spoken with at least one board member about the possibility of his return, the people said. The conversation with the director took place before the company’s earnings report and before Huang issued a public statement Tuesday that he’d be willing to return to the company if the board decides it is in the “best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.” Hours later, Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the company’s earnings call that the chipmaker wasn’t considering bringing Huang back and that the board had voted unanimously to accept his resignation. Spokespeople for Huang and Nvidia declined to comment. Despite the pushback from three directors, other board members are starting to narrow the search for Huang’s replacement, some of the people familiar with the deliberations said. ARM CEO Rene Haas and Marvell CEO Matt Murphy have both been considered, the people said. Haas has spoken to at least some Nvidia directors about taking the job, one of the people said, but he’s said he’s concerned about the optics of taking it over calls to bring Huang back to the helm. Spokespeople for ARM and Marvell didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s also unclear whether Marvell’s Murphy would be able to take over as Nvidia’s CEO given the company is navigating a mega-merger with rival Lumentum.

events.title: Troubled Australian retailer David Jones to cut 1,500 jobs, union says
events.summary: The administrators McGrathNicol said David Jones owed at least A$459 million (S$398 million) to an array of creditors. David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs as 19 stores close after the retailer entered administration, with the union saying only 170 workers were offered redeployment. Administrators said David Jones owes at least A$459 million, including A$11 million to 6,242 employees, as they seek buyers and plan to close 18 stores in Australia and one in New Zealand. The chain failed after weak trading, online competition and low household spending, while landlords would not agree rent cuts; the union is trying to protect unpaid worker entitlements. SYDNEY – Troubled Australian department store chain David Jones will cut about 1,500 jobs across 19 stores slated for closure following its collapse into administration , a union said on Nov 18. The Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association said only 170 of the 1,689 impacted store workers had been offered redeployment opportunities. David Jones entered administration on Nov 5, with directors citing difficult trading conditions, online competition and weak household spending as reasons for its failure. At the first meeting of creditors on Nov 17, administrators McGrathNicol said the retailer owed at least A$459 million (S$398 million) to an array of creditors, including A$11 million to 6,242 employees. “We are very disappointed that of the 1,689 jobs of directly employed David Jones workers at risk in the 19 stores set to close, the company is offering only 170 job redeployments, barely one in 10,” said Bernie Smith, secretary of the union’s New South Wales state branch. “This is a missed opportunity both for the workers and for the business to reset the service level they could provide that David Jones was once known for.” The union was continuing to work to secure members’ unpaid entitlements, Smith added. FTI Consulting, the appointed receivers, declined to comment when asked about the job losses. It has said it plans to close 18 of David Jones’ 37 stores across Australia and one in New Zealand by the end of the year. A sale process is also under way, with administrators saying on Nov 17 they had contacted 150 potential buyers, local and international. Founded in Sydney in 1838 by Welsh immigrant David Jones, the retailer describes itself as the world’s oldest continuously operating department store. Australian private equity firm Anchorage Capital Partners acquired the chain in 2023 with plans to turn the business around, yet losses continued as rent and employee costs rose. It entered administration after landlords did not agree to rent concessions and a plan to restructure the store network. REUTERS

events.title: One Nation surges, Labor overtakes Liberals in latest Tasmanian poll results
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmanian EMRS poll shows Labor, Liberals, One Nation in three-way battle, with health, cost of living biggest issues Despite a decline in the Liberals' fortunes, Jeremy Rockliff still came out on top as preferred premier. ( ABC News ) Labor, Liberals and One Nation are separated by just two points in the latest poll by EMRS. The Liberal vote is the lowest since 2001, while One Nation has climbed every quarter this year. A pollster says focusing on the cost of living and healthcare could help a party edge ahead. Labor, the Liberals and One Nation are locked in a three-way battle to be Tasmania's preferred party, with a pollster describing the situation as a "red hot mess". The latest polling by EMRS shows Labor has edged slightly ahead of the pack after being chosen by 25 per cent of responders, just ahead of the Liberals at 24 per cent and One Nation at 23 per cent. The polling firm's managing director, Brad Stansfield, said the results were all within the survey's margin of error of about 3 per cent, which suggested "any one of them could be in front next quarter". EMRS voting intentions, November 2026. ( Supplied: EMRS ) EMRS preferred premier, November 2026. ( Supplied: EMRS ) Cost of living and health dominated the results for major issues, which Mr Stansfield said could be driving the growth in support for both One Nation and Labor. While his party faltered, the state's premier, Jeremy Rockliff, saw his net favourability grow and he is still the preferred premier for 41 per cent of responders. However, support for Labor leader Josh Willie did rise to 33 per cent, which is his best result since taking the reins in August last year. It was Josh Willie's best result since taking over as leader. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) The poll results are produced through a survey of 1,000 people across Tasmania, with undecided voters excluded from results. Orange tap water called 'safe to drink' had metals above guidelines Survivalist says wearing cotton can kill in Tasmanian outdoors Hundreds waiting for their own records from Tasmania's education department England wins ODI series as Australia falters in chase after Duckett ton Liberals slide as One Nation surges Support for the Liberal government dropped two percentage points since August, with the November figure marking the party's lowest result in an EMRS poll since May 2001. Bridget Archer, the state's health minister, was asked about the findings at a press conference on Wednesday morning and said she would "leave the commentary to others". It's the first time Labor has been ahead of the Liberals since May last year, shortly before it called a no-confidence motion against the premier, resulting in a snap state election. Mr Stansfield said while the tight results showed Tasmanian politics was "a red hot mess right now", the Labor party would still be encouraged by the result, as it was "better to be ahead than behind". Cost of living was the most important issue for those polled. ( ABC News: Courtney Withers ) The popularity of One Nation has grown in every quarter since the party was first included in EMRS state polling in February this year, rising from 14 per cent to 23 per cent in nine months. Mr Stansfield, a former Liberal party adviser, said recent history, including the South Australian election and the Farrer by-election, showed poll numbers for One Nation had "tended to translate into votes". One Nation Tasmania marked the result with a post on social media, where it said it was "breathing down the necks" of the major state parties. Support for the Greens dropped slightly to 14 per cent, while independents were backed by 13 per cent of responders. Health came in at a close second. ( Pixabay : Engin_Akyurt ) Health, cost of living dominate issues vote When asked what the most important issue influencing their vote would be in a state election, 24 per cent of responders said the cost of living and 22 per cent said healthcare. There was a significant drop-off to the next most popular issue, which was government spending and the budget at 10 per cent. Some of the major topics which have dominated headlines in recent years were mentioned much less by responders, with just 6 per cent naming the Macquarie Point Stadium and 3 per cent saying data centres. The Macquarie Point stadium was not front of mind for respondents. ( ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough ) Mr Stansfield said these results were "starker than normal" and showed issues dominating discussions in parliament may be "not of top line concern for voters".

events.title: Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt
events.summary: Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday , up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies. The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year ; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year. But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor. Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.” Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications. It’s also become a big financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio. The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.” But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm. Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies. “We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital. events.title: Why the internet suddenly broke all at once
events.summary: Americans were locked out of bank accounts, blocked from boarding flights and unable to check emails in rapid succession over the past week. Why it matters: The internet immediately pointed fingers toward an AI agent doomsday, sending people into a frenzy that the Big One™was about to happen. Reality check: Experts tell Axios these disruptions don't appear linked to hacking. To the extent they involve AI, the incidents may have just as much to do with widespread efforts to fix outdated code as they do with slop software. Downdetector data also show that while the seven days through Monday represent the highest number of weekly outages in the last 12 months, the pattern over longer periods such as 30 days is far from unprecedented. Driving the news: Some Americans struggled to access JPMorgan Chase banking services Monday. United Airlines briefly delayed departing flights later that day, days after the FAA executed the longest nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Microsoft Outlook's outage left users unable to access emails and other Microsoft 365 services. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested Monday that AI systems capable of writing and changing code could be contributing to the outages. Yes, but: No evidence so far points to AI-assisted hacking. In most cases, the outages have been attributed to software patching and appear otherwise unrelated, even as small technical problems snowballed into big ones. Chase blamed an internal software bug that delayed transactions involving other banks. United cited a technology problem; the FAA said a flood of network traffic destabilized older, legacy equipment. Microsoft cited a months-old bug, increased traffic and reduced server capacity. Between the lines: There are ways AI may have played a role that have nothing to do with hacking. Institutions around the world are racing to update software in order to solidify systems, given that AI models are capable of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities with shocking speed. That race has accelerated a lot of coding work, a process that can lead to more downtime, outages and unexpected hiccups, experts say. AI has also dramatically accelerated the rate at which engineers write and improve software, leading to new bottlenecks for reviewing the safety and reliability of new code. To the extent reviewers or the systems they work with are overwhelmed, mistakes are possible. What they're saying : Increasingly complex systems are being pushed to operate faster and cheaper without enough attention to how they might fail, David Woods, a professor emeritus of integrated systems engineering at Ohio State University, told Axios. "We're cutting out the cross checks, we're cutting out the tests, we're cutting out the stress tests, we're cutting out the safeguards," Woods says. "Humans see patterns in everything, regardless of whether they're there, and generally interpret coincidences as conspiracies," said Bruce Schneier, a security technologist. "It's human psychology." "There's very little that these incidents have in common, actually," Liz Fong-Jones a technical fellow at Honeycomb tells Axios. "No one notices when things go right." By the numbers: Downdetector received nearly 6 million U.S. problem reports in the seven days ending Nov. 16, the highest weekly total in a year, Ookla analyst Luke Kehoe tells Axios. However, the past 30 days saw just three major outages, compared with a typical five. The intrigue: Some experts doubt that AI is to blame. "The outages that we've seen are a decades-old phenomenon ... cascading failures," Fong-Jones says. "Nothing to do with writing code, nothing to do with shipping code with AI." Zoom in: Fong-Jones compares cascading failures to a busy intersection where a traffic light stops working. Cars back up, drivers turn to surrounding streets, and soon the entire area is gridlocked. That's essentially what happened at Microsoft, where a software bug combined with increased traffic and reduced capacity, overwhelming servers as they tried to recover. The bottom line: New technology can make systems faster and more efficient, but it can't eliminate the unexpected. When companies rush to embrace it without preparing for what could go wrong, "the world bites back and bites your ass," Woods warns. Go deeper: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool

events.title: Europe’s AI sector not ‘doom and gloom,’ but still lags
events.summary: Europe’s tech scene is still fighting the same battles that have held it back in the global AI race, leaders and CEOs from the continent said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said the US, and to an extent China, are “radically in a different league” when it comes to scale and capital. Employing a soccer (or football) metaphor, he said those are the only two countries that are in AI’s Premier League, while the UK sits atop the Championship, the tier below. He’s “not happy enough” with that. Marco-Alexander Breit, director-general at Germany’s digital ministry, argued that Europe still needs more “innovation-friendly regulation” if it wants to compete. He said he agreed with most of the EU’s AI Act, but argued it “actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world.” Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak echoed some of the criticism, saying that “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, the continent is starting to figure out its niche: Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch pointed to a rising need for cheaper, open-source, and sovereign AI — models that companies can run on their own premises, without relying on US models or exposing their data. Germany is leaning on its industrial base, with Breit pointing to the troves of data that manufacturers like Siemens and Bosch sit on. Narayan said the UK is looking to make inroads in inference chips and AI for drug discovery. “It’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” Breit said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn. In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this." Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China. But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him." Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading. The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn. The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter. How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? Published 13 hours ago Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance. Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader. "The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment." Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation? Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry. "It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us." She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects". "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this." The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China. The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington. They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US. Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped. The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal Published 6 days ago Jensen Huang says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia CEO if board asked him Published 1 day ago Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement. He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection. "With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person." Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia. The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media. Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said. ( Coal River Farm ) Tasmanian cheese and chocolate brand Coal River Farm has entered voluntary administration. Apex Advisory's Adam Johnston has been appointed to handle the administration and sale process. The administrator says the business will continue to trade while its financial position and "path forward" is determined. A Tasmanian cheese and chocolate producer has entered voluntary administration, following what its director has described as prolonged "difficult trading conditions". Coal River Farm was established in southern Tasmania in 2015 by Daniel and Melanie Leesong. On Wednesday, Apex Advisory's Adam Johnston was announced as administrator of the business. It follows what Mr Leesong, the business's director, said had been "sustained efforts to find a solution" following difficult conditions in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. "We have undertaken an extensive process with the shareholder group, working through the available options to secure a lifeline for the business," Mr Leesong said. events.title: Recent AI cyberattacks are part of a ‘short period of transition,’ says Yann LeCun
events.summary: The world is “probably” going to enter an era of “unprecedented safety of software systems,” Advanced Machine Intelligence founder and chair Yann LeCun said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I’m worried about very few things when it comes to AI,” LeCun told Semafor’s Shelly Banjo. LeCun predicted a short period “where AI tools facilitate cyberattacks and favor the attacker over the defender,” but that will be “just a short period of transition.” Future software, he suggested, will be “hardened” by AI. LeCun, a winner of the 2018 Turing Award, has long been skeptical that scaling large language models will usher in superintelligence or artificial general intelligence. He left Meta to found his world-model company AMI in 2025; it raised more than $1 billion in seed funding, the largest ever for a European company. He told Banjo that “I think it’s called a coconut when it’s that big.” He spoke on Tuesday about world models’ practical application in physical AI, but acknowledged there is a long way to go in their development. “We’re going to need a few conceptual breakthroughs in AI to make domestic robots that are useful,” he said. “We can use humanoid robots for very narrow tasks in well-controlled environments at the moment,” but domestic robots are “not for tomorrow.” He said he and his peers working on world models are gravitating toward physical AI because it’s a “complete blind spot” of LLMs. When asked about open source models, he remarked that “it made a lot of people really sad in the US, including people who are in the current government, that the most powerful open-source systems are Chinese.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: House Dems can't stand the speaker vote drama anymore
events.summary: House Democrats aren't unanimous on whether House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) should be speaker, but they pretty much all agree on two things: He probably will be speaker, and they just want this to be over. Why it matters: Their phones and emails are still being blown up by constituents and grassroots activists urging them to do what they can to block Jeffries from securing the speaker gavel. There isn't much Jeffries' skeptics and detractors on Capitol Hill can do: He is set to easily win his caucus' nomination on Wednesday and then be formally elected to the role on Jan. 3. Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), who told Axios last week he was undecided, said Tuesday he met with Jeffries and was "assured" votes on his two key issues: Ending the Trump administration's tariffs and the war in Iran. "I'll be voting for Leader Jeffries," Johnson told Axios. State of play: The movement to deny Jeffries the speakership has proliferated online and among the progressive grassroots but has struggled to gain a foothold on Capitol Hill. A handful of members of the progressive "Bloc" — and some other newly elected members in deeply red district — have voiced skepticism of Jeffries, but only in a few cases has that evolved into outright opposition. "As of now, I'm a 'no,'" Rep.-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres (D-Calif.) told Axios on Wednesday. "The people are saying we deserve better, and better is possible." Reality check: Nobody is challenging Jeffries. Some people floated as potential potential challengers, such as Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), have firmly ruled it out . Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.), the subject of an online petition urging her to seek the role, has privately told colleagues she is not running but been more equivocal in public. "I'm very humbled to even be in conversation," Pressley said at a town hall on Monday. She added that she was "making no declarations or announcements" at that event and does not "need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people." What we're hearing: Some of Pressley's fellow Congressional Progressive Caucus members, granted anonymity to speak candidly, expressed frustration that she hasn't more forcefully tamped down the speculation. "She's only playing coy with people online," one CPC member told Axios. "The rest of us know she's not running. But that's generating additional calls and making people … even more pissed off in the end." Said another CPC member: "Many of us feel like she's stringing people along online to make them think that she's running and it's just not reality. " A third CPC member complained that it's "a bit selfish," with an incoming CPC member saying "it's not real" and chalking it up to Congress being an "attention economy." Yes, but: A second incoming CPC member said the grassroots would be "blowing us up regardless" of whether Pressley shut down the speculation or not. "It's true that the percentage of emails that mention her has grown, but the number was large to begin with," the member-elect added. What they're saying: "Everyone's trying to use whatever leverage they have and I think she's probably hoping that maybe this could be a way to make sure her voice is heard," said Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.). Gonzales-Torres said she is "fully behind" the policy agenda Pressley has laid out but, asked if she would vote for her for speaker, said, "Where does she stand? What is she doing? Do you know?" Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio), one of Jeffries' most outspoken critics in the freshman class, said in a Breaking Points interview that Pressley "would have my support." Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.) said Pressley "would be a great speaker but she's not running, so it's a hypothetical." What's next: House Democrats will meet behind closed-doors Wednesday to vote on their nominee for speaker and other caucus leadership roles. Jeffries plans to request a tallied vote, rather than being nominated by acclamation. He needs a simple majority among Democrats to secure the nomination but at least 218 votes on the House floor to formally win the gavel on Jan. 3. Democrats are expected to have a majority of at least 260 seats, giving Jeffries a wide margin for error. The bottom line: "The whole thing has been a stupid clusterfuck," the senior CPC member told Axios. "This is such a distraction from reality."

events.title: Nvidia promises that revenue will keep soaring — for now
events.summary: Despite the turmoil at Nvidia following the departure of its disgraced founder and CEO Jensen Huang , the company — as expected — delivered a solid quarter on Tuesday. More importantly, Nvidia reassured investors that its streak of record-breaking revenue won’t stop. On Tuesday, CFO-turned-interim CEO Colette Kress reported revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from the year-ago quarter and a beat above the company’s guidance. Nvidia had told Wall Street to expect $108 billion in revenue for its third quarter of fiscal 2027. Kress also projected an even bigger fourth quarter, with revenue expected to reach $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. She also said full-year revenue is on track to exceed expectations. “We are raising our fiscal year 2028 outlook. We expect revenue to grow approximately 75% year over year, up from 70% and off what is now a higher fiscal 2027 base,” Kress said on the quarterly conference call on Tuesday. “Our outlook considers data center readiness, the strength and durability of end customer demand, and our customers’ access to capital.” The company also reminded investors that it was using some of its billions in cash to buy back shares. In September 2026, Nvidia increased its share buyback program by $150 billion. It spent $28.1 billion on its own shares during the quarter and still had another $227.3 billion remaining in the kitty for additional repurchases. Ironically, Nvidia could also benefit from the plunge in its share price following Huang’s resignation last week, should shares remain depressed over the longer term. The stock is down about 10% since his departure. Investors, however, celebrated Tuesday’s quarterly results, sending shares up about 4% in after-hours trading. Kress stressed that the company was in good shape now and for the foreseeable future, even without Huang at the helm. “We have the best technologists on the planet with a world-class multi-year roadmap,” Kress stressed. “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual. We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners. They’re all 100% behind us.” She added that the company has secured memory and advanced packaging capacity and is working with its chip manufacturer, TSMC, to “narrow the supply and demand gaps.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Citi settles sexual harassment claims by managing director
events.summary: Ardith Lindsey alleged that a senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her family with violence after she ended it. Citigroup settled a lawsuit by managing director Ardith Lindsey, who said the bank allowed years of sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination in its equities division. Lindsey, a Citi employee since 2007, alleged an abusive relationship, threats to her family, and a sexual assault by a superior. She described a “boy’s club” culture. The deal was finalised after months of talks and a June “settlement in principle”. No terms were made public, and Citi said no one should be “discriminated against or harassed in the workplace”. Citigroup has settled a high-profile lawsuit by a managing director who claimed the bank had for years tolerated sexual harassment, assault and gender-based discrimination against her. Ardith Lindsey sued Citi three years ago, claiming she had been the subject of “prolonged, pervasive and outrageous mistreatment” during her 16 years in the bank’s global equities markets division. Lindsey had spent her entire Wall Street career at Citi, starting as the most junior member on the electronic sales trading desk, before later taking charge of the desk in 2021, when she was promoted to managing director. A lawyer for Lindsey, Jeremiah Iadevaia, told the court in a letter on the night of Nov 13 that they had finalised a deal to resolve the case, after months of negotiations. No terms of the agreement were made public. The two sides announced in June that they had reached a “settlement in principle” after engaging in mediation. Neither Citigroup nor Iadevaia immediately responded to phone messages seeking comment. “Our values and expectations are clear – no one should ever be discriminated against or harassed in the workplace,” Citigroup said in an earlier statement. Lindsey, a University of Virginia graduate, joined Citigroup in October 2007. She alleged that another, more senior Citigroup executive had coerced her into an abusive relationship and threatened her and her family with violence after she ended it in October 2022. Lindsey’s suit also alleged a sexual assault by a superior when she first started at the bank and claimed there was a “boys’ club” culture at Citigroup’s equities group, including suggestive comments, traders mocking the firm’s sexual harassment policies and frequent outings to strip clubs. events.title: Stripe backer Atomico calls for Europe to own its success stories
events.summary: Europe is home to many of the world’s fastest growing companies of all time, veteran VC firm Atomico highlighted in its latest annual State of European Tech report . The report, for instance, notes that the likes of Black Forest Labs and Microagi have reached $100 million in revenue in months, not years. “I think we can put to bed the idea that there’s a fundamental reason or constraint on the ability to scale a breakout company from here in Europe,” Atomico partner and head of intelligence Tom Wehmeier (pictured) told TechCrunch. Yet, there’s still more that the VC firm founded by Skype’s Niklas Zennström would like to see — and its call this year is for Europe to “build it” and “scale it,” but also “own it.” That’s a way of wishing these companies will remain European longer. But there’s also a sense that this success hasn’t been acknowledged enough, perhaps obscured by louder calls for improvements. Wehmeier, the report’s lead author, was quick to opine that “policy, procurement and capital are not moving at the same speed as our founders.” But he said the tech sector should advocate for itself in an inspiring way. “When it comes to policy, I think the language needs to be, ‘Hey, this is not us complaining. This is us saying here is an opportunity to make the magnitude of impact even greater,’” Wehmeier said. “When we frame it as problems, that becomes harder.” This reframing may also help European tech improve its image abroad, where complaints around overregulation may have overshadowed Europe’s potential to leverage its deep tech talent and growing pool of repeat entrepreneurs to have even more of success stories. Plenty could be still done to fully unlock this potential, and Wehmeier said that “the next few weeks are going to be a really important test, with EU Inc .” Also known as the 28th regime, this initiative would create a unified European corporate regime akin to the Delaware C Corp. If the last stretch of EU Inc’s grassroots campaign achieves it goal, it will become much easier to create and operate businesses across the EU. It would also show that the tech system got itself heard, which could open the door to the kind of endorsement Atomico is hoping to see more of. Politicians have strong incentives to give the tech sector what it wants. If it is Europe’s second largest sector, biggest contributor to growth, and biggest job creator, “Do we not want more of that?” Wehmeier asked rhetorically. But it is unclear whether it will win them any votes. To make the answer more straightforward, the tech sector will have to work on having public opinion on its side. For Wehmeier, one key is to “demonstrate that this is translating into value for citizens.” The report is supporting this endeavor with a mix of high-level data and examples from its portfolio; for instance, it notes that ICEYE ’s satellites monitor severe weather, flooding, and other hazards; and Daniel Ek’s Neko Health has now done more than 100,000 body scans, some of which helped identify severe or life-threatening health conditions. One limit to this argument is that Neko Health’s scans will seem pricey to most Europeans, who largely rely on collective, public health insurance. But Atomico seems to hope that its report will give readers FOMO not just as potential customers, but also as potential shareholders. There’s more to be done for this to happen. Beyond joining the sector’s push for an EU capital markets union, he hopes more of Europe’s institutional investors will invest in the region’s own tech companies. “We must get to the place where Europe and European beneficiaries are the biggest shareholders in the success that we create,” Wehmeier said. Before that can happen, the industry must overcome anti-industry beliefs like fears of AI-induced job destruction. But Wehmeier is a believer in the power of proof. “I think that trust is going to be earned through showing results to the public — be that lower energy bills, better healthcare, more homes built for cheaper and faster, and having infrastructure that we can rely on.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Europe plans to catch the next computer chip wave
events.summary: Photonic chips use light instead of electrons to process data Published 18 November 2026, 00:00 GMT "Photonic chips are on the verge of a breakthrough," says Ton van Mol of the Dutch research institute TNO. If van Mol is right – and TNO, the European Union and the Dutch government are backing the idea with millions of euros - then the technology could be a gamechanger. The chips which run today's society, from your phone and TV, to the vast data centres meeting our insatiable desire for AI, are mostly electrical. They process data by shunting electrons around tiny circuits – a single microchip produced today can contain billions of transistors, and sizes are measured in nanometres (one nanometre is a billionth of a metre). Because they use light instead of electricity, photonic chips are faster, use less energy and generate less heat than traditional computer chips. Van Mol hopes for an acceleration in photonics similar to the one seen in electrical chips since the 1970s. "With optical chips, you are now where electronic chips were maybe 40 [or] 50 years ago." American, Taiwanese and Chinese firms dominate the computer chip industry, but Europe sees the emergence of photonic chips as a fresh opportunity to lead, on what could be, a key future technology. Which is why the European Union has committed €400m ($450m; £330m) to a project called PIX Europe , external , with the stated goal of making the continent "a global leader in emerging technology for Photonic Integrated Chips". "Europe said 'we need to have our own manufacturing in-house'," says van Mol, who is leading a key part of the programme. "We cannot depend like in the past that everything is manufactured in the US or China - that's not wise, so the [European] Chips Act was called into life, and one of the parts of the act is to build pilot lines to really bring the technology, which is now in labs, to the next stage - manufacturing." Electronic and photonic chips are produced on wafers made up of hundreds of individual chips. Factories with machines that can handle bigger wafers can churn out chips more efficiently. "[Photonic chip] manufacturing worldwide is [currently] done on wafers which are four inches (10cm) in size, and the next step is to scale-up production to a six-inch wafer," says van Mol. His team are already building a 10,000 sq m factory to produce six-inch indium phosphide wafers on the High Tech Campus in the Dutch city of Eindhoven. It's due to fully open in 2030 and will be a major step forward, not just for photonics in Europe, but around the world, according to van Mol. "That's the development TNO is going to do, in a pilot line which is really serious. "In 2030, we hope that we have a stable, reproducible, high-yield process, and then the intention is that the pilot line [opens] to industrial parties who can make commercial production out of it." Netherland's based ASML is a crucial supplier of chip-making equipment Europe does have one crucial player in the current computer chip industry - ASML. The Netherlands-based tech giant is the only company in the world able to build the machines needed to make the most sophisticated semiconductors. Which is why ASML products will sit at the heart of the pilot line in Eindhoven - it's no coincidence that van Mol's project is based around the corner from ASML's headquarters. "The way you produce these [photonic] chips is very similar to the way you produce electrical or electronic chip," says van Mol. "You use the same type of equipment, you also need a high-end clean room, you also use wafers, so the production method is very similar to the traditional semiconductor technology." ASML itself is keen to explore the opportunities that the emerging technology of photonics could offer. "Europe has a strong position in photonics research. The next challenge is translating those innovations into industrial-scale manufacturing," says Stanislas Baron, who is the head of ASML's EU/US Customer Team. Peter Wennik says TNO's pilot production line is a "launchpad" for European tech ASML's unique success has helped build an influential and lucrative network of companies and institutions devoted to semiconductor technology in and around Eindhoven, and it's a model for what Europe is trying to achieve with photonic chips. The Eindhoven project has the backing of former ASML chief executive Peter Wennink, author of an influential report for the Dutch government called The Roadmap to Future Prosperity , external , which noted that the market for photonics was expected to grow 10 to 20 times in the next 10 years. In a news release backing the new pilot line, Wennink described it as "a launchpad for Europe's future digital economy". "By investing in scalable production capacity, we are creating an ecosystem that can help shape the global technological direction," he said. Of course, Europe is not alone in looking to the potential of photonics to earn a global economic advantage.

The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision met in Basel on 18 November 2026 to discuss a range of analytical, supervisory and regulatory initiatives. “ This week’s meeting of the Basel Committee provided the opportunity for the Committee to discuss its work programme and strategic priorities for 2027–28 and related modernisation initiatives, which will be submitted to the Group of Governors and Heads of Supervision for endorsement in early 2027. The Committee also continued its discussions on ensuring that its governance and delivery mechanisms continue to be results-oriented, relevant and responsive to developments in the global banking system. ” Erik Thedéen, Chair of the Basel Committee and Governor of Sveriges Riksbank The Committee exchanged views on operational resilience, with information security and third-party dependency continuing to be leading supervisory priorities. The expanding use of digital channels, cloud services and AI can improve efficiency and innovation, but can also increase exposure to cyber attacks, operational incidents, digital fraud, technology failures and correlated dependencies. Supervisors are responding through increased focus on incident response, contingency planning and the resilience of critical services. The Committee exchanged views on current financial risks and vulnerabilities facing the global banking system. Members noted that macroeconomic and geopolitical risks remain elevated, including due to energy and commodity prices, trade developments and the prospect of interest rates remaining higher for longer. Particular attention was given to interest rate risk in the banking book, unrealised losses, refinancing risks in commercial real estate and growing links between banks and non-bank financial institutions, including private credit and financing related to data centres and artificial intelligence (AI). Banks’ capital and liquidity positions remain broadly strong, and asset quality has not deteriorated materially overall. The Committee is continuing its review of targeted elements of its prudential standard for banks’ exposures to cryptoassets. Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision The Committee has also completed its assessment of targeted updates to its 2008 Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision . It agreed to consult on targeted revisions to the Principles. The consultation will be published next month. The Committee agreed to consult on technical amendments to the counterparty credit risk and Liquidity Coverage Ratio standards. The consultation will be published later this month. The Committee also discussed its Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP), which is a key aspect of ensuring full and consistent implementation of Basel III. The RCAP includes peer-reviewed assessments by the Committee of the extent to which domestic regulations in each member jurisdiction are aligned with the globally agreed standards. To date, the Committee has completed jurisdictional assessments of all aspects of the initial Basel III standards, the liquidity standards and the large exposures framework . The Committee is now commencing the jurisdictional assessments for the outstanding Basel III standards. The first assessment will cover the implementation of the revised credit risk and operational risk standards in Hong Kong SAR and will be published in the coming months. Separately, the Committee agreed that supervisors may allow banks to apply a 0% risk weight on claims to the Inter-American Investment Corporation (IDB Invest), in line with the criteria set out in paragraph CRE20.14 of the Basel Framework. The Committee also discussed the result of a stocktake of the application of proportionality in Pillar 2 across members jurisdictions. This review included how jurisdictions apply proportionality in the internal capital adequacy assessment process, the Supervisory Review Process and Pillar 2 capital add-ons. The Basel Committee is the primary global standard setter for the prudential regulation of banks and provides a forum for cooperation on banking supervisory matters. Its mandate is to strengthen the regulation, supervision and practices of banks worldwide with the purpose of enhancing financial stability. The Committee reports to the Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision and seeks its endorsement for major decisions. The Committee has no formal supranational authority, and its decisions have no legal force. Rather, the Committee relies on its members’ commitments to achieve its mandate. The Group of Central Bank Governors and Heads of Supervision is chaired by Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. The Basel Committee is chaired by Erik Thedéen, Governor of Sveriges Riksbank.

events.title: Scoop: White House drops Heidi Overton's FDA nomination
events.summary: The White House is dropping Heidi Overton 's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda. "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday. Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August. She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda. Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone. The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying." What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said. The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation. What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday. The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

events.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
events.summary: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order g rounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure , riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue . “As someone who started out as a hacker , I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfortable reality I think we're grappling with is that attackers don't always have to break our systems. Sometimes, our systems are already capable of breaking on their own.” For people who couldn’t withdraw money from their bank, board a flight, or use email at work on Friday, “the disruption was real regardless of the cause,” she said. “Cybersecurity has spent decades investing in detecting threats, identifying vulnerabilities, and generating reports,” according to Kollender. “Yet we still allow for these preventable weaknesses and configurations that can bring entire systems down.” Cynthia Kaiser, senior VP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, told The Reg that the recent disruptions show “how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software update can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems.” AI has entered the chat Then we go and add AI to this already delicate balance, and everything essentially blows up. AI-assisted bug hunting and exploit development has surfaced more than 100,000 CVEs so far this year, with Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday disclosing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities in each of the past two months. AI has also shrunk the elapsed time between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits . “We are in an era where AI is accelerating the discovery of legacy software flaws, forcing organizations to race to patch vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them, which inevitably creates friction and disruptions,” Kaiser said. “Even when an outage isn’t caused by a cyberattack, these moments of operational distraction leave dangerous gaps open for threat actors and opportunists to take advantage of, making it crucial for both institutions and everyday individuals to remain on high alert against social engineering and unsolicited outreach.” Even when attackers aren’t using AI to facilitate intrusions, the technology itself has become a source of risk to organizations. “Autonomous agents can execute actions, change configurations, access sensitive information, and interact with critical systems at machine speed,” Kollender said. “When those systems lack proper governance and safeguards, a mistake can develop just as quickly as an attack. Former US Department of Defense network exploitation and vulnerability analyst Mike Wiacek, when asked if these regular system outages are the new normal, told us: “The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in.” After the DoD, Wiacek founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. He's since founded Stairwell, a threat-intel firm he serves as chief technology officer. “The idea that we are going to patch ourselves to security is, dare I say, an antiquated concept,” he told The Register . One of Stairwell’s engineers was doing regular, daily software development tasks on an open source library with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, and the model told the engineer about a buffer-overflow vulnerability in the code. “We weren't even looking for it,” Wiacek said. “It found a vulnerability in open source software by accident. You used to need specialized bug hunters and really, really technical security folks to discover and develop vulnerabilities and exploits. Now, it’s almost too easy to do it.” This new reality, he said, necessitates a total rethink of how we build and maintain digital infrastructure. “How do we get to a world where we assume compromised by default, and continuously recompromised, and then develop the architectures and the systems necessary to make what was the expense of incident-response investigation really fast and cheap? Because we will not be able to patch our way out of it.” It requires vulnerability managers and system administrators to patch as soon as software updates become available. events.title: AI companies lost voters on narrative and execution, Alphabet's Porat says
events.summary: Alphabet’s longtime investment chief acknowledged that Google — and AI companies generally — have come up short convincing US voters that the trillions of dollars being plowed into data centers across the country are worth the cost. A bipartisan backlash against data center building galvanized voters, who almost uniformly moved to block expansion across the country in local measures earlier this month, and elected lawmakers in the midterms who largely backed a slowdown in the AI buildout. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta have been at the center of that expansion — either directly financing massive projects or signing up as the anchor tenants there. “I’ve been traveling the country quite a bit and the pain you saw reflected in polls, I’m hearing firsthand around affordability,” Ruth Porat told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. Like many executives at the heart of the buildout, Porat argued that most Americans are willing and excited by the job opportunities that the AI frenzy presents. “What’s most potent is when I have these conversations across the country,” she told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, “what I hear time and time again is, ‘This is creating opportunity that I hadn’t seen in my town.’” Porat also defended the dilutive — and expensive — capital that Alphabet and other big companies have been using to finance their ambitions. “It’s expensive, but the reason we’re investing is we see the extraordinary opportunity,” Porat said. “None of us have lived at a time like this.” Google is expected to spend up to $205 billion in capex this year, and has forecast even higher numbers for 2027. The company’s free cash flow has turned negative in recent quarters, worrying investors who believe that the company — and Big Tech generally — may be getting ahead of its skis. “We want to make sure we’re showing up with a full-stack approach that delivers value and a balance sheet that’s a fortress balance sheet so that we can continue to deliver in a high-quality way,” Porat said. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Nvidia is abandoning China after Jensen Huang’s ouster
events.summary: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China, acting CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday, ending the company’s participation in a controversial loophole in the U.S. ban on the sale of advanced chips to the country. China’s access to leading AI accelerators was an important topic during the company’s first earnings call since CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down last week. The disclosure comes the same day Nvidia announced it was creating a board-level committee to oversee national security policies , export control compliance, and global trade risks. Nvidia’s deal to sell H200 chips in China was brokered by Huang and President Donald Trump. The arrangement required the chips to be shipped through the U.S., allowing the government to collect a 25% tariff. The pathway angered China hawks who wanted to deny Chinese labs computing power and maintain the United States’ lead in AI, but Huang long argued that it was more important for the U.S. to compete in China. In April, he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that “to concede that market for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country.” Huang’s ouster — in part over an affair with the CEO of a company under investigation for smuggling chips into China — has coincided with new rules, issued Monday, barring advanced U.S. chips from foreign data centers that serve Chinese customers remotely. Investment bank Jefferies forecast that those rules might trim between $44 billion and $62 billion from Nvidia’s data center revenue next year. Referencing the new export controls, Kress said that the backlog of demand for advanced chips like Vera Rubin means the rules would have no impact on the company’s top-line revenue. In the long term, the company may face the loss of potential customers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia. Critics of Nvidia’s dependence on China claim that as much as 20% of its revenue comes from demand linked to the country — annual revenue at its Singapore subsidiary hit $104 billion in 2025 before Nvidia stopped disclosing those figures — but that’s clearly going to change. Even before Nvidia decided to stop shipping H200s, China had largely refused to accept their delivery. The government would prefer to generate demand for the country’s domestic chip industry, even if major AI compute users want the still-superior Nvidia equipment, according to Jacob Feldgoise, a researcher at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Meanwhile, Chinese frontier labs are finding ways to access Nvidia chips elsewhere. All of China’s leading AI models show evidence of having been trained on Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips that are prohibited from being exported to China. That training may have taken place at data centers outside of China, but sales to those facilities will be barred under the new rules. If large data centers suited for training AI models want to buy Nvidia chips, they will have to certify they aren’t serving any Chinese customers, export control attorney Dan Fisher-Owens told TechCrunch. If they can’t provide that certification, the new rules may force them toward other chip options and further eat into Nvidia’s market share. events.title: Lutnick must answer questions from Congress on Nvidia, Sen. Kelly says
events.summary: Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., demanded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before Congress as questions mount over his role in delaying restrictions on AI chip exports to China. “He needs to come to Congress,” Kelly, who serves on the Senate Intelligence Committee, told Ashley Gold at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “I would like to hear answers to a lot of questions that we have about why he made the decisions he made.” Kelly also alluded to Lutnick’s family business interests in the AI industry, saying they raised additional questions that the commerce secretary needs to address. The Arizona senator added that he believed Lutnick should have been removed from his position at earlier points during President Donald Trump’s second term, saying there had been “multiple times” when his “expiration date in this job had already expired.” Kelly also said he wants answers from Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang, who stepped down last week amid revelations about his reported extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. “We haven’t received answers to the questions that I have and my colleagues have,” Kelly said, noting that Huang had volunteered to testify before Congress. “What we need is answers.” Kelly also expressed skepticism about the Justice Department’s ability to conduct an impartial investigation into the matter, citing his own experience with the department. The senator said the department had been “weaponized” against individuals — including himself, noting that Trump called for his prosecution over remarks he made reminding military personnel they must refuse unlawful orders. “I might be a little biased here, but I do not have a lot of faith in the folks that are currently running the Justice Department,” Kelly said. Kelly also voiced support for three bipartisan provisions in the Senate’s version of must-pass defense policy legislation that would strengthen restrictions on exports to countries of concern, including China, saying the US must be careful about transferring its most advanced technologies. He specifically called for more “guardrails” on AI technologies and argued that companies and individuals should face penalties when those standards are violated. Liability, he said, “depends on the outcome,” but in cases involving particularly egregious conduct, “individuals could be held accountable.” — Lauren Morganbesser
