events.title: Exclusive: Donald Trump Jr. signals investors underestimated AI pushback
events.summary: Donald Trump Jr. signaled that investors underestimated the political pushback to the AI ecosystem in an interview at Axios' annual BFD summit in New York. The big picture: The 2026 midterms reflected deep distrust of the AI race, with voters approving dozens of moratoriums on data centers — which President Trump rallied around. Driving the news: Trump Jr. asserted that "a lot of" the pushback "is manufactured." But he added "that doesn't mean it's not real" in an interview with Axios Pro Rata author Dan Primack Tuesday. "I think some of the big founders of the biggest [AI] companies out there probably have not done themselves the best service as [a] marketing department," he said, adding that they're "probably not the best messengers when they basically say, 'AI is gonna rule the world, and you should be thrilled about it.'" Asked by Primack if investors, peers or the pair themselves underestimated the populist pushback to AI, Trump Jr. said, "I think we saw that very clearly." He likened AI to other "any great innovation," but said, "This is gonna be one of those things, but it is going to take some time for people to learn how to adapt that into their regular lives." State of play: Trump Jr. spoke with Primack alongside 1789 Capital co-founder Omeed Malik, whose venture Trump Jr. joined in 2024. The investment firm has since exploded from overseeing a few hundred million dollars to billions. Zoom in: Trump Jr. agreed that the rage toward data centers represents a broader concern over growing AI influence. That public anger is becoming key to candidates: Democrats in six early 2028 primary states expect their presidential nominee to prioritize AI regulations, according to new polling data first reported by Axios' Maria Curi. Ahead of the midterms, Republicans took note of the sagging views of the data centers needed to power the AI boom. While Trump has prioritized self-regulation for the industry, the November results raise questions about how Republicans will tackle the tech moving forward. Zoom out: Asked if there was anything Democrats and the White House could agree on after a November shellacking that could be good for business, he said "we've got to focus" on costs and inflation. But he argued that "the second they win ... it's about investigations" — which Trump Jr. could find himself targeted by. Editor's note: This story was updated with additional context throughout.

events.title: "We will remain thoughtful": Nvidia says it will continue to backstop AI ecosystem
events.summary: Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward. Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital . What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said on at the end of conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this." She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added. In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds . Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world." Coreweave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each rose by more than 10% in after-hours trading. Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly. Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said. The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make." Catch-up quick: Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence. She was also a major Nvidia customer and helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country. On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones through cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang . "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said. The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.

events.title: Nvidia says its open source AI strategy remains intact after Jensen Huang’s exit
events.summary: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress reaffirmed the company’s commitment to open source AI during Tuesday’s earnings call with analysts — the first since CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation. “At Nvidia, we are committed to fostering a vibrant open model ecosystem, so every country, company, and industry can build its own intelligence,” Kress said in her opening remarks. She also noted that open models were accelerating AI adoption, citing a 35-fold year-over-year surge in weekly token volume on OpenRouter, including a 3.5-fold increase over the past three months. Kress also spoke about Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face, a platform for open source AI models that the company agreed to acquire for $12.9 billion in September, in what would be the second-largest acquisition in Nvidia’s history. The platform, which serves more than 18 million developers and 200,000 companies, is still on track to join Nvidia, despite Huang’s ouster. Huang had heavily advocated for open source AI technology. His departure had raised questions about the company’s future approach to open source AI models, with Hugging Face’s CEO calling Huang’s departure “a sad day,” and promising to “keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever.” So far, Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face appear unchanged. The acquisition was not directly addressed during the Q&A portion of the earnings call. “Together, we will scale its platform and make intelligence more open, more capable, and more accessible,” said Kress of Nvidia’s plans for Hugging Face. Last week, Nvidia founder Huang resigned from his position as CEO following news about his extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. He’s also accused of having extramarital affairs with two direct reports and is now set to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving. Meanwhile, the SEC is investigating Nvidia over whether the company’s disclosures misled investors, The WSJ reported . Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads. On today’s call, Kress noted that Nemotron is now the “most widely used U.S. open model on OpenRouter,” and it’s “where developers start to build their own intelligence.” “That foundation is empowering the ecosystem,” she said. Correction: Due to a typo, an earlier version of this article incorrectly stated the number of developers served by Hugging Face; it is 18 million, not 118 million. events.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
events.summary: Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week. For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures. Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship. US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency. The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions. For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology. Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech. Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this. Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger. Watch: Jensen Huang speaks to the BBC's Faisal Islam in 2025 Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China. The BBC has approached the White House for comment. Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China". "The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week. The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state". For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill. The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified. It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips. Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim , advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise. Now that opening may be under threat. History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world. Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course. The suspected Chinese spy balloon was shot down days after it was spotted over the US But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply. The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze. "The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal. "No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.

events.title: Nvidia says it doesn’t plan to reappoint Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Despite Nvidia founder and former CEO Jensen Huang’s recent offer to return to the chip company he helped build from the ground up, the company is not looking to take him back. During the company’s earnings call on Tuesday, Nvidia chairman Harvey C. Jones told listeners that Huang’s return was not something that company leadership was considering. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms,” Jones said, “Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions as president, CEO, and board member. The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Tuesday, Huang had posted on X that since he left the company, he has “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” and added that “if the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Huang resigned last week in dramatic fashion following revelations of a number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who has been accused of being a Chinese intelligence agent. That woman, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, has maintained close ties to the former Nvidia CEO for years. Critics worry that the relationship may have influenced Nvidia’s dealings with China , and U.S. intelligence officials have expressed suspicions that she works for China’s Ministry of State Security. The development has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry at a moment when the future of the AI business, in which Nvidia plays a pivotal role, hangs in the balance. It has also spurred investigations, including an independent investigation into Huang’s activities by Nvidia’s board and an SEC probe into Nvidia . Huang has been replaced by interim CEO Colette Kress , who is also the chipmaker’s chief financial officer and executive vice president, while the board searches for a permanent replacement. events.title: GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs
events.summary: At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC). The creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028. According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the new chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities. This is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads. “Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg . “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.” Details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community. Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions. The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists. When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well. Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains. Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a new strategy: FP64 emulation. We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme. The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance. Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS. While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation. Assessing the new chip's vector performance is much easier. With more than 50 thousand CUDA cores (by our calculation, it should be closer to 53,248), the chip should deliver at least 86 percent higher vector performance at double precision. AMD’s HPC beast AMD is also cooking up new HPC chips. In a blog post published late last week, AMD revealed the HPC-tuned version of its MI400-series GPUs. The Instinct MI430X boasts 432 GB of HBM4, 23 TB/s of memory bandwidth and a whopping 288 teraFLOPS of peak double precision grunt. AMD isn’t relying on FP64 emulation. Instead, AMD took advantage of its modular chiplet architecture to build two distinct versions of its MI400-series accelerators: one optimized for AI and another designed to excel in HPC and scientific computing workloads. AMD has shared predictions as to how the chips will perform in several of the Top500’s headline benchmarks. In a total non-surprise, the House of Zen says systems like EuroHPC’s Alice Recoque and Oak Ridge National Laboratories’ upcoming Discovery supers would enjoy significant performance gains if they upgrade from its earlier Instinct MI300A and MI250X-based offerings. ®

events.title: Trump ‘reaches out a lot’: Jeff Bezos says shutting out business leaders is a mistake
events.summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos says he doesn’t regret aligning himself with President Donald Trump, calling him unusually “communicative.” “He reaches out a lot,” Bezos told Liz Hoffman at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, adding that it was “quantitatively unusual.” It’s a two-way street, with the billionaire and the president both calling one another, he added. The billionaire said he’s worked closely with every president since Bill Clinton and plans to work with “every president going forward as long as they’ll have me,” sidestepping a question on whether tying himself so closely to the administration might create difficulties in a Democrat-controlled Congress. “I’m on the side of America,” he said. “I have never tried to take advantage for Amazon or myself or any of my companies. So, you know, presidents need advice from business leaders, and shutting out business leaders is a mistake. It’s not smart.” Former President Barack Obama was very communicative too, Bezos said. “I still reach out to Obama for advice,” but none of the other presidents “were half as communicative as Trump is” when it comes to the sheer volume of conversations, Bezos said. Blue Origin taps Prometheus Bezos said he’s spending most of his time these days focusing on Prometheus, his artificial intelligence startup that aims to bring AI to the physical world. He said his space company, Blue Origin, is already utilizing Prometheus tools on two projects, though he declined to provide details of how the space business is putting the startup’s products to work. When asked whether he’d follow rival Elon Musk, who’s trying to merge all of his businesses together, Bezos said he didn’t have plans to stitch Prometheus, Blue Origin, and Amazon together. “That’s such a funny idea,” he said. “I have nothing to announce.” Prometheus was founded in 2025 and has so far raised $14.5 billion and employs around 250 people, Bezos said. Vik Bajaj, co-founder of Prometheus, said that they respect the “proprietary nature” of engineering when working with other companies, but can help to shorten their product development significantly. “We help them perform their work much, much, much faster than is possible without the tools that we’re developing,” Bajaj said. Nvidia Bezos also had some advice for the Nvidia board: Don’t hire from outside the company. He urged the board to look internally for a replacement — if it doesn’t bring former CEO Jensen Huang back on, that is. Bezos did skirt around the question of whether or not Huang should be reinstated, saying he didn’t “know enough of the details.” “There’s probably a bunch of stuff that happened inside those board meetings and so on that we don’t know,” he said. He said that an outside pick would have a “vanishingly small chance of success” given Nvidia’s complex business. An outside candidate for CEO should be treated as a “last resort.” Bond It was immediately clear to everyone in the room, including director Denis Villeneuve, that Robert Pattinson should be the next James Bond, Bezos said. Although they weren’t always sold on the actor due to his level of fame, the choice became clear through “old-fashioned” screen testing. “He is James Bond,” Bezos said. The search had previously been whittled down to just five names, but ultimately the choice was “undebated.” — Ellen DiMauro

events.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
events.summary: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

events.title: Nvidia’s Board Has No Plans to Bring Back Jensen Huang
events.summary: As Nvidia reported its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday, the company’s financial performance was overshadowed by the drama surrounding its former CEO . And Nvidia’s board made one thing clear right off the bat: Jensen Huang isn’t coming back . At the start of the earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones emphasized the company’s strength and “groundbreaking technology” before turning to the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure. “On November 12, our board of directors announced that, after disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards, and cultural norms, Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned his positions … and the board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO,” Jones said. Asked about the company’s strategy for retaining talent and navigating the leadership transition, interim CEO Colette Kress emphasized the importance of the company’s workforce. “Our employees are absolutely instrumental to everything in this company,” Kress said. “We will take care of our employees during this transition to make sure that they are safe and that the work can be done in the current environment.” Jones added that the Nvidia board is taking the search for a new CEO “very seriously” and is considering both internal and external candidates. National security dynamics are changing the chip industry, Jones said, and “our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully. So the search will be thorough. We want to install the permanent CEO as quickly as possible, but we won’t expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person.” One recurring theme emerged from the earnings call, aside from the Huang saga: Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains as strong as ever. Kress said that Nvidia expects that it will keep growing throughout 2027 and into 2028, fueled by the rise of agentic AI. Less than a week after Huang resigned as chief executive, Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended on October 25. That exceeded analysts’ expectations of roughly $109 billion and was nearly double the revenue reported in the same quarter a year ago. The vast majority of Nvidia’s revenue came from its data center business, which generated $107.6 billion, up 110 percent from a year ago. Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, who had served as an executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider called Megaspeed. Then, reports emerged that Nvidia’s longtime leader additionally had an affair with one of his direct reports; following Huang’s resignation, Reuters reported he had an affair with a second employee. Huang’s relationship with the alleged Chinese operative has raised questions about what he knew about Nvidia’s advanced chips making their way into China despite US export restrictions. Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list in June 2025, but The New York Times reported that, according to third-party data, a subsidiary of Megaspeed “received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia AI technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips,” which were subject to export restrictions. On the heels of Tuesday’s earnings, Nvidia’s stock rose in after-hours trading. The company had lost more than $1 trillion in market value over the past month amid the fallout from Huang’s scandal. Earlier on Tuesday, Huang released his first statement since his resignation. Huang thanked allies for their support, writing he’d “seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” He admitted to failing to “live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia,” adding that he is “committed to cooperating with the board’s independent investigation.” However, Huang concluded, if the board “decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” Nvidia, which is headquartered in Santa Clara, California, has roughly 60,000 employees, and sentiments have varied in the wake of Huang’s departure. “In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” an employee told WIRED last week. But in his 33 years leading Nvidia, Huang earned a loyal army of supporters by minimizing layoffs and red tape. Some employees have been calling for his return to the helm. And a few tech industry heavyweights are similarly eager for Huang to be reinstated. Executives including Elon Musk , Replit CEO Amjad Masad , and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan took to X to voice support for Huang, signing a petition to “Bring Jensen Back.

events.title: NVIDIA Expands Commitments With Supply Chain Partners to Support AI Infrastructure Buildout
events.summary: News Summary: New agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics support additional substrate capacity and expanded production capabilities at existing factories. NVIDIA’s work with Amkor and SPIL expands advanced packaging capacity for current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs began volume shipments in the third quarter, leveraging TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. Foxconn is deepening its collaboration with NVIDIA, drawing on its global production network to support next-generation GPU and networking platforms. NVIDIA today announced expanded commitments with supply chain partners to support sustainable long-term growth, aligning supply and manufacturing capacity with demand for its accelerated computing and AI infrastructure platforms. Working with Amkor Technology, Foxconn, Kinsus Interconnect Technology, Samsung Electro-Mechanics , Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and TSMC, NVIDIA is expanding manufacturing capacity across substrates, advanced packaging, wafer and contract manufacturing to scale production of its current and next-generation accelerated computing platforms. “Our supply chain is a strategic advantage,” said Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations at NVIDIA. “Our work with these partners builds on our manufacturing foundation for long-term growth, expanding capacity across components, advanced packaging and system production to deliver the accelerated computing platforms our customers need.” Increasing Substrate Capacity and Production Capabilities NVIDIA is expanding its substrate supply commitments with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics, adding manufacturing capacity and improving production capabilities at existing factories. Under a new agreement with NVIDIA, Kinsus plans to expand its advanced ABF package substrate manufacturing capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by more than 3.5x over current levels from its Youth campus in Taoyuan, Taiwan. Production is expected to begin in the second half of 2027, with the additional capacity targeted for the third quarter of 2028. This multiyear agreement builds on the companies’ existing supplier relationship and supports NVIDIA’s long-term supply planning for its accelerated computing platforms. “We believe AI will be one of the most important technology transitions of our lifetime,” said Scott Chen, CEO and president of Kinsus. “After more than a decade of partnership with NVIDIA, we are excited to continue building the future together.” NVIDIA and Samsung Electro-Mechanics have amended their existing substrate supply agreement to improve operational capabilities at existing factories in support of increased production of NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platforms. The amendment builds on the companies’ previously announced multiyear collaboration supporting substrate manufacturing in Sejong and Busan, South Korea, for NVIDIA’s compute and high-speed networking technologies. “By combining our world-class substrate fine-processing technology and high-reliability MLCC technology, we will perfectly fulfill our role as a total solution provider so that NVIDIA’s AI platform can be supplied to the global market on time, with the highest performance and quality,” said Duck-Hyun Chang, CEO of Samsung Electro-Mechanics.   Scaling Advanced Packaging Through Multiyear Agreements NVIDIA’s advanced packaging plans include a new capacity expansion with SPIL and previously announced agreements supporting Amkor’s manufacturing expansion in the U.S. and South Korea. NVIDIA is supporting Amkor’s expansion of advanced packaging capacity in Arizona and South Korea through multiyear agreements announced in July and October 2026, totaling nearly $3 billion. The agreements include prepayments to help Amkor scale manufacturing capacity for NVIDIA’s long-term production needs. “Our agreements with NVIDIA support investments in Arizona and South Korea that will serve multiple generations of AI platforms,” said Kevin Engel, president and CEO of Amkor. “That long-term planning allows us to advance our packaging technologies and add manufacturing capacity as NVIDIA’s production needs grow.” NVIDIA and SPIL are expanding advanced packaging operations in Taiwan under a multiyear agreement supported by multibillion-dollar funding from NVIDIA. The expansion will increase contracted advanced packaging capacity dedicated to NVIDIA by mid-2029. The project includes new production lines with turnkey support spanning bumping, interposer wafer fabrication, assembly and testing. These capabilities support semiconductor products with demanding requirements for computing performance, bandwidth, power efficiency and system integration. “SPIL is proud to strengthen our collaboration with NVIDIA,” said C.W. Tsai, CEO and chairman of the board of SPIL. “This agreement enhances our ability to support next‑generation packaging technologies and deliver the performance and reliability required for future AI systems.” Next-Generation Technologies for Agentic AI The third quarter marked the first volume shipment of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs for agentic AI. These products take advantage of TSMC’s 5nm, 3nm and CoWoS advanced packaging technologies. “TSMC and NVIDIA share a longstanding partnership built on semiconductor innovation,” said Dr. Kevin Zhang, senior vice president and deputy co-COO at TSMC. “This deep collaboration allows us to plan for future technology requirements and prepare our manufacturing capabilities as NVIDIA brings new platforms to market.” Leveraging Global Manufacturing Footprint for GPU and Networking Platforms “Foxconn continues to deepen its collaboration with NVIDIA across next-generation GPU and networking platforms,” said Young Liu, chairman of Foxconn. “By leveraging its integrated global production network spanning Asia, North America, and Europe, Foxconn is well-positioned to support the volume ramp-up of next-generation AI infrastructure.” Building on Global Supply Chain Expansion These commitments build on NVIDIA’s decades-long partnerships and recent commitments announced in October for manufacturing expansions with Amkor, IBIDEN, King Yuan Electronics (KYEC), Samsung Electro-Mechanics, SPIL and Unimicron. Those plans included an aggregate 2.5x increase in substrate capacity over three years, expanded advanced packaging, a doubling of semiconductor testing capacity from 2026 to 2027 and a 15x increase in SPIL’s optical-engine capacity by mid-2027, with aims for another doubling by the end of 2028. “Our strong and long-standing collaboration with NVIDIA has continued to develop in the area of high-performance IC package substrates,”

events.title: Nvidia posts strong earnings amid Jensen Huang exit, reported SEC probe
events.summary: Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation. Why it matters: Nvidia remains squarely at the center of the AI economy — and investors are anxious for guidance on the company's strategic roadmap following Huang's sudden exit. Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier. S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion. The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion. The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke. The stock was up 2% in after-hours trading Tuesday. It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history. She didn't mention Huang on Tuesday in the earnings report but touted Nvidia's role as "an exceptional technology leader" and said sales of the company's new, advanced Vera Rubin chips are "off to an explosive start." "Our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater," she said. What we're watching: Whether Nvidia discloses any additional details about its CEO search or other investigations on its earnings call. WSJ reported Tuesday afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into the company. An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Huang posted a public letter Tuesday saying he'd be "honored" to return as CEO. Newly appointed Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on Tuesday afternoon's earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation "and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO." Tech analyst Dan Ives earlier said the board could face a special shareholder meeting called by at least 15% of shareholders. What's next: Tech analyst Gene Munster said on X that the Nvidia earnings call Tuesday is "the most anticipated conference call of all time, and the one we'll likely get the least information from." events.title: Duffy's $50 billion request gets chilly reception from Senate GOP
events.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. But Democrats are also expressing skeptcism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't." The intrigue : Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab. "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters. "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said. "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

events.title: Europe the natural location for Mistral IPO, CEO says
events.summary: French AI champion Mistral will likely go public in Europe, and is in preparations to do so, CEO Arthur Mensch said Tuesday. “The natural place to list is Europe,” Mensch said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “We’re not going to do this this year, but we’re definitely getting ready for it.” Mistral, which mostly makes open-weight AI models, aims to carve out a lane as a sovereign AI provider, pitching it as an alternative to closed US models or open Chinese models. That’s especially salient in Europe: Mensch said most of the investor base and half of its customer base is European. A US IPO, though, could offer the company access to more capital: Other European tech companies including Arm, Spotify, and Klarna have listed in New York, drawn by higher valuations and a bigger pool of investors. Mensch also said that regardless of who wins the French presidential elections next year, “we’re very confident as well that in Europe we will still have a lot of support. Support is needed.” He said he has met with most of the candidates to explain how AI and the industry works. “Many of them are not technical, and so they need to get a little more technical because that’s going to be five years of very technical discussions,” he said. He tied the country’s recent protests to young people’s anxiety around AI: “The youth need answers to what they’re going to do. So I think part of the unrest and part of the anguish that the youth is having is because of AI changing the way their jobs are going to be.” He criticized companies’ decisions not to hire young people because of AI. “You can invest in them, they will use AI much better, and they will create a lot of value,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Nvidia posts strong outlook as board rejects return of Jensen Huang as CEO
events.summary: Nvidia forecast quarterly revenue above estimates on Tuesday in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang 's resignation as chief executive. The chip maker, which said it has launched the search for a new chief executive, announced that it expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, compared to analyst expectations of $125.5 billion, according to LSEG data. It posted an earnings per share of $2.68 on revenue of $115.8 billion for the quarter, up 20 per cent for the quarter and 103 per cent from the same period last year. Estimates compiled by LSEG data projected an EPS of $2.47 and revenue of $109.15 billion. “Our momentum is real, with the market-leading multi-year road map, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand. We are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position,” interim chief executive Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call. Addressing the company's leadership vacuum , Ms Kress said Nvidia wants to install its next chief executive “as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person”. With Mr Huang out at the company at the heart of the AI buildout, investors were turning attention towards the company's outlook. The earnings come amid growing negative sentiments towards chip makers and the AI buildout , and rising concerns over financing to build AI data centres . Data centre revenue was $107.6 billion, up 21 per cent from the previous quarter and 110 per cent from a year ago, Nvidia said, compared to an anticipated $101.85 billion. Ms Kress said the company expects fiscal 2028 revenue to grow roughly 75 per cent year-on-year. The company's cloud industry backlog currently sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion three months ago. Nvidia said it is “not assuming any data centre compute revenue from China in our outlook”. Ms Kress also said Nvidia's total CPU revenue will at least double in fiscal year 2028. Coreweave , Meta, NScale and Open AI have since adopted the Vera Rubin processing platform, joining AWS, OCI and SpaceX. The earnings cap a frenetic week for the company and a widening fallout after Mr Huang left the company. Shares in the company are down more than 17 per cent this year, while the S&P 500 is up 8 per cent. Nvidia was up nearly 5 per cent during after-hours trading, after closing 0.48 per cent lower at $155.39 a share in Tuesday's trading session. The S&P 500 declined 1.03 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74 per cent, while the Dow Jones dropped 848 points, or 1.64 per cent. Nvidia not considering reinstating Huang as CEO Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board of directors, said the company does not intend to reinstate Mr Huang as chief executive. Nvidia has retained Heidrick and Struggles to lead the search for Mr Huang's replacement. “While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners, and shareholders,” he said. The company has lost about $410 billion in market value since Mr Huang's resignation last week after revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a spy for China. In his first public comments since his resignation, Mr Huang on Tuesday said he would be open to returning as Nvidia chief executive if the company's board asked him to. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he said. President Donald Trump said he would support Mr Huang's return as chief executive, while a petition calling for his reinstatement has received more than 178,000 signatures. Mr Huang has agreed to testify before three US congressional committees on December 1. Nvidia's general counsel will testify on December 2. The Wall Street Journal reported the Securities and Exchange Commission is reporting the chip maker after Mr Huang's resignation last week, quoting people familiar with the matter.

events.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
events.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives." Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows. "Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella. AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world . Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software. "Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot." Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, " Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365 ," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric. He also talked up Microsoft IQ , the company's new enterprise context management platform. "The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot. Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion , its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench , a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal. Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model. Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available. "We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it." He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available. It's a question of trust After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust. "Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted. "And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable." Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative . The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative." Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®

events.title: FAA pauses tech upgrade linked to nationwide ground stop
events.summary: The Federal Aviation Administration is halting the installation of new routers following Friday's nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop , the agency confirmed to Axios Tuesday. Why it matters: The technology rollout is suspected to be connected to massive travel disruptions that continued through the weekend, inconveniencing travelers across the country. Catch up quick: Over 12,000 flights were canceled Friday after the telecommunications failure, and thousands more were delayed. The issue stemmed from routine work to upgrade the FAA's aging telecommunications network, replacing copper wires with fiber-optic connections. The agency is adding Juniper routers to the network as part of the transition. The FAA said its system became overwhelmed by roughly 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds after a router was installed, disabling communication and radar in 17 of the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers. Investigators identified two potential sources of the problem — one in Arkansas and another in Texas. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the device functioned as programmed by the installer and wasn't faulty. The FAA is still investigating the root cause. What they're saying: "We believe we have addressed the initial cause of the disruption by immediately disabling the functionality of the originating Juniper routers," the FAA announced in a statement . "As a precaution, we disabled the same functionality on more than 60 other Juniper routers in the system, and we have paused installing them." Zoom in: A group of Democratic senators demanded the agency halt the router installation on Tuesday, though the agency had already done so. "DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote in a letter to Transportation Secretary Scott Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. "Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed." They added that identifying the problematic router is not the same as determining why it malfunctioned. The senators — all part of the Senate Committee for Commerce, Science and Transportation — requested a response to its questions by no later than Nov. 23. The FAA did not address Axios' questions about whether the agency would meet all the senators' demands. "[T]he Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so," a spokesperson said. By the numbers: The FAA is slated to convert more than 3,600 routers to Juniper devices, and 400 are already installed, per the senator's letter. Just 69 are operational. events.title: Sheehy, Klobuchar look to solve hemp dispute
events.summary: Sens. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont., and Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., are introducing a new, far-reaching hemp regulatory bill that could smooth over a major point of contention in the government funding negotiations, according to details shared first with Semafor. The bipartisan proposal would bar sales of consumable hemp products to people under 21, ban “gas station” marijuana products derived from hemp and copycat advertising for those products, and also restrict synthetic cannabis products from China. The bill would also require hemp products be produced in the US, preserve access to CBD products, and empower the FDA to inspect hemp facilities. The timing of the compromise is crucial: A new federal definition of hemp goes into effect on Dec. 11 — the same day as the government funding deadline — and without action could upend the industry in the US. Internal Republican disagreements over the issue complicated the last funding bill. Sheehy has made solving the hemp issue within his party a major priority; he’s holding a hemp roundtable on Tuesday afternoon with veterans to discuss the issue. In a statement, the Montana Republican said the compromise with Klobuchar will put “every bad actor in the hemp space out of business and keep intoxicating [productsout of the hands of children,” while shielding farmers, cancer patients, and veterans from criminal penalties. Klobuchar, who will leave the Senate in January after being elected governor of Minnesota, touted her state’s hemp industry and warned that the “looming federal ban on hemp products is threatening farmers, brewers, small businesses, and consumers across Minnesota and the country.” A coalition of veterans groups is also asking congressional leaders to support the bill, according to a letter shared with Semafor . Republican Sen. Ted Budd, R-N.C., is a leading opponent of delaying the new hemp definition deadline and is gearing up for another push ahead of the December funding deadline. Sheehy and Klobuchar’s bill would go into effect on Dec. 11 if passed.

events.title: Data center industry should repurpose older infrastructure, SambaNova CEO says
events.summary: Data center builders must adapt to AI pushback, SambaNova CEO Rodrigo Liang said on Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. One way to do that, Liang said, is to repurpose existing data centers. This approach “disrupts the communities less,” he told Semafor’s Liz Rappaport. AI backlash has presented a formidable obstacle for the data center buildout. People voted to limit data center development in 40 out of 41 ballot measures across the US on Election Day, and some newly elected Democratic leaders have laid out plans to pass data-center moratoria. Existing data centers tend to be much smaller than the massive ones being built for AI, and repurposing old infrastructure will require the industry to be “much more energy-efficient in the chips that we build,” Liang said. Still, he said, it’s good for the industry to get more value out of what it has available now. “To distribute the data center into existing environments where power already exists, the infrastructure already exists, the cooling already exists and fits within the ecosystem — it’s not a bad way to do it,” he said. Compute is a precious resource for companies right now. Voice AI company ElevenLabs CEO Mati Staniszewski told Rappaport that “compute constraint” in the near term is a real possibility. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
events.summary: No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. Huang out to dry The US Department of Justice made the rare point of commenting on one of the pillars of the Jensen Huang story on Tuesday when it confirmed that it’s investigating Megaspeed, the Singaporean company formerly helmed by Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), the alleged Chinese spy. The DoJ has been checking the company out since 2024, when Alice Huang was still in charge, over potential export control violations. In other words, the DoJ is hinting that even if Alice Huang isn’t a spy, Megaspeed may have still been moving illegal chips. The DoJ added that Nvidia blacklisted Megaspeed in 2025, and that the Department of Commerce previously interviewed Alice Huang around the same time. It was immediately after that, the DoJ said, that it took over the investigation. “The Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security working together will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred,” the DoJ said. In other words, this is far from over and Nvidia might be justified in wanting not to touch its founder with a ten-foot pole. ®

events.title: Europe needs ‘innovation-friendly’ regulation to catch up on AI, German official says
events.summary: Europe must enact more innovation-friendly regulation if it wants to compete in the AI race, Germany’s director-general for digital policy and economic affairs at the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization said Tuesday. There are “a lot of things we need to do to catch up in the race,” Marco-Alexander Breit said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “One of these is actually having a more innovation-friendly regulatory framework, especially in Brussels.” Germany also needs to “step up” its capacities and capabilities, he told Semafor’s Mohammed Sergie, adding that the country hopes to quadruple its data center capacity by 2030. Steve Jurvetson, managing director and founder of Future Ventures, who joined Breit on stage, went further, saying Europe is “trapped in a sort of regulatory doom loop” that smothers innovation. Jurvetson said “regulation is the elephant in the room” that “is stifling European innovation at every step of the way.” While Breit pushed back, saying, “it’s not all doom and gloom in Europe,” he acknowledged that red tape and regulation needed to be cut, arguing that change would ensure European AI leaders “don’t need to leave Europe to work on AI and change the world and make a lot of money.” Breit said he agreed with the vast majority of the EU AI Act, for example, but continued on to say that “it actually adds to a higher threshold for European companies to step up their game in the AI world,” he said. “So it actually hurts our economy, even more than people maybe think in Silicon Valley that it hurts the US companies.” Speaking earlier at Silicon Valley & The World, former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak also criticized the EU AI Act, saying “trying to legislate for every conceivable use case was not the right approach.” Still, Sunak said he supports some regulation, because despite being bullish on new AI technologies, “they bring new risks with them.” — Ben Kesslen

events.title: Medical practice squeezed as business confidence slumps in SA
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Business confidence takes hit in SA amid cost and profitability concerns Clinical psychologist Quentin Black is among those dealing with rising business costs. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Business confidence in SA has again been dented, according to the latest snapshot produced by the state's Business Chamber. The group's CEO says confidence has slumped to levels "we haven't seen since COVID". The most recent quarterly survey found almost 75 per cent of respondents felt the pressure of wage, energy, rent and other costs. Quentin Black helps people deal with life's pressures, but he himself knows what it's like to be under the pump. The clinical psychologist manages a not-for-profit practice in Adelaide, which he said was currently being squeezed. Dr Black said the practice was too big for small business support, but too small to qualify for other forms of financial assistance. "There's a lot of pressures on businesses at the moment," he said. "Small enterprises like PsychMed that employ a lot of South Australians actually don't get any assistance whatsoever. In fact, we end up paying a lot of the burden. "Even though we're running not-for-profit programs, we pay payroll tax to the state government for employing people on the programs." Dr Black's comments reflect a mood that is corroborated by the latest snapshot of business confidence in South Australia. According to the September quarterly survey produced by the South Australian Business Chamber, confidence has again been dented, slumping to its fourth-lowest level since 2001. Among the factors driving that result — which reversed an uptick in confidence in June — were cost pressures and government policies, the chamber's CEO Andrew Kay said. "Business confidence in South Australia is back to levels we haven't seen since COVID," he said. Andrew Kay says businesses are feeling the pressure of rising government charges. ( ABC News: Daniel Litjens ) About three quarters of survey respondents listed costs — including wages, energy and rent — as major obstacles to confidence. Dr Black, who is a long-time member of the ALP, said he was all-too-familiar with those challenges. "There's been regular increases in wages as part of the inflationary spiral. That's a yearly event now," he said. "Also, insurance costs have gone up significantly along with energy costs which have really skyrocketed for businesses." More than two thirds of respondents to the confidence survey were anxious about profitability, while more than 60 per cent highlighted government policies and legislation. "Government needs to find ways to reduce cost pressures on businesses, to reduce red tape, and to find ways to encourage investment, rather than detract from investors coming to this country," Mr Kay said. "We're seeing at the moment government putting pressure on businesses through increased credit card surcharges, through changes to trusts on businesses — these are simply additional costs or additional taxes on businesses." The SA opposition said the pressures were being exacerbated by inflation caused by excessive government spending. "Inflation and red tape are absolutely hammering small businesses right across South Australia," opposition leader Ashton Hurn said. "They're being squeezed in every direction because they've got their costs that are going up, but we also know that families at home are really feeling the pinch in their own hip pockets." Ashton Hurn has been critical of government spending. ( ABC News: Carl Saville ) But business confidence in South Australia nevertheless remains higher than it does nationally, according to the survey. "The national economy is clearly under a bit of strain, and under a bit of pressure, yet South Australia is outperforming the rest of the nation, with the exception of maybe Western Australia," SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said. "That doesn't change the fact that we are subject to the national economic headwinds which are clearly under strain at the moment." events.title: Should court filings related to the search of Ilhan Omar's home be released? A judge will decide
events.summary: It's been more than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar WASHINGTON -- More than a month after federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar , a federal judge heard arguments Tuesday on a request by media organizations to unseal court records related to the search — and to an immigration-fraud investigation that the Minnesota Democrat claims is politically motivated. Over a dozen news organizations, including The Associated Press, maintain that the public has a First Amendment right to access the search warrant and other court filings that led to the Oct. 12 search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home by Department of Homeland Security agents. During a hearing on the request, Chief Judge James Boasberg said he agrees with Justice Department attorneys that it's premature to unseal a search warrant affidavit containing sensitive details of the government's investigation. But the judge said he will privately review other sealed court filings for possible public release as soon as next week. Omar, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has been a target of anti-immigrant rhetoric by President Donald Trump and many Republican allies. Omar, who has denied wrongdoing, said in a social media post that the search was an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives , a person briefed on the investigation told The AP last month on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. Agents conducted the court-authorized search less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Omar won her reelection bid. The Justice Department historically has avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election. Omar has said DHS agents seized 17 items , including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift. Boasberg gave the government until Friday to provide him with proposed redactions to sealed court filings that could shed light on some of the underlying legal arguments involved in the Omar investigation. The judge said redacted versions of those documents could be released as soon as next Monday. The 67-page search warrant affidavit, which contains information about witnesses and other details of the investigation, will remain under wraps for now. In a court filing last month, the government argued that it would jeopardize the investigation to unseal the court records before a charging decision is made. JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech The news organizations' attorneys argue that the government's privacy concerns are outweighed by the “enormous public interest in and historic significance of a search warrant executed at the home of a sitting member of Congress.” Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano said the government isn't trying to keep the affidavit under seal permanently. “It's not our position. It's never been our position,” she told the judge. Boasberg noted that Vice President JD Vance and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin already have publicly commented on the contours of the Omar investigation. Serano said she can't control what others in the Trump administration say about the case. “It seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg replied. Boasberg, who was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama, is himself a frequent target of Trump's ire. Trump called for Boasberg's impeachment last year after the judge blocked the president's administration from deporting planeloads of Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador under the Alien Enemies Act. ___ Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed to this report.
