events.title: Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft Ignite 2026: Empowering human ambition, intelligence and trust Microsoft Source | 5 minutes One year ago at Microsoft Ignite, we introduced Frontier Transformation. The premise was simple: technology exists to serve humanity and deliver real business outcomes. Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. Ignite 2026 is the next milestone in this journey as we introduce new innovations that deliver on the promise of all three of these pillars. Our goal is to build a frontier ecosystem , one that lets every organization benefit from progress at the frontier while preserving what makes it unique.   “We need to parlay any technological advance into real outcomes and new points of leverage for people, organizations and society at large,” said Satya Nadella, Microsoft Chairman and CEO, in his opening keynote at Ignite. “For us, that comes down to three things: keeping human ambition at the center, ensuring you have ownership over your organization’s intelligence and learning, and trust.” Human ambition: AI should serve humanity, not the other way around It starts with the work people are trying to do, which is why we think of Microsoft Copilot as the new operating system for work.   New Copilot Workspaces gives people and agents a shared space to work together as a team. Autopilot, a long-running agent, can manage recurring tasks and move projects forward without being prompted at every step, and Copilot Code lets anyone build dashboards, trackers and apps in natural language with enterprise security and governance built in. Together with Office in Copilot, and features like Today, they make up the new Copilot, which is built to translate raw intelligence into real value. Copilot is already driving transformation at scale among our customers. Volkswagen Group is equipping more than 330,000 employees with Copilot and The Estée Lauder Companies has expanded Copilot to more than 14,000 people across its global workforce. Copilot is also connecting to the systems teams rely on most, including Dynamics 365, as well as announcing Salesforce in Copilot , a plugin available in preview with more than 38 pre-built sales skills. Intelligence: Compound your intelligence without giving away your IP Agents are only as effective as the context they work with. Microsoft IQ is the enterprise context management platform that helps organizations build their own IQ by capturing, governing and reusing the business knowledge apps and agents need. New business plugins let teams package that knowledge into reusable, trusted context, skills and tools that can be shared across the business.  Customers are already turning that intelligence into business outcomes. Publicis Groupe is empowering employees to build custom AI skills that combine Microsoft IQ with Publicis’ industry expertise and proprietary data, then test them against real-world client scenarios. The result is faster innovation, quicker decision-making and greater value for clients. In Microsoft Foundry , new continuous improvement tools help customers develop more powerful agents and even train models automatically based on real production signals: optimizing for quality, latency and cost-effectiveness. New models for coding, cyber image and audio are also being introduced, as well as the general availability of Microsoft-Decision-1.1 , a fast, low-cost decision model for tasks like routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control. Trust: Observability at every layer of the stack and for every person As agents move from answering questions to taking action, trust becomes the deciding factor. There should never be a choice between innovation and safety. Microsoft Perception , now generally available, brings together specialized agents to find, defend and remediate vulnerabilities — powered by models including our MAI-Cyber line — to help defenders stop threats at machine speed. Agent 365 Business Analytics gives leaders a clear view of what their AI is costing and what it is delivering, from task success to hours assisted. And Windows is expanding its operating-system-level protection for agents, with more granular containment with Microsoft Execution Containers, built-in agent identity with Entra support and Agent 365 policies enforced on every device, giving IT more control over agent activity in their organizations. Building on its use of Microsoft Defender, Entra and Purview, BNY is exploring capabilities in Project Perception to further strengthen security and governance. These efforts support BNY’s broader AI ambitions, including its collaboration with Microsoft to complete the first agentic negotiation of a U.S. Treasury trade. Infrastructure: A cloud built for AI at global scale Microsoft builds Azure as a single system, co-designing silicon, servers, networking and racks around what we learn running workloads at scale. As agents increasingly work outside the model, from running tools to compiling code, CPUs matter even more. Cobalt 200 virtual machines , generally available today, deliver up to 50% better performance than the previous generation. Cobalt will reach 23 regions by year end and becomes a significant share of new Azure compute capacity in 2027. Azure Catalyst brings Azure and GitHub agentic tools together in one connected experience for modernizing the applications, databases and infrastructure that AI depends on, and hybrid intelligence on Windows lets AI run wherever it makes the most sense, on the device or in the cloud, starting with GitHub Copilot for coding and Copilot for everyday work. Taken together, today’s announcements demonstrate that the organizations that pull ahead in this next phase are the ones that connect intelligence to their people, their data and their processes, with trust built in from the start. That is the frontier ecosystem we are building with our customers and partners. To see it in action, watch the Microsoft Ignite keynote and explore the full set of announcements in the Book of News . events.title: US tech billionaire flags interest in Hurricanes, Hobart stadium
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil expresses interest in buying into Hobart Hurricanes, new stadium Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in buying into the Hobart Hurricanes Big Bash League team. ( Getty Images: Steve Bell ) Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in buying into the Hobart Hurricanes and the Hobart stadium precinct. The government's appetite for such a deal is unclear, and any public-private partnership agreement for the stadium would signal a change in policy. An updated cost for the Hobart stadium project is expected in the next few weeks. Cricket looms as a wildcard in the Tasmanian government's hunt for more funds to build the new Macquarie Point stadium. And at least one American billionaire has expressed an interest in investing in the stadium precinct , as part of a potential power play involving the Hobart Hurricanes cricket team. Tech billionaire Sanjay Govil wants to buy at least a 50 per cent share in the Hobart Hurricanes, following Cricket Australia's decision to green-light the privatisation of the Big Bash League. As part of a broader cricket and infrastructure play, Mr Govil is interested in a slice of the Macquarie Point stadium and precinct, envisioning a place where American college football-style parties may be held before future Hurricanes games. "I think it's going to be very, very exciting. And to be part of that? Imagine," he told the ABC. Sanjay Govil has expressed interest in the Hobart Hurricanes and Macquarie Point stadium project. ( Supplied: Eagle Team ) Mr Govil, who founded Infinite Computer Solutions and digital healthcare company Zyter, is worth upwards of US$2 billion. Orange tap water called 'safe to drink' had metals above guidelines Survivalist says wearing cotton can kill in Tasmanian outdoors Hundreds waiting for their own records from Tasmania's education department England wins ODI series as Australia falters in chase after Duckett ton He owns the Welsh Fire, which plays in the UK Hundred competition, the Ricky Ponting-coached Washington Freedom in America's Major League Cricket competition, and is funding the construction of a 10,000-capacity cricket stadium for the Freedom in Frederick, Maryland. He wants a stake in the Big Bash League and has targeted the Hurricanes — and its prospective new stadium. "There are two elements to it, part A and part B," he said. "We would come in, and part A is the operations team, taking ownership of the Hobart Hurricanes team. The Hurricanes would then, in turn, lease the ground and facility from entity B, which would have different shareholders including us," he said. Sanjay Govil says it would be "exciting" to have a stake in the Macquarie Point stadium. ( Supplied: Cox Architecture ) The Auburn college football fan, who also owns a stake in entertainment and events company Mari, envisages a college football-style atmosphere and fan experiences before and after Hurricanes games at Macquarie Point. "That infrastructure would not just include the stadium, but a tailgating area, shops, restaurants, a whole experience centre," he said. "It's all about experience. That's the expertise I want to bring to the Hobart Hurricanes. More stadium money sought amid cost blowout concerns The Tasmanian government has begun the process of courting financial partners to help fund its Hobart stadium, as the $1.13 billion project faces a budget crunch. The prospect of cricket-induced private investment was floated with Premier Jeremy Rockliff at a September 8 meeting between him and Cricket Tasmania bosses. The government's appetite for such a deal is unclear, and any public-private partnership agreement would signal a backflip. It had previously explored a public-private partnership for the stadium, commissioning reports by Perth consultants Paxon Group and Melbourne-based Infrastructure Advisory Group last year — but ultimately decided against the model, deeming it too high a risk to the state . But with a stadium budget crunch on the horizon, a cricket-flavoured public-private partnership might become enticing to a government desperately needing outside funds to help fund the build. The stadium looks set to exceed its project budget of $1.13 billion, with state funding constrained to $875 million, as part of a government agreement with upper house MLC Bec Thomas in exchange for her support for the project in Tasmania's parliament last year. BESIX Watpac won the tender to construct the Macquarie Point stadium.

events.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
events.summary: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap. Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period. The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018. The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say. "What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. "The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026." Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions. Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall. The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses. ®

events.summary: The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over. Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans. The Guardian’s year in review 2026. events.title: Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft and organizations across industries launch AI Transparency Initiative to strengthen enterprise trust in AI models and agents Through the new AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to advance a common approach to AI transparency, security and governance across models and providers. Microsoft will also bring greater visibility into how AI models and agents interact with enterprise data across its products and services Microsoft Source | 5 minutes REDMOND, Wash. — Nov. 17, 2026 — Organizations can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they often cannot reconstruct what happened between a request and an outcome, making it difficult to independently verify model behavior. At Microsoft Ignite on Tuesday, Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella announced the next phase of Microsoft’s commitment to making AI safer: the AI Transparency Initiative, a collaborative effort with customers and partners to establish a common, open approach to security and governance across models and providers. The initiative reflects a simple principle: Greater AI autonomy requires greater transparency. “For security controls to be effective, every organization needs greater transparency into the model itself,” said Hayete Gallot, Executive Vice President, Microsoft Security. “With this work, we will bring more transparency to all models. This is a critical step in making containment smarter and stronger, allowing us to better inform accountability and traceability.” Enterprises are connecting AI models to data, tools, credentials and infrastructure, enabling agents to take actions without human approval at every step. Existing controls can observe much of the activity around AI models, but they cannot see what happens within them or independently verify their accounts of their own behavior. This limits organizations’ ability to understand the context behind an agent’s actions. That evidence gap creates security, compliance, audit and accountability risk. Security teams need a new trust architecture to address the growing insider risks posed by increasingly capable AI agents. “As AI agents become more deeply integrated into enterprise operations, security teams need clear visibility into what those agents are accessing, what actions they’re taking and how those actions can be verified,” said Aanchal Gupta, Chief Security Officer, Adobe. “Building a common approach to AI transparency across the industry is essential to strengthening trust and helping organizations innovate with confidence while maintaining security and accountability.” From principles to practice The initiative has three parts. First, Microsoft will expand its participation in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s SI Agent Standards Initiative and draw on its research to develop open, industrywide standards for AI transparency, security and governance. Second, Microsoft is collaborating with more than 40 organizations, including Accenture, Adobe, KPMG, Mastercard and Volvo Cars, to help develop open standards for AI systems that are accountable, independently verifiable and safe by design, regardless of the model or provider. Third, Microsoft will incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Microsoft Foundry and Microsoft Copilot, enabling customers to use the resulting evidence with their security and compliance tools, whether from Microsoft or other providers. “Our clients want to move faster with AI, and they shouldn’t have to choose between innovation and safety,” said John Israel, Global Chief Information Security Officer, KPMG International. “Trust in AI requires transparency, explainability and responsible oversight. We’re proud to work with Microsoft on the AI Transparency Initiative to help establish open, industrywide standards that give organizations the visibility and control they need to deploy AI responsibly at scale.” Clear accountability Agents with access to data, tools and credentials carry the risk profile of a privileged insider but operate at machine speed and scale, making independent oversight essential. Accountability stays with the organization. When something consequential happens, leaders answer to customers, employees, boards, auditors and regulators. Blaming the AI isn’t an answer, and “trust the model” isn’t a control. The initiative is designed to work across models and providers, including closed and open-weight models, so developer teams can change or update the models powering their agents without compromising IT and security teams’ ability to govern them securely or compliance teams’ ability to audit their actions. “As organizations take the next step in their AI reinventions, they need a solid foundation of trust and confidence to build from,” said Harpreet Sidhu, global cybersecurity lead, Accenture. “Initiatives like this from Microsoft to take an open, industry-driven approach to AI transparency can help as we secure AI models and fit them with controls and governance. Accenture is proud to partner with Microsoft and other leaders in this space.”  See, verify, control Microsoft believes every organization should be able to see what AI systems access and do, verify their actions independently and control what they are permitted to do. See: Know what the AI was asked and authorized to do, which model and runtime were used, what data and tools it accessed, and what actions it took. Monitor agent activity and risk signals continuously against policies and thresholds. Verify: Agents cannot be the sole source of truth about their own behavior, and frontier models cannot be trusted to govern themselves. Evidence covering agent identity, delegated intent and actions should identify its source (the model, the runtime around it, or independent systems such as identity and policy) so model-reported signals can be checked against independently observed records. Organizations should be able to independently verify AI activity using their own security and compliance systems, without relying solely on the model provider’s account of its behavior. Control: Stay in charge of what AI is permitted to do. Clear evidence of each workflow’s purpose, owner, data and delegated authority helps organizations enforce their policies before consequential actions occur and reconstruct what happened during investigations, containment, recovery and audits. That evidence should stay with them when models and providers change. Organizations should retain control over what data their agents can access and how that access is governed, regardless of the model or provider. Get involved Organizations interested in helping shape the initiative or following its progress can learn more and sign up at aka.ms/learnmoreAItransparency . events.title: Voters broke with Democrats on ballot initiatives
events.summary: The News PALO ALTO, Calif. — Democrats swept Republicans on Nov. 3, but some of their party’s progressive ideas didn’t make it with them, as a host of liberal ballot initiatives failed and conservative proposals passed across the country. In California, where Republicans lost every major race by landslides, voters rejected a billionaire wealth tax, made it harder to create one, and likely killed a measure that would have piloted public financing of elections. In Colorado, a deep blue electorate voted to ban gender surgeries on minors by 4 points and to bar trans athletes’ participation in female sports by 5 points. A similar sports proposal prevailed by 12 points in Washington, even as Democrats padded their state legislative majorities. And in Iowa, where Gov.-elect Rob Sand led a Democratic comeback, voters endorsed a two-thirds legislative supermajority for any income tax increase. The success of some conservative ideas down the ballot — largely focused on taxes and social issues — gave some hope to Republicans after a hopeless election night. Voters rejected their party, but took multiple opportunities to oppose tax increases and roll back progressive social policies.Democrats were not taking that as advice to their party. Instead, they believe that opposition money and muddled messaging overwhelmed them, and they could win if they made another run at the ballot. “The margin was narrow enough that if we do more education with voters, we could significantly narrow it and win this,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff at the union SEIU-UHW and a proponent of the California wealth tax. Saikat Chakrabarti, an unsuccessful House candidate who was a top contributor to the wealth tax campaign, agreed. “When you have nearly half a billion dollars against you, and they spend it to spread straight-up lies about an issue, it’s hard to win unless you can get your own message out,” Chakrabarti said. “The campaign had a winning issue,” he said, “but failed to get its own message out.” Different ways to lose The Proposition 40 campaign was heavily outspent, with some of California’s wealthiest residents funding its opposition. According to state campaign finance records , $152 million went into the “no” effort, compared to a bit more than $33 million for “yes.” Spending for and against Proposition 42, which bars new wealth taxes, was similarly lopsided —nearly $128 million for, and nearly $35 million against. Some of the funding to kill the wealth tax also came from members of the Democratic Party’s coalition, like Planned Parenthood, which advocated for a long-term funding source over the proposed one-time levy. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed it, as did Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, giving voters permission to support their ticket while voting against an idea backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. “Since it failed, I look forward to Gov. Newsom leading the fight by championing a national wealth tax, which he claimed he heavily supports,” said Chakrabati. The spending in other conservative down-ballot victories was more mixed. Supporters of Washington’s ban on transgender girls playing in girls sports out-spent opponents by a 3-1 margin. One of the coalition’s other priorities, which would have required schools to notify parents if their children identified as a different gender at school than at home, failed by 5 points. In Colorado, where transgender sports and medicine bans for minors passed narrowly, the “yes” side was heavily outspent by its opponents, the Families Not Politics coalition. “It’s unfortunate that this is an issue that’s been politicized,” said Erin Lee, the Democrat-turned-Independent whose Protect Kids Colorado coalition got the measures on the ballot. “Democrats have chosen this as a hill to die on, and Republicans have grabbed this as a political tool to wield. But when we started putting the team together, it became clear that this issue transcends the parties.” The Democratic Party in both blue states opposed the measures. Shasti Conrad, the chair of the Washington state Democratic Party, said that the sports measure “was very confusingly written,” while Republicans brought out their base to support it. Sources who worked to beat the measure told Semafor that their campaign was beset by bad planning and bad luck. The Gender Justice League, an LGBTQ+ rights group that was working against the measure, claimed to have “lost 80% of our foundation support and 35% of our government funding” as the Trump administration enforced its executive order on gender. The “no” campaign also resisted help from Third Way, the centrist Democratic think tank not beloved by progressives. Lanae Erickson, a Third Way vice president, shared research with campaigners in every state where a sports ban could appear on the ballot. “We found that most persuasive messages were around the gender checks component of the measure,” said Erickson, referring to language in the Washington initiative that required female athletes to prove their biological sex . Colorado campaigners used Third Way’s research; Washington campaigners opted not to until the campaign’s final weeks, when they ran some digital ads based on the information. Democrats in both states believed that their eventual messaging was not effective enough. “We had an extremely long ballot, and I think it was confusing to folks,” said Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo. “I think a lot of people didn’t know exactly what those provisions stood for. We have to make sure we’re protecting folks, and that we’re doing so clearly and specifically.” In no state where conservatives passed their preferred tax or social issue measures did Democrats say that their party’s position might change. Erickson, pointing to the margins in both Washington and Colorado, said that Third Way had been trying to find a winning path for trans rights for years, and that the results showed progress. “Funders kept telling us it’s an 80-20 issue, so they didn’t help us,” she said, referring to polling on trans participation in girls sports. “It’s not an 80-20 issue. But if the question is put to voters as the status quo or a blanket ban, people will say yes to the blanket ban.” David’s view Roughly speaking, there are two kinds of ballot measures – those designed to bring out voters for one of the major parties, and those designed to pass no matter what the parties do. For years, Democrats hoped that ballot measures raising the minimum wage would help them change the electorate. Two decades ago, Republicans thought the same about ballot measures that banned same-sex marriage. But in many cases, voters simply took the chance to separate their partisan preference from their issue preference. This is what happened on Nov. 3, when Republicans got no lift at all from measures that were most attractive to their hardcore voters. events.title: Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences
events.summary: November 17, 2026 Category: AI Microsoft and Salesforce Announce Copilotforce, Bringing Trusted Customer Context and Action into Microsoft AI Experiences Microsoft Source | 8 minutes New integrations connect Salesforce with Microsoft Copilot, Teams and Fabric, helping enterprises turn Salesforce customer insights into action while maintaining existing security and permissions. New two-way Zero Copy integrations between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric enable organizations to securely query and analyze data across both platforms without maintaining duplicate datasets. Accenture is serving as design and implementation partner and pilot customer, deploying the integrations in its own global sales organization. REDMOND, Wash., and SAN FRANCISCO — Nov. 17, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) and Salesforce Inc. (NYSE: CRM) today announced Copilotforce, a new partnership that helps employees get more done in the tools they already use by bringing Salesforce customer context, business processes and actions into Microsoft Copilot and other AI-powered productivity experiences.   Unveiled at Microsoft Ignite, the partnership introduces new integrations across Microsoft Copilot, Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Fabric, including Salesforce in Copilot, a plugin available in public preview with 38+ prebuilt sales skills. Together, these capabilities help businesses move faster, reduce manual work and get more value from their existing technology investments — while maintaining the security, governance and permissions they already rely on.   Bringing Salesforce workflows together with conversations, meetings and documents in Microsoft 365 means less time spent moving between systems and more time on the work that matters. Salesforce in Copilot connects customer context with the work happening across the business so employees can make more informed decisions and take action without constantly switching applications. Microsoft Work IQ, the intelligence layer powering Copilot, provides relevant context from Teams meetings, Outlook emails and documents across SharePoint and OneDrive. Work IQ and Salesforce help sellers understand not only what’s recorded in CRM, but what’s happening across customer conversations and collaboration — and what needs to happen next.  Through authenticated Salesforce MCP access, sellers can securely retrieve customer information and take supported business actions within their existing Salesforce permissions. Salesforce continues to govern access and business actions, while Microsoft applies its existing enterprise compliance controls to communications and documents. Data, context and the apps where sellers work come to life in practical workflows across the sales cycle, including:  Grow Revenue . Use the Pipeline Review and Close Planning skills to decide which opportunities deserve attention and build a concrete path to signature. Customer priorities and deal context inform the proposals and business cases sellers develop in Word and PowerPoint, with clear owners, milestones and next steps.  Manage Risk. Connect Salesforce opportunity data with customer concerns raised in Outlook, escalations discussed in Teams and unresolved commitments. The Deal Review, Customer Health and Renewal Radar skills see beyond the recorded stage or renewal date to the customer concern in an Outlook thread, the escalation discussed in Teams or the unresolved commitment behind a stalled deal, helping sellers identify where to intervene.  Move faster. Turn customer conversations into follow-up drafts, internal recaps and proposed CRM activities using the Call Follow-Up skill. Sellers can review and confirm next steps instead of manually reconstructing conversations and updating multiple systems.    With Copilot as the front door to business process, Salesforce in Copilot allows organizations to bring together Salesforce data, workflows, agents and prebuilt skills from the systems they already rely on through Copilot’s open and interoperable platform.  “AI is only as powerful as the data and context that grounds it,” said Judson Althoff, CEO, Microsoft Commercial Business . “Bringing Salesforce customer data and sales skills together with the work context delivered by Work IQ in Microsoft Copilot allows our joint customers to unlock actionable insights across their core business applications. Copilotforce will give sales teams the intelligence they need to make faster, higher-confidence decisions while maintaining the governance and trust enterprises demand.”  “Through Copilotforce, we’re bringing Salesforce to the largest surface in enterprise software today, embedding trusted Salesforce context and intelligent sales workflows directly where sellers work,” said Miguel Milano, President & Chief Operating Officer, Salesforce . “By bringing together the #1 CRM with the #1 productivity surface, we’re transforming AI from a standalone tool into a powerful driver of productivity, smarter decisions and customer success.”  Expanding connection in the places people work   For many organizations, the work first starts in Microsoft Teams, where people share files, make decisions and hand work to each other. Sales Cloud in Teams, now available in pilot, brings Salesforce customer context directly into those conversations, so sellers can see pipeline and quota progress, get deal notifications and find briefing materials without leaving the place where decisions are already being made.   Across these Microsoft and Salesforce integrations, customer data remains protected at every boundary: Salesforce controls data access and governs supported business actions, while Microsoft ensures communications and documents adhere to existing enterprise compliance policies. Supported writeback actions to the CRM require explicit user confirmation and respect existing validation rules, so teams can act with confidence while customer records stay governed and auditable.  AI is only as useful as the context it can reach, and for many enterprises customer data lives in Salesforce while operational and financial data lives in Microsoft Fabric. Microsoft and Salesforce are bringing a two-way Zero Copy connection between Salesforce Data 360 and Microsoft Fabric, so teams can work with fuller context across both platforms without building pipelines or maintaining duplicate datasets.  With Data Federation, now generally available, joint customers can now directly query and analyze supported Microsoft Fabric OneLake data within Salesforce Data 360. A service agent can see a customer’s recent purchases on their account, a marketer can build a segment from spending behavior and an AI agent can answer from current data, all without moving the source data out of Fabric. events.title: Hank Paulson warns of ‘underestimating’ risk of AI unwind
events.summary: Markets are underestimating the risk surrounding AI, and governments worldwide must work more closely with private businesses in order to better mitigate the chances of a catastrophe or financial crisis, former US Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson said Tuesday. “I’ve never seen so much money chasing one opportunity with not a lot of earnings and ROI backing it up,” Paulson, a former Goldman Sachs executive, said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “People are underestimating the risk.” “It boggles my mind … people just brush aside this catastrophic risk,” he continued, speaking to Semafor’s Gina Chon. Former UK Prime Minister Rishi Sunak largely concurred with Paulson, adding that while regulatory efforts thus far — such as the EU’s AI Act — were “not the right approach … that doesn’t mean we do nothing.” “The worst thing would be if we had some type of catastrophic accident … then we will have, as we all know, an overreaction on the other side.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: GP clinic bought by Bupa encouraged doctors to bill expensive Medicare items
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bupa GP clinic urged doctors to bill costly Medicare items to lift revenue Topic: Doctors and Medical Professionals A Bupa clinic encouraged doctors to increase revenue by billing extra Medicare items. ( ABC News: Nic MacBean ) Bupa emailed GPs at one of its clinics to encourage increased billing of chronic condition management plans, which cost more than standard appointments. Senior doctors say they are concerned corporatised GP practices are prioritising profit over patient care, but Bupa has defended the email. The Department of Health says it is spending $147 million over four years to review the industry and improve compliance. A GP clinic operated by health insurance giant Bupa has encouraged doctors to lift their billing of more costly Medicare items. The ABC obtained a June email from a Bupa clinic to its GPs, which told doctors to ensure "revenue is increasing". The email asked doctors to do this by increasing the bookings of patients for costly Medicare checks known as "chronic condition management plans" (CCMPs). It further encouraged doctors to re-book patients, if they were eligible for further checks but Medicare rules prevented them from being claimed on the same day. CCMPs are personalised plans written by GPs, designed to create a structure to improve outcomes for people struggling with complex health conditions. The plans can be used for conditions ranging from eczema to heart disease, and while often beneficial to patients, they may not be essential for everyone with a chronic condition. The Medicare schedule fee for a GP to prepare a CCMP is $160.60, compared to $87.10 for a standard GP appointment lasting at least 20 minutes. The federal government's spending on the plans is rising rapidly and it is now spending nearly $1.3 billion a year on these chronic care plans out of the $35 billion Medicare budget. 'Need to explain' why items not billed In the email, Bupa told doctors their appointment books were closely scrutinised each day through the popular software portal Cubiko, for "possible service opportunities", and notes were left about what could be billed. Bupa operates 33 medical centres. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The booking software includes a specific function to check for chances to bill patients for "possible service opportunities", including the costly chronic care plans. The email also detailed how the "ops team" had tasked the practice managers with "ensuring revenue is increasing by ensuring there is an uptick in billings of HA [health assessments]". Cubiko spruiks that its "QuickCheck" function can help identify opportunities for billing patients more Medicare items. ( ABC News: Screenshot ) Bupa's email went on to list the Medicare item numbers for these health assessments, including chronic condition management plans and a nurse item. GPs were reminded that practice managers need to "ensure" an increase in patients being charged for these more expensive Medicare items, otherwise practice managers "need to explain why these are not being billed". In a statement, Bupa said the email was sent at one clinic and was an attempt to remind doctors to consider preventative care. "Patient needs, clinical judgement and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first," it said. Bupa said practice managers provided "administrative support to our doctors. Patient needs, clinical judgement, and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first and we reinforce this through ongoing guidance and training". Do you know more? Share it with us here . If GPs coerced, that 'has to be stopped' Policy analyst Terry Barnes was a senior adviser to two health ministers in the Howard government. He told the ABC he was not surprised by Bupa's email, and it was a window into how much corporate owners of GP clinics "called the shots". Terry Barnes says optional extras like chronic condition management plans should not become mandatory Medicare billings. ( ABC News: Billy Draper ) "If corporates are putting pressure on their doctors to order health assessments or any other type of extra service, and the optional extras become mandatory, then there is a real problem there," he said. "If they are actually putting pressure on the doctors, coercing them internally to behave in a certain way in relation to billing services and generating services, then that has to be stopped." Are private health insurers moving to US-style model? Increasing partnerships among health insurers, GP centres, and telehealth services raise concerns about a potential two-tier system in which privately insured patients have more affordable access to GP consultations.

events.title: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
events.summary: Flight delays are becoming more common, causing financial and emotional stress for travelers CHICAGO -- New airline tickets: $300. Hours waiting for luggage: four. And the topper: a four-hour Uber ride from Detroit to Chicago that cost $400. Call it outage math, a hellish calculation spawned by ever-more-common flight delays. This one was part of Angelina and Kyle Phoenix's anniversary trip to Chicago. On Friday, they flew from Jacksonville, Florida, into the maw of the Great Ground Stoppage of 2026 with as many as a million other travelers. Instantly, the financial and emotional toll of the four-hour flight outage radiated outward from the airports as everyone involved scrambled for costly workarounds to a crisis no one expected, can fully explain or wants to pay for. Emergency child care. Outrageous taxi ride fees. Rebooked tickets, lost vacation rentals and little idea what expenses might be reimbursed. But beyond finances, travelers told The Associated Press on Monday, perhaps the most consequential cost is also the most intimate: Stress and grief over time lost — a cumulative toll that is generally not, as customer service might say, eligible for reimbursement. Kyle Phoenix got a whiff of it more than 12 hours and hundreds of dollars of unexpected expenses into the couple’s journey, as he watched chaos unfold in the baggage claim area of Detroit airport. Officials, he noticed, had stopped announcing which canceled flights would disgorge checked baggage onto which turnstiles. Answers were hard to come by. That made decisions about what to do next increasingly difficult. “A lot of confusion, a lot of scrambling from a lot of people,” Kyle recalls of the scene. “I think that was probably the roughest part, not knowing anything.” When the couple finally retrieved their luggage at midnight, the $400 Uber ride began to look like the best option. They forfeited their rebooked flight — as well as a hotel room they would have stayed in for a few hours — and embarked on the four-hour ride to Chicago. “We just took the loss,” Angelina Phoenix said. Dread lingers around such events because they're getting more commonplace, with no end in sight. Even as travelers spoke to the AP about Friday's ground stop, United Airlines suffered a malfunction and halted its flights for 90 minutes. Several top U.S. banks reported significant slowdowns. And that was after AI chaos and Microsoft’s global meltdown just a few days earlier. Ahead loomed the busy Thanksgiving travel week, when TSA agents typically screen more than 2 million passengers nationwide. It was enough to make any thinking person ask: Could everything be broken? And it forced humanity to reckon once again with the fragility of the systems that anchor modern life. Delays are accelerating faster than the increase of scheduled passenger flights since the COVID-19 pandemic, the International Air Transport Association reported in July. Between 2015 and 2025, delays affecting scheduled passenger flights generated about $10.9 billion in costs for airlines and travelers, with sharp increases in holdups starting in 2021. The issues are costing travelers time, which even the Federal Aviation Administration agrees is worth money. Federal guidance issued a decade ago valued airline passengers’ time at $47.10 an hour, expressed in 2015 dollars. That's about $66 an hour today. The figure accounted for travel time that would otherwise be available for work or leisure. More recently, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond estimated that last year’s 43-day federal government shutdown caused roughly 1 million additional hours of passenger delays at six airports. Economist Russell Wong calculated the lost time’s value at $66 million, based on metro area wage data and the higher-than-average incomes of people who take flights. Wong excluded canceled flights. JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech Harder to measure is the loss absorbed by the population downstream from the airports, including hourly workers, freelancers and caregivers — in short, everyone affected by the ripples. Another cost: Trust in government, which has been low for years . The nationwide shutdown, the nation's longest in 25 years, could cost billions of dollars, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said over the weekend. He blamed a contractor and aging infrastructure . President Donald Trump testily pointed to Democrats , who in turn demanded answers about how the administration has spent billions it’s already been given and why its funding request has soared to $50 billion. Downplaying the event as a glitch with a faulty router raised questions, if not suspicions, one communications expert says. “It wasn’t simply a crisis, it was an actual emergency of impending disaster-level scale,” Shannon A.

events.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
events.summary: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source. Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.  Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September. Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.  Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.  The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.  But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.  Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA. El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions. Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

events.title: Amazon CEO says US AI lead over China depends on building more data centers
events.summary: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said Tuesday it would be a “historic mistake” for the US to pull back on its AI infrastructure buildout following the data center backlash during the midterm elections. “I cannot fathom any scenario where the United States stops building data centers and allows another country like China to establish all the norms,” Jassy said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. The US would regret such a move “for a very long time,” said Jassy, who has directed hundreds of billions into data centers around the world. Still, he acknowledged that tech companies need to “do it better and partner more closely with our communities.” Given Nvidia is so central to the AI buildout, Jassy said he didn’t think Jensen Huang’s departure would impact Amazon and pledged to continue working closely with the chipmaker. The growth in AI stems from “more than one company,” he said. Nvidia GPUs help power AWS data centers and Amazon works with the chip giant on infrastructure and robotics. “They’ll have to work out how they move forward as a company, but we’ll be partners with them either way.” Jassy also said that Amazon, which currently doesn’t let Meta’s Muse and other consumer agents access its site, is still talking to companies like Meta about how to open up the e-commerce giant to consumers who want to use the agents. He said the company would open up the site to agents if it could find a “good exchange of value” and a positive experience for customers, which isn’t happening at the moment. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
events.summary: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now , was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader . Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List , a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma , which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices . Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco . The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun. Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS project that is used by nearly half a million non-techie people. For many of Crosspoint Reader's users, it's the first time they have ever used open source. Some want tech support. Many demand features that can't fit into these tiny devices. Even when the requests are modest and feasible, such a large user base means that people want a wide range of functionality – and thanks to inexpensive cloud LLMs, even totally non-technical users can try to add new functions for themselves. The result is multiple code submissions every day. Many might fit on their own, but it's impossible to fit them all in. So many queries and submissions puts considerable stress on the volunteer maintainers. Mitchell mentioned a possibility that they – and we – had never dreamed of: that of pull requests (GitHub parlance for code submissions) from people using such extensive automation that the submitters don’t realize that they’re sending them. One submitter sent 10,000 pull requests in a single month. The problems aren't just technical, or workload-related: there's also a delicate balance of how to refuse well-intentioned and technologically viable submissions that just won't fit for non-technical reasons, such as being too niche for the typical use-case of a sub-£60 gadget. The problem is that this FOSS firmware is making these cheap gadgets so much more useful that re-flashing them is an implicit part of the purchase. That introduces all kinds of unexpected side-effects, for the users and for the developers. Crosspoint Reader is a microcosm of the rapid growth of Linux and FOSS in general – and a taste of what will happen if it ever goes truly mainstream with mass-market consumers. One of his "what I got wrong about this job" points we particularly liked was: “The scarce resource isn’t code. We have more code than we know what to do with." Instead, it's… "Judgement. Trust. Responsibility." There are lessons for the whole IT industry in there, we reckon. Even for the biggest players . In the meantime, though, these tiny cheap e-readers are an interesting new thing. As Mitchell put it, paraphrasing The Atlantic , they're: "Fun in a way gadgets haven’t been for a long time." Just being fun is a goal that is far too often forgotten… Especially in FOSS. ®

events.title: Defect-Aware Chiplet Matching For Heterogeneous Integration Yield (ASU, Ampere)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at Arizona State University and Ampere Computing published “DT-MATCH: Defect- and Topology-Aware Chiplet Matching for Yield Optimization in Heterogeneous Integration.” “Heterogeneous integration (HI) and advanced packaging enable chiplet-based system-on-chip (SoC) designs; however, they also introduce new yield challenges arising from manufacturing defects and complex die-to-die (D2D) interconnect constraints. In particular, lane-level defects, limited spares, and strict structural compatibility requirements impede the efficient assembly of functional systems from defective but repairable chiplets. We present DT-MATCH, a defect- and topology-aware chiplet matching framework that maximizes the number of functional SoCs under realistic assembly constraints. DT-MATCH provides two complementary approaches. The integer linear programming (ILP)-based approach is implemented using a batching strategy to approximate the exact formulation. The greedy randomized adaptive search procedure (GRASP)-based approach provides substantial acceleration, but it does not guarantee yield optimality. Both approaches use a preprocessing pipeline to reduce the problem size. Experimental results on industrial designs demonstrate that, as expected, the ILP-based approach achieves superior solution quality. The GRASP-based approach leads to lower runtimes while still achieving solution quality that is comparable to the ILP-based solution. Together, these methods provide a trade-off between solution quality and efficiency for practical chiplet assembly optimization.” Find the technical paper here . November 2026. events.title: Jensen Huang Says He’s Open to Coming Back to Nvidia
events.summary: Jensen Huang said that he is open to returning as chief executive of Nvidia , five days after he resigned from the company . In a statement published Tuesday morning on X, Huang said that since stepping down he has received an “ outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO.” “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote. Huang also thanked people who showed “kindness” to him and his family and acknowledged “the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met.” He reiterated his love for America and Nvidia and his remorse for his unfaithfulness to his wife, which he also expressed in a company-wide email sent last week. Huang resigned four days after Nvidia launched an internal investigation into an affair he had admitted to having with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen. Huang reportedly misled the company’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about the affair with Alice. The day before Huang stepped down, The New York Times reported that he'd had a second affair with one of his direct reports at Nvidia. After his resignation, Reuters reported on an alleged third affair with another Nvidia employee. The company’s code of conduct discourages "personal relationships" that "may create a conflict of interest." Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, was installed as interim CEO upon Huang’s resignation. The New York Times first reported Jensen’s association with Alice, also known as Huang Le, in October 2025. On November 6 of this year, citing an intelligence memo that reportedly circulated among Trump administration officials last spring, The New York Times and the Financial Times reported that intelligence officials believed Alice may be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump administration officials, including tech executive and White House Science and Technology advisory council cochair David Sacks, have questioned whether Alice was associated with the MSS. The Chinese government has rejected claims that Alice spied for the nation. WIRED reported last week that on the same day Huang resigned, Nvidia employees began using an existing petition to the board to call for his reinstatement . It gained more than 1,600 comments in just a few hours. A separate, public petition titled “ Stand With Jensen ” similarly calls for the executive’s return. At the time of writing, it has more than 193,000 online signatures, including more than 11,000 self-identified current and former Nvidia employees and more than 100,000 self-identified shareholders. On Friday, Elon Musk said that he was going to sign the petition, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan claimed that he had signed. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as CEO, adding that he believed Huang had “learned a big lesson.” Nvidia’s board of directors, however, reportedly said on Monday that it was not considering reinstating Huang as CEO. On Tuesday, the board announced that it had established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee “for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” In your inbox: For life-tested picks, sign up for our Gear newsletters Building social media apps isn’t cool anymore RIP to the unloved, unwanted Cybertruck Want better search results? events.title: SAP's cloud migration chief is migrating to Ionos as CEO
events.summary: SAP chief customer officer Thomas Saueressig is leaving the German software giant to become CEO of hosting and cloud provider Ionos. The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1. In January, Saueressig will begin handing over responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, currently a regional customer success president, who will take charge on an interim basis. SAP's supervisory board is searching for a permanent successor. Saueressig joined SAP's executive board in 2019 and became chief customer officer in April 2026. He leads the Customer Value Group and is charged with overseeing sales, customer success, services, and delivery, including adoption of SAP's cloud and AI products. In previous roles at SAP, Saueressig was responsible for customer services and delivery. He has also led product engineering, and has served as SAP's in-house CIO responsible for IT strategy and cloud transformation. He joined SAP in 2004 through its combined work-and-study program. His departure follows several changes at the top of SAP in recent years. In September 2024, CTO Jürgen Müller left by mutual agreement following an "incident" at a company event earlier in the year. In a statement, Müller said his behavior had been inappropriate. The company announced he would get paid €7.1 million following his departure. Chief revenue officer Scott Russell also left in 2024 by mutual agreement with the supervisory board. Julia White left the role of chief marketing and solutions officer in August 2024. "Thomas Saueressig has been a valued member of the Executive Board and has made significant contributions to SAP's transformation," said Pekka Ala-Pietilä, chair of SAP's supervisory board. "Over many years, he has helped sharpen SAP's focus on execution, customer value and operational excellence. We thank him for his commitment and wish him all the best for the future." Saueressig's departure comes as SAP pushes to move the ERP systems underpinning thousands of customers' businesses into the cloud – an effort whose operations and infrastructure he helped oversee. ®

events.title: Jensen Huang agrees to face Congress over Nvidia scandal
events.summary: Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter will officially testify before Congress in early December, lawmakers announced Tuesday. Why it matters: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology. Huang and Teter will participate in transcribed, closed-door interviews with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China select committees. Context: House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast (R-Fla.), House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Mich.) and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent letters to Huang, Teter and Commerce undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler on Nov. 12 , requesting they appear. The chairmen told Teter they were seeking information on alleged chip smuggling and the use of Nvidia products by U.S. adversaries, as well as the company's alleged export-control investigations. Kessler was expected to join a classified briefing with Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, but the meeting was postponed. What they're saying: "We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," the three committee chairmen said in a release . "We look forward to meeting with the Chairmen on December 2," Nvidia said in a statement. When reached for comment Tuesday, a representative for Huang pointed to a statement the former CEO made Tuesday about returning as CEO . What's next: Huang will appear before the committees on Dec. 1, and Teter will appear on Dec. 2. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced last week that Huang had stepped down as CEO over an alleged affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy and former executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International. Huang's resignation ignited requests from Congress to investigate his relationship with Megaspeed , a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to Nvidia's AI chips. Megaspeed faces its own investigations for allegedly smuggling chips into China, which the company denies. The big picture: Huang ties to President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have raised concerns from lawmakers about whether the government did enough to crack down on Nvidia's chips finding their way to China. events.title: Tech leaders tell Fed chairman Warsh how AI could transform the economy
events.summary: Just maybe, both the extreme techno-optimists and AI doom-and-gloomers are wrong about the economic impact of the technology. That's the argument that venture capitalist Marc Andreessen — who is co-leading a Federal Reserve task force on the topic — made in a high-profile panel Monday. Why it matters: The argument could help shape how the Fed assesses AI's economic consequences, with major implications for its outlook on growth, inflation and interest rates. Andreessen's argument offered an early glimpse of the thinking that will underpin his recommendations to the central bank's leaders. What they're saying: "My line has been both utopians and the doomers are going to be disappointed, specifically disappointed by the scope and magnitude of the real-world impact, and specifically the economic impact," Andreessen said at the San Francisco Fed. Andreessen, a co-leader of Fed chairman Kevin Warsh's Jobs and Productivity Task Force, spoke alongside former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo at a hearing in the Bay Area, where Warsh studied at Stanford and later spent 15 years teaching and conducting research. (Fellow task force member Chad Jones, a Stanford economist on leave for Anthropic, was in the audience but did not speak because the company is preparing to go public, Andreessen said.) Zoom in: Andreessen previewed his contribution to the task force's report, arguing that the economy is divided into two groups: Fast-changing industries, such as technology and media, where innovation drives productivity gains and lower prices. Slower-changing industries, including health care, education and housing, where regulations, limited competition and other barriers make technological progress harder. The intrigue: These slower-changing sectors account for some of Americans' biggest expenses. Those sectors of the economy "are not legally allowed to have rapid change," Andreessen said. Andreessen argued that regulations and other barriers could prevent AI from transforming large parts of the economy, which he says would limit job losses and productivity gains. " You might interpret this as good news because it means the AI revolution is not going to destroy all the jobs or kill everybody," he said. "You can also view this as very negative. Productivity growth just simply may not grow very much. Economic growth just simply may not grow very much. We may just continue to stagnate," he added. The big picture: Warsh is turning to influential outsiders to challenge how the central bank thinks about the economy. Affirm CEO Max Levchin told Warsh that AI has made the company's engineers five times more productive, cutting the cost of developing new features by 80%. Stripe CEO Patrick Collison said new businesses launching on its platform each week have doubled from a year ago, an unprecedented surge in its 15-year history. Unlike established companies, startups are more willing to let AI independently develop products and fix bugs, potentially allowing them to grow faster with fewer employees. What to watch: Executives said AI is already delivering productivity gains in traditional industries — including sectors Andreessen said are more resistant to technological change. Erik Wexler, CEO of Providence, a large nonprofit health system, said AI tools that transcribe patient appointments are saving some physicians two to four hours a day on paperwork. Wexler said that one doctor called it "life-changing." What's next: Warsh has asked all five task forces to recommend ways to improve Fed policymaking by year-end, though he cautioned last month that some may miss the deadline.

events.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
events.summary: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles. "Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public." Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update. That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months." It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note. Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models. In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. Google has been in touch to tell us that, despite its own FAQ saying that submitting feedback on Gemini conversations may mean they’re used to train AI, that’s definitely not happening. “This retained data will be used strictly for safety and security purposes,” a Google spokesperson told us. The spokesperson added that the increased retention is necessary because Gemini is so much more capable than it used to be, which has also increased risk vectors. “To ensure a more thorough and robust process, we’re lengthening the time from the 72-hour window to around two months to detect, report, and investigate complex emerging abuse scenarios,” Google added. “To be clear, this data [retained for ~two months] will strictly not be used for GAI model training or for other product improvement purposes.” ® Updated on November 18 to include comment from Google.

events.title: Iraq resumes pumping crude oil for export through pipeline to Turkey
events.summary: Iraq has resumed pumping crude oil for export through Turkey in a move expected to boost the economy and revitalise an industry paralysed by the war in Iran . Crude will be pumped through the 960km Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline at an initial rate of 120,000 barrels per day, Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Khudair said, the state-owned Iraqi News Agency reported on Tuesday. That will be gradually increased to hit a capacity of 500,000 bpd, after the “successful completion of maintenance, rehabilitation, technical and operational tests”, he added. “This achievement represents an important strategic step in enhancing Iraq's export capacity and diversifying crude oil export outlets.” It will also help in “generating additional financial revenues for the national economy, especially since exporting through the northern outlet allows for the marketing of crude oil without price discounts”, he added. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. More than 90 per cent of Iraq's budget is funded in dollars from oil exports, almost all of which must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The regional conflict has led to a sharp supply collapse for Iraq. Exports fell from 3.36 million bpd in February to 131,000 bpd in April. The result was a drop in monthly oil revenue that previously hovered around $7 billion. Baghdad has also announced the start of work on a new pipeline linking Basra to Haditha with a capacity of 2.5 million bpd, as it seeks new routes to export crude. But the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline remains crucial. In August, Iraq and Turkey signed a ​one-year agreement ⁠to continue crude oil ⁠flows at an export capacity of 750,000 bpd. Iraq is also driving efforts to boost its standing. At September's UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi appealed to the world to invest in Iraq as he pitched his economic and anti-corruption plans. Last month, the International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said it was advancing discussions with Iraq , as well as Lebanon , as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa. Iraq is also debating a draft federal budget for 2027 that would be the biggest in its history but the plan is also the most detached from the country's financial reality.
