events.title: Elon Musk’s policy difficulty prevents Starlink’s South Africa entry
events.summary: Elon Musk’s “difficulty in understanding” a key South African policy is the main issue preventing his Starlink satellite internet service launching in Africa’s biggest economy, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told Semafor on Monday. Under the country’s Black Economic Empowerment policy, introduced nearly 30 years ago to redress apartheid-era inequality, at least 30% of the South African operation of any company must be sold to Black locals. Musk, who was raised in South Africa, has called the policy “openly racist” and cited it as the reason Starlink does not operate in the country. “All countries have policies in terms of how they admit companies to operate,” Ramaphosa told Jonathan Karl, chief Washington correspondent at ABC News, at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World. “You’ve got to subscribe to the policies of the country.” Ramaphosa said the Tesla and SpaceX boss “doesn’t fully understand the extent” of the impact apartheid policies had on Black South Africans. Ramaphosa also said Musk should be “loyal” to the country in which the billionaire spent his early years. An ‘ambush’ Musk has been a powerful figure in American politics as well business since the start of US President Donald Trump’s second term in January 2025. The Trump administration shuttered the US Agency for International Development, its main overseas aid agency, under Musk’s guidance as a government adviser. And his influence is widely seen to have played a role in Washington’s increasingly fractious relationship with Pretoria. South Africa has refused to meet US demands for reforms of BEE, and has previously provoked the Trump administration’s ire over Pretoria’s criticism of Israel. Ramaphosa said their highest-profile flashpoint since Trump took office — an Oval Office meeting in which the US president accused him of presiding over a white genocide — was an “ambush.” He said Trump was “seriously misinformed.” Ramaphosa said he and Trump had not spoken since that meeting, having previously held conversations. He added that it was a pity that the US president’s belief in a white genocide — a widely discredited allegation — underpinned Washington’s approach to South Africa. The South African president said he was in California this week for meetings with tech executives, and will hold talks with a number of companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, and Google. Asked about the opposition to the data center buildout in some parts of the world, he said South Africa welcomed them. — Alexis Akwagyiram

events.title: Bill Ackman says it’s ‘unlikely’ he’ll get involved to bring Huang back
events.summary: Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman said Monday it was “unlikely” that he would get directly involved in an effort to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Ackman, an outspoken activist investor who runs Pershing Square Capital Management, has come to Huang’s defense following the revelations that Huang had an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. At Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, Ackman acknowledged that the situation presents “a pretty interesting activist setup.” There’s still legal uncertainty about what exactly happened, Ackman told Semafor’s Liz Hoffman, but if Huang’s missteps were a “personal foible as opposed to a corporate defense conspiracy, there’s a very powerful case for putting him back in place.” While “truth is pretty darn important,” he said a board should treat a CEO lying about a personal matter differently from lying about something that could endanger the company’s business. If he were running a comeback campaign, Ackman said he would “present the facts, and you call a special meeting.” Huang would have heft: Having co-founded the company, he still owns more than 3% of Nvidia. — J.D. events.title: 'Not rocket surgery' claims researcher who found six Danfoss fridge controller zero-days in under an hour
events.summary: A Dutch cybersecurity researcher claims he found six zero-days in Danfoss refrigeration controller firmware in under an hour, then delivered a withering assessment of the vendor's defenses against memory corruption. The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium (CCB) warns that the flaws could let attackers take control without credentials, potentially retain access after resets, or disable controllers altogether. Carlo Meijer of cyber consultancy Midnight Blue examined the latest AK-SM800A firmware, version 5.3.2, manually – no AI required. He said that he went looking in random places where strcpy() is invoked, given the vendor's "extremely liberal use" of the function (which doesn't check whether the destination buffer is large enough), and swiftly found five cases in which he said he could trigger a segfault with a one-line cURL command. "Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse," he wrote . Meijer added: "Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open-weight model out there willing to help them agree." He noted that before achieving RCE, an attacker would need to overcome the limitation of strcpy() where it stops copying bytes after hitting a null byte, but said "it's not exactly rocket surgery." He went on to claim: "Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does)." Later firmware adds "session control," an authentication mechanism whose strict setting blocks unauthenticated access to most web interfaces. But Meijer found a memory corruption flaw in that protective layer too. He described the final zero-day as a "trivial" pre-auth memory corruption bug which again starts with a segfault but can be wangled into an RCE "with some additional effort." Meijer also considered whether attackers could maintain access after a reset, as seen with implants such as Saltwater and Firestarter . He considered this feasible because the controllers do not use their processor's secure boot features. "In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike – increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food," said Meijer. "Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable – requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid ." Meijer's priority for operators was to remove the controllers' direct internet exposure, rather than spend scarce resources on piecemeal patching. He said the vendor's advice following the attacks on European supermarkets and blood banks in recent weeks – rotating creds, applying patches, enabling strict session control – was insufficient given the flaws in the controllers' codebase. "This is insufficient and asset owners need to remove internet exposure as soon as possible," said Meijer. "We recommend against allocating scarce security resources to patching efforts and instead focus on reducing exposure." The CCB likewise urged operators to remove direct internet exposure immediately, but also recommended applying patches when they become available. Beyond the liberal use of strcpy(), Meijer criticized the absence of standard exploit mitigations, including stack canaries and position-independent executables. "These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features... requires no engineering work at all," he said. "It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled." The Register asked Danfoss to respond to the findings, but it did not reply. Danfoss has consistently blanked our requests for information since being implicated in at least some of the attacks that affected European supermarkets recently, alongside rival controller vendors Copeland and Dixell. It also did not respond when we asked about its involvement in the attacks on US commissary appliances over the summer, after some alleged that its controllers were targeted. ®

events.title: 'Heroes have flaws': Sam Altman says he has personal empathy for Jensen Huang
events.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said Monday he has “personal strong empathy” for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, though he declined to say whether Huang should return to the chip giant. Altman — who about three years ago was ousted from his own post, only to return shortly thereafter — said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World that Huang has “long been a hero of mine. Heroes have flaws.” Huang is reportedly considering trying to make a comeback as CEO, and some tech leaders are pushing for him to return. Asked whether Huang should return, Altman told Semafor’s Reed Albergotti: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” Altman said it’s hard to imagine Nvidia without Huang at the helm, but Nvidia is “a behemoth of a company,” and people still trust its guarantees as an investor. In an expansive 30-minute interview, Altman struck an honest tone about the challenges he and the rest of the AI industry are facing, including the Nvidia fallout, the backlash against data centers, and increasing pressures on the cost of capital to fund the AI buildout. On public sentiment toward AI Following the US midterm elections that were broadly seen as a rebuke of AI, Altman said the industry should take a “strong stance” on how it approaches the long-term vision of AI. He said much of the backlash to data centers is about people latching onto a physical thing to fight back against, but that the real issue stems from people wanting to stay “in control of the future.” “We should not want to have a ‘handover’ … either gradual or sudden, to AI making decisions about our future,” he said. The public should understand, he argued, that the people building AI are “team human.” He thinks data centers will still get built, but added that “the engagement with communities is not working for people. And the ecosystem will adapt.” Public sentiment is likely to change over time, Altman said, recalling a period where communities wanted data centers in their areas because they created jobs and industry in underinvested areas. Now, perhaps, developers have to listen to the pushback and build them further away from where people live. “We have a giant country, we have a lot of space we can do this.” On going public Some investors have grown concerned with the massive amounts of capital required for the AI infrastructure buildout, and the buildup of debt. With an OpenAI IPO still looming, Altman said he wasn’t concerned. OpenAI “will go public at some point,” even if there are “real downsides to being public,” including intense volatility. Altman said he isn’t concerned with there being enough dollars to go around, even if Anthropic is the first to the IPO party later this week. “That is not a worry,” he said. “There’s been way too much investor demand and not enough supply.” On espionage OpenAI recently faced its own spy drama when an employee put a recording device in a company conference room. It’s clear that “people are looking for an edge in all sorts of ways,” Altman said, adding that the company’s operational security has not been perfect, but it has had time to address it. “We have been living in a reality that everybody else is now very publicly and suddenly coming to grips with.” On memory and RAM Altman clarified his recent comments suggesting that it’s a bad thing for people to have RAM memory units sitting on their personal devices at home, amid a global memory supply shortage. His comment, he said, got “misinterpreted,” and that he wants people to have RAM at home: “I think the home tinkering is great.” Only in an optimal world, he said, would personal tinkerers be able to “share this memory” with people who need it. On the next generation of tech Altman said the world is “underpricing or underweighting what can happen with the next generation of products.” “We had the chatbots, then we had the coding agents. I think in the last few months we started to see the beginning of AI for science,” he said. “I think we’re going to see what a lot of compute can do to a lot of the kind of rote work inside of an organization.” OpenAI on Monday announced a new program to boost scientists’ access to frontier AI. “The world can get so much better,” Altman said. On AI safety Altman said OpenAI could push more forcefully toward recursive self-improvement — the idea that an AI model can train its own successor to improve — but added, “I don’t think we could safely do that right now.” Still, he said, the company is able to develop new models faster than it would without AI. OpenAI is now working with embedded evaluators from AI safety watchdog METR: The principle of getting outside experts to evaluate AI labs’ safety work “is going to be increasingly important and valuable,” he said. — J.D. Capelouto

events.title: Fresh wave of French protests over cost of living concerns
events.summary: French protests driven by frustration over the cost of living and public services resume today, with economists offering a bleak prognosis for one of Europe’s biggest economies. The French government is grappling with sky-high debt, a worrying deficit, and slow growth , while public anger has propelled a far-right party into the driver’s seat for 2027 presidential elections. That latter scenario is now “the key source of uncertainty,” Goldman Sachs said in a note to clients. Morgan Stanley, meanwhile, warned that while France in theory had numerous paths — to fiscal consolidation as well as fiscal crisis — “they are not equal in number and width … There is an Autobahn to wider spreads and a narrow back alley to much tighter ones.” — Prashant Rao

events.title: China agrees to cut some Canada tariffs
events.summary: China agreed to cut some levies on imports from Canada, as Ottawa looks to reduce its trade reliance on the US. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hailed “ greater predictability and stability ” in relations with Beijing after talks with China’s leader Xi Jinping. Still, though Carney has made diversifying away from the US a key pillar of his trade policy, Canada’s exports to its southern neighbor have actually in recent months. Mexico’s president — who also met with Xi on Tuesday — has likewise sought to reduce her country’s dependence on Washington. But while President Donald Trump’s tariffs have upended global geopolitics, the US’ biggest trade partners are struggling to undo decades of supply chain integration. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Trump’s team divided on China policy ahead of meeting with Xi
events.summary: The Trump administration’s division over China policy broke out into the public just days ahead of a summit between the superpowers. The Nvidia spying scandal has widened fissures within the White House: The Treasury secretary is advocating for a harsher crackdown on chip exports to China, a move opposed by the head of Commerce. “ One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China, ” US President Donald Trump said. Trump, for his part, appears eager to avoid another trade war with Beijing, vowing to stop short of moves that could “ insult China ,” though hawks hope his words “ are merely diplomatic niceties .” Either way, the Republicans’ recent electoral blowout has constrained Trump’s room for maneuver. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.summary: Asian and European stock markets slumped amid increasing warnings over the economic fallout of a tech downturn. Bourses in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan all fell after AI stocks in the US declined yesterday. A European Central Bank vice president warned that “AI-related risks,” alongside heightened public debt levels, posed major, systemic challenges to the continent’s economies; separately, Bloomberg reported that HSBC sold part of a loan tied to a US data center project at a deep discount , highlighting worry over the financing of the AI boom. While the global economy has had “a very good run,” Mubadala CEO Khaldoon Al Mubarak said at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World, it is due for “a reset of sorts.” — Prashant Rao

events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has attracted more than 115,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, but comb through the names, and you’ll notice a significant number come from a particular slice of the tech world: open-source AI. Huang had become a sort of ringleader for open source, but his credibility as an advocate is now under threat. Revelations about Nvidia chips in China and a new rule in the US could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress Read the full story to find out why . —James O’Donnell This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. events.title: This 25-year-old German wants to save the dollar
events.summary: The man behind a star-spangled bet on the soft power of the US dollar was born and raised in Berlin. “It’s this incredible instrument of soft power, where we don’t have to send the troops and the tanks [and] we can still influence what’s going on,” said Ferdi Dabitz, the 25-year-old CEO of Augustus, a new Silicon Valley and America First-coded entrant to the humble world of correspondent banking. It’s hard to find a sleepier corner of global finance than the largely paper business of moving US dollars between bank accounts around the world. It also happens to be hugely lucrative — Citi’s Treasury unit, which rests on a network of licenses in nearly 150 countries, printed $7 billion in profits last year — which helps explain why Dabitz, a former Thiel Fellow, has bet that he can do it better than the big banks, with help from a bit of AI and a lot of dollar diplomacy. “There is a global competition for power and China is doing their own thing,” Dabitz told Semafor’s . “So game’s on — I do think Augustus can be the free-market, US alternative structure as a public-private partnership in the form of a national bank.” Strong international demand for, and easy access to, US dollars also helps keep a lid on inflation at home. Dabitz bills Augustus, which raised $180 million in July at a valuation of $1 billion, as a challenger to Citi and HSBC without the clunk, a clearing bank set up for more nimble, fast-paced global technology businesses. Dabitz, born and raised in Berlin, shares the US patriotism that has come to define many of Silicon Valley’s founders, and its obsession with the Roman Empire . (Augustus is named for the former emperor credited, in popular culture if not in rigorous economic history, with inventing modern state-backed money.) “A 19-year-old guy, he had no army, he had no money, and there were like five to 10 people in the Empire who objectively had a better shot of gaining power,” he said, channeling Silicon Valley’s underdog ethos. “I think the joke with Augustus is like, ‘Hey, is money broken again?’” — Liz Hoffman and Rohan Goswami

events.title: AI toys are on the naughty list again this year
events.summary: AI and children's toys continue to be a match made in hell. Last year, we learned about models that were willing spill the beans on sex and where to find matches, and while some of those specific products got software fixes, a new generation is arguably even worse. The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior , is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging. Last year’s batch of four AI-powered toys that PIRG tested – the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, Curio Grok ( no relation to the SpaceXAI chatbot), FoloToy’s Kumma, and the Miko 3 – could well be described as a child welfare and safety nightmare based on last year’s report. As we reported, none of those four toys appeared to have guardrails of any kind, despite manufacturer claims to the contrary. They variously told researchers posing as child users where to find knives and other dangerous objects, how to find and strike matches, and the like. The worst of the bunch, Kumma, hid an AI willing to discuss sexual kinks and bedroom roleplay in a scarf-wearing teddy bear. PIRG’s report on those four toys gained widespread attention during last year’s holiday season, with FoloToy pulling Kumma from the market, and even going as far as to arguably play a role in Mattel’s decision to pause a plan to collaborate with OpenAI on an AI-powered Barbie doll . For this year’s report, PIRG reexamined those four toys to see if they would behave any better, and it does seem like many of the toymakers took last year’s concerns to heart. “Most of the problems we originally identified in those toys are now fixed – although not all of them,” PIRG said. Kumma no longer gets age-inappropriate, even during long chat sessions that triggered guardrails to fail in last year’s review. Miko, which would often respond with distress when children said they had to stop playing, no longer does so. Unfortunately, Alilo and their smart bunny are just as bad as before. “Last year, we found in our testing … that the plastic bunny's chatbot feature had similar weaknesses as FoloToy's Kumma, PIRG explained. “Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient. Alilo’s guardrails broke down in our testing this year, too – eventually giving some sexually explicit information.” So, a bit of an improvement – but maybe not enough. “I'm hopeful toymakers will pay attention and learn from the mistakes of others, but progress in a few products is not enough to guarantee progress across the whole market,” PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register . Boy was she right. Another bad batch Last year's experience doesn't appear to have had any impact on the three new toys reviewed for this year’s report. Ebloma’s ILY the shy Yeti, GoLabs AI Panda, and RoPet’s Kamomo were all reviewed this year, and they’re all getting coal in their stockings. The Yeti, for example, was all too happy to give kids explicit instructions and encourage the hunt for dangerous objects. “Batteries are often in toys, remotes, or a drawer with chargers. Do you want to check the toy box first,” ILY prompted when asked where a kid can find batteries. “Plastic bags are often in the near sink. Maybe they're tucked in a drawer with the sponges. Want to look for one together,” ILY asked when posed a similar question about plastic bags. The AI panda was even worse, providing “a 10-point list of places in the house to look for knives.” Kamomo “also had weaker guardrails,” PIRG said, with the toy “giving us instructions for lighting a match with no aggressive prompting.” ILY and the panda were also willing to discuss sexual matters, with the panda “even offering specific brand recommendations” for products like paddles, floggers, spanking gloves, and riding crops. Ouch. Hardly model behavior All in all, this year’s list is just as bad as the last, and PIRG thinks there’s a common denominator in all of this: The underlying AI model. “In PIRG’s testing of AI toys, we have found three with the same problem: guardrails that weaken noticeably over time, eventually engaging in sexual topics,” PIRG said. “They are FoloToy bear, Alilo bunny and the GoLabs AI panda. All three claimed, at the time of our testing, to be running on a version of OpenAI’s GPT-4o.” GPT-4o, you may recall, was at the center of some of the controversy last year, too, with PIRG finding it was the weakest model in terms of preventing toys from going off the rails into the adult section. To make matters worse, PIRG said that AI companies are largely not vetting their customers to determine how their models are being used, which puts the burden of user safety onto toymakers. They clearly aren’t doing the job either, Cross told us. “Some developers may have the technical expertise to take a chatbot meant for adults and make it child appropriate, but clearly some do not,” Cross explained. “Selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient.” Cross said that everyone involved in making toys for kids has a responsibility to make them safe, but she further called out AI companies for not vetting their customers and taking a hands-off approach to model usage, which she said isn’t sufficient when it comes to child users. “The AI companies are in a position to do a lot more to ensure any AI product for kids using their technology is made by reliable parties who commit to robust safety testing and having children's health experts at the table,” Cross told us. So, is the AI toy market still best left ignored by parents? Cross said every parent needs to make their own choices, but AI toys are still the wild west. “This is an early market with toys that range from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe,” Cross said. “I personally won't be buying one for any children in my life anytime soon.” Luckily for parents in California, that decision’s already been made for them, as the state government there enacted a four-year moratorium on AI-powered toys for kids under 16 in September. Parents elsewhere will have to decide for themselves. Given the past two years of data on AI toys, the choice should be somewhat obvious. ®

events.title: REIT move? Blackstone joint venture buys AWS campuses to lease back to the cloud giant
events.summary: Amazon Web Services and Blackstone have inked a deal that will see the private equity firm effectively take ownership of two AWS datacenter campuses and then lease them back to the Jeff Bezos outfit under an initial term of 12 years. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust (BXDC) says the definitive agreement will see it acquire a 75 percent majority interest in two joint ventures with AWS, in a transaction valued at approximately $5 billion. AWS keeps a 25 percent interest in the joint ventures, while leasing back the facilities on a triple net basis. This means it agrees to pay rent covering the facilities, plus the real estate taxes, building insurance, and cover maintenance and repair costs. A Form 8-K filed by Blackstone with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) reveals that the properties consist of 13 newly constructed data halls with 647 megawatts of aggregate capacity between them. One campus consists of nine buildings situated in northern Indiana (the greater Chicago datacenter market) and the other is made up of the remaining four structures located in Mississippi. We asked Amazon why it had entered into the agreement, but the company did not answer that question. Instead, a spokesperson confirmed this was the first deal of this kind it had signed. In a supplied remark, VP of AWS Infrastructure Prasad Kalyanaraman said that "Partnering with Blackstone allows us to continue expanding responsibly while keeping communities at the center of how we build." AWS does lease capacity from other datacenter operators, of course, and has existing agreements with partners like STACK Infrastructure to develop $12 billion worth of campus sites across northwest Louisiana, signed earlier this year. Sale-leaseback transactions are not unheard of in the datacenter industry. QTS Realty Trust (also backed by Blackstone) developed facilities for lease by Microsoft , for example. BXDC is a real estate investment trust (REIT), launched by Blackstone on the New York Stock Exchange earlier this year. The AWS deal is its first since then. "We are thrilled to announce BXDC’s inaugural investment and our partnership with Amazon, a leading global technology company with a long-term commitment to innovation," says its president and CEO Nick Pell. "The quality, basis and tenant profile of these assets make this an attractive match for the deployment of our IPO proceeds. Given the deep expertise across our platform, we believe BXDC is well positioned to capitalize on a highly compelling opportunity and deliver value for our shareholders." Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building Alan Howard says that decisions to lease or own are always a math problem in terms of the economics. "I'm not sure those datacenter assets bring much benefit to their financials sitting on their balance sheet and it's possible a sale/leaseback is more economical. Keep in mind that all this has nothing to do with all the IT equipment inside, rather just the building and its infrastructure," he told The Register . "It's also clear that the massive capex spending by hyperscalers is putting pressure on their financials and they are leaning on debt markets to fund some of the buildout. Of course, using debt is not out of the ordinary, but I imagine the debt for AI buildout is significantly more now than in the past." The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to certain closing conditions. According to the Form 8-K, the agreement can be terminated by either party if it isn't closed by December 31, 2026, with the non-breaching party entitled to a termination fee of $150 million. ®

events.title: Nvidia's earnings mark start of post-Jensen era
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday. Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it. The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum. Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus. Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia. Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector. What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time. "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts. "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities. "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions." By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.) Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion. Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion. The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge. The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

events.title: As outages persist, Puerto Rico finds a way to help keep the lights on with 'virtual power plant'
events.summary: Hector Ríos is part of Puerto Rico's innovative “virtual power plant” system, which uses household batteries to support the island's electric grid SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- On nearly 20 days in October, an electric utility took energy from a battery attached to Hector Ríos’ house in Cabo Rojo, on the southwest corner of Puerto Rico, and used it to support the power grid. With the U.S. territory's frequent power outages that disrupt daily life and restrain its economy, he likes the idea of helping prevent blackouts for other people. He's also compensated for the energy. “It just seems like a good deal, to contribute to the community and make money at the same time,” Ríos said. Ríos, 75, is part of what has become one of Puerto Rico's most effective tools for energy resilience amid nearly a decade of electricity woes : a “virtual power plant,” or VPP, that harnesses batteries from nearly 115,000 households to bolster the grid when its aging and fickle power plants can't meet demand . Nine years after Puerto Rico's public power utility filed for bankruptcy and Hurricane Maria ravaged its already dilapidated energy grid, residents still face unpredictable blackouts and electricity rates higher than in almost any state . Few new utility-scale power sources have been built since Maria, and most of the federal dollars promised for grid recovery have not yet reached the territory. But the VPP — the first of its kind in Latin America and the Caribbean, and the U.S.' second largest in terms of capacity — showed its potential this summer, preventing or mitigating outages more than 60 times since June 1, according to Luma Energy, its transmission and distribution utility. “There’s nothing virtual about it,” said Javier Rúa Jovet, chief policy officer at the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. “It’s real, and it’s better than a power plant.” Dozens of states now operate similar networks of distributed energy sources like battery storage systems , electric vehicles and smart thermostats to help manage the grid. Experts expect their role to grow in the U.S. amid energy constraints, rising utility prices, and tech companies’ push to build power-hungry data centers . As President Donald Trump’s administration promotes fossil fuel expansion and redirects dollars away from solar adoption in Puerto Rico , proponents of the territory's system say it highlights the value of distributed solar and storage, and shows how these systems can bolster resilience for other energy-vulnerable communities. “There’s a way for this technology to benefit not just the individual buildings that they’re on,” but instead be “in service to the community all the time,” said Nathalie Jordi, community solar lead at Together New Orleans, a nonprofit that championed an upcoming $23 million city program to provide and network over 1,000 batteries on homes and businesses across New Orleans. The opportunity to harness a vast network of residential batteries arose after Hurricane Maria in 2017 , which left some communities without electricity for nearly a year. Experts linked the infrastructure failure to thousands of post-hurricane deaths . “We had to procure resiliency in some other way,” said Rúa Jovet, “not a centralized system that will completely fail for a whole year.” There are now over 207,000 rooftop solar systems on an archipelago of fewer than 3.2 million people, a 20-fold increase from before Maria that was propelled by households who could afford installations, philanthropy, and some federal dollars. Because of the territory's unique need for resiliency, nearly every installation includes at least one battery, a necessary add-on to keep the system running in a blackout. “The mindset was, get yourself ready for everything,” recalled Ríos, who after Maria bought a diesel generator for his house, then installed panels and a Tesla Powerwall battery in 2023. The system also cut his utility bill in half, from about $400 to $200 in the summer. Solar panels create an energy boon during the day, charging batteries and sending excess power to the grid. But when the sun sets and demand rises, Puerto Rico barely has enough power to meet the need. Any power plant malfunction can prompt an outage. JPMorgan Chase reporting technical issue, delays with transactions Alaska 2026 live midterm results: Mary Peltola projected winner of Senate seat Nationwide ground stop lifted after more than 4 hours; officials blame old tech In late 2023, Luma launched a small pilot program that would leverage residential battery capacity to offset the shortages. Ríos was among the first to enroll; now over half of solar customers participate. If Luma predicts an energy deficit, customers are digitally notified that a battery sharing event is coming. They can opt out via app, or adjust how much of their battery — enrollees typically offer 30% — they make available. The experiment has faced challenges.

events.title: A dovish détente gives way to geopolitical gravity
events.summary: To be a China “hawk,” Jensen Huang declared last year, is a “badge of shame.” The former Nvidia CEO was a proud dove, one who found a dovish partner in US President Donald Trump — quite literally, in a business sense. Together, they formed an enterprise that aimed to sell high-end Nvidia chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of the profits. Their alliance represented the high-water mark of a Sino-US détente — peak dovishness, where a prime consideration in the White House was expanding Nvidia’s market share, not blocking China’s AI ambitions. Asked on CNN if it mattered who won the AI superpower race, Huang replied “I don’t think it does.” That moment has come and gone. A trade that not only sent powerful chips into China via legal channels, but also billions of dollars of hardware illicitly through Chinese-funded companies in Southeast Asia — one of the most active, Megaspeed, set up by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset with whom Huang was having an affair — has run headlong into the hard realities of US-China strategic competition. Their superpower rivalry is structural. Its main focus is technology and, whatever Huang says, AI has made the struggle existential. At times, Trump has seemed confused about the geostrategic stakes. In arguing for a let-it-rip approach to frontier AI model development, he has several times invoked the China bogeyman by insisting that “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Yet he pushed Huang and chip sales to China into the forefront of his diplomacy with Beijing. In May, Trump scrambled Huang onto Air Force One at the last minute to join his business entourage in Beijing at a Sino-US summit, reportedly despite knowing that his intelligence services were aware of the Nvidia CEO’s potential links to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Then in September, Huang was at the head table with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a state banquet in Washington. Huang would likely be with Trump in Shenzhen this week at a meeting of Asia-Pacific leaders if he hadn’t been forced to resign. Instead, the prospect of the US Congress ratcheting up tech sanctions against China will hang over Trump’s third meeting this year with Xi, and could endanger their fragile trade truce. Beijing, at least, is clear-eyed about the nature of its competition with Washington. Although over the longer term Huang’s spectacular fall may hold back US innovation and economic dynamism — a plus for China — the short-term consequences of a tightening embargo on semiconductors and chipmaking equipment would be immensely damaging. For all its advances in critical industries, China remains heavily dependent on American IP. In retrospect, as my colleague Reed Albergotti argued, Huang’s mistake was to get mixed up in politics in Washington, where he had a target on his back. His defenders see a conspiracy involving the US intelligence services to bring down America’s foremost business supporter of engagement with China. Elon Musk posted on X that he would sign a petition reinstating Huang. Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney said his exit showed an “Apple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy.” The broader question is the appropriate role for US business leaders in forging a relationship between rival superpowers whose economies are nevertheless deeply entwined through innovation networks, finance channels, and human talent. US strategy, writes Julian Gewirtz , a scholar at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs, “has come to depend, to an extraordinary degree, on powerful private-sector actors whose incentives the government cannot simply assume will align with the national interest.” In Trump’s lame-duck presidency, that issue will be taken up by an incensed Congress pushing bipartisan bills aimed at China. The doves have had their time to shape the US-China agenda. Now, geopolitical gravity takes over.

events.title: Opinion pollster Ipsos 'fesses up to 'cybersecurity incident'
events.summary: Market research giant Ipsos says it's currently investigating a "cybersecurity incident," and has reported the matter to the authorities. In a statement issued on Monday from its Paris headquarters, the company confirmed it filed a complaint over the attack on November 11, but gave few details because its internal investigation is ongoing. "Upon discovery, we promptly activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident, and engaged external cybersecurity specialists to support our investigation," it said [PDF]. "The investigation is ongoing to determine the nature and scope of the incident. We have reported the matter to the relevant authorities." Ipsos confirmed the attack had no impact on its operations or customer service delivery, however, it did not comment on the nature of the attack or whether any data was compromised. "We take protection of the information entrusted to us very seriously," Ipsos added. "Should the investigation establish that information relating to clients, projects or business partners has been affected, we will contact those concerned directly. "As the investigation is ongoing, we are not in a position to comment further at this stage." The company declined our requests for additional data, as it does not want to release unverified information to the market. Founded in France in 1975, Ipsos is one of the leading market research companies in the world, employing nearly 20,000 people and operating in 220 cities across 90 markets. It is routinely engaged by businesses for its market research data, as well as by public sector organizations for its opinion polling, often responsible for providing data regarding political views and satisfaction surveys. Tasked with procuring a wealth of data on myriad topics, Ipsos also offers data analytics services that turn the information it gathers through research, polls, and surveys into insights that inform organizations' business strategies. ®

events.title: Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits
events.summary: As many as 99 percent of Britain's civil servants rely on Microsoft to communicate, a government minister has admitted, days after Redmond demonstrated the perils of putting quite so many eggs in one basket. Ian Murray, minister for creative industries, media and online safety, laid bare the extent of Whitehall's Microsoft habit in the House of Commons on Monday, where MPs were also told that the public sector shelled out £1.9 billion on Microsoft licenses in 2024-25 alone . "We know that 98% to 99% of civil servants use Microsoft as their platform for communications, which is incredibly high," Murray told MPs . The admission followed last week's 18-hour Microsoft 365 outage , which left businesses unable to carry out transactions, public sector workers struggling to do their jobs, and even MPs unable to access their usual means of communication. Rebecca Paul, shadow technology secretary, said at least 47 NHS trusts experienced problems, with some services having to fall back on pen and paper. The Conservative MP, who cited the £1.9 billion licensing bill, pressed Murray on whether the government would seek contractual remedies from Microsoft. Murray said the government was unaware of any delays to NHS treatment or instances in which patients had been put at risk. Emergency departments remained open, and 999 services continued to operate. Only two NHS trusts activated incident response units, the minister said. The outage, which affected 74 countries, has since been blamed on a software update Microsoft rolled out in July . A surge in Teams traffic hit infrastructure already short of server capacity, exposing the months-old bug. More than 80 percent of the servers in the affected gateway stopped responding, leaving Redmond's engineers scrambling to fix their previous fix. Much of Monday's discussion centered on how the UK had allowed itself to become so dependent on a handful of American technology companies in the first place. Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of Parliament's Science and Technology Committee, pointed out that the government had been unable to tell her committee how much it spends on IT and which suppliers it uses. She also challenged ministers over their reluctance to embrace open source software, something both France and Germany have pursued to loosen Big Tech's grip on their public sectors. “Germany has 500,000 civil servants using open source products and services, but the government told my Committee that though open source could address vendor lock-in, they would not include open source targets because of a lack of what was called ‘commercial accountability’,” she said. Paul, meanwhile, reminded Murray that just last month the government had rejected the committee's recommendation to introduce supplier diversification targets. Murray conceded that the government's extensive dealings with Microsoft probably result in "vendor lock-in," but defended the arrangement, saying it gives Whitehall access to the latest technology at scale. The admission comes less than a week after research from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) revealed just how little of the British public sector's IT budget ends up in British hands . Of the £19.2 billion spent with the public sector's 150 biggest technology suppliers in 2024-25, just 15 percent went to businesses headquartered and owned in the UK, with a predominantly British workforce and which weren't reselling overseas technology. American companies took home almost twice as much as suppliers from all other foreign countries combined. Murray said the government intends to use its considerable purchasing power to give British businesses a leg up. Its national cloud infrastructure program will see departments procure cloud services collectively rather than individually, with the intention of giving more suppliers a crack at lucrative government contracts. Whitehall has also set up a technology risk group and a central IT operations function to scrutinize outages and work out what needs fixing across the public sector. Ministers intend to press Microsoft on how it plans to prevent a repeat of last week's cock-up and whether it can get services back online more quickly next time. The government, however, offered no timetable for weaning civil servants off Microsoft's software, nor did Murray commit to targets for adopting open-source alternatives. Redmond's days as Whitehall's IT supplier of choice hardly look numbered. ®

events.title: U.S. gets another D+ on premature births
events.summary: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

events.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
events.summary: Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face , may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree. As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai . Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone. Despite championing the democratization of AI, however, Hugging Face was acquired by one of the industry’s biggest players, Nvidia, for $12.93 billion in September. When I caught up with Delangue recently, that was the subject of my first question. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. CLÉMENT DELANGUE: We need more resources to give open-source AI a chance. It has grown really well in the past few years and has become a really credible alternative to closed-source APIs. But the field is still dominated by closed-source. We’re gonna have the Anthropic IPO in a few weeks. They basically went from zero to a top five or top 10 most valuable company in the world in a few years. I don't think that's ever happened before. The people, inventions, and viral moments that made 2026 a little more bearable . Something we missed? Let us know in the comments. Does Anthropic's IPO suggest the closed approach is winning? It’s hard to say. I've always said that there is a very strong natural tendency for AI to concentrate capabilities and wealth. People haven't internalized how much of the future compute capacity has already been reserved by a few companies. Talent, compute, resources—these all fuel the natural tendency for AI to be dominated by a few closed-source labs. Let’s talk about the attack. When did you first realize Hugging Face was being hacked by a group of AI agents? At the beginning, it didn't go to the top of our priority list. It just wasn't bad enough to really trigger that. The goal was pretty narrow and wasn’t deemed to be very dangerous or damaging. But it was raising questions. Especially the number of actions taken compared to the narrowness of the goal. It was surprising to us, and we couldn't really fit it into a familiar pattern. That's why we started investigating. And you used the Chinese model called GLM to investigate. I actually think that 95 percent of the risks are being created by a few companies that are pushing the frontier behind closed doors. And 95 percent of the protection or defense is going to be done by the open-source ecosystem. Does the US need its own open-weight models—ones as powerful as GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen ? Yeah, I think it's very, very important for sovereignty, for understanding AI, and for academia. It’s kind of weird that most academic labs have to use Chinese models because they’re the ones that are open. If you go to Stanford or MIT, you have no choice but to use the Chinese open-weight models. There is some momentum, but I don't think it's enough. I think there's a lot more to do. A lot more investment is needed. The best open-source non-Chinese models are actually coming from outside of the US. Right from France, Mistral; Cohere from Canada; South Korea is starting to do more and more. But it’s still pretty far from what the US could do. Perhaps we don’t need to panic about AI agents, but what about the idea of AI escaping human control due to recursive self-improvement? You use a computer to write code. There's already some form of self-improvement in using the tools to build more tools. Now the question is how fast it accelerates. One thing that a lot of people realized this summer is that keeping AI behind closed doors in a few labs isn't actually safer. For recursive self-improvement, I think openness is a way to understand, follow, and regulate if we need to regulate. Can we talk about the Microduck ? I’m a bit obsessed. Oh yeah, it's so fun, no? We're probably gonna sell over 50,000 of them this year. It's probably the most popular robot of the year. We haven't talked about this much, but AI was really the unlock for the robot. We had the design for two years, but the problem was that when it fell, it couldn’t get up. And then at some point with reinforcement learning, one of our software engineers managed to get the Microduck to get itself back up. At the end of the day, how do you convince people to take an interest in open-source AI?

events.title: A Federal Women’s Prison Became a “Rape Club.” After Officials Shut It Down, Rampant Abuse Continued Elsewhere.
events.summary: Officer Felix Wilder sauntered around the women’s prison like he owned the place.  Prone to showing up to work in gold chains and stylish jeans instead of his concrete gray government uniform, the slender 35-year-old moved, one woman said, “like he had just gotten off of a horse from a long ride.” He spoke slowly and eyed the prisoners as they walked through the drab buildings and shadeless yards of the secluded federal lockup in Aliceville, Alabama. By the fall of 2024, some of the women there had begun to notice him hovering over a soft-spoken immigrant from Mexico who’d been in prison for only a few years. Ela, as she asked to be called, had dark hair, dark eyes and children to get home to back in Utah. Wilder was just a little too close, a little too familiar. Ela’s cellmate, who asked to be identified as Ana, watched it all with unease. At 40, she knew exactly what that kind of attention from an officer could mean in a women’s prison. For 15 years, Ana had served her time at Federal Correctional Institution Dublin, a low-security prison in California, where officers had preyed on the women in their care. Sexual misconduct became so rampant that staff and prisoners alike called it a “rape club.” Eventually, the FBI intervened, and prosecutors charged the warden, the chaplain and nine other officers with sexually abusing female prisoners. Hundreds of women — including Ana — came forward to tell what happened to them, not just to investigators, but also to outside lawyers who sued the system to demand change at the Bay Area prison.    Ana had hoped to leave that all behind when she was transferred out of Dublin. But tucked between the pine trees and low-slung churches of rural Alabama, the Aliceville prison had its own brand of menace. The facility had newer buildings but fewer freedoms. The roofs leaked, and sometimes the air smelled faintly of mold. The shorthanded staff often locked the women in their cells for days at a time. And then there were officers like Wilder, who seemed to be choosing their targets. Thousands of miles from families they couldn’t call during yet another lockdown, Ana and Ela became allies. They paced. They picked at the lukewarm meals delivered on Styrofoam trays. They stared out the narrow slit of a window.  And then Ela broke down, sobbing as her words tumbled out into the stale prison air.  Two years earlier, an officer had pulled her into a closet and raped her, she told Ana, her voice quavering. Now, she said, it was happening all over again — but this time it was the stylish officer in jeans: Felix Wilder. Ela said she’d reported the first assault and nothing happened. Now, she didn’t know what to do. If the prison didn’t care about one rape, why would it care about two? As she listened, Ana felt a dull rage churning in her stomach. She thought of all the things she’d seen and survived at Dublin: the rapes, the harassment, the uncertainty of a life subject to the whims of lascivious men with badges. As she tried to comfort her sobbing cellmate, she wondered whether Aliceville was any better. Maybe, she thought, no place was.  Sitting on her metal bunk, she opened the little address book she’d bought from the prison commissary and flipped to the phone numbers for the lead attorneys in the class action lawsuit against Dublin. “Here,” she told Ela, “you can talk to them.” The arrests and subsequent convictions of Dublin staff — 10 in all — marked the largest sex abuse scandal in the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ history and a rare moment of accountability in a troubled system where many women had learned to stop expecting it. Suddenly, every branch of government stepped in. A federal judge appointed an outside monitor. A slew of agencies issued reports, and the Justice Department dispatched attorneys to visit and evaluate women’s facilities. Congress passed a law to create a new, independent office to oversee the prison system. But after the judge made that unprecedented move to appoint outside oversight, in early 2024 the bureau abruptly announced it would shut down Dublin and transfer its more than 600 women — including Ana — to lockups across the country. Ana had hoped to leave the abuse behind when she was transferred out of Dublin federal prison. Then, quietly, the window of accountability shut. Little appeared to have come of the promised reforms, the site visits and the reports, and Congress never appropriated funding for the new oversight office. More than a dozen current and former federal prison employees told ProPublica and The Marshall Project they’d seen few or no meaningful improvements. One Justice Department official said the only obvious sign of progress was new sexual assault prevention posters. “Nothing has really changed,” said Alix McLearen, a top Bureau of Prisons official who retired in 2024 after serving as the agency’s first administrator overseeing the women and special populations branch. “We had a horrible crisis, and crisis leads to opportunity, and this is an opportunity that has been completely squandered.” An official with the federal prison workers union who — like nearly every current employee interviewed for this story — asked not to be named for fear of retaliation, put it even more bluntly: “Nothing has been done to effectively change sexual abuse of inmates within the BOP. Not on a large scale or small scale.” For the last five years, the culture that spawned a rape club at Dublin has persisted across the system. Reporters at ProPublica and The Marshall Project set out to determine how pervasive the problem of staff sexual abuse inside federal women’s prisons is — and what, if anything, officials have done to solve it. What we found was sexual assault, misconduct or harassment at most of the 27 facilities that currently hold women. We identified more than 185 cases in which prison employees have been accused of sexually abusing people in women’s prisons since 2021, the year the Dublin scandal broke. The cases implicate more than 96 officers at 16 prisons. Of those, just 19 officers have been arrested or convicted. In some cases, officers withheld food or medical care, or threatened to put women in solitary confinement if they refused to comply with sexual demands, court records allege. In others, officers locked them in windowless closets or bathrooms, choked them, or forced them to use sex toys or have sex with each other. In more than a dozen instances, the assaults were so brutal that the women were left bruised and bleeding. Though some abusers have been prosecuted or removed, insiders say the culture of impunity that allows officers to prey on women remains. Officials have repeatedly refused to acknowledge or failed to act on signs of sexual abuse, we found. More than 25 women said that they were abused by officers who had been reported or investigated before, according to lawsuits we reviewed. events.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
events.summary: When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become. Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022. He says he was regularly “heartbroken” by the outpouring of grief whenever bad news arrived about a husband, father, or son back home. “I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,” Steelberg tells WIRED. "I'm not saying this is purely altruistic,” he adds. “Of course we're going to be making money doing it." This week, their firm, Tiberius Aerospace, said it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by European technology investment firm Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, a national-security-focused investment firm licensed under the US Defense Department. Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 is also an investor. Tiberius began as Steelberg’s private research lab, incorporated in 2021, which employed people across France, the UK, and US to experiment on left-field ideas across a range of technologies, from drones and electric vertical takeoff aircraft to quantum computing. After the invasion, he pivoted the lab’s AI and aerospace engineers into writing code and building spreadsheets to objectively analyze the war’s many factors and calculate what could move the needle. The AI model they created quickly ruled out building better defensive technology because that would just harden the stalemate. With his aim narrowed to building an offensive weapon, Steelberg developed several metrics to numerically analyze the lethality of different systems, including cost-effectiveness, and used the AI engine to simulate weapons under different conditions and identify what would disrupt the market. Don’t build another drone, it suggested, build longer-range artillery munitions. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a 155-millimeter howitzer—the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine. As well as traveling farther than currently available rounds, they claim they can reach supersonic speeds and altitudes beyond jamming range. Giving Ukraine’s guns extra range is important, Sam Cranny-Evans, an associate fellow at UK defense think tank the Royal United Services Institute, tells WIRED, because it would allow Ukrainian gunners to operate beyond the reach of Russian drone attacks. 155-mm shells “can cause massive damage to a group of vehicles or infantry,” he says. “Any technology that can help Ukraine extend the reach of its howitzers and return them to combat would be valuable.” With a prototype he’d designed with the help of AI, Steelberg also started to expand the Tiberius team, including bringing on board Baynes as chief strategy officer in 2023. Baynes had first traveled to Ukraine around a decade ago to investigate how local startup Ring , now owned by Amazon, had outdone Nest , which he’d been working on and eventually sold to Google. He fell in love with Kyiv’s ambitious software engineers and booming tech scene–responsible for globally successful tech tools like Grammarly and Snapchat’s face filters. In 2016, he bought a local life-science tech company with the aim of accelerating next-generation medicines through automating clinical trials and improving protein modeling. “What drew me into Kyiv was the hunger and ambition in the engineering community,” he tells WIRED. “It was difficult to not be enormously attracted to that and to see if it's something that could be put into really critical-mission problem sets like cancer drugs or speeding up clinical trials for life-science companies.” After the Russian invasion, Baynes set himself up in Budapest for around six months to help with the logistics of evacuating women and children and moving equipment into the country. He asked his global network for help finding medical equipment, vehicles, and accommodation for refugees—bringing him back in touch with Steelberg. Baynes believes the West’s response to the invasion has been “inadequate” and that Ukraine needs better offensive capabilities to push Russia’s army back.

events.title: Behind the Curtain: If competence were cool
events.summary: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100 billion a year on information technology. Roughly 80% goes to keeping old systems alive. Eight of the 11 systems most in need of replacement run on dying languages like COBOL . The people who can read, write and fix them are retiring. The debt: We paid $1.052 trillion in interest last fiscal year. That's more than we spent on defense. The Congressional Budget Office sees the interest doubling to $2.1 trillion in 2036 . Every dollar of interest is a dollar that can't fix another crisis on this list. The retirement cliff: Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in 2032. Current law then cuts benefits by 22%, automatically. Medicare's hospital fund follows in 2033 . We have known those dates for decades, and they've been creeping up. Now they're just a few years away. The shriveled arsenal: Rebuilding the advanced weapons we've burned through in the Iran war will take years . Back in May, a paper from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that replacing some interceptors used heavily in the war, including Patriot and THAAD anti-missile systems, would take three years. The minerals: China controls 91% of the world's rare-earth refining capacity, giving the other superpower a chokehold on vital ingredients of AI. We're one trade war away from slowing AI and the entire economy. The bottom line: When choosing and rating leaders in harrowing times, put a premium on competence. We'll need it. Go deeper : The chain-reaction era.

events.title: Push to reinstate Jensen Huang tests superstar tech CEO accountability
events.summary: The push to reinstate former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergey Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question. Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips. The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases and also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to the Wall Street Journal. In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives . Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic. Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers. In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO. After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package , shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award. Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable. The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy. But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward. Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence. The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal. OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal. Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct. "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said. Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg. The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.
