events.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
events.summary: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions. For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need. Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform: CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server . A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard. CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months. CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation. The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink. At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built. Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies . events.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
events.summary: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack , so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time. AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights , advancing scientific research. Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster. MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times. NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks. For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. Every AI service has to balance serving many users at once against responding quickly to each one. Vera Rubin shifts that entire curve, serving more users while responding faster. Leadership Across Benchmarks and Workloads NVIDIA partners participated extensively in MLPerf Training, with submissions from 20 organizations: ASUS, Azure , Cisco, CoreWeave, Crusoe, Dell Technologies, Firmus , Giga Computing, Google Cloud, HPE , Inventec, Krai, Lambda, Nebius, Oracle, Quanta Cloud Technology (QCT), Supermicro, TTA and the University of Florida . Their submissions show how NVIDIA’s programmable platform, with open source libraries and frameworks, lets a vast ecosystem of partners innovate and optimize AI training performance. Vera Rubin also delivers leading performance on independent benchmarks including SemiAnalysis AgentX and Artificial Analysis AgentPerf, showcasing how the same NVIDIA infrastructure can productively run everything from pretraining and post-training to agentic inference, as well as workloads beyond AI, such as the high-performance computing showcased at SC26 this week. Dive deeper into the results in the MLPerf Training and MLPerf Endpoints technical blogs. events.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
events.summary: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever. Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process. With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit , black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes. By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull. Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results. Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron -powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design. Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research , accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions. NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER , NAMD , GROMACS , LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows. Cadence , Fathom Therapeutics , Topos Bio , Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery. Daviator , a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs. At Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory , the NVIDIA DAQIRI networking library connects a high-speed electron microscopy detector to GPU processing, moving analysis into the experiment itself. Researchers can identify useful signals, discover previously unknown regions of interest and decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken. The workflow supports atomic-resolution materials studies that can distinguish elements, laying the groundwork for future automated experiments. The newly open source cuSpa accelerates cell polygon calculations, enabling developers to generate massive spatial graphs for next-generation patient and cancer models at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center , with a 900x speedup compared with using CPUs. Codeveloped with scverse , the rapids-singlecell framework accelerates single-cell analysis — and is now available in a single, agent-ready container. Using the tool, Therna Biosciences processed data 200x faster for therapeutic design. 10x Genomics integrated rapids-singlecell in its new Sentira platform, helping academic researchers, biopharma teams and foundation model builders accelerate the path from large-scale spatial data to biological insights. And the NVIDIA GPU-accelerated HMMER library, also open source, accelerates the annotation of predicted protein sequences, supporting data preparation for biological foundation models. At Basecamp Research , benchmark searches ran up to 84x faster than with standard HMMER, reducing the time required to annotate the large biological datasets used to train the company’s therapeutic design models. events.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
events.summary: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. Honoring the Architects of Progress Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI: At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics , tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters , one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time. In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition , helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution . These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more. Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26 . events.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
events.summary: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes. And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates. Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028. events.title: NVIDIA Announces Collaboration With IBM and Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory to Launch Quantum-Classical Codesign Platform, Plus Error-Correction Breakthrough to Advance Practical Quantum Computing
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA and IBM announce a growing quantum supercomputing collaboration combining NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to advance quantum error-correction research, scientific applications and integration into supercomputing workflows. NVIDIA DGX B200 systems will connect with IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the most powerful processor IBM has yet built. A quantum computing codesign platform with Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, alongside IBM and NVIDIA, will support quantum error-correction and applications research for future systems. NVIDIA releases TCBP-JOBS, a new decoding algorithm part of the CUDA-Q platform, that delivers up to a 13,000x speedup for quantum error-correction research, accelerating fault-tolerant quantum computation. NVIDIA is expanding Slurm to simplify scheduling quantum processors within supercomputing workflows, with IBM contributing integration through its Quantum Resource Management Interface. NVIDIA today announced plans for new collaborations with IBM and the U.S. Department of Energy’s Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory that will span research into next-generation modular architectures for quantum computers, scientific applications and supercomputing integration. These efforts, including a new modular quantum computing codesign platform with IBM and Fermilab, combine NVIDIA accelerated computing and software with IBM quantum computers to help researchers scale quantum computers and explore their scientific capabilities. Separately, NVIDIA also announced a new quantum algorithm that delivers up to 13,000x faster decoding compared with existing leading algorithms — cutting the computation time for researching new quantum computing designs from 12 weeks to just 45 minutes. The collaboration with IBM also brings together new Slurm capabilities integrations to simplify how quantum computers can be added into supercomputing workflows. Modular Quantum Computing Codesign Platform IBM and NVIDIA are colocating NVIDIA DGX™ B200 systems with state-of-the-art IBM quantum computers, including those powered by IBM Quantum Nighthawk, the fastest quantum processor IBM has ever delivered. This integrated system is supporting a jointly developed IBM, Fermilab and NVIDIA modular quantum codesign platform. The codesign platform will allow researchers to develop and evaluate error-correction codes, decoding algorithms and quantum-classical applications driving scientific discoveries in high-energy and nuclear physics (HENP), as well as how classical systems can scale alongside multiple linked quantum processors within modular architectures. Fermilab’s expertise will allow work at the platform to focus on quantum error correction and HENP applications — helping define requirements for future fault-tolerant quantum computers and the science that can be achieved with them. “Making quantum computers useful for science requires advances in error correction, applications and the systems that bring quantum processors and accelerated computing together,” said Krysta Svore, vice president of applied research for quantum computing at NVIDIA. “NVIDIA’s research software and our collaboration with IBM give scientists more powerful tools to investigate quantum designs and develop applications across these systems.” “Some of the most fundamental problems in science remain out of reach without access to quantum computing. Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond,” said Jerry Chow, IBM Fellow and chief technology officer of quantum-centric computing. “With Fermilab and NVIDIA, we plan to explore how these real-world problems can help us shape the modular, interconnected architectures that will define the next generation of quantum computers and accelerated classical computing.” “The future of quantum computing depends on more than advances in quantum hardware alone,” said Anna Grassellino, Fermilab chief technology officer and director of the SQMS Center. “Accelerated computing and superintelligence will play an important role in how we design algorithms, study errors and coordinate increasingly complex quantum systems. This proposed platform would combine NVIDIA’s computing capabilities with IBM’s quantum technologies and Fermilab’s scientific expertise, and would enable researchers to explore new approaches to codesigning quantum computers that meet the needs of challenging HENP science problems.” Advancing Quantum Error-Correction Research Errors inherent to quantum processors limit the complexity and duration of the computations they can perform. Quantum error correction protects quantum information by encoding it across multiple physical qubits. A classical algorithm called a decoder interprets measurement data to identify likely errors so they can be corrected. Available through the NVIDIA CUDA-Q™ QEC 0.9.0 library today, NVIDIA’s new TCBP-JOBS decoding algorithm accelerates the computationally intensive parts of quantum error-correction research by up to 13,000x while delivering high accuracy. Faster decoding in research workloads allows scientists to evaluate candidate error-correction approaches more efficiently and explore how different codes and decoder configurations perform. The new decoding algorithm provides researchers with tools to identify designs that use physical qubits more efficiently, and better measure their performance improvements, shortening the path to practical fault-tolerant quantum computing. Advancing Quantum Chemistry  IBM and RIKEN are advancing quantum-classical chemistry research powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. The work, which combines IBM’s quantum computer with RIKEN’s JHPC-quantum GPU supercomputer ROQUO, has been named a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The researchers calculated binding energies for two protein-ligand complexes to study interactions relevant to drug discovery. By dividing the systems into fragments and combining quantum sampling with GPU-accelerated calculations, they modeled complexes containing up to 12,635 atoms — more than 40x the size of the previous 303-atom quantum-classical benchmark.  ROQUO uses NVIDIA GB200 systems and NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking to support research in quantum algorithms, simulation and hybrid computing. This research is supported by NEDO (New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization), an organization under the jurisdiction of Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry’s “Research and Development of Quantum-Supercomputers Hybrid Platform for Exploration of Uncharted Computable Capabilities.” Bringing Quantum Into Supercomputing Workflows NVIDIA is expanding the open source Slurm workload

events.title: NVIDIA Expands Vera CPU Platform to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
events.summary: The NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform combines NVIDIA processors, NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking and breakthrough scientific software to boost weather, climate and molecular simulations. DKRZ has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer for climate science. The full Vera CPU platform is coming from Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro. NVIDIA today announced the NVIDIA Vera CPU rack-scale platform for high-performance computing — combining NVIDIA’s first fully custom data center CPU with the gold standard for HPC networking to drive extreme efficiency and throughput for state-of-the-art scientific modeling, simulation and agentic science. The rack-scale platform brings together 192 Vera CPUs interconnected by NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking to meet the massive performance demands of climate modeling, molecular dynamics and other unaccelerated, next-generation scientific workloads. The liquid-cooled system delivers more than 200TB/s of aggregate peak memory bandwidth to support scientific simulation and AI workflows. “Scientific simulations need CPUs that can keep large datasets moving and sustain performance as applications scale,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Vera brings custom CPU cores, high-bandwidth memory and InfiniBand networking together to address those bottlenecks. With compilers and libraries optimized for Vera, researchers can run demanding simulations more efficiently and explore more complex scientific problems.” Engineered for Memory-Intensive HPC Each Vera CPU features 88 custom NVIDIA Olympus cores, 176 threads and compact, serviceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X memory delivering up to 1.2TB/s of bandwidth to accelerate data-intensive scientific applications. The rack combines 192 Vera CPUs with approximately 300TB of memory and 1 petabyte of storage in a fully liquid-cooled NVIDIA MGX™ design. Each 1U tray integrates eight Vera CPUs, and NVMe storage and management. The platform reuses NVL72 rack components, including chassis, power distribution and cooling infrastructure, to simplify deployment and service. NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking connects the system, and NVIDIA SHARP™ In-Network Computing helps scientists finish complex simulations faster by reducing the time processors spend coordinating their work. In NVIDIA’s tests, Vera delivered 1.9x the performance and 2.4x the performance per watt of x86 systems on OpenFOAM’s motorBike Large airflow simulation. Advancing Climate Science Research NVIDIA has benchmarked the open source Weather Research and Forecasting model on Vera CPUs, with projected performance gains of 1.6x and energy-efficiency gains of 2x compared with x86. DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera CPUs for its HLRE-5 supercomputer, alongside NVIDIA GB200 Grace Blackwell systems and NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking. Built by Bull and expected to be available in early 2028, the system will support climate simulation and AI research, enabling global kilometer-scale climate simulations with lower energy consumption than on the current system. Software and Availability To help researchers speed scientific applications, NVIDIA HPC SDK 26.11 is available now, providing compilers and libraries optimized for Vera. NVIDIA is also introducing a public beta of its next-generation Fortran compiler, which was built in collaboration with leading HPC centers and national labs. The new compiler gives developers a way to run their existing programs built on Fortran — the language that scientific computing was built on — with greater speed on NVIDIA platforms, without needing to rewrite their code. Vera CPU racks are expected to be available from Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro beginning in early 2027. Learn more about the NVIDIA Vera CPU . events.title: NVIDIA Introduces Nemotron for Science to Accelerate Discoveries With Agents
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA Nemotron for Science brings together the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model, scientific evaluations, a new open chemistry dataset and recipes to help researchers build domain-specific science agents. LitmusBench v0.2 supports both evaluation and post-training for chemistry reasoning, helping researchers assess model capabilities and adapt models to scientific tasks. NVIDIA DGX Spark and data center infrastructure take Nemotron 3.5 Super VL from researchers’ desktops to supercomputing centers, enabling secure scientific workflows on infrastructure organizations control. Leading global research institutions, including the U.S. Department of Energy’s Argonne National Laboratory, are using Nemotron to build agents to speed scientific discovery. NVIDIA today introduced NVIDIA Nemotron for Science, bringing together scientific applications of its NVIDIA Nemotron™ 3.5 Super VL open model, a new open chemistry dataset and post-training recipes to help researchers build specialized agents for scientific discovery. Built on Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Nemotron for Science helps researchers develop agents that reason through scientific problems and put specialized research tools to work. With post-training, scientists can adapt the model to specialized tasks such as conducting experiments for chemistry, protein design and more. Part of Nemotron for Science, LitmusBench v0.2 is a new open dataset with nearly 50,000 questions for training and evaluating language models on chemistry reasoning. Drawing on molecular properties and experimental drug discovery data, it helps researchers improve models’ ability to predict how molecules behave, including their solubility and how the human body processes them. Life sciences companies Lila Sciences, Terray Therapeutics and Therna are using and customizing NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for science applications. Use cases include extracting chemical knowledge, planning experiments and designing therapeutics and laboratory protocols. Major research centers like Argonne and Jülich Supercomputing Centre are integrating it into their drug and scientific discovery AI agents. “Accelerated computing is transforming how scientists tackle the world’s most complex challenges,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Nemotron for Science gives researchers open models, scientific data and post-training recipes to build specialized agents that reason through scientific problems and use CUDA-X accelerated tools to turn ideas into discoveries.” Post-Training Nemotron Open Models for Scientific Discovery Researchers can post-train Nemotron open models with domain-specific data to improve performance on specialized scientific tasks. They can integrate the resulting model into agent workflows that interpret scientific information, generate code and call computational tools. These workflows can use NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ accelerated tools to perform scientific computation. Terray Therapeutics post-trained Nemotron to extract reactants, products and reaction conditions from scientific diagrams, surpassing previously published results on two benchmarks. On the RxnScribe test, it recovered about 76% of annotated reactions under the benchmark’s matching criteria, helping turn published chemistry discoveries into structured data for synthesis planning and scientific agents. Lila Sciences used Nemotron to design execution-ready laboratory protocols for its automated labs, matching frontier-level performance without requiring additional fine-tuning. Post-training with laboratory feedback nearly doubled the model’s accuracy for making quantum dots — nanoscale crystals used in screens and solar panels — to 61%, exceeding GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at 10-20x lower inference cost. These gains help agents and materials scientists translate desired material properties into synthesis recipes, advancing the discovery of new materials. Therna collaborated with NVIDIA to post-train Nemotron for agentic mRNA therapeutic design, nearly doubling accuracy in predicting protein-expression ranges over frontier models. Scientists preferred its explanations over those from the base model in 96% of comparisons. These gains could help scientists tailor mRNA designs for the desired protein production in specific cell types as they scale to human use. Researchers Speed Science With Nemotron Models and Datasets Leading research institutions are using NVIDIA Nemotron models and datasets to advance scientific discovery at every scale, from individual researchers’ desktops to labs and supercomputing centers. By helping researchers rapidly design and evaluate novel molecules across the periodic table, the work has the potential to open new pathways for applications in critical materials and minerals, national security and cancer treatment. Argonne is integrating Nemotron into its StructBioReasoner multi-agent system to design and evaluate protein-based therapeutic candidates for treatment of cancer and other diseases. KTH Royal Institute of Technology has built an AI agent on Nemotron that repairs broken GROMACS molecular dynamics setups on its own. In one overnight run on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark ™ system, the agent fixed 81% of test cases with reasoning enabled, and every fix was checked independently by GROMACS itself. RIKEN has made NVIDIA Nemotron, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, available on its RIKYU AI supercomputing platform through RiVault, its inference gateway, enabling researchers to access the models for scientific research and the development of accelerated applications. Availability NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and the LitmusBench v0.2 chemistry dataset are available now on Hugging Face. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model was also optimized to run locally on a 128GB NVIDIA DGX Spark system . Learn more in this technical blog on post-training NVIDIA Nemotron to increase accuracy across scientific domains. ]]>

events.title: U.S. attorney targets another Democrat over congressional investigtions
events.summary: A U.S. attorney put likely incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on notice about her intent to investigate corporations and expected probes into the president's inner circle. Why it matters: The letter demanding Warren preserve documents related to her congressional oversight is the latest in a string of threats levied against congressional Democrats ahead of the party assuming the congressional majority — and gavels — next year. Congress' authority to investigate, hold hearings and gather testimony is a core legislative power. Analysts have long forecasted a Democratic subpoena storm into President Trump's lucrative presidency. But Democrats' plan to exercise that power and hone their focus on the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption," as reported by Axios' Hans Nichols, is already facing Justice Department pushback. Driving the news: U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of the Southern District of Texas contended in his Sunday letter that Warren appeared "eager to wield" her "gavel like a tomahawk," instructing her to preserve oversight records. In the strongly worded letter, he warned Warren about targeting private citizens close to the president and reiterated that any probes must serve a legislative purpose or risk violating those individuals' First Amendment rights. Those arguments echo his prior letters to Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller , shared Reitz's letter and referenced two civil rights statutes. Warren's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zoom in: Reitz's letter referenced Warren, Blumenthal and incoming Oversight chair Rep. Robert Garcia's (D-Calif.) recent inquiry into Trump fundraiser Meredith O'Rourke's role in coordinating contributions for the president's ballroom and other projects. It also referenced letters Warren, with Slotkin and other lawmakers, sent to tech CEOs probing the extent to which their AI investments were subsidized by GOP-led tax breaks. What they're saying: The White House did not respond to detailed questions but referred Axios to White House counsel Will Scharf's letter to Garcia that argued Democratic threats of investigations "may cross the line into blatant criminality." Asked if Warren was the subject of a criminal probe or other proceedings, a Justice Department spokesperson told Axios that "the Department does not confirm or deny the existence of ongoing investigations." "The Department has both the statutory authority and the responsibility to examine potential violations of the law," the spokesperson added. Asked if DOJ leadership authorized or reviewed the letter, the DOJ referred Axios to Attorney General Todd Blanche's prior statement that "DOJ leadership is working with every U.S. attorney, including U.S. Attorney Reitz, on ongoing investigations." Friction point: Blanche refused to rule out prosecuting Democrats set on investigating administration officials in an interview earlier this month, claiming lawmakers' rhetoric had overstepped their authority. That came after Trump demanded the DOJ look into what he labeled as "Weaponization and Lawfare" from his political opponents. What we're watching: Reitz asked Warren to respond to his letter by next Monday. He described the letter as his "first arrow shot." Go deeper: Corporate America's Trump trap

events.title: US moves to close 'remote access' chip loophole
events.summary: The US Commerce Department on Monday issued interim rules aiming to close the so-called remote access loophole by which Chinese AI firms used cutting-edge US-made chips via data centers in third countries. The new rules limit access to advanced AI chips and servers in a limited number of countries, including in the Southeast Asian nations of Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand where the practice was most intensely applied. The updated rules come with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick facing increasing pressure over his department’s allegedly poor enforcement of export control rules, particularly when it came to a Singapore-based company accused of smuggling chips into China. The company hit the limelight after one of its executives, alleged by US officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset, had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Entrepreneur launches $50M African film fund
events.summary: Entertainment entrepreneur Mo Abudu launched a $50 million fund aimed at helping African filmmakers to showcase their “creativity to the world.” The Afro Film Fund, backed by Abudu’s EbonyLife Media and a Paris-based investment vehicle, plans to finance around 35 films over eight years. events.title: Private investments in African climate projects tripled in 2024
events.summary: Private sector investment in carbon-cutting and adaptation projects in Africa tripled in four years to reach $26.5 billion in 2023-24, pointing to a shift in the continent’s climate finance landscape. African banks and businesses provided three-quarters of the investment, which overwhelmingly funded energy projects, while household spending on solar PV alone rose nearly fivefold to $3.3 billion a year, according to a report jointly published by the Climate Policy Initiative think tank, development agency FSD Africa, and the UK and Norwegian governments. Africa has the lowest proportion of private climate finance of any region in the world. Public funding provides almost two-thirds of flows, although it is increasingly being used to de-risk and leverage private capital. But the growth is uneven, and CPI’s CEO said many projects were too small and fragmented for investors to reach. — Chloé Farand

events.title: Uncertainty deters green investors from Africa's biggest economies
events.summary: Many of Africa’s biggest economies remain unattractive for major renewables investors because of legislative, regulatory, and security uncertainty, the head of one of the continent’s biggest clean energy developers told Semafor. Infinity Power, a privately owned joint venture between Infinity and the UAE’s Masdar, has been fast expanding its green power generation targets in Egypt, and sees Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal as attractive markets for growth. But Ethiopia, Kenya, and Nigeria — among the continent’s biggest economies — are not as much of a draw, Nayer Fouad, Infinity Power’s co-founder and CEO said in an interview. Kenya had recently renegotiated the terms on its power-purchase agreements, causing unease among prospective investors, while Ethiopia and Nigeria carried security risks.

events.title: MTN eyes $2B takeover of state-backed rival Telkom
events.summary: Telecoms giant MTN revived its $2 billion pursuit of state-backed rival Telkom, a buyout that would present a tricky choice for South Africa’s government and regulators. A deal would confront South Africa’s coalition government with a choice over the future of Telkom, in which the state owns a stake of about 40%. It would also test competition regulators’ willingness to accept a more concentrated market, with MTN and Vodacom a de facto duopoly in exchange for the prospect of a larger entity pumping more money into digital infrastructure. The two companies said they had started early-stage takeover talks that could see MTN making a cash-and-shares offer for Telkom, reviving a courtship that collapsed three years ago. Investors have already started pricing in the possibility of a deal; they sent shares in Telkom soaring 15%. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
events.summary: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell , the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die . The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies , the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke. “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics , based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away. Christie Hemm Klok The screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga , who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit. Why Telesurgery Starts With Stroke As recently as the early ’90s , physicians who treated stroke struggled with “ therapeutic nihilism .” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery . In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event. Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right. The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.” Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter. Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray. I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. events.title: Americans are eating way less turkey than we used to
events.summary: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line experts take part in cooking and carving classes in 2009. AP Photo/M. Spencer Green One of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm , Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays . I find turkeys fascinating , because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway . Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies , researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving . Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken , according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound , while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched . Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken . So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans . And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn . The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds . Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken . In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week . Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours , while a 4-pound chicken takes about two . That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society . In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut . He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one . They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take . I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. events.title: Trump arrives in the Philippines, a key ally in resisting Chinese aggression
events.summary: President Donald Trump’s trip to the Philippines ahead of the APEC summit this week takes him to a key US ally on the front lines of resisting alleged Chinese aggression in Asia. Though Trump has upended relations with many longtime partners throughout his second term, ties with Manila have remained sturdy, with joint military drills increasing in scope and sophistication. Washington sees the Philippines — a potential launchpad for American defense of Taiwan were China to attack the self-ruled island — as a key linchpin in projecting its power across the East, The Wall Street Journal reported. Trump should expect a warm welcome: Almost 70% of Filipinos said they trusted him to do the right thing, the highest level of 36 countries polled. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: China's economic activity slows more than expected
events.summary: China’s economic activity slowed more than expected last month, a sign that Beijing’s efforts to bolster growth are having limited impact. Retail sales and industrial output missed forecasts, feeding fears that the country could slip into deflation. Meanwhile, investment plummeted in the worst monthly drop outside the COVID-19 pandemic. Policymakers fear conditions will worsen further in 2027 and 2028 , prompting them to hold back some stimulus to weather those headwinds. The disappointing data weakens Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s hand ahead of this week’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Elsewhere, Japan’s economy unexpectedly cooled , too, as it reeled from higher energy prices sparked by the war in the Middle East. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Oil up on renewed hostilities in the Middle East
events.summary: Oil prices rose on renewed fears of a resumption of hostilities between Washington and Tehran, despite both sides’ otherwise conciliatory rhetoric. US President Donald Trump said he would proceed “ a bit more civilly ” as part of an American focus on economic pressure; a powerful Iranian politician, meanwhile, said a path remained for a deal between the two countries to end the war. But Washington also said a third aircraft carrier group had arrived in the Gulf, while Tehran struck an American base in Bahrain over the weekend. US intelligence now reportedly estimates that Iran maintains up to 2,500 missiles , giving it the ability to hit back hard at American forces and Gulf allies if conflict resumes. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Average diesel prices are under $6 per gallon for the first time in months
events.summary: Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Average U.S. diesel prices inched below $6 per gallon on Monday for the first time since Sept. 10 amid lower oil prices recently, per AAA data. Why it matters: Diesel soared even more than gasoline during the Iran war, and those costs rippled throughout the economy. Democrats featured high prices, especially for farmers, en route to midterm wins in typically red agricultural states. Zoom out: The worldwide diesel supply crunch remains acute even as the broader oil market is starting to fitfully stabilize. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, damage to Middle Eastern production and shipments, throttled oil supplies, and expanded U.S. exports to meet overseas demand helped raise domestic costs. The bottom line: Prices are now far below the Sept. 22 record of nearly $6.53 per gallon. The recent relief is real, but it's limited. Average U.S. prices remain well above the prior record $5.82 per gallon set in 2022.

events.summary: Headwinds facing the AI boom — an unfurling Nvidia scandal, mounting public opposition, a newly elected US Congress more favorable to regulation — are unlikely to stall a huge infrastructure buildout, a major CEO told Semafor. The remarks by the head of Acwa , one of the world’s top clean energy developers, came as Samsung indicated that it wanted to deepen its involvement in the AI sector by constructing data centers . Their bullishness comes despite persistent voter frustration in the US. “The onus really is on everyone serving in government … to do a better job of communicating to the public the opportunity and the upside of this great technology ,” a top US government official told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & the World. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Government pressure grows on Nvidia over spying scandal
events.summary: US government pressure on Nvidia mounted over whether the chip giant knowingly allowed the sale of restricted technology to China, as the scandal resulting from its ousted CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset widened. The ex-Nvidia boss has agreed to testify behind closed doors before US lawmakers; the Treasury secretary, meanwhile, questioned whether the firm pursued sales to China in order to boost revenues, demanding a “ dramatic shakeup ” at the company as reports circulated of Huang seeking a path back to his job . Supporters of Huang who focus solely on his infidelity, however, risk underestimating the scale of the crisis he faces, four experts wrote in Fortune: “ There is no comeback here ,” they warned. — Prashant Rao

events.title: The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Are we there yet? Six technologies that promised to change the world How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , our series “ Are we there yet? ” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises. We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten. Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise. Nuclear-powered spaceships Exercise in a pill Interspecies communication Solid-state batteries Cleaning up PFAS Eliminating traffic deaths Subscribe now to get every issue of our print magazine as soon as it lands. Inside the quest for cognitive immortality Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality. Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow. Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST . events.title: Ex-Barclays CEO Bob Diamond on investing in the Gulf and the irrelevancy of Bitcoin
events.summary: The News Speaking from the Bahrain capital Manama, which a few months earlier had been bombarded in Iranian attacks, Bob Diamond, chief executive of private equity firm Atlas Merchant Capital, says he’s still optimistic about the outlook for the Gulf’s future, the US economy, and the prospect to raise more capital to consolidate the banking industry around the world. Panmure Liberum, a UK investment bank he’s invested in, is expanding into the Gulf. Wall Street investors increasingly see the region as a place to invest, not just a place to raise money, and the war isn’t deterring that. “This is a really serious economy,” he said. Diamond has experience in the region spanning decades. His contacts in Abu Dhabi and Qatar helped secure a £11.8 billion bailout for Barclays during the Great Financial Crisis, enabling the bank to avoid a taxpayer-funded rescue. He left Barclays in 2012 in the wake of a scandal around its role in manipulating interbank rates, and has since reinvented himself as a private equity investor, backing bank consolidation deals and fintechs. He is also chairman of the advisory committee of the Export-Import Bank of the US and chairman of Abu Dhabi’s tokenization platform Finstreet. Diamond also said that Bitcoin, the most well-known and biggest digital asset by market capitalization, is “irrelevant” (though useful as a store of value untethered from governments) and that the future of finance is tokenization — an industry is being led by the US as well as the Middle East. Q&A Matthew Martin: You just announced Panmure Liberum, the UK investment bank you own, is expanding into the Gulf — how do you think about the opportunities in the Gulf now, particularly with the conflict that’s still going on? Bob Diamond: I don’t mean to be dismissive of the severity of the situation here for a second, with the invasion of Iran, but when you’re here, as you and I are today, it feels pretty normal. For people who have not spent time in this region, I don’t think there’s a recognition of how developed the economies are, how developed the leadership is. And then I’d say that since we started Atlas Merchant Capital just over 10 years ago, I’ve been as interested in investing Middle Eastern money in other parts of the world as I have been in how we can find ways to help develop business here on the ground. I think there’s just a tremendous opportunity in this region for an on-the-ground advisory and M&A business for middle-market and family-owned businesses, because, as we are seeing here, the entrepreneurial spirit is very, very strong in many of these countries. Financial services here is a great example of an industry where the vast majority of banks are ultimately state-controlled. As governments need to redirect capital to other things in the wake of the war, is there an opportunity for private equity investors to come in and play more of a role in the financial services industry in the Gulf? One hundred percent. But I think you hit on a key issue, which is that traditionally that state control made things more opaque, so you couldn’t get outside investment because it was opaque. And two, it was intrusive and more focused on subsidized business. And you can see why, right? Because as the Middle East was growing, much of the commercial real estate, for example, had to be “if we build it, they will come.” So some of the unbelievable commercial real estate, whether it’s in Abu Dhabi or Dubai or Qatar, or the financial services center that was built in Riyadh, was done really with strategic impetus, if you will, as opposed to pure commercial activity. And I think that’s changing, because a lot of those initial strategic investments have been done. I think it was the same in the early days of the development of Singapore. You could say the same thing, that it was strategic investing, but if you go to Singapore today, it’s a very commercial city. You don’t see commercial buildings being put up. What impact do you see the conflict in the region having on how Wall Street sees the Gulf? I think sometime around 2024, 2025, we hit an inflection point where the Middle East being seen purely as a source of funding for the Western world changed to “this is a really serious economy.” Going forward the Gulf will be focused much more on inward investment, as well as outward investment. I think it probably happened already with Saudi Arabia, and they’ve been a little bit ahead of it. But I think it’s really true across the region. But there are still significant pools of capital in this region — if you just look at the sovereign wealth funds, that’s the best example but not the only example — for investment in good ideas wherever they happen to be. Dubai and Abu Dhabi are both making this big play into fintech and tokenization. How much are you getting involved in that, and what do you see as the chances of centers in the region becoming hubs for this new asset class? I feel very strongly. Bitcoin’s irrelevant. It’s not that Bitcoin isn’t going to go up or down, and I’m not questioning whether Bitcoin’s going to have a significantly higher price or not. I’m personally not an investor, but I have a number of close associates who believe strongly. My point is different. In its best version, Bitcoin is a store of value away from a government, much as gold is. And if it doubles or triples or quadruples in value, it doesn’t have a single strategic implication for financial services. It’s just made somebody money, and it’s a good store of value. Compare and contrast that to stablecoins, basically making payments electronic institutionally for the major currencies around the world. Compare and contrast that to blockchain, which is 24/7, instantaneous settlement, a permanent record of every transaction that happens, everything at the speed of the internet and a fraction of the cost of conventional financial services. That’s the future. That’s the underpinning of financial services going forward: blockchain, and finally tokenization. events.title: Africa’s power drive is short of developers, Gridworks CEO says
events.summary: The News Africa has plenty of investors ready to finance much-needed electricity projects, but too few developers with the expertise and early funding to get them off the ground, the head of a UK government-backed power developer told Semafor. More than 40% of sub-Saharan Africans lack electricity, with private investment central to a World Bank and African Development Bank push to connect 300 million across the whole continent by 2030. “People spend a lot of time talking about a lack of capital for infrastructure projects in Africa. There is not a lack of capital,” said Chris Flavin, chief executive of Gridworks, which develops and invests in electricity networks across Africa. The issue for him is that investors generally want to get involved once projects are ready for construction, leaving the four or five years of preparatory work harder to finance. Gridworks, which has electricity projects in countries including Uganda and Mozambique, is set to become the majority shareholder in a planned $300 million power line linking Zambia’s grid to DR Congo’s copper-mining region, under an agreement signed in October. Lenders have shown “very strong interest” in the line, Flavin said. When it develops its own projects, though, Gridworks faces the same hurdles as others despite its UK backing, he added, from permits and environmental approvals to years of planning “before you even get close to the financing.” In DR Congo, for example, commercial banks will not lend at that stage, said Archip Lobo, co-founder of Nuru, a solar mini-grid operator in the country’s east. “They will take the risk on something that exists,” he told Semafor. Instead, Lobo highlighted the existence of state support for early development costs and World Bank Group insurance against political risks. But the World Bank’s own evaluators are less sure capital is plentiful. They found in a recent review that private financing remained too limited to meet Africa’s electrification needs. The narrow pool of investors, such as development lenders’ private arms, government-sponsored funds, foundations, and impact funds “are unlikely to meet the scale of financing needed for electrification growth,” the group said. Industrial advantage Private power projects in Africa are easier to develop when they serve large industrial buyers, such as mines, rather than households and small businesses, Flavin said. A mine with a strong balance sheet and known electricity consumption gives developers a clear customer to design around. For projects aimed at individual customers “the challenge is one of guaranteed demand.” In southeastern DR Congo, CrossBoundary Energy, a Mauritius-based power producer, commissioned a 233-megawatt solar farm with battery storage in August to supply Kamoa-Kakula, a copper complex co-owned by Ivanhoe Mines. “Kamoa’s books are very good,” Auguy Bakome, a project manager at the mine, told Semafor in an earlier interview. He said its expected 40-year operating life and a 15-year contract to buy the electricity helped reassure lenders. Utilities must estimate consumption across tens of thousands of customers. Building networks to serve them is “at the much harder end of the spectrum, full stop,” Flavin said. Moyi Power, a Gridworks-backed utility planned for three cities in northern DR Congo, relies on donor grants for about a quarter of its $190 million first phase and is not expected to deliver electricity before 2029. Notable Africa’s shortage of reliable power is stalling its industrialization , Bloomberg reported, citing World Bank data that put manufacturing at 11% of sub-Saharan Africa’s GDP , half East Asia’s share.

events.title: Zambia's mining investor seeks to borrow $700M
events.summary: The News Zambia’s majority state-owned mining and energy investor plans to borrow about $700 million by 2028 to expand its business, its CEO told Semafor, as Africa’s second-largest copper producer seeks a bigger share of the wealth from its minerals. The money, which ZCCM Investments Holdings has yet to secure, will help fund a $2.7 billion investment proposal it unveiled on Monday. Over the next decade, the company looks to back new infrastructure including a coal-fired power plant in southern Zambia and to raise its stakes in copper mines , among them a project led by Bill Gates-backed Kobold Metals. “We don’t want to be a quiet minority shareholder,” CEO Kakenenwa Muyangwa said. He added that any changes would be negotiated on commercial terms, and that “investors who share the ambition will find us a committed long-term partner.” ZCCM-IH holds stakes in mines run by other companies and earns much of its income from their dividends, which depend on what is left after the mines pay their costs and debts. “For a country that owns a share of its mines, that is not good enough,” Muyangwa said. The company now aims to earn more from royalties, a share of a mine’s sales that is paid regardless of profit. Its only such arrangement, with Canadian miner First Quantum’s Kansanshi mine, will bring in more than $990 million over the next decade, the company forecasts. ZCCM-IH aims to add at least one more later this decade. The investment company said it now owes $5 for every $100 of its own capital, down from about $66 in 2021. Muyangwa said a cleaner balance sheet had put ZCCM-IH in a strong position to fund its expansion. Trading ambitions ZCCM-IH also plans to negotiate with its mining partners to get a share of the copper produced at each mine, which it would then sell directly. That would give the company “a trading income on top of its investment income” and build “the skills to market Zambian metal from Zambia,” Muyangwa said. The plan comes as state-backed companies across Africa’s copper belt seek a more influential role over the trade of the metal. In neighboring DR Congo, state miner Gécamines sells copper through a venture with Swiss trader Mercuria. Zambia’s state-owned Industrial Development Corporation also has a trading venture with Mercuria, which last month named ZCCM-IH as a regional partner. The goal is greater control over the money countries earn from their minerals, Ekpen Omonbude, a senior policy adviser at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, told Semafor. As demand for critical minerals grows, governments are looking to take a more active role in their sale, an approach he said is more common in oil and gas than in mining. Notable Zambia’s copper output rose just 1.5% in the first nine months of the year , far short of what it needs to meet its goal of 3 million tons a year by 2031.
